fragments.text: Height per unit x; it can exceed 1 provided areas are valid probabilities.

fragments.label: Median
fragments.text: A value m with equal probability on either side for a continuous distribution.

fragments.label: Support
fragments.text: The interval on which the density is non-zero.
Valid density functions

fragments.label: Valid density functions
fragments.text: A pdf f(x) must satisfy f(x)≥0 on its support and ∫f(x)dx=1 over the whole support. Use normalisation to find unknown constants, checking they keep the density non-negative.

fragments.label: Valid density functions
fragments.text: A density value is not itself a point probability.

fragments.label: Valid density functions
fragments.text: Outside the stated support, f(x)=0.

fragments.label: Valid density functions
fragments.text: Normalisation: ∫ f(x) dx=1 over the support
Probabilities as areas

fragments.label: Probabilities as areas
fragments.text: P(a < X < b)=∫ₐᵇf(x)dx after intersecting the requested interval with the support. For continuous X, endpoints make no difference: P(X=a)=0.

fragments.label: Probabilities as areas
fragments.text: Draw the support and shade the required interval.

fragments.label: Probabilities as areas
fragments.text: Use complements for awkward tails.
Percentiles

fragments.label: Percentiles
fragments.text: A pth percentile q satisfies ∫ from the lower support limit to q of f(x)dx=p/100. The median uses 0.5. Solve and select the root that lies within the support.

fragments.label: Percentiles
fragments.text: Do not assume median equals mean unless symmetry justifies it.

fragments.label: Percentiles
fragments.text: Reject algebraic roots outside the support.
Moments

fragments.label: Moments
fragments.text: Calculate E(X)=∫xf(x)dx and E(X²)=∫x²f(x)dx over the support, then Var(X)=E(X²)−[E(X)]². Interpret the mean in the same units as X and variance in squared units.

fragments.label: Moments
fragments.text: Normalise before calculating moments.

fragments.label: Moments
fragments.text: Keep exact values until the variance subtraction is complete.
Can a pdf exceed 1?

fragments.label: Can a pdf exceed 1?
fragments.text: Yes; only areas must be between 0 and 1, and total area must equal 1.
What is P(X=a) for continuous X?

fragments.label: What is P(X=a) for continuous X?
fragments.text: Zero.
How is the median found?

fragments.label: How is the median found?
fragments.text: Set the area from the lower support boundary to m equal to 0.5.
Which root of a percentile equation is valid?

fragments.label: Which root of a percentile equation is valid?
fragments.text: Only a root lying in the stated support.

Understand sampling distributions and construct confidence intervals to estimate an unknown population parameter. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Population
fragments.text: The full set about which an inference is made.

fragments.label: Sample
fragments.text: A subset observed to learn about the population.

fragments.label: Sampling distribution
fragments.text: The probability distribution of a statistic over repeated samples.

fragments.label: Standard error
fragments.text: The standard deviation of a sampling distribution.

fragments.label: Confidence interval
fragments.text: A range generated by a method that captures the true parameter at a stated long-run rate.
Random samples and bias

fragments.label: Random samples and bias
fragments.text: Every population member should have an appropriate chance of selection. Convenience, voluntary-response and incomplete-frame samples can be biased. Random numbers help choose units without personal judgement.

fragments.label: Random samples and bias
fragments.text: A large biased sample is still biased.

fragments.label: Random samples and bias
fragments.text: Distinguish sampling variation from measurement error.

fragments.label: Random samples and bias
fragments.text: Sample mean moments: E(X̄)=μ; Var(X̄)=σ²/n
Sample mean distribution

fragments.label: Sample mean distribution
fragments.text: If population mean is μ and variance σ², then E(X̄)=μ and Var(X̄)=σ²/n. X̄ is normal if the population is normal and approximately normal for large n by the CLT.

fragments.label: Sample mean distribution
fragments.text: Standard error is σ/√n.

fragments.label: Sample mean distribution
fragments.text: Increasing n reduces standard error by the square-root law.
Unbiased estimates

fragments.label: Unbiased estimates
fragments.text: Estimate μ by x̄. Estimate population variance with s²=Σ(x−x̄)²/(n−1), equivalently [Σx²−(Σx)²/n]/(n−1). The n−1 correction makes the estimating process unbiased.

fragments.label: Unbiased estimates
fragments.text: Use the sample variance requested, not the descriptive variance with denominator n.

fragments.label: Unbiased estimates
fragments.text: Keep x̄ unrounded in the variance formula.
Confidence intervals

fragments.label: Confidence intervals
fragments.text: For known σ or a large sample, a confidence interval for μ is x̄±z*σ/√n, replacing σ by s for a large sample when needed. For a large-sample proportion p, use p̂±z*√[p̂(1−p̂)/n]. Interpret the confidence level as a property of the method.

fragments.label: Confidence intervals
fragments.text: 90%, 95%, 99% use different central z-values.

fragments.label: Confidence intervals
fragments.text: Give interval endpoints in context and sensible units.
What is the standard error of X̄?

fragments.label: What is the standard error of X̄?
fragments.text: σ/√n.
Why is n−1 used in the sample variance?

fragments.label: Why is n−1 used in the sample variance?
fragments.text: It corrects the systematic underestimation and makes the estimator unbiased.
What does a 95% confidence method mean?

fragments.label: What does a 95% confidence method mean?
fragments.text: Across repeated samples, about 95% of intervals produced by the method contain the true parameter.
What happens to standard error if n is quadrupled?

fragments.label: What happens to standard error if n is quadrupled?
fragments.text: It is halved.

Set up null and alternative hypotheses, use a critical region or p-value, and draw a conclusion in the context of the question. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Null hypothesis
fragments.text: H₀, the model or parameter value tested as the default claim.

fragments.label: Alternative hypothesis
fragments.text: H₁, the direction or difference supported if H₀ is rejected.

fragments.label: Significance level
fragments.text: The maximum chosen probability of rejecting H₀ when it is true.

fragments.label: Critical region
fragments.text: Test-statistic values that lead to rejection of H₀.

fragments.label: p-value
fragments.text: The probability under H₀ of an outcome at least as extreme as observed in the direction(s) of H₁.

fragments.label: Type I error
fragments.text: Rejecting a true H₀.

fragments.label: Type II error
fragments.text: Failing to reject a false H₀ under a specified alternative.
Setting up the test

fragments.label: Setting up the test
fragments.text: Define the parameter, write H₀ with equality, and make H₁ match the claim. 'Increased' gives an upper tail, 'decreased' a lower tail, and 'changed' two tails. The test calculation always uses the H₀ parameter.

fragments.label: Setting up the test
fragments.text: Use population parameters, not sample statistics, in hypotheses.

fragments.label: Setting up the test
fragments.text: Choose the tail before seeing the result.

fragments.label: Setting up the test
fragments.text: Mean test statistic: Z=(X̄−μ₀)/(σ/√n)
Discrete tests

fragments.label: Discrete tests
fragments.text: For X binomial or Poisson, find the probability of the observed result or something more extreme under H₀. Reject if that p-value is ≤α. A critical region is chosen so its H₀ probability is at most α; discreteness means the actual size may be smaller.

fragments.label: Discrete tests
fragments.text: For two tails, identify both extremes rather than blindly doubling if the distribution is asymmetric.

fragments.label: Discrete tests
fragments.text: State the actual critical-region probability when requested.
Normal and mean tests

fragments.label: Normal and mean tests
fragments.text: Use a continuity-corrected normal approximation for binomial/Poisson when conditions hold. For a mean, standardise Z=(X̄−μ₀)/(σ/√n), using s for σ in a large-sample setting as allowed, then compare with the relevant critical value or p-value.

fragments.label: Normal and mean tests
fragments.text: Put μ₀ from H₀ in the numerator.

fragments.label: Normal and mean tests
fragments.text: A two-tailed α test places α/2 in each tail.
Errors and conclusions

fragments.label: Errors and conclusions
fragments.text: Type I probability is the rejection-region probability under H₀. Type II probability is the acceptance-region probability under a specified alternative. Finish with 'reject H₀' or 'do not reject H₀', followed by a contextual evidence statement—never say H₀ is proved.

fragments.label: Errors and conclusions
fragments.text: Power=1−P(Type II error).

fragments.label: Errors and conclusions
fragments.text: The conclusion must use the direction in H₁.
Where does equality belong in hypotheses?

fragments.label: Where does equality belong in hypotheses?
fragments.text: In H₀.
What tail matches 'the mean has decreased'?

fragments.label: What tail matches 'the mean has decreased'?
fragments.text: A lower-tailed test.
What is a Type I error?

fragments.label: What is a Type I error?
fragments.text: Rejecting H₀ when H₀ is true.
How should a non-significant result be stated?

fragments.label: How should a non-significant result be stated?
fragments.text: Do not reject H₀; there is insufficient evidence for the contextual alternative claim.

Everything a computer stores is a pattern of bits, so Paper 1 repeatedly asks you to convert between number bases, use binary and decimal prefixes, represent signed integers in two's complement, add and subtract in binary and spot overflow. Questions also test BCD, the uses of hexadecimal and character sets, usually with a short justification of why one representation suits a given use. Most calculation questions award a mark for visible working and a mark for the answer.

fragments.label: Bit
fragments.text: A binary digit, 0 or 1; the smallest unit of data a computer stores.

fragments.label: Byte
fragments.text: A group of 8 bits, treated as a single unit of storage. A nibble is 4 bits.

fragments.label: Binary prefix
fragments.text: A multiplier based on powers of 2: kibi (Ki, 2^10), mebi (Mi, 2^20), gibi (Gi, 2^30) and tebi (Ti, 2^40).

fragments.label: Decimal prefix
fragments.text: A multiplier based on powers of 10: kilo (k, 10^3), mega (M, 10^6), giga (G, 10^9) and tera (T, 10^12).

fragments.label: Hexadecimal
fragments.text: A base-16 number system using the digits 0–9 and A–F; each hex digit represents exactly 4 bits.

fragments.label: Sign and magnitude
fragments.text: A signed representation in which the most significant bit shows the sign (0 = +, 1 = −) and the remaining bits hold the size of the number.

fragments.label: One's complement
fragments.text: The binary number obtained by inverting every bit (each 0 becomes 1 and each 1 becomes 0).

fragments.label: Two's complement
fragments.text: The one's complement of a binary number plus 1; as a representation, the most significant bit has a negative place value.

fragments.label: Overflow
fragments.text: When the result of a calculation is too large (or too small) to be stored in the number of bits available.

fragments.label: Binary Coded Decimal (BCD)
fragments.text: A representation in which each denary digit is stored separately as a 4-bit binary code (a nibble).

fragments.label: Packed BCD
fragments.text: BCD in which two 4-bit digit codes are stored in one byte.

fragments.label: Character set
fragments.text: The complete list of characters a computer recognises, each paired with a unique binary code.
Binary, denary and hexadecimal

fragments.label: Binary, denary and hexadecimal
fragments.text: Denary (base 10) uses ten digits, binary (base 2) uses 0 and 1, and hexadecimal (base 16) uses 0–9 and A–F. In every base the value comes from place values that increase by a power of the base from the right. For a byte, the binary place values are 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1. To convert denary to binary, either subtract the largest place values that fit, or divide repeatedly by 2 and read the remainders from the last to the first. To convert between binary and hexadecimal, split the binary into groups of four bits from the right and replace each group with one hex digit; to go from hex to binary, replace each hex digit with its 4-bit pattern. Converting hex to binary first is often the easiest route from hex to denary.

fragments.label: Binary, denary and hexadecimal
fragments.text: Hex to denary directly: multiply each digit by its place value (256, 16, 1) and add, e.g. 3F = 3 × 16 + 15 = 63.

fragments.label: Binary, denary and hexadecimal
fragments.text: Pad the leftmost group to 4 bits before converting to hex, e.g. 101 becomes 0101 = 5.

fragments.label: Binary, denary and hexadecimal
fragments.text: An n-bit unsigned binary integer can represent 0 to 2^n − 1, so a byte holds 0 to 255 and two bytes hold 0 to 65,535.

fragments.label: Binary, denary and hexadecimal
fragments.text:
202 ÷ 2 = 101 remainder 0
101 ÷ 2 = 50 remainder 1
50 ÷ 2 = 25 remainder 0
25 ÷ 2 = 12 remainder 1
12 ÷ 2 = 6 remainder 0
6 ÷ 2 = 3 remainder 0
3 ÷ 2 = 1 remainder 1
1 ÷ 2 = 0 remainder 1
Read the remainders from the bottom up: 1100 1010
Check: 128 + 64 + 8 + 2 = 202
Hex: 1100 = C, 1010 = A → CA
Binary magnitudes and prefixes

fragments.label: Binary magnitudes and prefixes
fragments.text: Decimal prefixes multiply by powers of 10: kilo = 10^3, mega = 10^6, giga = 10^9, tera = 10^12. For many years the computing industry also used 'kilo' to mean 1024 (2^10), which caused confusion: a '1.6 GHz' processor uses the decimal meaning while '8 GB of RAM' usually meant 8 × 2^30 bytes. Binary prefixes were introduced to remove the ambiguity: kibi (KiB) = 2^10, mebi (MiB) = 2^20, gibi (GiB) = 2^30 and tebi (TiB) = 2^40. When presenting a calculated size, choose the prefix that gives one or two digits before the decimal point, and convert all values to the same prefix before combining them.

fragments.label: Binary magnitudes and prefixes
fragments.text: Each step up a binary prefix multiplies by 1024; each step up a decimal prefix multiplies by 1000.

fragments.label: Binary magnitudes and prefixes
fragments.text: The gap grows with size: 1 KiB is 2.4% larger than 1 kB, but 1 TiB is about 10% larger than 1 TB.

fragments.label: Binary magnitudes and prefixes
fragments.text: Use the prefix named in the question; if it says MiB, divide by 1024 twice, not by 1,000,000.

fragments.label: Binary magnitudes and prefixes
fragments.text: Storage manufacturers use decimal prefixes, which is why a '500 GB' drive appears as about 465 GiB in an operating system.

fragments.label: Binary magnitudes and prefixes
fragments.text:
3 MiB = 3 × 1024 × 1024 = 3,145,728 bytes; 3 MB = 3,000,000 bytes.
A file of 45,000 bytes = 45,000 ÷ 1024 ≈ 43.9 KiB.
How many 3.2 MiB files fit on a 4 GiB memory stick?
Convert to the same prefix: 4 GiB = 4 × 1024 = 4096 MiB
4096 ÷ 3.2 = 1280 files
Sign and magnitude, one's and two's complement

fragments.label: Sign and magnitude, one's and two's complement
fragments.text: Unsigned integers are stored as plain binary. For signed integers, the simplest idea is sign and magnitude, where the most significant bit (MSB) is the sign; but it has two zeros (+0 and −0) and needs special rules for arithmetic, so computers use two's complement instead. The one's complement of a number is found by inverting every bit; the two's complement is the one's complement plus 1. To store a negative denary number: write the positive value in binary with a leading 0 (fill the byte), invert every bit, then add 1. In two's complement the MSB has a negative place value (−128 in a byte), so 8 bits represent −128 to +127. To read a two's complement value, add the negative MSB value to the positive values of the other 1 bits.

fragments.label: Sign and magnitude, one's and two's complement
fragments.text: A leading 1 means the number is negative; a leading 0 means it is zero or positive.

fragments.label: Sign and magnitude, one's and two's complement
fragments.text: Two's complement has only one zero, and the same adder circuit performs both addition and subtraction.

fragments.label: Sign and magnitude, one's and two's complement
fragments.text: Quick method: from the right, copy bits up to and including the first 1, then invert every remaining bit.

fragments.label: Sign and magnitude, one's and two's complement
fragments.text: Taking the two's complement again changes the sign back, e.g. from −44 to +44.

fragments.label: Sign and magnitude, one's and two's complement
fragments.text: Range of n-bit two's complement: −2^(n−1) to 2^(n−1) − 1.

fragments.label: Sign and magnitude, one's and two's complement
Sign and magnitude, one's and two's complement
fragments.text:
+44 = 0010 1100
Copy from the right up to and including the first 1: 100
Invert the rest (00101 → 11010): 1101 0100 = −44
Check: −128 + 64 + 16 + 4 = −44

Read 1110 0110: −128 + 64 + 32 + 4 + 2 = −26

fragments.label: Sign and magnitude, one's and two's complement
fragments.text:
+5: sign and magnitude 0000 0101; two's complement 0000 0101
−5: sign and magnitude 1000 0101; two's complement 1111 1011
0: sign and magnitude has 0000 0000 and 1000 0000; two's complement has only 0000 0000
Binary addition and subtraction

fragments.label: Binary addition and subtraction
fragments.text: Binary addition works from right to left using four rules: 0 + 0 = 0, 0 + 1 = 1, 1 + 1 = 0 carry 1, and 1 + 1 + 1 = 1 carry 1. Subtraction can be done directly by borrowing (0 − 1 = 1 after borrowing from the next column), but computers subtract by adding the two's complement: A − B = A + (−B). In two's complement arithmetic, any carry out of the most significant bit is discarded.

fragments.label: Binary addition and subtraction
fragments.text: Show carries or borrows above the columns; examiners award method marks for visible working.

fragments.label: Binary addition and subtraction
fragments.text: Convert the answer back to denary to check it.

fragments.label: Binary addition and subtraction
fragments.text: Discarding the final carry is not the same as overflow; check the signs instead.

fragments.label: Binary addition and subtraction
fragments.text:
1110  (14)
− 0101  (5)
Column 1: 0 − 1 → borrow, 10 − 1 = 1
Column 2: 1 becomes 0 after the borrow; 0 − 0 = 0
Column 3: 1 − 1 = 0
Column 4: 1 − 0 = 1
Result = 1001 = 9
Overflow

fragments.label: Overflow
fragments.text: A register has a fixed number of bits, so a result outside the representable range cannot be stored correctly. In two's complement, overflow is shown when two numbers of the same sign are added and the result has the opposite sign: two positives giving a negative, or two negatives giving a positive. The processor records this in the overflow flag of the status register so that software can react.

fragments.label: Overflow
fragments.text: Adding numbers of opposite signs can never overflow.

fragments.label: Overflow
fragments.text: With unsigned numbers, a carry out of the MSB shows the result was too large.

fragments.label: Overflow
fragments.text: Using more bits (for example 16 instead of 8) widens the range and makes overflow less likely.

fragments.label: Overflow
fragments.text:
0110 0100  (+100)
+ 0011 0010  (+50)
= 1001 0110
The correct answer, +150, is above +127. The MSB is 1, so the result reads as −128 + 16 + 4 + 2 = −106: overflow has occurred.

fragments.label: Overflow
fragments.text:
1001 1100  (−100)
+ 1100 1110  (−50)
= (1) 0110 1010  (carry out discarded)
The result reads as +106, but the correct answer, −150, is below −128: overflow has occurred.
Binary Coded Decimal (BCD)

fragments.label: Binary Coded Decimal (BCD)
fragments.text: BCD stores each denary digit separately in its own nibble, using the codes 0000 (0) to 1001 (9); the codes 1010 to 1111 are never used. Digits can be stored one per byte (leaving four bits unused) or as packed BCD, two digits per byte. BCD is used where denary digits must be displayed or processed individually, such as digital clocks, calculators and seven-segment displays, and for currency, where values such as 0.10 cannot be stored exactly as binary fractions. When two BCD digits are added and the result is above 1001, the processor adds a correction of 0110 so that the digit is valid and a carry passes to the next digit.

fragments.label: Binary Coded Decimal (BCD)
fragments.text: BCD is less storage-efficient than pure binary: 6 of the 16 possible nibble codes are unused.

fragments.label: Binary Coded Decimal (BCD)
fragments.text: BCD avoids rounding errors for exact denary values, such as money.

fragments.label: Binary Coded Decimal (BCD)
fragments.text: When justifying BCD, link it to each digit being processed or displayed separately.

fragments.label: Binary Coded Decimal (BCD)
fragments.text:
0011 1000  (38)
+ 0100 0111  (47)
Low digit: 1000 + 0111 = 1111, which is not a valid BCD digit
Add the correction 0110: 1111 + 0110 = 1 0101 → store 0101, carry 1
High digit: 0011 + 0100 + 1 = 1000 (valid)
Result = 1000 0101 = 85
Uses of hexadecimal

fragments.label: Uses of hexadecimal
fragments.text: The computer always stores binary; hexadecimal is only a way of writing binary for people. It is shorter and far less error-prone to read, write and remember than long binary strings, yet it converts directly to binary because each hex digit is exactly 4 bits. A 48-bit MAC address, for example, becomes just 12 hex digits.

fragments.label: Uses of hexadecimal
fragments.text: Memory addresses and memory dumps when debugging.

fragments.label: Uses of hexadecimal
fragments.text: MAC addresses, e.g. 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E.

fragments.label: Uses of hexadecimal
fragments.text: Colour codes in HTML/CSS, e.g. #FF8000 = red FF, green 80, blue 00.

fragments.label: Uses of hexadecimal
fragments.text: Error codes and machine-code or assembly listings.

fragments.label: Uses of hexadecimal
fragments.text: URL encoding of special characters, e.g. a space written as %20 (hex 20 = 32, the ASCII code for a space).
Character sets

fragments.label: Character sets
fragments.text: Text is stored by giving each character a numeric code from a character set. Standard ASCII uses 7 bits, giving 128 codes covering English letters, digits, punctuation and control characters; it is usually stored in a byte with the MSB set to 0. Extended ASCII uses all 8 bits for 256 codes, adding accented and graphical characters. Unicode can use up to 4 bytes per character, so characters from almost every writing system, plus symbols and emoji, can be represented; its first 128 codes match ASCII.

fragments.label: Character sets
fragments.text: Codes are allocated in sequence: 'A' = 65, 'B' = 66; 'a' = 97; the digit '0' = 48, so a lower-case letter is 32 more than its capital.

fragments.label: Character sets
fragments.text: Because codes are sequential, strings can be sorted and compared by comparing their codes.

fragments.label: Character sets
fragments.text: Unicode needs more storage per character than ASCII but supports international text in one system.

fragments.label: Character sets
fragments.text: The character '7' (code 55) is different from the integer 7; converting between them is a common exam point.
How many bytes are in 1 KiB and in 1 kB?

fragments.label: How many bytes are in 1 KiB and in 1 kB?

fragments.text: What is the range of an 8-bit two's complement integer?

fragments.label: What is the range of an 8-bit two's complement integer?

fragments.text: How do you find the two's complement of a negative number?

fragments.label: How do you find the two's complement of a negative number?
fragments.text: Write the positive value in binary with a leading 0, invert every bit, then add 1.
Why is two's complement preferred to sign and magnitude?

fragments.label: Why is two's complement preferred to sign and magnitude?
fragments.text: It has only one zero, and addition and subtraction use the same simple adder with no special rules.
How is overflow detected when adding two's complement numbers?

fragments.label: How is overflow detected when adding two's complement numbers?
fragments.text: Two numbers of the same sign are added and the result has the opposite sign.
What is 0011 1001 in BCD?

fragments.label: What is 0011 1001 in BCD?
fragments.text: 39 — each nibble is one denary digit (3 and 9).
What is packed BCD?

fragments.label: What is packed BCD?
fragments.text: BCD with two digit codes stored in one byte.
Give two uses of hexadecimal.

fragments.label: Give two uses of hexadecimal.
fragments.text: Any two of: memory addresses, MAC addresses, HTML colour codes, error codes, machine-code/assembly listings, URL encoding.
Why is Unicode needed when ASCII exists?

fragments.label: Why is Unicode needed when ASCII exists?
fragments.text: ASCII has only 128 (or 256 extended) codes, which cannot represent characters from all languages; Unicode can.

Images and sound must be turned into binary before a computer can store them. Paper 1 asks you to explain how bitmaps and vector graphics are encoded, calculate bitmap and sound file sizes, describe how changing resolution, colour depth, sampling rate or sampling resolution affects quality and size, and justify choosing a bitmap or a vector graphic for a given task.

fragments.label: Pixel
fragments.text: The smallest addressable element of a bitmap image; a single dot of one colour.

fragments.label: Image resolution
fragments.text: The number of pixels in an image, given as width × height (for example 1920 × 1080).

fragments.label: Screen resolution
fragments.text: The number of pixels a display screen can show horizontally and vertically.

fragments.label: Colour depth
fragments.text: The number of bits used to represent the colour of one pixel; n bits allow 2^n different colours.

fragments.label: Bit depth
fragments.text: The number of bits used to store each of the red, green and blue components of a pixel's colour; a bit depth of 8 gives 24 bits per pixel.

fragments.label: File header
fragments.text: Data at the start of an image or sound file describing the file, such as its type, dimensions, colour depth or sampling rate.

fragments.label: Drawing object
fragments.text: A single shape in a vector graphic, such as a line, rectangle or circle.

fragments.label: Property
fragments.text: A value that defines how a drawing object looks, such as its coordinates, size, line colour, line width or fill colour.

fragments.label: Drawing list
fragments.text: The set of commands in a vector graphic file that define every drawing object and its properties.

fragments.label: Sampling rate
fragments.text: The number of samples of a sound wave's amplitude taken per second, measured in hertz (Hz).

fragments.label: Sampling resolution
fragments.text: The number of bits used to store each sound sample; it sets how many amplitude levels can be recorded.
Encoding bitmap images

fragments.label: Encoding bitmap images
fragments.text: A bitmap image is a two-dimensional grid (matrix) of pixels. A pixel has just two properties: its position in the grid and its colour. Each pixel's colour is stored as a binary code, and the codes are stored in order, row by row. The number of bits per pixel is the colour depth: 1 bit gives 2 colours (black and white), 4 bits allow simple greyscale, 8 bits give 256 colours and 24 bits give over 16.7 million colours. Bit depth is the number of bits for each of the red, green and blue components, so a bit depth of 8 means 3 × 8 = 24 bits per pixel. A high colour depth is needed for areas of gradually changing colour, such as a sky; with too few bits the image shows visible bands of colour. A file header at the start of the file records information the software needs to rebuild the image, such as the file type, image width and height, and colour depth.

fragments.label: Encoding bitmap images
fragments.text: Image resolution is a property of the image (how many pixels it contains); screen resolution is a property of the display.

fragments.label: Encoding bitmap images
fragments.text: If the image resolution is higher than the screen resolution, the image is scaled down or only part of it is shown.

fragments.label: Encoding bitmap images
fragments.text: Enlarging a bitmap beyond its resolution makes the individual pixels visible (pixelation).

fragments.label: Encoding bitmap images
fragments.text:
Colour depth 4 bits → 2^4 = 16 colours
Colour depth 8 bits → 2^8 = 256 colours
Colour depth 24 bits → 2^24 = 16,777,216 colours
Calculating bitmap file size

fragments.label: Calculating bitmap file size
fragments.text: The pixel data in a bitmap take up (number of pixels) × (colour depth) bits. Multiply the width by the height to find the number of pixels, multiply by the colour depth, then divide by 8 to convert bits to bytes. The result is an estimate, because the file header adds a small amount of extra data.

fragments.label: Calculating bitmap file size
fragments.text: Divide by 8 for bytes, then by 1024 for KiB or by 1000 for kB, depending on the unit the question asks for.

fragments.label: Calculating bitmap file size
fragments.text: Keep the calculation in one line of working so method marks can be awarded.

fragments.label: Calculating bitmap file size
fragments.text: State that the file header makes the real file slightly larger than the estimate.

fragments.label: Calculating bitmap file size
fragments.text:
An 800 × 600 image has a bit depth of 8 (per RGB component).
Bits per pixel = 3 × 8 = 24, i.e. 3 bytes
Size = 800 × 600 × 3 = 1,440,000 bytes ≈ 1406.3 KiB

fragments.label: Calculating bitmap file size
fragments.text:
A 6 × 4 inch photo is scanned at 300 dots (pixels) per inch with 24-bit colour.
Pixels = (6 × 300) × (4 × 300) = 1800 × 1200 = 2,160,000
Bytes = 2,160,000 × 3 = 6,480,000 bytes
= 6,480,000 ÷ 1024 ÷ 1024 ≈ 6.2 MiB
Effect of changing resolution and colour depth

fragments.label: Effect of changing resolution and colour depth
fragments.text: Increasing the image resolution gives more pixels, so finer detail can be shown and the image can be enlarged further before pixelation appears. Increasing the colour depth allows more colours, so shades and gradients look more realistic with less colour banding. Both changes increase the file size in direct proportion: doubling the colour depth doubles the size, and doubling both the width and the height quadruples it.

fragments.label: Effect of changing resolution and colour depth
fragments.text: Reducing resolution or colour depth reduces file size but lowers quality; this is a trade-off, not a free saving.

fragments.label: Effect of changing resolution and colour depth
fragments.text: A larger file takes longer to download or transmit and uses more storage.

fragments.label: Effect of changing resolution and colour depth
fragments.text: Always link a change to both effects the question asks for: quality and file size.

fragments.label: Effect of changing resolution and colour depth
fragments.text:
An image is 2 MiB. Its width and height are both halved and its colour depth is changed from 24 bits to 8 bits.
Pixels fall to ½ × ½ = ¼ of the original
Bits per pixel fall to 8 ÷ 24 = ⅓ of the original
New size = 2 MiB × ¼ × ⅓ ≈ 0.17 MiB
Encoding vector graphics

fragments.label: Encoding vector graphics
fragments.text: A vector graphic does not store pixels. Instead it stores a drawing list: a set of commands describing each drawing object and its properties, such as a circle's centre coordinates, radius, line colour, line width and fill colour. Dimensions are defined relative to an imaginary drawing canvas rather than in fixed units. When the image is displayed, the software reads the drawing list and recalculates every object at the required scale, so the graphic can be resized without losing quality or being distorted. Vector graphics are produced by drawing and computer-aided design (CAD) packages. Most screens and printers work with pixels, so a vector graphic is converted to a bitmap (rasterised) at the moment it is displayed or printed.

fragments.label: Encoding vector graphics
fragments.text: File size depends on the number and complexity of objects, not on the display size.

fragments.label: Encoding vector graphics
fragments.text: Scaling only changes property values, so edges stay sharp at any size.

fragments.label: Encoding vector graphics
fragments.text: Vector graphics are poor at representing photographs, because natural scenes cannot be broken down into simple shapes.

fragments.label: Encoding vector graphics
fragments.text:
Circle: centre (120, 80), radius 40, line colour black, line width 2, fill colour red
Rectangle: top-left (20, 20), width 60, height 30, line colour blue, fill none
Choosing a bitmap or a vector graphic

fragments.label: Choosing a bitmap or a vector graphic
fragments.text: Choose a bitmap when the image has continuous tones and fine, irregular detail, such as a photograph or a scanned document. Choose a vector graphic when the image is built from lines and shapes and must be resized, such as a logo, a diagram, a map, a font or a technical drawing. In a justification, name the feature of the task and link it to a property of the format.

fragments.label: Choosing a bitmap or a vector graphic
fragments.text: Logo printed on a pen and on a billboard → vector, because it must scale without pixelation.

fragments.label: Choosing a bitmap or a vector graphic
fragments.text: Photograph from a digital camera → bitmap, because each pixel's colour can be captured individually.

fragments.label: Choosing a bitmap or a vector graphic
fragments.text: Simple diagrams are often smaller as vectors; complex photographs would need a vast drawing list.

fragments.label: Choosing a bitmap or a vector graphic
fragments.text: Useful questions to decide: Must the image be resized? Must it be drawn accurately to scale (e.g. an architect's plan)? Must it look photo-realistic?

fragments.label: Choosing a bitmap or a vector graphic
fragments.text: Images captured by a digital camera or scanner are always bitmaps.
Sampling sound

fragments.label: Sampling sound
fragments.text: Sound is an analogue wave: its amplitude varies continuously over time. To store it digitally, a sound encoder first passes the signal through a band-limiting filter, which removes very high frequencies that humans cannot hear and that would cause coding problems. An analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) then measures (samples) the amplitude at regular time intervals, and each measurement is rounded to the nearest level that can be stored with the sampling resolution. These binary sample values are stored in order, with a file header recording details such as the sampling rate and sampling resolution. Played back, the samples are converted into an approximation of the original wave.

fragments.label: Sampling sound
fragments.text: Analogue data vary continuously; digital data take discrete values.

fragments.label: Sampling sound
fragments.text: The sampling rate controls how often the wave is measured; the sampling resolution controls how precisely each measurement is stored.

fragments.label: Sampling sound
fragments.text: A sampling resolution of n bits gives 2^n possible amplitude levels, e.g. 3 bits gives only 8 levels, while 16 bits gives 65,536.

fragments.label: Sampling sound
fragments.text: Nyquist's theorem: the sampling rate must be at least twice the highest frequency in the sound. Human hearing reaches about 20 kHz, which is why CDs sample at 44.1 kHz with 16-bit resolution.
Sound quality and file size

fragments.label: Sound quality and file size
fragments.text: A higher sampling rate captures changes in the wave more often, so rapid changes (higher frequencies) are represented and the playback is closer to the original. A higher sampling resolution rounds each sample less, so the amplitude is recorded more accurately with less quantisation error. Both improve accuracy but increase the file size: file size = sampling rate × sampling resolution × duration in seconds (× number of channels).

fragments.label: Sound quality and file size
fragments.text: Doubling the sampling rate or the sampling resolution doubles the file size.

fragments.label: Sound quality and file size
fragments.text: Stereo sound has two channels, so it needs twice the data of mono.

fragments.label: Sound quality and file size
fragments.text: Beyond a certain point, extra quality cannot be heard, so a larger file brings no practical benefit.

fragments.label: Sound quality and file size
fragments.text:
Sampling rate = 44,100 Hz, sampling resolution = 16 bits, 2 channels, 30 seconds
Bits = 44,100 × 16 × 2 × 30 = 42,336,000 bits
Bytes = 42,336,000 ÷ 8 = 5,292,000 bytes
MiB = 5,292,000 ÷ 1024 ÷ 1024 ≈ 5.05 MiB
What is colour depth?

fragments.label: What is colour depth?
fragments.text: The number of bits used to represent the colour of each pixel.
How many colours can a 12-bit colour depth represent?

fragments.label: How many colours can a 12-bit colour depth represent?
fragments.text: 2^12 = 4096 colours.
How do you estimate the file size of a bitmap?

fragments.label: How do you estimate the file size of a bitmap?
fragments.text: Width × height × colour depth gives bits; divide by 8 for bytes.
What does a vector graphic's drawing list contain?

fragments.label: What does a vector graphic's drawing list contain?
fragments.text: Commands defining each drawing object and its properties, such as coordinates, size and colours.
Why does a vector graphic not pixelate when enlarged?

fragments.label: Why does a vector graphic not pixelate when enlarged?
fragments.text: Each object is recalculated from its properties at the new size rather than stretching stored pixels.
What is the difference between sampling rate and sampling resolution?

fragments.label: What is the difference between sampling rate and sampling resolution?
fragments.text: Sampling rate is how many samples are taken per second; sampling resolution is how many bits store each sample.
What is the formula for the size of a sound file?

fragments.label: What is the formula for the size of a sound file?
fragments.text: Sampling rate × sampling resolution × duration in seconds × number of channels (in bits).
What does Nyquist's theorem say about the sampling rate?

fragments.label: What does Nyquist's theorem say about the sampling rate?
fragments.text: It must be at least twice the highest frequency in the sound being sampled.
What does a file header store?

fragments.label: What does a file header store?
fragments.text: Information about the file needed to decode it, such as file type, dimensions and colour depth, or sampling rate and resolution.

Compression reduces the size of a file so it takes less storage and transmits faster. Paper 1 asks why compression is needed, what separates lossy from lossless methods, which method suits a given file and use, and how different file types are compressed, with run-length encoding (RLE) as the method you must be able to apply and trace.

fragments.label: Compression
fragments.text: Encoding data so that it uses fewer bits than the original representation.

fragments.label: Lossless compression
fragments.text: Compression in which no data are lost, so the original file can be reconstructed exactly.

fragments.label: Lossy compression
fragments.text: Compression that permanently removes data judged to be unnecessary, so the original cannot be reconstructed exactly.

fragments.label: Run-length encoding (RLE)
fragments.text: A lossless method that replaces a run of identical consecutive values with a single copy of the value and a count of how many times it repeats.

fragments.label: Dictionary (token) compression
fragments.text: A lossless method that replaces repeated words or patterns with short codes stored in a dictionary.

fragments.label: Huffman coding
fragments.text: A lossless method that gives frequently occurring characters shorter bit codes and rarer characters longer codes, using codes with the prefix property.

fragments.label: Perceptual coding
fragments.text: A lossy technique that removes the parts of a sound or image that human senses are least able to notice.

fragments.label: Compression ratio
fragments.text: Original size divided by compressed size; a higher ratio means greater compression.
Why compression is needed

fragments.label: Why compression is needed
fragments.text: Uncompressed images, audio and video are very large. Compressing them means less storage space is used, files transfer and download faster, less bandwidth is used on a network, and media can be streamed in real time without long buffering. Compression is used for email attachments, web pages, streaming services, backups and archives.

fragments.label: Why compression is needed
fragments.text: Smaller files → faster transmission → lower data costs and less network congestion.

fragments.label: Why compression is needed
fragments.text: Compression and decompression take processing time, which is the price paid for smaller files.

fragments.label: Why compression is needed
fragments.text: Both sender and receiver need compatible software to compress and decompress.
Lossless and lossy compression

fragments.label: Lossless and lossy compression
fragments.text: Lossless compression finds patterns or redundancy in the data and records them more efficiently; decompressing gives back every original bit. Lossy compression goes further by discarding data, usually detail that people will barely notice, so it achieves much smaller files, but the removed data are lost permanently and quality falls with each extra level of compression.

fragments.label: Lossless and lossy compression
fragments.text: Lossless is essential for text, program files, spreadsheets and databases, where one changed bit could corrupt meaning or stop a program working.

fragments.label: Lossless and lossy compression
fragments.text: Lossy suits photographs, music and video for streaming or the web, where a small loss of quality is acceptable for a large saving.

fragments.label: Lossless and lossy compression
fragments.text: Once lossy compression has been applied, the discarded data cannot be recovered by decompressing.

fragments.label: Lossless and lossy compression
fragments.text: Many real formats combine both: a lossy step removes detail, then a lossless step encodes what remains efficiently.

fragments.label: Lossless and lossy compression
fragments.text:
A program's executable file must be sent to users → lossless, because any lost bit would change the instructions and the program might not run.
A holiday photo is uploaded to social media → lossy, because the file becomes much smaller and the loss of fine detail is not noticeable on a phone screen.
Run-length encoding (RLE)

fragments.label: Run-length encoding (RLE)
fragments.text: RLE replaces each run of repeated consecutive values with a count and one copy of the value. It works well on data with long runs, such as simple graphics with large areas of one colour, but can make data with few repeats larger, because every single value now needs a count as well.

fragments.label: Run-length encoding (RLE)
fragments.text: RLE is lossless: expanding each count/value pair gives back the exact original.

fragments.label: Run-length encoding (RLE)
fragments.text: In a bitmap, each row of pixels is encoded as runs of colour codes.

fragments.label: Run-length encoding (RLE)
fragments.text: In binary, each run is stored as a count followed by the value, e.g. a count byte and then the byte being repeated.

fragments.label: Run-length encoding (RLE)
fragments.text: The decompressor must be able to tell a count from a data value, for example by using fixed-size pairs or a flag character that marks where an encoded run starts.

fragments.label: Run-length encoding (RLE)
fragments.text:
Original: AAAAABBBCCCCCCCCD (17 characters)
Runs: 5 × A, 3 × B, 8 × C, 1 × D
Encoded: 5A 3B 8C 1D (8 characters)
The data have been reduced from 17 to 8 characters.

fragments.label: Run-length encoding (RLE)
fragments.text:
Original: ABCDEF (6 characters)
Encoded: 1A 1B 1C 1D 1E 1F (12 characters)
With no repeated runs, RLE doubles the size, which is why it only suits data with long runs.

fragments.label: Run-length encoding (RLE)
fragments.text:
Original bytes: 01000001 repeated 4 times ('AAAA', 32 bits)
Encoded as a count byte then a data byte: 00000100 01000001 (16 bits)
A 1-bit black-and-white row 0001111111000 becomes the runs 3 × 0, 7 × 1, 3 × 0
Compressing text files

fragments.label: Compressing text files
fragments.text: Text must always be compressed losslessly, because losing any character changes the meaning. In Huffman coding, the text is analysed to find how often each character occurs; frequent characters are given short bit codes and rare characters longer ones, instead of every character using a full byte. The codes have the prefix property: no code is the start of another, longer code, so the compressed bit stream can be decoded without ambiguity. Dictionary methods are another approach: repeated words or groups of characters are stored once in a dictionary, and each occurrence is replaced by a short index into it.

fragments.label: Compressing text files
fragments.text: Huffman coding turns a stream of bytes into a stream of bits of different lengths.

fragments.label: Compressing text files
fragments.text: The code table (or dictionary) must be stored with the file or known to the decompressor, which adds a small overhead.

fragments.label: Compressing text files
fragments.text: The more uneven the character frequencies, or the more often words repeat, the greater the saving.

fragments.label: Compressing text files
fragments.text:
Codes: e = 10, t = 01, o = 111, h = 110, l = 0001
'tee' → 01 10 10 = 6 bits, compared with 3 × 8 = 24 bits in 8-bit ASCII
Decoding 011010: 01 must be t (no other code starts 01), then 10 = e, 10 = e
Because no code is the prefix of another, there is only one way to split the bits.

fragments.label: Compressing text files
fragments.text:
Dictionary: 1 = 'the', 2 = 'cat', 3 = 'sat'
'the cat sat the cat' → 1 2 3 1 2
Compressing bitmap images and vector graphics

fragments.label: Compressing bitmap images and vector graphics
fragments.text: A bitmap can be compressed losslessly with RLE, which is effective on images with large areas of the same colour. Lossy methods reduce the resolution, or reduce the colour depth by setting up a smaller palette and changing each pixel to the closest colour in it, which works well on photographs where neighbouring pixels are similar. JPEG is the most common lossy format for photographs. A vector graphic is already compact because it stores a drawing list; to compress it further it can be converted to Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG), which describes the image in a text-based markup language that compresses well with lossless methods.

fragments.label: Compressing bitmap images and vector graphics
fragments.text: Reducing colour depth or resolution before saving is a form of lossy compression.

fragments.label: Compressing bitmap images and vector graphics
fragments.text: Lossy image compression can create visible artefacts such as blockiness or colour banding at high compression levels.

fragments.label: Compressing bitmap images and vector graphics
fragments.text: Vector graphics should use lossless compression so that object properties are not altered.
Compressing sound files

fragments.label: Compressing sound files
fragments.text: Lossy sound compression uses perceptual coding: it removes sounds outside the range of human hearing, and quieter sounds that are masked by louder sounds at the same time. MP3 works this way and typically cuts a music file by up to about 90%. Another technique uses the fact that successive samples rarely change much: the file stores the differences between samples, using a lower sampling resolution for them. The sampling rate or sampling resolution of the whole recording can also be reduced. Video formats such as MP4 apply similar compression to both sound and pictures. Lossless audio compression exists for situations where perfect quality is needed, such as studio master recordings, but it gives much smaller savings.

fragments.label: Compressing sound files
fragments.text: Removing frequencies humans cannot hear reduces size with no audible loss.

fragments.label: Compressing sound files
fragments.text: Reducing the sampling rate or resolution lowers accuracy, so quality falls noticeably at extreme settings.

fragments.label: Compressing sound files
fragments.text: Streaming services use lossy compression so music plays without buffering on limited bandwidth.
Give two reasons for compressing files.

fragments.label: Give two reasons for compressing files.
fragments.text: Any two of: less storage space, faster transmission or download, less bandwidth used, allows real-time streaming.
What is the key difference between lossless and lossy compression?

fragments.label: What is the key difference between lossless and lossy compression?
fragments.text: Lossless allows the original to be reconstructed exactly; lossy permanently removes data.
Encode WWWWWBBBWW using RLE.

fragments.label: Encode WWWWWBBBWW using RLE.
fragments.text: 5W 3B 2W.
Why must text files use lossless compression?

fragments.label: Why must text files use lossless compression?
fragments.text: Losing any character would change the content and meaning of the text.
What is perceptual coding?

fragments.label: What is perceptual coding?
fragments.text: Lossy sound compression that removes sounds humans cannot hear or would not notice, such as quiet sounds masked by louder ones.
What is the prefix property in Huffman coding, and why does it matter?

fragments.label: What is the prefix property in Huffman coding, and why does it matter?
fragments.text: No code is the start of another code, so the compressed bit stream can be decoded in only one way.
When does RLE work badly?

fragments.label: When does RLE work badly?
fragments.text: When the data contain few consecutive repeated values, because each value needs a count too and the file may grow.
How can a bitmap be compressed with a lossy method?

fragments.label: How can a bitmap be compressed with a lossy method?
fragments.text: Reduce the resolution or colour depth, or group similar colours together and store them as one colour.

This single subtopic covers the whole of the syllabus chapter on communication, so it is one of the broadest in Paper 1. You need to compare LANs and WANs, client-server and peer-to-peer models, topologies and transmission media; describe LAN hardware, Ethernet and CSMA/CD; explain how the internet is built from ISPs, routers, the telephone network and cell networks; explain the WWW, cloud computing and bit streaming; and explain IP addressing, URLs and DNS. Most marks come from precise definitions, ordered descriptions and choices justified for a scenario.

fragments.label: Local area network (LAN)
fragments.text: A network connecting computers in a single room, building or site, owned by the organisation that uses it.

fragments.label: Wide area network (WAN)
fragments.text: A network connecting computers or LANs on different sites, possibly thousands of kilometres apart, usually using links leased from a telecommunications company.

fragments.label: Client-server model
fragments.text: A network model in which servers provide applications, files or services that clients request and use.

fragments.label: Thin client
fragments.text: A client that only sends input to, and receives output from, an application running on a server.

fragments.label: Thick client
fragments.text: A client that carries out at least some of the processing itself, or downloads and runs the application locally.

fragments.label: Peer-to-peer model
fragments.text: A network model with no central server, in which each computer (peer) stores some of the files and can act as both client and server.

fragments.label: Topology
fragments.text: The configuration of a network, defining how the devices are connected by links.

fragments.label: Bandwidth
fragments.text: A measure of the amount of data that can be transmitted per second.

fragments.label: Router
fragments.text: A device that forwards packets between networks, choosing a route using the destination IP address; routers form the nodes of the internet.

fragments.label: Switch
fragments.text: A device at the centre of a star LAN that sends each message only to the device it is addressed to.

fragments.label: CSMA/CD
fragments.text: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection: the method used on a shared Ethernet medium to detect collisions and retransmit after a random delay.

fragments.label: Bit rate
fragments.text: The number of bits transmitted or processed per second.

fragments.label: IP address
fragments.text: A numerical address that identifies a device's network interface so that packets can be routed to it.

fragments.label: Domain Name Service (DNS)
fragments.text: A hierarchical, distributed database held on domain name servers that translates domain names into IP addresses.

fragments.label: Cloud computing
fragments.text: Providing computing services, such as storage, platforms and software, on remote servers accessed over the internet.
Why networks are used; LANs and WANs

fragments.label: Why networks are used; LANs and WANs
fragments.text: Networking lets computers share resources and communicate. Connecting PCs in a LAN means software can be installed once on an application server, files can be stored centrally and shared on a file server, several users can share high-quality printers through a print server, staff can communicate by email, and files can be kept digitally rather than on paper. A LAN covers one room, building or site, is owned by the organisation, uses twisted pair cable or Wi-Fi, has user computers and servers connected to it, and includes a device that connects it to other networks. A WAN connects sites that may be thousands of kilometres apart. It is usually not owned by the organisation but leased from a telecommunications (PSTN) company as dedicated links, typically fibre-optic, with switches connecting each site. The internet is an internetwork: LANs connect to WANs, which connect to the internet.

fragments.label: Why networks are used; LANs and WANs
fragments.text: LAN: small area, organisation-owned, high speed, end-systems attached directly.

fragments.label: Why networks are used; LANs and WANs
fragments.text: WAN: large area, leased third-party links, connects sites rather than individual computers.

fragments.label: Why networks are used; LANs and WANs
fragments.text: A benefit of networking should always be linked to a resource being shared or a task being centralised.
Client-server and peer-to-peer models

fragments.label: Client-server and peer-to-peer models
fragments.text: In the client-server model, clients request and servers provide; on the internet the client is typically a web browser and the server is a web server. A thin client chooses an application to run on the server, sends it input data and receives the output. A thick client may do some processing before and after using the server, or may download the application and run it itself. Client-server is the choice when the server holds a database the clients access, provides a web application for finding or supplying information, or handles e-commerce and financial transactions. In a peer-to-peer network each peer stores some of the files and can act as a client (requesting a file) or a server (supplying one).

fragments.label: Client-server and peer-to-peer models
fragments.text: Peer-to-peer advantages for file sharing: avoids congestion at a single server when many users download at once, and parts of a file can be downloaded separately from several peers.

fragments.label: Client-server and peer-to-peer models
fragments.text: Client-server advantages: the organisation controls which files are available and who uses them, and files on one server can be regularly scanned and protected from malware.

fragments.label: Client-server and peer-to-peer models
fragments.text: Thin client: cheap devices and central management, but needs a constant connection. Thick client: can work offline and reduces server load, but needs more powerful hardware.

fragments.label: Client-server and peer-to-peer models
fragments.text:
Question: Describe the roles of clients and servers on the internet. [2]
Mark-scoring answer:
Web pages and files are stored on servers. (1)
Clients send requests to the servers, which send back the requested pages or files. (1)
Bus, star, mesh and hybrid topologies

fragments.label: Bus, star, mesh and hybrid topologies
fragments.text: A data communication system needs a sender, a receiver, a transmission medium, a message and a protocol. In a bus topology all end-systems share one link with a terminator at each end; every message is broadcast along the whole bus and each device checks whether it is the destination. It is cheap, but a break in the bus stops the whole network and collisions increase with traffic. In a star topology each end-system has its own link to a central device, normally a switch, which sends each message only to its destination; a failed link affects one device, but the central device is a single point of failure. In a mesh topology devices have direct links to several others, so messages can take alternative routes; it is very reliable but needs a lot of cabling. The internet's core is a partial mesh of routers. A hybrid network joins LANs that use different topologies.

fragments.label: Bus, star, mesh and hybrid topologies
fragments.text: Star is the most common LAN topology: easy to add devices and no shared-medium collisions with a switch.

fragments.label: Bus, star, mesh and hybrid topologies
fragments.text: A Wi-Fi LAN behaves like a star, with the wireless access point at the centre.

fragments.label: Bus, star, mesh and hybrid topologies
fragments.text: Justify a topology by linking it to the scenario: cost, reliability, number of devices and expected traffic.
Transmission media: cable and wireless

fragments.label: Transmission media: cable and wireless
fragments.text: Cable can be twisted pair or coaxial (both copper) or fibre-optic (light). Fibre is the most expensive but has by far the highest bandwidth, suffers least from interference and attenuation (loss of signal strength), and needs fewer repeaters, so it is used for long-distance and backbone links. Twisted pair is cheapest and is used for telephone lines and most LAN connections. Wireless transmission uses radio, microwave or infrared. Moving from radio to microwave to infrared, bandwidth increases but the ability to pass through walls decreases; infrared is limited to indoor use in one room, while microwave offers the best balance for most applications. Satellites extend communication to remote areas: geostationary (GEO) satellites at about 35,800 km appear fixed in the sky and three give global coverage, while medium- and low-Earth-orbit satellites provide GPS and support mobile networks. The long distances introduce a transmission delay.

fragments.label: Transmission media: cable and wireless
fragments.text: Wired: faster, more reliable and more secure; costly to install and needs permission to lay cables across land.

fragments.label: Transmission media: cable and wireless
fragments.text: Wireless: no cabling and supports mobile devices; more interference, limited range, easier to intercept, and some frequencies need a licence.

fragments.label: Transmission media: cable and wireless
fragments.text: Repeaters are needed less often for wireless links.

fragments.label: Transmission media: cable and wireless
fragments.text: For global links the competing technologies are undersea and underground fibre-optic cable and satellites.

fragments.label: Transmission media: cable and wireless
fragments.text:
Altitude ≈ 35,800 km; speed of light ≈ 300,000 km/s
Up to the satellite: 35,800 ÷ 300,000 ≈ 0.12 s
Up and back down: ≈ 0.24 s before any processing
This delay is noticeable in phone calls and games, which is why fibre is preferred where it is available.
LAN hardware

fragments.label: LAN hardware
fragments.text: Each end-system (a user computer or a server) needs a network interface card (NIC), which has a unique address set during manufacture that identifies the device on the network; a wireless NIC (WNIC) does the same job on Wi-Fi. A server provides a service, such as files, printing or applications, to end-systems. In a star network the central connecting device is normally a switch, which directs each message to a specific end-system. A repeater receives a weakened (attenuated) signal and sends it on at full strength, extending a cable. A bridge connects two segments of a LAN and stores the addresses of the devices on each side. A bus network needs a terminator at each end to stop signals reflecting back. In a Wi-Fi LAN (IEEE 802.11) the central device is a wireless access point (WAP), which connects wireless devices to the wired network.

fragments.label: LAN hardware
fragments.text: NIC/WNIC: identifies the device on the network. Switch: sends a message only to the device it is addressed to.

fragments.label: LAN hardware
fragments.text: Repeater: restores signal strength. Bridge: joins two LAN segments into one network.

fragments.label: LAN hardware
fragments.text: A router connects the LAN to other networks such as the internet; a home 'router' often combines a router, switch, WAP and modem.
Ethernet and CSMA/CD

fragments.label: Ethernet and CSMA/CD
fragments.text: Ethernet is the dominant LAN technology, standardised as IEEE 802.3, with generations from the original speed up to 100 gigabit. Legacy Ethernet used a bus, or a star with a hub, so every message was broadcast to all end-systems, each of which checked the destination address. Because the medium was shared, two devices transmitting at once caused a collision that corrupted both messages. CSMA/CD manages this: a device checks the medium for activity; if it is busy it waits a random time and checks again; if it is idle it transmits while continuing to monitor; if a collision is detected it stops, sends a jamming signal to warn all devices, waits a random time and tries again. Modern Ethernet is switched: each end-system has its own full-duplex link to the switch, which buffers messages until the link is free, so collisions cannot happen and CSMA/CD is no longer needed.

fragments.label: Ethernet and CSMA/CD
fragments.text: The random wait is the key point: a fixed wait would make both devices collide again.

fragments.label: Ethernet and CSMA/CD
fragments.text: Ethernet frames carry the source and destination addresses of the NICs.

fragments.label: Ethernet and CSMA/CD
fragments.text: Full-duplex means data can travel in both directions on a link at the same time.

fragments.label: Ethernet and CSMA/CD
fragments.text:
1. The device listens to (senses) the medium before transmitting.
2. Data are only sent when the medium is free.
3. While transmitting, the device checks for a collision; if one is detected it stops and sends a jamming signal.
4. It waits a random time before trying to transmit again.
(One mark per point, up to 4.)
The internet's infrastructure

fragments.label: The internet's infrastructure
fragments.text: The internet was never designed as a whole; it evolved as networks joined together. Users connect through an access Internet Service Provider (ISP), which connects to regional ISPs, which connect to tier 1 (backbone) ISPs; ISPs connect to each other at Internet Exchange Points (IXPs). The busiest links are fibre-optic cables under the sea and across land, forming a mesh whose nodes are routers, each choosing the best route for the data passing through it. The public switched telephone network (PSTN) was built for voice. Early dial-up connections used a modem to convert the computer's digital signals to analogue for the telephone line, with another modem converting them back. Organisations could rent leased lines: dedicated, permanently connected links with a guaranteed speed. Today PSTN companies use digital fibre and act as ISPs themselves, offering broadband and Wi-Fi hotspots. Mobile devices connect through the cell phone network: the phone communicates with a cell tower, and the mobile company acts as the ISP.

fragments.label: The internet's infrastructure
fragments.text: Modem: converts between digital and analogue signals (modulator-demodulator).

fragments.label: The internet's infrastructure
fragments.text: Leased (dedicated) line: permanent, guaranteed speed and more secure, but expensive; used to build WANs.

fragments.label: The internet's infrastructure
fragments.text: Cell network: towers (base stations) give radio coverage in cells, connected to the wider network.
The WWW and cloud computing

fragments.label: The WWW and cloud computing
fragments.text: The internet is the internetwork: the physical infrastructure of connected networks. The World Wide Web is a distributed application that runs on the internet: a vast collection of websites whose pages contain hyperlinks giving immediate access to other pages, accessed with HTTP/HTTPS through a browser. Email and file transfer are other internet applications. Cloud computing provides computing services over the internet from large server farms. A public cloud is owned and managed by a cloud service provider and used by many customers. A private cloud is used only by one organisation: it may build and manage it on site itself, have a third party build and manage it on site, or have a third party provide it over the internet. Services can be infrastructure (storage and processing power), platforms (for developing and testing software) or software (applications run in the cloud).

fragments.label: The WWW and cloud computing
fragments.text: Benefits: better performance and more storage than local systems, access from any device anywhere, no need to buy expensive hardware or software, and no need for in-house technical expertise.

fragments.label: The WWW and cloud computing
fragments.text: Drawbacks: the provider can access all stored data, the user cannot be sure data are not shared with third parties, the user relies on the provider for security and backups, and access depends on the internet connection.

fragments.label: The WWW and cloud computing
fragments.text: A one-mark definition: using services, files or software on a remote server accessed over the internet.
Bit streaming

fragments.label: Bit streaming
fragments.text: Streamed media are compressed and sent as a continuous bit stream that is played as it arrives, rather than downloaded first. On-demand streaming sends stored content, such as a film, when the user chooses; real-time (live) streaming sends content as it is produced, such as a sports match, usually via many content-provider servers because so many people watch at once. On the user's computer the incoming data go into a buffer, and the media player takes data from the buffer at exactly the bit rate the media need. Data should arrive faster than they are played so the buffer can absorb delays. The player monitors the buffer against a low-water mark (ask the server to send more) and a high-water mark (pause transmission so the buffer does not overflow).

fragments.label: Bit streaming
fragments.text: The rate data can enter the buffer is limited by the connection's bandwidth, so broadband is essential for video.

fragments.label: Bit streaming
fragments.text: If the buffer empties, playback stops to rebuffer.

fragments.label: Bit streaming
fragments.text: Services offer each video at several compression levels so users with low bandwidth receive a lower bit rate at lower quality.

fragments.label: Bit streaming
fragments.text:
Data arrive at 2 Mbps; the video plays at 500 kbps. Low-water mark 100 KiB, high-water mark 700 KiB.
Net fill rate = 2,000,000 − 500,000 = 1,500,000 bits per second
Data to add = 600 KiB = 600 × 1024 × 8 = 4,915,200 bits
Time to fill = 4,915,200 ÷ 1,500,000 ≈ 3.3 s
With input paused, time to drain back to the low mark = 4,915,200 ÷ 500,000 ≈ 9.8 s
IP addressing

fragments.label: IP addressing
fragments.text: An IPv4 address is 32 bits, written in dotted decimal notation as four denary numbers from 0 to 255. It is hierarchical: a network part (netID) is used to route data to the right network, and a host part (hostID) identifies the device once there. The original scheme used fixed classes (A, B, C) with 8, 16 or 24 bits for the netID, which wasted addresses. Classless inter-domain routing (CIDR) adds a suffix giving the number of netID bits, e.g. /21, so the split can suit each organisation. Subnetting divides one network's hostID range into sub-networks, e.g. one per department, so addresses are not wasted and traffic stays local. Private addresses (10.x.x.x, 172.16–31.x.x and 192.168.x.x) are used inside organisations and can be reused by every private network; a NAT (network address translation) device lets them share one public address on the internet. A static IP address never changes, which suits servers; a dynamic address is allocated by the ISP each time a user connects, so addresses can be reused. IPv6 uses 128 bits, written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons, giving a vastly larger address space.

fragments.label: IP addressing
fragments.text: IPv4 gives 2^32 ≈ 4.3 billion addresses, which is not enough, hence CIDR, NAT and IPv6.

fragments.label: IP addressing
fragments.text: In IPv6, leading zeros in a group can be dropped and one run of all-zero groups can be replaced by ::.

fragments.label: IP addressing
fragments.text: A router has one IP address for each network interface.

fragments.label: IP addressing
fragments.text:
11000000 10101000 00000001 00001010 → 192.168.1.10
172.20.14.9/20 → 20 bits for the netID, 32 − 20 = 12 bits for the hostID
2^12 = 4096 host addresses on that network

fragments.label: IP addressing
fragments.text:
The organisation has one network: 200.15.7.0 to 200.15.7.255 (8 hostID bits).
Use 3 of the hostID bits as a subnet ID: 2^3 = 8 subnets, enough for 6 departments.
The remaining 5 bits give 2^5 = 32 addresses per subnet.
One network address is shared, instead of wasting a separate network for each department.

fragments.label: IP addressing
fragments.text:
192.168.300.4 → invalid IPv4: 300 is greater than 255
2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329 → valid IPv6
Shortened form: 2001:db8::ff00:42:8329
URLs and the Domain Name Service

fragments.label: URLs and the Domain Name Service
fragments.text: A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) gives the location of a resource on the web, for example https://www.example.com/notes/index.html: the protocol (https), the domain name (www.example.com) and the path to the resource (/notes/index.html). Routers work with IP addresses, so the domain name must be translated. The browser sends the domain name to a DNS server. If that server holds the entry, it returns the IP address; if not, it passes the request to other DNS servers in the hierarchy until the address is found. The IP address is returned to the browser, which then sends its request to the web server at that address.

fragments.label: URLs and the Domain Name Service
fragments.text: Domain names are easier to remember than IP addresses.

fragments.label: URLs and the Domain Name Service
fragments.text: DNS results are cached so repeat lookups are faster.

fragments.label: URLs and the Domain Name Service
fragments.text: If a website moves to a server with a new IP address, only the DNS record changes, not the URL.

fragments.label: URLs and the Domain Name Service
fragments.text:
1. The user types the URL into the browser's address bar
2. The browser extracts the domain name and sends it to a DNS server
3. The DNS server looks up the IP address, asking other DNS servers if it does not hold it
4. The IP address is returned to the browser
5. The browser sends an HTTP(S) request to that IP address
6. The web server returns the page, which the browser displays
Give two characteristics of a typical WAN.

fragments.label: Give two characteristics of a typical WAN.
fragments.text: Any two of: connects sites far apart, not owned by the organisation, leased from a telecommunications company, uses fibre-optic links, no end-systems connected directly.
What is the difference between a thin client and a thick client?

fragments.label: What is the difference between a thin client and a thick client?
fragments.text: A thin client only sends input and receives output from an application running on the server; a thick client does some or all of the processing itself.
Give one advantage of peer-to-peer file sharing over client-server.

fragments.label: Give one advantage of peer-to-peer file sharing over client-server.
fragments.text: It avoids congestion at one server, as parts of a file can be downloaded from several peers at once.
Why is fibre-optic cable used for long-distance links?

fragments.label: Why is fibre-optic cable used for long-distance links?
fragments.text: It has the highest bandwidth and suffers least from interference and attenuation, so fewer repeaters are needed.
What does a repeater do?

fragments.label: What does a repeater do?
fragments.text: It receives a weakened signal and transmits it again at full strength, so the cable can be extended.
Why is CSMA/CD not needed on switched Ethernet?

fragments.label: Why is CSMA/CD not needed on switched Ethernet?
fragments.text: Each device has its own full-duplex link to the switch, so collisions cannot occur.
What is the difference between on-demand and real-time streaming?

fragments.label: What is the difference between on-demand and real-time streaming?
fragments.text: On-demand sends stored content when the user chooses; real-time sends content as it is being produced.
What does a NAT device do?

fragments.label: What does a NAT device do?
fragments.text: It lets devices with private IP addresses share one public IP address when communicating over the internet.
Why is a static IP address used for a web server?

fragments.label: Why is a static IP address used for a web server?
fragments.text: So its address never changes and DNS records keep pointing to it.
What is the role of DNS?

fragments.label: What is the role of DNS?
fragments.text: It translates a domain name into the IP address of the server hosting the resource.

A computer system must process, store, input and output data, and Paper 1 expects you to explain why each component is needed and how the named devices work internally. Questions ask for ordered descriptions of the laser printer, 3D printer, hard disk, flash memory, optical disc, touchscreen, VR headset, microphone and speaker; comparisons of RAM and ROM, SRAM and DRAM, and PROM, EPROM and EEPROM; and explanations of buffers, embedded systems and monitoring and control systems. Mark schemes award one mark per correct, correctly sequenced point.

fragments.label: Primary storage
fragments.text: Memory the processor can access directly: registers, cache and main memory (RAM and ROM).

fragments.label: Secondary storage
fragments.text: Non-volatile storage, such as a hard disk or SSD, used for long-term storage of programs and data.

fragments.label: Volatile
fragments.text: Describes memory that loses its contents when the power is switched off.

fragments.label: Embedded system
fragments.text: A computer system with a processor, memory and input/output built into a larger device to carry out a dedicated function.

fragments.label: Microcontroller
fragments.text: A processor, memory and input/output capability constructed together on a single chip.

fragments.label: Random-access memory (RAM)
fragments.text: Volatile memory that can be read from and written to any number of times.

fragments.label: Read-only memory (ROM)
fragments.text: Non-volatile memory that can be read from any number of times but not written to during normal operation.

fragments.label: Buffer
fragments.text: Temporary storage, usually in memory, for data being transferred from one part of a system to another; it works as a queue.

fragments.label: Sensor
fragments.text: A hardware device that measures a physical property and transmits a value to a controlling computer.

fragments.label: Actuator
fragments.text: A hardware device, such as a motor, that receives a signal from a computer and adjusts the setting of a controlling device.

fragments.label: Feedback
fragments.text: Using the effect of a control action, measured by the next sensor reading, to decide the next action.
Input, output, memory and storage

fragments.label: Input, output, memory and storage
fragments.text: A computer system must process data (the CPU), store data, and input and output data. Input devices capture data and instructions, and output devices present results. Storage forms a memory hierarchy: registers, cache, main memory, then secondary storage such as hard disks. Moving down the hierarchy, capacity rises and cost per byte falls, but access becomes slower. Users would like large, cheap and fast storage, which is impossible, so systems combine a small amount of fast primary storage with large, cheap secondary storage. Main memory (RAM) is also volatile, so separate non-volatile secondary storage is needed to keep programs and data when the power is off.

fragments.label: Input, output, memory and storage
fragments.text: The processor can only execute programs that are in main memory; they are loaded there from secondary storage.

fragments.label: Input, output, memory and storage
fragments.text: Storage may be internal (hard disk, SSD), inserted into a drive (optical disc), a connected peripheral, portable (memory stick, used for carrying data and personal backup) or remote over a network (cloud, often for backup).

fragments.label: Input, output, memory and storage
fragments.text: Input and output, including reading and writing the internal disk, are handled by an I/O subsystem.
Embedded systems

fragments.label: Embedded systems
fragments.text: An embedded system contains a processor, memory and input/output capability built into a larger product to perform a dedicated function; if these are all on one chip it is a microcontroller. Almost every manufactured item with electrical or mechanical parts contains one, for example washing machines, car engine management, lane-detection systems, traffic lights and fitness trackers. Its program is stored in ROM or flash memory and runs when the device is switched on. Some embedded systems have no user interface, some show a little output to the user, and some, like a mobile phone, provide a full user interface.

fragments.label: Embedded systems
fragments.text: Benefits: special-purpose, so small, cheap to mass-produce (economies of scale), low power and reliable.
