fragments.text: Library benefits: saves development time, routines are already tested so they are reliable, and expert code can be used for complex tasks.

fragments.label: Program libraries and DLLs
fragments.text: DLL benefits: executable files are smaller, one copy in memory can be shared by several programs, and updating the DLL improves every program that uses it without recompiling them.

fragments.label: Program libraries and DLLs
fragments.text: DLL drawbacks: the program relies on the DLL being present and working; if it is missing, corrupted or a new version contains bugs, the program fails or gives wrong results, and the user will find it hard to work out what is wrong.
Give two reasons why a computer needs an operating system.

fragments.label: Give two reasons why a computer needs an operating system.
fragments.text: Any two of: provides a user interface, hides hardware complexity, provides a platform for applications, manages resources between programs.
What does the OS do in memory management?

fragments.label: What does the OS do in memory management?
fragments.text: Allocates and frees memory for processes, tracks memory use, protects each process's memory, and manages virtual memory.
What is a device driver?

fragments.label: What is a device driver?
fragments.text: Software that translates OS commands into signals a specific hardware device understands.
Why is defragmentation useful on a hard disk?

fragments.label: Why is defragmentation useful on a hard disk?
fragments.text: It stores each file contiguously, so the read/write heads move less and files are accessed faster.
How does a virus checker detect malware?

fragments.label: How does a virus checker detect malware?
fragments.text: It compares files against a database of known virus signatures and monitors for suspicious behaviour.
What is a DLL?

fragments.label: What is a DLL?
fragments.text: A library file linked to a program when it runs, which can be shared by several programs.
Give two benefits of using DLLs.

fragments.label: Give two benefits of using DLLs.
fragments.text: Any two of: smaller executables, one shared copy in memory, updates apply to all programs without recompiling.
Give one drawback of DLLs.

fragments.label: Give one drawback of DLLs.
fragments.text: The program will not run if the DLL is missing, or an incompatible update can break it.

Programs are written in assembly language or high-level languages, but the processor only runs machine code, so a translator is needed. Paper 1 asks why assemblers, compilers and interpreters are needed, the benefits and drawbacks of compiling versus interpreting, how languages such as Java are partly compiled and partly interpreted, and which features of an Integrated Development Environment (IDE) help programmers write, check, present and debug code.

fragments.label: Source code
fragments.text: A program as written by the programmer in assembly language or a high-level language.

fragments.label: Object code
fragments.text: The machine code produced by translating source code.

fragments.label: Compiler
fragments.text: A translator that converts the whole of a high-level program into machine code in one go, producing an executable file.

fragments.label: Interpreter
fragments.text: A translator that analyses and executes a high-level program one statement at a time, without producing a separate executable file.

fragments.label: Assembler
fragments.text: A translator that converts assembly language into machine code.

fragments.label: Intermediate code (bytecode)
fragments.text: Partly translated code that is independent of any processor and is run by a virtual machine.

fragments.label: Integrated Development Environment (IDE)
fragments.text: A single program providing the tools needed to write, translate, test and debug code.

fragments.label: Breakpoint
fragments.text: A marker set on a line of code at which execution pauses so the programmer can inspect variables.
Why translators are needed

fragments.label: Why translators are needed
fragments.text: A processor can only execute machine code in its own instruction set. Programmers write in assembly language or high-level languages because they are far easier to write and read, so the source code must be translated before or while it runs. An assembler translates assembly language, with each instruction becoming one machine-code instruction. A compiler or interpreter translates high-level languages, where one statement may become many machine-code instructions.

fragments.label: Why translators are needed
fragments.text: Assembly language → assembler (one-to-one).

fragments.label: Why translators are needed
fragments.text: High-level language → compiler or interpreter (one-to-many).

fragments.label: Why translators are needed
fragments.text: Translators also detect errors, such as syntax errors, during translation.
Compilers

fragments.label: Compilers
fragments.text: A compiler needs the source code but no data. It reads each line in turn and analyses it; if a line contains an error, the error is recorded and compilation continues, otherwise the line is converted to intermediate code. When the whole source has been processed, either the complete intermediate code is converted into object code, or, if any errors were found, a list of them is output and no object code is produced. The program can only run once compilation finds no errors. The object code can then be run straight away, or stored and run later without the compiler.

fragments.label: Compilers
fragments.text: For the programmer: an executable file can be distributed, so users never see the source code; but errors are only listed after the whole program has been analysed, and the program must be recompiled after every change.

fragments.label: Compilers
fragments.text: For the user: only the object code is needed to run the program, and it executes faster than interpreted code; but compiled object code could contain a virus, which is harder to spot than in source code.

fragments.label: Compilers
fragments.text: A compiled program only runs on the type of processor (and OS) it was compiled for.

fragments.label: Compilers
fragments.text: Compilers are the right choice once the program is as near error-free as possible and is to be distributed for general use.

fragments.label: Compilers
fragments.text:
A program has syntax errors on lines 12 and 40.
Compiler: reads all the lines, records both errors, outputs a list of the two errors and produces no object code.
Interpreter: runs lines 1–11, then reports the error on line 12 and stops. The error on line 40 is only found after line 12 is fixed, and only if that line is actually reached.
Interpreters

fragments.label: Interpreters
fragments.text: An interpreter needs the source code and the data the program uses. It reads the first line of source code and analyses it. If there is an error, it is reported and the interpreter stops. If not, the line is converted to intermediate code, which the interpreter uses to carry out the action straight away. It then reads the next line and repeats. No executable file is produced: the source code and the interpreter are needed every time the program runs, and each statement is translated again each time it is executed, including inside loops.

fragments.label: Interpreters
fragments.text: For the programmer: errors are identified as they occur and can be corrected immediately, and parts of an unfinished program can be tested; but code that is not reached during a run is not checked, so some syntax errors may stay hidden until later.

fragments.label: Interpreters
fragments.text: For the user: the interpreter and the source code must be available every time the program runs, and execution is slower.

fragments.label: Interpreters
fragments.text: An interpreter is the right choice during development: one error can cause several others, so finding and fixing the first error at once limits the rest, and the associated debugging tools speed this up.

fragments.label: Interpreters
fragments.text: The source code must be given to users, so it can be copied or changed.
Partly compiled, partly interpreted languages

fragments.label: Partly compiled, partly interpreted languages
fragments.text: Some languages combine both approaches. A Java Virtual Machine (JVM) is written for each type of computer. Java source code is compiled into Java Byte Code, an intermediate code that does not depend on any particular processor. When the program is run, the byte code is interpreted by the JVM on the target computer, so the byte code can be transferred to any computer with a JVM installed. The same bytecode can therefore run on any device with a JVM, while the initial compilation catches syntax errors and does much of the translation work in advance.

fragments.label: Partly compiled, partly interpreted languages
fragments.text: 'Write once, run anywhere': the bytecode is portable between platforms.

fragments.label: Partly compiled, partly interpreted languages
fragments.text: Faster than a pure interpreter because the source has already been analysed and translated to bytecode.

fragments.label: Partly compiled, partly interpreted languages
fragments.text: Python is also compiled to bytecode before being interpreted.
IDE features for coding and error detection

fragments.label: IDE features for coding and error detection
fragments.text: An IDE brings an editor, translator and debugging tools together. When coding, context-sensitive prompts (auto-complete) suggest suitable keywords, variable names and the parameters a function expects, based on what has been typed so far, which saves time and reduces typing errors. For initial error detection, dynamic syntax checking checks each line as it is typed and highlights syntax errors, such as a missing bracket or a misspelled keyword, immediately, before the program is translated.

fragments.label: IDE features for coding and error detection
fragments.text: Context-sensitive prompts reduce the need to remember exact names and parameter orders.

fragments.label: IDE features for coding and error detection
fragments.text: Dynamic syntax checks find syntax errors only; logic errors still need testing and debugging.
IDE features for presentation

fragments.label: IDE features for presentation
fragments.text: Prettyprint formats code automatically to make its structure clear, for example by colour-coding keywords, variables and comments and by indenting the contents of loops and selection statements. Expanding and collapsing code blocks lets the programmer hide the body of a procedure, loop or other block, showing only its first line, so they can see the overall structure of a long program and focus on the part they are working on.

fragments.label: IDE features for presentation
fragments.text: Colour coding makes typing errors stand out, e.g. a keyword that is not highlighted is probably misspelled.

fragments.label: IDE features for presentation
fragments.text: Consistent indentation makes it easier to see where each block starts and ends.
IDE features for debugging

fragments.label: IDE features for debugging
fragments.text: Debugging tools help find logic and run-time errors. Single stepping executes the program one statement at a time, so the programmer can follow the exact path taken. A breakpoint pauses execution at a chosen line, so the program runs normally up to the suspected problem area and then stops. A report window (variable watch window) displays the current values of variables as the program runs or while it is paused, so the programmer can see where a value first becomes incorrect.

fragments.label: IDE features for debugging
fragments.text: Breakpoints and single stepping are usually combined: run to a breakpoint, then step line by line.

fragments.label: IDE features for debugging
fragments.text: Watching variables replaces adding temporary output statements to the code.

fragments.label: IDE features for debugging
fragments.text: These tools find the location of an error; the programmer still has to work out the correction.

fragments.label: IDE features for debugging
fragments.text:
A loop should total 10 values but gives the wrong answer.
1. Set a breakpoint at the start of the loop
2. Add the total and loop counter to the watch/report window
3. Single step through each pass of the loop
4. Notice that the loop counter starts at 2, so the first value is never added
5. Correct the starting value and run the program again
Which translator converts assembly language into machine code?

fragments.label: Which translator converts assembly language into machine code?
fragments.text: An assembler.
Give two benefits of a compiler.

fragments.label: Give two benefits of a compiler.
fragments.text: Any two of: faster execution, no translator needed to run, source code not distributed, compiled once and run many times.
Give two benefits of an interpreter during development.

fragments.label: Give two benefits of an interpreter during development.
fragments.text: Errors are reported at the line they occur, and parts of a program can be tested before it is complete.
How is Java partly compiled and partly interpreted?

fragments.label: How is Java partly compiled and partly interpreted?
fragments.text: Source code is compiled to bytecode, which is then interpreted by the Java Virtual Machine on the target computer.
What is a context-sensitive prompt?

fragments.label: What is a context-sensitive prompt?
fragments.text: An IDE suggestion of keywords, identifiers or parameters that fit what the programmer is currently typing.
What is dynamic syntax checking?

fragments.label: What is dynamic syntax checking?
fragments.text: The IDE checks each line for syntax errors as it is typed and highlights them immediately.
What does a breakpoint do?

fragments.label: What does a breakpoint do?
fragments.text: It pauses execution at a chosen line so variable values can be examined.
What is the purpose of the report (watch) window?

fragments.label: What is the purpose of the report (watch) window?
fragments.text: To display the current values of variables while the program runs or is paused.

Data must be kept safe from loss, seen only by the right people, and kept accurate. Paper 1 asks you to distinguish security, privacy and integrity; name and describe threats such as malware, hackers, phishing and pharming; and describe measures that protect the computer system (accounts, passwords, authentication, firewalls, anti-malware) and the data itself (backup, disk mirroring, access rights, encryption). The highest marks go to answers that match a specific measure to a specific threat and say how it reduces the risk.

fragments.label: Data security
fragments.text: Protecting data against loss, damage or corruption, so it is available when needed and can be recovered if lost.

fragments.label: Data privacy
fragments.text: Keeping data available only to authorised users, protecting it from unauthorised access.

fragments.label: Data integrity
fragments.text: The requirement for data to be accurate, complete and up to date, and unchanged except by authorised processes.

fragments.label: Malware
fragments.text: Malicious software written with the intention of causing harm to a computer system or the data it holds.

fragments.label: Hacker
fragments.text: A person who attempts to gain unauthorised access to a computer system.

fragments.label: Phishing
fragments.text: Sending an email or message that appears to come from a legitimate source in order to trick the recipient into giving away confidential information.

fragments.label: Pharming
fragments.text: Redirecting a user to a fake website that looks legitimate, for example by altering DNS or browser settings, so that confidential details are entered there.

fragments.label: Authentication
fragments.text: Verifying that a user is who they claim to be, for example by password, biometrics or a security token.

fragments.label: Authorisation (access rights)
fragments.text: Defining which files and resources each user may access and what they are allowed to do with them (e.g. read only, read/write).

fragments.label: Firewall
fragments.text: Hardware or software that monitors incoming and outgoing network traffic and blocks traffic that does not meet a set of rules.

fragments.label: Encryption
fragments.text: Converting plain text into cipher text using an algorithm and a key, so that intercepted data cannot be understood without the decryption key.

fragments.label: Disk mirroring
fragments.text: Writing every item of data to two separate disks at the same time, so an identical copy is always available if one disk fails.
Security, privacy and integrity of data

fragments.label: Security, privacy and integrity of data
fragments.text: These three terms are often confused, and examiners reward precise definitions. Data security means the data are protected from being lost or corrupted, so they are available when needed and are the same data that were originally stored. Data privacy means the data can only be seen by people who are authorised to see them. Data integrity means the data are accurate, complete and up to date. Privacy of personal data is supported by data protection laws, which require organisations to keep the data they hold private and accurate and to use them only for the purposes agreed with the individual; the law acts as a deterrent because offenders can be prosecuted.

fragments.label: Security, privacy and integrity of data
fragments.text: Security → protection against loss. Privacy → protection against unauthorised access. Integrity → accuracy.

fragments.label: Security, privacy and integrity of data
fragments.text: Security is needed first: lost or corrupted data cannot be private or accurate.

fragments.label: Security, privacy and integrity of data
fragments.text: But security alone does not guarantee privacy or integrity; secure data can still be wrong or seen by the wrong people.

fragments.label: Security, privacy and integrity of data
fragments.text:
Question: Describe the difference between the security and the privacy of data. [2]
Mark-scoring answer:
Security is protecting data against loss or corruption. (1)
Privacy is protecting data against access by unauthorised people. (1)
Why both the system and the data need protecting

fragments.label: Why both the system and the data need protecting
fragments.text: Protecting data depends on protecting the computer system that stores it. System security has two aims: to keep the system running and carrying out the tasks users need, and to ensure that only authorised users can access it. Data security measures, such as backups and encryption, then protect the data itself in case the system's defences fail. An organisation needs both: a secure system that is down after a disaster cannot provide its data, and a system that is running but has no backups can lose its data permanently.

fragments.label: Why both the system and the data need protecting
fragments.text: System security measures: user accounts, passwords, authentication, firewalls, anti-malware, disaster recovery planning.

fragments.label: Why both the system and the data need protecting
fragments.text: Data security measures: backup, disk mirroring, access rights, encryption.

fragments.label: Why both the system and the data need protecting
fragments.text: Threats come from people inside and outside the organisation, from software and from natural disasters.
Threats from networks and the internet

fragments.label: Threats from networks and the internet
fragments.text: Threats include careless users, internal mismanagement, natural disasters (fire, flood, earthquake), hackers and malware. A hacker tries to gain unauthorised access, usually by exploiting weaknesses such as weak passwords, unpatched software or out-of-date anti-malware; once in, they may steal, delete or change data, install malware or disrupt the system. Malware takes several forms. A virus attaches itself to other executable code and replicates, corrupting or deleting data. A worm runs independently and spreads itself across a network. A Trojan horse appears to be useful, legitimate software but carries hidden malicious code. Spyware secretly gathers information, such as keystrokes, and sends it to a third party. A logic bomb stays inactive until a condition, such as a date, is met. A bot takes control of a computer so it can be used in attacks on others.

fragments.label: Threats from networks and the internet
fragments.text: Phishing: a fake but legitimate-looking email or message persuades the user to reveal confidential details or click a link.

fragments.label: Threats from networks and the internet
fragments.text: Pharming: malicious code alters DNS or browser settings so a correctly typed web address leads to a fake site.

fragments.label: Threats from networks and the internet
fragments.text: Keylogging: recording the user's keystrokes to capture passwords and card numbers.

fragments.label: Threats from networks and the internet
fragments.text: Users often introduce malware accidentally by opening email attachments, downloading files, visiting infected websites or attaching portable storage devices.

fragments.label: Threats from networks and the internet
fragments.text: Systems have their own weaknesses, such as operating system flaws found after release and buffer overflow, where a program writes beyond the end of a memory buffer and overwrites other data or code.

fragments.label: Threats from networks and the internet
fragments.text:
A bank customer receives an email with the bank's logo asking them to 'confirm their account' using a link → phishing: the user is tricked by a message into acting.
A customer types the bank's correct web address but lands on a copy of the site that records their login → pharming: the redirection happens without any message, because settings or DNS have been tampered with.
Restricting the risks posed by threats

fragments.label: Restricting the risks posed by threats
fragments.text: Each threat has matching preventative measures, and good answers pair them. Against hackers: strong passwords, two-factor authentication, firewalls and keeping software patched. Against malware: up-to-date anti-virus and anti-spyware, a firewall, and restricting which files users can download or run. Against phishing: spam filters, training users to recognise suspicious messages, and never following links in unexpected emails. Against pharming: anti-malware that detects altered settings, and checking that the URL is correct and the site uses HTTPS with a valid certificate. Against natural disasters and system failure: backups stored off site and a disaster recovery plan.

fragments.label: Restricting the risks posed by threats
fragments.text: Organisations can ban or restrict portable storage devices to reduce the risk of malware being brought in.

fragments.label: Restricting the risks posed by threats
fragments.text: Software updates (patches) close security holes that attackers exploit.

fragments.label: Restricting the risks posed by threats
fragments.text: Good user practice: log off or lock the computer when unattended, do not share or write down passwords, and do not let others watch you log in.
Security measures for computer systems

fragments.label: Security measures for computer systems
fragments.text: Every user should have a user account, which controls what they can do and allows their activity to be logged. Access is protected by authentication. Passwords should be long and use a mix of character types, and are stored in encrypted (hashed) form so that stealing the password file does not reveal them. Biometric methods (fingerprint, face, iris or voice recognition) use a unique physical characteristic that cannot be forgotten or easily copied. Security tokens and one-time codes sent to a phone add a second factor, so a stolen password alone is not enough. A digital signature authenticates the sender of a message and shows it has not been altered. A firewall sits between a network and the internet, checking traffic against rules such as permitted IP addresses and ports and blocking anything not allowed; hardware firewalls protect the whole network while software firewalls protect individual devices. Anti-virus software scans files, attachments and downloads, comparing them with a database of known malware signatures and removing or quarantining threats, so it must be updated regularly; anti-spyware detects and removes spyware in the same way. An intrusion detection system analyses records of system use to spot activity that does not match normal patterns.

fragments.label: Security measures for computer systems
fragments.text: Two-factor authentication combines two different types: something you know (password), something you have (token or phone), something you are (biometric).

fragments.label: Security measures for computer systems
fragments.text: Longer passwords with more character types increase the number of combinations an attacker must try.

fragments.label: Security measures for computer systems
fragments.text: Disaster recovery planning keeps an organisation running after a major failure, for example by having a remote 'hot site' ready to take over.

fragments.label: Security measures for computer systems
fragments.text:
There are 95 printable ASCII characters.
8-character passwords: 95^8 ≈ 6.6 × 10^15 combinations
12-character passwords: 95^12 ≈ 5.4 × 10^23 combinations
Each extra character multiplies the number of possibilities by 95, making a brute-force attack far slower.
Security measures for data

fragments.label: Security measures for data
fragments.text: Data can be lost through corrupted or damaged disks, system crashes, accidental deletion or overwriting, as well as through attacks. A backup is a copy of the data made so it can be restored. A typical procedure makes a full backup regularly (such as weekly), keeps at least two generations of full backups, and makes incremental backups of changed data daily, with copies stored off site in a fireproof and flood-proof location. Disk mirroring writes all data to two disks simultaneously, so if one fails the other takes over immediately with no data lost; the second disk can be at a remote site. Access rights (authorisation) give different users different permissions for each file, such as no access, read-only, or read and write, so staff see only the data their role requires. Encryption means that even if data are stolen or intercepted, they cannot be understood without the key.

fragments.label: Security measures for data
fragments.text: Backup protects against loss but the data restored are only as recent as the last backup; mirroring gives an up-to-the-moment copy.

fragments.label: Security measures for data
fragments.text: Mirroring does not protect against accidental deletion or malware, because the change is copied to both disks, so backups are still needed.

fragments.label: Security measures for data
fragments.text: Encryption does not stop data being stolen or deleted; it stops it being read.

fragments.label: Security measures for data
fragments.text: Symmetric encryption uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt; asymmetric encryption uses a public key and a private key (covered fully in topic 17.1).

fragments.label: Security measures for data
fragments.text:
Doctors: read and write access to their patients' medical records.
Receptionists: read access to appointment details only; no access to medical notes.
IT technicians: access to system settings but no access to patient records.
Each group gets only the access its job requires, protecting patients' privacy.
What is the difference between data security and data privacy?

fragments.label: What is the difference between data security and data privacy?
fragments.text: Security protects data against loss or corruption; privacy protects data against access by unauthorised people.
How does a worm differ from a virus?

fragments.label: How does a worm differ from a virus?
fragments.text: A worm runs independently and spreads itself across a network; a virus attaches to other executable code to replicate.
What is pharming?

fragments.label: What is pharming?
fragments.text: Redirecting a user to a fake website, for example by altering DNS or browser settings, so they enter confidential details there.
Give two ways of reducing the risk of phishing.

fragments.label: Give two ways of reducing the risk of phishing.
fragments.text: Any two of: spam filters, training users to recognise fake messages, not clicking links in unexpected emails, checking the sender's address.
How does a firewall protect a network?

fragments.label: How does a firewall protect a network?
fragments.text: It checks incoming and outgoing traffic against rules and blocks traffic that is not permitted.
What is disk mirroring?

fragments.label: What is disk mirroring?
fragments.text: Writing data to two disks at the same time, so an identical copy is always available if one disk fails.
What is the difference between authentication and authorisation?

fragments.label: What is the difference between authentication and authorisation?
fragments.text: Authentication confirms a user's identity; authorisation sets which resources that user may access and what they can do with them.
Why must anti-virus software be updated regularly?

fragments.label: Why must anti-virus software be updated regularly?
fragments.text: It detects malware by comparing files with a database of known signatures, so new malware is missed unless the database is updated.

Data integrity means data are accurate and up to date, and it is most at risk when data are entered or transmitted. Paper 1 asks you to explain how validation and verification protect integrity, describe and apply the validation checks (range, format, length, presence, existence, limit, check digit), and describe and carry out verification during data entry (visual check, double entry) and data transfer (parity checks, parity block checks and checksums). A classic trap is claiming that validation proves data are correct.

fragments.label: Data integrity
fragments.text: The requirement for data to be accurate, complete and up to date.

fragments.label: Validation
fragments.text: An automatic check by the computer that data entered are reasonable and meet set rules; it does not prove the data are correct.

fragments.label: Verification
fragments.text: Checking that data have been entered or transferred exactly as intended, i.e. the copy matches the original.

fragments.label: Check digit
fragments.text: An extra digit calculated from the other digits of a code and added to it, so that errors in entering or reading the code can be detected.

fragments.label: Parity bit
fragments.text: An extra bit added to a byte so that the total number of 1s is even (even parity) or odd (odd parity), as agreed by sender and receiver.

fragments.label: Parity block check
fragments.text: Parity applied to each byte and to each bit position (column) across a block of bytes, so a single-bit error can be located and corrected.

fragments.label: Checksum
fragments.text: A value calculated from a block of transmitted data (e.g. the sum of its bytes) and sent with it; the receiver recalculates it to detect errors.
How validation and verification protect integrity

fragments.label: How validation and verification protect integrity
fragments.text: Errors most often enter a system when data are typed in or when they are sent from one device to another. Validation checks that input data are sensible and follow the rules set for that field, rejecting data that are the wrong type, in the wrong format or out of range. Verification checks that the data entered or received are the same as the original data. Used together, they greatly reduce errors, but neither can guarantee the data are true: a valid date of birth can still be the wrong person's date of birth, and a correctly verified copy of a wrong value is still wrong.

fragments.label: How validation and verification protect integrity
fragments.text: Validation = is it reasonable? (performed by the computer against rules).

fragments.label: How validation and verification protect integrity
fragments.text: Verification = is it the same as the original? (checked on entry or on transfer).

fragments.label: How validation and verification protect integrity
fragments.text: Several validation checks can be applied to one field, e.g. a password may have presence, length and format checks.
Validation checks

fragments.label: Validation checks
fragments.text: A range check ensures a value lies between a lower and an upper bound, such as a percentage between 0 and 100. A limit check tests only one boundary, such as an age of no more than 120. A format check ensures data follow a set pattern, such as a date in DD/MM/YYYY form or a student ID of two letters followed by four digits. A length check ensures the number of characters is exactly, at least or at most a given number, such as a password of at least 8 characters. A presence check ensures a required field has not been left blank. An existence check ensures the value entered refers to something that actually exists, such as a customer ID in the customer file or a file name on disk. A type check ensures the data are of the expected data type, such as a whole number for a quantity.

fragments.label: Validation checks
fragments.text: Range vs limit: range has two boundaries, limit has one.

fragments.label: Validation checks
fragments.text: Format checks the pattern of characters; length checks only how many there are.

fragments.label: Validation checks
fragments.text: Validation is carried out by software as the data are entered, before they are stored or processed.

fragments.label: Validation checks
fragments.text:
Number of guests (1 to 8) → range check and type check (integer)
Email address → presence check and format check (contains @ and a domain)
Membership number → existence check (must be in the members file) and length check (exactly 6 characters)
Arrival date → format check (DD/MM/YYYY)
Check digits

fragments.label: Check digits
fragments.text: A check digit is calculated from the other digits of an identification number, such as an ISBN or a product barcode, and added to the end. When the number is entered or scanned, the same calculation is repeated; if the result does not match the check digit, an error is reported. One common method is modulo 11: multiply each digit by a weight, add the products, divide by 11 and use the remainder to produce the check digit (a remainder that would give 10 is written as X). Check digits detect most single-digit errors and transpositions, where two digits are swapped.

fragments.label: Check digits
fragments.text: A check digit is a validation check on the number itself; it is part of the stored code.

fragments.label: Check digits
fragments.text: It detects incorrect digits, transposed digits, and extra or missing digits.

fragments.label: Check digits
fragments.text: Do not confuse a check digit (part of a stored code) with a checksum (sent with a block of transmitted data).

fragments.label: Check digits
fragments.text:
Code: 3 7 2 6, weights 5 4 3 2
Sum = 3×5 + 7×4 + 2×3 + 6×2 = 15 + 28 + 6 + 12 = 61
61 ÷ 11 = 5 remainder 6
Check digit = 11 − 6 = 5 → full code 37265

Checking on entry (weights 5 4 3 2 1): 61 + 5×1 = 66, and 66 ÷ 11 has remainder 0 → valid
If 73265 is typed by mistake: 35 + 12 + 6 + 12 + 5 = 70, remainder 4 → error detected
Verification during data entry

fragments.label: Verification during data entry
fragments.text: In a visual check, the user reads through the data on screen and compares it with the original source document before confirming it. In double entry, the data are entered twice, often by different people or, for a new password, twice by the same person; the computer compares the two versions and only accepts the data if they match. Both reduce copying mistakes, but neither guarantees correctness: a visual check depends on the person noticing the error, and in double entry the same mistake could be made twice.

fragments.label: Verification during data entry
fragments.text: Visual check: cheap and quick, but unreliable for long or repetitive data.

fragments.label: Verification during data entry
fragments.text: Double entry: catches most typing errors, but takes twice as long to enter the data.

fragments.label: Verification during data entry
fragments.text: Neither method checks whether the source document itself is correct.
Parity checks during data transfer

fragments.label: Parity checks during data transfer
fragments.text: During transmission a bit can be flipped from 0 to 1 or 1 to 0 by interference. Before sending, the sender and receiver agree on even or odd parity. The sender counts the 1s in the seven data bits of each byte and sets the eighth (parity) bit so that the total number of 1s is even (or odd). The receiver counts the 1s in each byte it receives; if the count does not match the agreed parity, an error has occurred and the byte is re-sent. A single parity bit detects any error in an odd number of bits, but it cannot detect two bits being flipped in the same byte, and it cannot show which bit is wrong.

fragments.label: Parity checks during data transfer
fragments.text: Parity only detects errors; it does not correct them, so retransmission is requested.

fragments.label: Parity checks during data transfer
fragments.text: An even number of flipped bits in one byte keeps the parity correct, so the error goes undetected.

fragments.label: Parity checks during data transfer
fragments.text: The parity bit is usually the most significant bit of the byte.

fragments.label: Parity checks during data transfer
fragments.text:
Data bits: 1001101 → four 1s
Even parity: parity bit 0 → 0 1001101
Odd parity: parity bit 1 → 1 1001101
Even parity byte received as 0 1011101: five 1s, which is odd → an error is detected and the byte is re-sent
Parity block checks

fragments.label: Parity block checks
fragments.text: A parity block check extends parity to a block of bytes. Each byte gets its own parity bit (row parity) and, after the block, an extra parity byte is sent in which each bit is the parity of that bit position across all the bytes (column parity). If one bit is flipped, one row and one column will both fail their parity check, and the wrong bit is at the point where they cross. The receiver can therefore correct the error by flipping that bit, without needing a retransmission.

fragments.label: Parity block checks
fragments.text: Row parity finds which byte is wrong; column parity finds which bit position is wrong.

fragments.label: Parity block checks
fragments.text: It can locate and correct a single-bit error in the block.

fragments.label: Parity block checks
fragments.text: Some combinations of several errors can still cancel out and go undetected.

fragments.label: Parity block checks
fragments.text:
Bit positions:  P 6 5 4 3 2 1 0
Byte 1:         0 1 0 1 1 0 0 1
Byte 2:         1 0 1 1 0 1 1 1
Byte 3:         1 1 1 1 0 0 1 0   ← five 1s: row parity fails
Byte 4:         1 0 0 0 1 0 1 1
Parity byte:    1 0 0 0 0 1 1 1
Column 4 contains 1, 1, 1, 0 with parity-byte bit 0 → three 1s: column parity fails
The error is in byte 3, bit 4. It was sent as 0 (byte 3 was 1 1100010), so flipping it back corrects the data.
Checksums

fragments.label: Checksums
fragments.text: With a checksum, the sender treats each byte in a block of data as a binary number and adds them all together; the result (or a value derived from it, for example the remainder after division) is sent with the block. The receiver performs the same calculation on the data it receives and compares its result with the transmitted checksum. If they differ, an error has occurred and the block is sent again. Like a single parity bit, a checksum detects errors but does not show where they are.

fragments.label: Checksums
fragments.text: A checksum checks a whole block, so it can detect errors that single-byte parity misses, such as two flipped bits in one byte.

fragments.label: Checksums
fragments.text: If the total is too large for the checksum's size, the overflow is discarded or the remainder after division is used.

fragments.label: Checksums
fragments.text: Checksums are used in network packets and file downloads.

fragments.label: Checksums
fragments.text:
Bytes: 01000001 (65), 00110010 (50), 01111000 (120)
Checksum = 65 + 50 + 120 = 235 → sent with the block
Received bytes add to 65 + 50 + 122 = 237
237 ≠ 235 → error detected, block re-sent
What is the difference between validation and verification?

fragments.label: What is the difference between validation and verification?
fragments.text: Validation checks data are reasonable and follow rules; verification checks data match the original after entry or transfer.
What is an existence check?

fragments.label: What is an existence check?
fragments.text: A check that the value entered refers to something that exists, such as a customer ID in the customer file.
Give two errors a check digit can detect.

fragments.label: Give two errors a check digit can detect.
fragments.text: Any two of: an incorrect digit, two digits transposed, a missing or extra digit.
Name two methods of verification during data entry.

fragments.label: Name two methods of verification during data entry.
fragments.text: Visual check and double entry.
Set the even parity bit for 0110100.

fragments.label: Set the even parity bit for 0110100.
fragments.text: The data contain three 1s, so the parity bit is 1: 1 0110100.
What is a limitation of a single parity bit?

fragments.label: What is a limitation of a single parity bit?
fragments.text: It cannot detect an even number of flipped bits in a byte and cannot identify which bit is wrong.
How does a parity block check locate an error?

fragments.label: How does a parity block check locate an error?
fragments.text: The error is at the intersection of the byte (row) and bit position (column) whose parity checks fail.
How does a checksum detect an error?

fragments.label: How does a checksum detect an error?
fragments.text: The receiver recalculates the sum of the received block and compares it with the checksum sent; a difference means an error.

This topic asks you to think like a computing professional. Paper 1 tests why professionals need ethics and codes of conduct (BCS, ACM/IEEE), the impact of acting ethically or unethically in a given scenario, why copyright legislation is needed, the differences between commercial software, shareware, freeware, open source and free software licences (and which suits a situation), and the applications and social, economic and environmental impact of artificial intelligence. Marks come from applying a principle to the scenario in the question, not from general statements.

fragments.label: Ethics
fragments.text: The moral principles that guide a person, and the rules of conduct recognised in a particular profession.

fragments.label: Code of conduct
fragments.text: A set of principles published by a professional body describing how its members are expected to behave.

fragments.label: Copyright
fragments.text: Formal legal recognition of the ownership of a created and published original work, giving the owner control over how it is copied and used.

fragments.label: Software licence
fragments.text: An agreement that gives the buyer permission to use software under stated conditions; the vendor keeps ownership.

fragments.label: Shareware
fragments.text: Commercial software provided free of charge for a limited trial period, without the source code.

fragments.label: Freeware
fragments.text: Software provided free of charge with no time limit, but without the source code.

fragments.label: Open source software
fragments.text: Software provided with its source code, which users may use, modify, copy and distribute according to the licence (Open Source Initiative).

fragments.label: Free software
fragments.text: Open source software (Free Software Foundation) that users are free to use as they wish, under a copyleft licence.

fragments.label: Copyleft
fragments.text: A licence condition that if the software is modified, the modified source code must be made available to others under the same conditions.

fragments.label: Artificial intelligence (AI)
fragments.text: The use of a computer or computer-controlled device to perform tasks normally associated with intelligent human behaviour.
What ethics means for computing

fragments.label: What ethics means for computing
fragments.text: Ethics can mean the moral principles that guide a person, or the rules of conduct recognised in a profession. Professional rules of conduct must reflect moral principles of right and wrong, which can be viewed from philosophical, religious, legal or pragmatic (common-sense) points of view. Computing professionals need ethics because the systems they build affect employers, clients and the public: software controls money, personal data, safety-critical equipment and communication for millions of people, so a careless or dishonest decision can cause serious harm.

fragments.label: What ethics means for computing
fragments.text: Laws set the minimum standard; ethical codes go further, covering honesty, competence and responsibility to others.

fragments.label: What ethics means for computing
fragments.text: Religious and cultural beliefs of colleagues and users must also be respected in the workplace.
Professional bodies and codes of conduct

fragments.label: Professional bodies and codes of conduct
fragments.text: Any professional is expected to act ethically, and joining a professional organisation provides guidance through its code of conduct. The British Computer Society (BCS) code is organised under four headings: public interest; professional competence and integrity; duty to relevant authority; and duty to the profession. The IEEE-CS/ACM Software Engineering Code of Ethics sets out eight principles: Public (act consistently with the public interest), Client and employer (act in their best interests, consistent with the public interest), Product (meet the highest professional standards), Judgement (keep integrity and independence), Management (managers should promote an ethical approach), Profession (advance its integrity and reputation), Colleagues (be fair to and supportive of them) and Self (keep learning throughout one's career). The codes differ in detail but agree that the public interest is the key concern, that they state principles rather than detailed rules, that professionals must use their own judgement, and that they should seek advice when unsure.

fragments.label: Professional bodies and codes of conduct
fragments.text: Benefits of joining a professional body: guidance on ethical behaviour, recognition of competence, professional development and support if challenged.

fragments.label: Professional bodies and codes of conduct
fragments.text: Do not accept work you are not competent to do, and do not claim a level of competence you lack.

fragments.label: Professional bodies and codes of conduct
fragments.text: Documentation is stressed repeatedly in the codes because it records decisions, lets others maintain the software and shows the work met the specification.

fragments.label: Professional bodies and codes of conduct
fragments.text:
Scenario: your manager halves the testing time on a client's payroll system to meet a deadline.
Product: an under-tested system may contain errors, so it will not meet professional standards.
Client and employer: the client could be harmed by wrong payments, and your employer's reputation could suffer.
Management: cutting testing is poor, unethical management.
Colleagues: the team is put under unrealistic pressure.
Judgement: you should raise your concern with the manager and, if ignored, seek advice. Keeping quiet and planning to 'fix it later in maintenance' would be unethical.

fragments.label: Professional bodies and codes of conduct
fragments.text:
Any two of:
So team members feel valued. (1)
To get the best work from the team. (1)
So the team works well together. (1)
So the team produces the best product for the client. (1)
Acting for the public good

fragments.label: Acting for the public good
fragments.text: Codes of conduct refer to the health, safety and welfare of the public and to the public interest; the BCS asks members to have due regard for public health, privacy, security, wellbeing of others and the environment. Poor engineering has wasted huge sums of public money. The Ariane 5 rocket exploded in 1996 because code converting a 64-bit floating-point number to a 16-bit integer overflowed. NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter failed because one team used imperial units while the rest used SI units. The UK's National Programme for IT in the NHS was scrapped after costing about £12 billion without producing a workable system. Applying the codes' requirements on specification, testing and project management could have prevented such losses. Other public concerns involve the purpose or effect of systems: systems not secure against unauthorised access, organisations hiding security breaches, private communications stored for security services, social media carrying abusive or illegal content, and powerful companies pressuring others to use their products.

fragments.label: Acting for the public good
fragments.text: Acting ethically: protects users and the public, produces reliable software, maintains trust in the employer and the profession.

fragments.label: Acting for the public good
fragments.text: Acting unethically: can cause financial loss, harm to users, legal action, loss of reputation and loss of the professional's job or membership.

fragments.label: Acting for the public good
fragments.text: Public attitudes to some issues vary, which makes individual judgement difficult, and whistle-blowers can suffer serious personal consequences.
Ownership and copyright

fragments.label: Ownership and copyright
fragments.text: Copyright is formal recognition of ownership of an original, published work. The creator owns it, unless they created it while working for an organisation, in which case the organisation can claim copyright. Copyright cannot protect an idea, only its expression, and cannot be claimed for material previously published by someone else. It applies to written works, music, films, recordings, broadcasts, art and computer programs. Copyright legislation is needed for two reasons: creating the work took time, effort and originality, so the owner should be able to earn from it; and it is unfair for others to copy the work and profit from it without paying the creator. Laws differ between countries, but international agreements mean the protection cannot be avoided by publishing in another country. In the UK the relevant law is the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act, under which copyright applies automatically when the work is created.

fragments.label: Ownership and copyright
fragments.text: Copyright laws typically define how long copyright lasts, what happens when the owner dies, how copyright is indicated (e.g. the © symbol) and may record the date of creation.

fragments.label: Ownership and copyright
fragments.text: The owner can state how the work may be used, for example 'may be published unchanged as long as it carries this copyright notice'.

fragments.label: Ownership and copyright
fragments.text: A buyer of a copyrighted product may normally make copies only for their own use.

fragments.label: Ownership and copyright
fragments.text: Distributing a copyrighted work, for example posting it online, without the owner's permission breaks the law.
Software licensing

fragments.label: Software licensing
fragments.text: When you buy software you do not own it: the vendor keeps ownership and you pay for a licence to use it under stated conditions, and the source code is not provided. Commercial software is sold for profit, with options such as a fee per copy, a site licence allowing a set number of copies to run at once, or special rates for education. A vendor may also give away licences: shareware is commercial software offered free for a limited trial period (possibly a limited version, or a beta test version), and freeware is free with no time limit (often a limited or older version); neither includes the source code. The Open Source Initiative makes open source software available, normally free of charge, with the source code, so users may use, modify, copy and distribute it under the licence terms; its philosophy is collaborative development. The Free Software Foundation believes users should be free to use software however they wish. Its software is also open source and may carry a small fee to cover distribution; its licence includes copyleft, so any modified version must be released with its source code under the same conditions.

fragments.label: Software licensing
fragments.text: Commercial software is justified when it provides exactly the functionality needed immediately, works with software already installed, or comes with continuous maintenance and support.

fragments.label: Software licensing
fragments.text: Shareware lets users try before buying and suggest improvements; freeware may be enough for limited needs.

fragments.label: Software licensing
fragments.text: Open source or free software is justified when full functionality is available at little or no cost, when a few changes to the source code would make it suitable, when developers are collaborating on a new product, or when the user wants to control the software's future development.

fragments.label: Software licensing
fragments.text: Only open source and free software provide the source code.

fragments.label: Software licensing
fragments.text:
User can edit the source code → Free Software Foundation, Open Source Initiative
Source code is provided → Free Software Foundation, Open Source Initiative
Free only for a trial period → shareware
User must pay to keep using it and cannot see the source → commercial
Modified versions must be shared under the same terms → Free Software Foundation (copyleft)
Artificial intelligence

fragments.label: Artificial intelligence
fragments.text: AI is the use of a computer or computer-controlled device to perform tasks normally associated with intelligent human behaviour. Applications can be grouped by the human behaviour they imitate. Problem solving: game-playing programs such as chess, and expert systems for medical diagnosis, which hold more knowledge than one doctor but cannot handle situations outside their rules creatively. Linguistics: voice recognition and speech synthesis, such as automated telephone help lines. Perception: autonomous robots and driverless cars that use sensors to decide what to do, rather than repeating fixed tasks regardless of what happens. Reasoning: drawing conclusions from evidence, for example proving mathematical theorems or checking that software meets its specification. Learning: machine learning, where a system improves its performance with experience by applying statistical algorithms to very large data sets, for example recommending products or filtering spam.

fragments.label: Artificial intelligence
fragments.text: Social impact: more leisure and less dangerous or repetitive work, but job losses in some areas, new skills needed, safety worries about driverless vehicles, uncertain consequences if expert systems replace doctors and nurses, and huge amounts of personal data collected by global organisations.

fragments.label: Artificial intelligence
fragments.text: Economic impact: new jobs manufacturing, installing and servicing AI systems and greater productivity, but fewer jobs where machines do the work, and a risk that the rich get richer and the poor get poorer.

fragments.label: Artificial intelligence
fragments.text: Environmental impact: robots can work in environments dangerous to humans and AI can optimise energy use, but manufacturing robots uses limited raw materials and disposing of them adds to electronic waste.

fragments.label: Artificial intelligence
fragments.text: If the data collected are not stored securely they could be used for criminal activity.

fragments.label: Artificial intelligence
fragments.text:
Any three of:
The rules, past games and decision-making algorithms are stored. (1)
The program is trained by playing many games. (1)
It looks ahead at possible moves and chooses the one most likely to succeed. (1)
It stores whether each choice led to a good or bad result. (1)
It changes future choices, learning from its mistakes. (1)
Why should a computing professional join a professional body?

fragments.label: Why should a computing professional join a professional body?
fragments.text: It provides a code of conduct and guidance on ethical behaviour, recognition of competence, and support and professional development.
Name four of the eight principles in the IEEE-CS/ACM code.

fragments.label: Name four of the eight principles in the IEEE-CS/ACM code.
fragments.text: Any four of: Public, Client and employer, Product, Judgement, Management, Profession, Colleagues, Self.
What is the key concern shared by all professional codes of conduct?

fragments.label: What is the key concern shared by all professional codes of conduct?
fragments.text: The public interest (public good).
Give two reasons copyright legislation is needed.

fragments.label: Give two reasons copyright legislation is needed.
fragments.text: The creator should be able to earn from the time and effort spent creating the work, and it is unfair for others to copy and profit from it without paying.
What is copyleft?

fragments.label: What is copyleft?
fragments.text: A licence condition that modified versions of the software must be released with their source code under the same conditions.
What is the difference between shareware and freeware?

fragments.label: What is the difference between shareware and freeware?
fragments.text: Shareware is free only for a limited trial period; freeware is free with no time limit. Neither includes the source code.
Give three areas of AI application.

fragments.label: Give three areas of AI application.
fragments.text: Any three of: problem solving (games, expert systems), linguistics (voice recognition), perception (robots, driverless cars), reasoning (theorem proving), learning (machine learning).
What is machine learning?

fragments.label: What is machine learning?
fragments.text: A system improving its performance at a task as it gains experience, by applying statistical algorithms to large data sets.

This topic covers why organisations moved from separate data files to relational databases, the vocabulary of the relational model (tuple, attribute, primary, candidate, secondary and foreign keys, referential integrity, indexing), how E-R diagrams document one-to-one, one-to-many and many-to-many relationships, and normalisation to Third Normal Form. Paper 1 regularly gives a scenario, a set of data or a set of tables and asks you to draw the E-R diagram, say whether the tables are in 3NF and justify it, or produce a normalised design with every primary and foreign key identified. Marks come from precise terms applied to the given data, not from general statements.

fragments.label: Tuple
fragments.text: The formal name for one row of a relation (table): the set of attribute values stored for a single instance of the entity. Commonly called a record.

fragments.label: Attribute
fragments.text: A named column of a relation holding one property of the entity, such as MemberName. Commonly called a field. Each attribute value in a tuple must be atomic (a single value or no value).

fragments.label: Primary key
fragments.text: The attribute, or combination of attributes, chosen to identify each tuple in a table uniquely; every tuple must have a value for it and no two tuples may share that value.

fragments.label: Candidate key
fragments.text: Any attribute, or minimal combination of attributes, that is guaranteed to be unique for every tuple and so could be chosen as the primary key.

fragments.label: Secondary key
fragments.text: A candidate key that was not chosen as the primary key. It is still unique and is often indexed so that tuples can also be searched for quickly by it.

fragments.label: Foreign key
fragments.text: An attribute in one table that refers to the primary key of another table, so that the two tables are linked in a relationship.

fragments.label: Referential integrity
fragments.text: The rule, enforced through a foreign key, that a value can only be stored in the foreign key if the same value already exists as a primary key in the table it refers to.

fragments.label: Index
fragments.text: A small secondary structure holding the values of one key attribute in order, each with a pointer to the matching tuple in the main table, so searches on that attribute are much faster than scanning every tuple.

fragments.label: Data redundancy
fragments.text: The same data being stored more than once, either within one file or across several files, which wastes storage and creates the risk of inconsistent copies.

fragments.label: Third Normal Form (3NF)
fragments.text: A table design in 2NF in which no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute: every non-key attribute depends on the key, the whole key and nothing but the key.
Limitations of a file-based approach

fragments.label: Limitations of a file-based approach
fragments.text: In a file-based approach each department or program keeps its own data files, usually text files whose layout is defined by the program that uses them. Imagine a sports centre that keeps one file of member details for the front desk, another for the finance office and another for the coaches. The problems fall into three groups. First, integrity within a file: nothing checks data as it is typed, so a member can be entered twice with slightly different spellings, a required item can be left blank, or a class code can be entered for a class that does not exist. Second, redundancy across files: the member's name and phone number are stored in every department's file, so when the member changes their number only some copies may be updated and the files then contradict each other (data inconsistency). Third, data dependency: each program is written around the exact layout of its file (for example, that the fourth item on each line is the phone number), so adding a new item of data means rewriting the file and every program that reads it, and the files are poorly suited to any new application, such as analysing attendance over several years. A single shared file does not help either, because a file cannot restrict access to part of its contents, so staff who need contact details could also read bank details (a data privacy problem).

fragments.label: Limitations of a file-based approach
fragments.text: Data redundancy: the same data held in several files, wasting storage and making every change a multi-file job.

fragments.label: Limitations of a file-based approach
fragments.text: Data inconsistency: when only some of the redundant copies are updated, different files give different values for the same fact.

fragments.label: Limitations of a file-based approach
fragments.text: Poor data integrity: no built-in validation or checks when data is entered, so errors, duplicates and references to things that do not exist go undetected.

fragments.label: Limitations of a file-based approach
fragments.text: Data dependency (program-data dependence): programs rely on the file's physical layout, so any change to the data structure forces the programs to be rewritten.

fragments.label: Limitations of a file-based approach
fragments.text: Poor privacy and security: access cannot be controlled for part of a file, so anyone who can open the file can read all of it.

fragments.label: Limitations of a file-based approach
fragments.text: Difficult to share and to use for new purposes: each file suits the program it was built for, so extracting combined data for a new task is slow and complex.
Features of a relational database that address these limitations

fragments.label: Features of a relational database that address these limitations
fragments.text: A relational database stores data in a collection of related tables (relations), each holding data about one entity, and all access goes through a database management system (DBMS). Each limitation of the file-based approach has a matching feature. Data about one thing is stored once, in the table for that entity, and other tables refer to it through a key rather than copying it, which removes redundancy and with it the chance of inconsistent copies. Every table has a primary key, and the DBMS refuses a new tuple whose key value already exists, so duplicates cannot be created. Foreign keys give referential integrity: a value cannot be entered that refers to something missing from the linked table. Data types and validation rules defined for each attribute are checked whenever data is entered. Because programs send queries to the DBMS rather than reading files directly, new attributes or tables can be added without rewriting existing programs (data independence), and any combination of tables can be queried for a new purpose. Finally, access rights can be set per user or group and per table, so different staff see only the data they need.

fragments.label: Features of a relational database that address these limitations
fragments.text: Redundancy and inconsistency are removed because each fact is stored in one place and linked by keys.

fragments.label: Features of a relational database that address these limitations
fragments.text: Primary keys guarantee each tuple is unique; foreign keys enforce referential integrity between tables.

fragments.label: Features of a relational database that address these limitations
fragments.text: Validation (data types, ranges, required fields) is applied centrally, whatever program enters the data.

fragments.label: Features of a relational database that address these limitations
fragments.text: Programs are independent of the physical storage, so the structure can be extended without breaking them.

fragments.label: Features of a relational database that address these limitations
fragments.text: Queries can join any related tables, making new uses of the data straightforward.

fragments.label: Features of a relational database that address these limitations
fragments.text: Access rights can be granted to individual users or groups for individual tables, solving the privacy problem of a single shared file.

fragments.label: Features of a relational database that address these limitations
fragments.text:
File-based data (one line per class booking):
BookingNo | MemberName | MemberPhone | ClassName
1 | O. Haddad | 555-0104 | Yoga
2 | O. Haddad | 555-0104 | Spin
3 | O. Haddad | 555-0104 | Pilates

Problem: O. Haddad's phone number is stored three times. If it changes and only line 1 is edited, lines 2 and 3 are now inconsistent.

Relational design:
Member(MemberID, MemberName, MemberPhone)       primary key MemberID
Booking(BookingNo, ClassName, MemberID)         primary key BookingNo, foreign key MemberID

Member:
MemberID | MemberName | MemberPhone
M104 | O. Haddad | 555-0104

Booking:
BookingNo | ClassName | MemberID
1 | Yoga | M104
2 | Spin | M104
3 | Pilates | M104

The phone number is now stored once, so one edit updates it for every booking. Referential integrity also stops a booking being entered for a MemberID that is not in the Member table.
Relational terminology: entity, table, tuple and attribute

fragments.label: Relational terminology: entity, table, tuple and attribute
fragments.text: An entity is a type of thing (a person, object, event or transaction) about which data is stored and of which there are many instances, such as Member or Class. In a relational database each entity becomes a table, which the formal model calls a relation. A table's columns are its attributes (informally, fields) and each row is a tuple (informally, a record) holding the data for one instance of the entity, such as one particular member. A table design is written as the table name followed by its attributes in brackets, with the primary key underlined (or labelled PK in typed answers), for example Member(MemberID, MemberName, MemberPhone). Two principles of the model matter in exam answers: each attribute value in a tuple is atomic, meaning it holds one value or none (never a list), and neither the rows nor the columns have a defined order, which is why data is always retrieved by a query rather than by position.

fragments.label: Relational terminology: entity, table, tuple and attribute
fragments.text: Entity = the type of thing (Member); tuple/record = one instance (the row for member M104).

fragments.label: Relational terminology: entity, table, tuple and attribute
fragments.text: Attribute = field = column; tuple = record = row. Use the formal terms when a question asks for relational terminology.

fragments.label: Relational terminology: entity, table, tuple and attribute
fragments.text: Atomic values: a MemberPhone attribute holds one number; storing 'Yoga, Spin' in a single ClassName attribute breaks this rule.

fragments.label: Relational terminology: entity, table, tuple and attribute
fragments.text: Do not confuse a relation (a table) with a relationship (a link between two tables).
Primary, candidate and secondary keys

fragments.label: Primary, candidate and secondary keys
fragments.text: Every table must have a primary key: an attribute, or combination of attributes, that has a value in every tuple and whose value is never repeated. The DBMS rejects an insert that would duplicate an existing primary key value, which is how the key guarantees each tuple is unique. Sometimes a table has more than one attribute that is guaranteed unique. For a Member table, both MemberID and a unique EmailAddress might qualify; each is a candidate key. One candidate is chosen as the primary key (usually the short, stable one that never changes, here MemberID) and any candidate not chosen becomes a secondary key, which can still be used, and indexed, to find tuples. Often no natural attribute is guaranteed unique, for example names repeat, so an identifier such as MemberID is created specifically to be the primary key. When no single attribute is unique but a combination is, the primary key is a composite (compound) key, as in a ClassMember table where neither ClassID nor MemberID is unique alone but the pair is.

fragments.label: Primary, candidate and secondary keys
fragments.text: Primary key: unique and never empty; one per table (it may be composite).

fragments.label: Primary, candidate and secondary keys
fragments.text: Candidate key: any attribute or minimal attribute combination that could serve as the primary key.

fragments.label: Primary, candidate and secondary keys
fragments.text: Secondary key: a candidate key that was not chosen as the primary key (some textbooks also use the phrase for any attribute indexed for searching; the coursebook meaning is the candidate-key one).

fragments.label: Primary, candidate and secondary keys
fragments.text: Choose a primary key that is guaranteed unique for all possible data, not just the current rows: a name that happens to be unique today is still unsuitable.
Foreign keys and referential integrity

fragments.label: Foreign keys and referential integrity
fragments.text: Tables are linked by a foreign key: an attribute in one table whose values are primary key values of another table. In Class(ClassID, ClassName, Day, InstructorID) the attribute InstructorID is a foreign key referring to the primary key of Instructor(InstructorID, InstructorName). The referenced table must be created first, then the foreign key is declared in the referring table. From then on the DBMS enforces referential integrity: it will not accept an InstructorID in Class unless that value already exists in Instructor, and it will not allow an Instructor tuple to be deleted (or its key changed) while Class tuples still refer to it, unless the change is cascaded. This prevents 'orphan' tuples that point to nothing. A foreign key does not have to be unique in its own table: many classes can share the same InstructorID, which is exactly what makes a one-to-many relationship.

fragments.label: Foreign keys and referential integrity
fragments.text: The foreign key goes in the table on the 'many' side of a one-to-many relationship and refers to the primary key on the 'one' side.

fragments.label: Foreign keys and referential integrity
fragments.text: A foreign key may repeat within its table and may be part of a composite primary key (as in a link table).

fragments.label: Foreign keys and referential integrity
fragments.text: Referential integrity means every foreign key value matches an existing primary key value in the referenced table.

fragments.label: Foreign keys and referential integrity
fragments.text: The foreign key and the primary key it references must have the same data type (and normally the same meaning), even if the names differ.
Indexing

fragments.label: Indexing
fragments.text: Finding a tuple by scanning every row of a large table is slow. An index is a separate, much smaller structure associated with one attribute of a table, normally the primary key or a secondary key. It holds that attribute's values in order, each with a pointer to the position of the matching tuple in the main table. To find a tuple, the DBMS searches the ordered index (which can use a fast method such as a binary search or a tree) and follows the pointer straight to the tuple. The DBMS normally indexes the primary key automatically, and further indexes can be created on attributes that are searched or joined on frequently. The cost is extra storage, and slightly slower inserts, updates and deletes, because each index must be updated whenever the indexed data changes.

fragments.label: Indexing
fragments.text: Purpose: faster searching and sorting on the indexed attribute, especially for tables with many tuples.

fragments.label: Indexing
fragments.text: An index contains only the key values and pointers, not the rest of each tuple.

fragments.label: Indexing
fragments.text: Worth adding to attributes that are searched or used in joins often; not worth it for small tables or rarely searched attributes.

fragments.label: Indexing
fragments.text: Trade-off: faster retrieval versus extra storage and extra work on every change to the data.

fragments.label: Indexing
fragments.text:
Member table (stored in the order members joined):
Row | MemberID | MemberName | EmailAddress
1 | M120 | T. Reyes | treyes@mail.test
2 | M104 | O. Haddad | ohaddad@mail.test
3 | M117 | L. Ortiz | lortiz@mail.test

Index on EmailAddress (sorted, with pointers):
EmailAddress | Row
lortiz@mail.test | 3
ohaddad@mail.test | 2
treyes@mail.test | 1

Searching for ohaddad@mail.test: search the sorted index, find pointer 2, read row 2 directly instead of checking every row of the table.
E-R diagrams and relationship types

fragments.label: E-R diagrams and relationship types
fragments.text: An entity-relationship (E-R) diagram documents a database design before any tables are built. Each entity is drawn as a rectangle containing its name, and each relationship as a line between two entities. The ends of the line show the cardinality: a single line end means 'one', and a crow's foot (three prongs) means 'many'. There are three types of relationship. In a one-to-one (1:1) relationship each instance of A is linked to at most one instance of B and vice versa, such as Member and Locker when each member rents one locker; these are rare and can be implemented with a foreign key on either side. In a one-to-many (1:M) relationship one instance of A is linked to many of B but each B to only one A, such as one Instructor teaching many Classes; the foreign key goes in the 'many' table. In a many-to-many (M:M) relationship each A is linked to many B and each B to many A, such as Member and Class (a member attends many classes, a class has many members). To design an E-R diagram from a scenario: pick the entities (nouns with many instances), decide which pairs are directly related, then decide the cardinality by reading the relationship in both directions, one instance at a time: 'one Instructor teaches many Classes' and 'one Class is taught by one Instructor' gives 1:M. More detailed diagrams also label each relationship with a verb and show the minimum as well as the maximum cardinality (for example, a new class may have zero members so far).

fragments.label: E-R diagrams and relationship types
fragments.text: Always read a relationship both ways, starting each sentence with 'one': one Member attends many Classes; one Class has many Members, so the relationship is M:M.

fragments.label: E-R diagrams and relationship types
fragments.text: The crow's foot is drawn at the 'many' end: on a 1:M line between Instructor and Class it touches the Class box.

fragments.label: E-R diagrams and relationship types
fragments.text: The entity at the crow's-foot end of a 1:M relationship is the one that will hold the foreign key.

fragments.label: E-R diagrams and relationship types
fragments.text: An E-R diagram shows entities and relationships, not every attribute; list attributes and keys separately in a key table or table designs.

fragments.label: E-R diagrams and relationship types
fragments.text:
Scenario: Each class is taught by one instructor; an instructor can teach many classes. A member can attend many classes and a class has many members. Each member may rent one locker and each locker is rented by at most one member.

Entities: Instructor, Class, Member, Locker

Relationships (| = one, <  or > = crow's foot / many):
Instructor |------< Class          1:M  one Instructor teaches many Classes; one Class is taught by one Instructor
Class      >------< Member         M:M  one Class has many Members; one Member attends many Classes
Member     |------| Locker         1:1  one Member rents one Locker; one Locker is rented by one Member

The M:M relationship between Class and Member cannot be implemented directly and must be resolved with a link entity (next section).
Resolving a many-to-many relationship with a link table

fragments.label: Resolving a many-to-many relationship with a link table
fragments.text: A many-to-many relationship cannot be implemented directly. A foreign key attribute holds one value in each tuple, so a single ClassID attribute in Member could not record the several classes that member attends (and storing a list would break the atomic-value rule). Putting a foreign key in both tables fails as well, because each table would have to exist before the other. The solution is to add a link (associative) entity between the two, turning one M:M relationship into two 1:M relationships. For Class and Member the link entity ClassMember holds one tuple for each member in each class. Its primary key is the composite of the two foreign keys (ClassID, MemberID), since neither is unique alone but the pair is, and it is also the natural place for any data that belongs to the pairing itself, such as whether that member has paid for that class. The resulting logical E-R model can be summarised in a key table listing each table with its primary and foreign keys.

fragments.label: Resolving a many-to-many relationship with a link table
