fragments.text: Class >----< Member becomes Class |----< ClassMember >----| Member.

fragments.label: Resolving a many-to-many relationship with a link table
fragments.text: The link table holds a foreign key to each of the original tables; together they usually form its composite primary key.

fragments.label: Resolving a many-to-many relationship with a link table
fragments.text: Attributes that describe the combination (FeePaid, date enrolled, grade) belong in the link table, not in either original table.

fragments.label: Resolving a many-to-many relationship with a link table
fragments.text: Every many end in the logical model is a table that contains a foreign key.

Table | Primary key | Foreign key(s)
Instructor | InstructorID | (none)
Class | ClassID | InstructorID
Member | MemberID | (none)
ClassMember | ClassID + MemberID | ClassID, MemberID
Locker | LockerNo | MemberID

Locker holds MemberID as its foreign key for the 1:1 relationship (it could equally have been LockerNo in Member).
The normalisation process: 1NF, 2NF and 3NF

fragments.label: The normalisation process: 1NF, 2NF and 3NF
fragments.text: Normalisation is a step-by-step technique for turning a list of data items (from a form, a description or an existing table) into a set of table designs with no unnecessary redundancy. Start by listing all the attributes, marking any repeating group: a set of attributes that takes several sets of values while the other attributes have one value each. First Normal Form (1NF): a table is in 1NF when it has a primary key, all attribute values are atomic and there are no repeating groups; to get there, move the repeating group into a new table whose primary key combines the original key (now also a foreign key) with the attribute that identifies each repeat. Second Normal Form (2NF): a 1NF table is in 2NF when every non-key attribute depends on the whole primary key; a partial dependency, where a non-key attribute depends on only part of a composite key, is removed by moving that attribute to a new table keyed by that part. A table with a single-attribute primary key is automatically in 2NF once it is in 1NF. Third Normal Form (3NF): a 2NF table is in 3NF when no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute; such a non-key (transitive) dependency is removed by moving the dependent attributes to a new table whose primary key is the attribute they depend on, and leaving that attribute behind as a foreign key. Each step splits tables but never loses data: the keys let the original data be rebuilt by joining tables.

fragments.label: The normalisation process: 1NF, 2NF and 3NF
fragments.text: 1NF: remove repeating groups; every table has a primary key and atomic values.

fragments.label: The normalisation process: 1NF, 2NF and 3NF
fragments.text: 2NF: remove partial dependencies (only possible when the primary key is composite).

fragments.label: The normalisation process: 1NF, 2NF and 3NF
fragments.text: 3NF: remove non-key dependencies (a non-key attribute determined by another non-key attribute).

fragments.label: The normalisation process: 1NF, 2NF and 3NF
fragments.text: Each time an attribute group is moved out, the attribute it depends on stays behind as a foreign key so the link is kept.

Explaining whether tables are in 3NF and producing a normalised design

fragments.label: Explaining whether tables are in 3NF and producing a normalised design
fragments.text: To decide whether a given set of tables is in 3NF, test each table in turn with three questions and quote the attributes involved in your answer. Is there a repeating group or a non-atomic value? If so, it is not in 1NF. Does the table have a composite primary key with a non-key attribute that depends on only part of it? If so, it is not in 2NF. Is there a non-key attribute that depends on another non-key attribute? If so, it is not in 3NF. If a table passes all three it is in 3NF, and the set of tables is in 3NF only if every table is. To produce a normalised design from a written description, pick out the entities and their attributes, decide the relationship between each pair, resolve any many-to-many relationship with a link table, give every table a primary key and place a foreign key at the many end of each 1:M relationship; then check the result against the three questions. From a given set of data or tables, follow the 1NF to 2NF to 3NF steps and state which dependency each split removes.

fragments.label: Explaining whether tables are in 3NF and producing a normalised design
fragments.text: Name the exact dependency: 'SubjectName depends only on SubjectCode, part of the composite key' earns the mark; 'it has redundancy' does not.

fragments.label: Explaining whether tables are in 3NF and producing a normalised design
fragments.text: A table with a single-attribute primary key cannot have a partial dependency, so only non-key dependencies need checking for it.

fragments.label: Explaining whether tables are in 3NF and producing a normalised design
fragments.text: Write every final table in the form TableName(PK, attributes, FK(fk)) and clearly identify both primary and foreign keys.

fragments.label: Explaining whether tables are in 3NF and producing a normalised design
fragments.text: State any assumption the design depends on (for example, 'each class has only one instructor').

fragments.label: Explaining whether tables are in 3NF and producing a normalised design
fragments.text:
Student(StudentID, StudentName, TutorID, TutorName)               PK StudentID
Result(StudentID, SubjectCode, SubjectName, Grade)                 PK StudentID + SubjectCode

Student: single-attribute key, so no partial dependency. But TutorName depends on TutorID, a non-key attribute -> non-key dependency, so NOT in 3NF.
Result: SubjectName depends only on SubjectCode, part of the composite key -> partial dependency, so NOT in 2NF (and therefore not in 3NF). Grade depends on both StudentID and SubjectCode, which is correct.

3NF design:
Student(StudentID, StudentName, TutorID(fk))
Tutor(TutorID, TutorName)
Result(StudentID(fk), SubjectCode(fk), Grade)       PK StudentID + SubjectCode
Subject(SubjectCode, SubjectName)

Description: A vet practice records owners (name, phone) and their pets (name, species). An owner can have several pets; each pet has one owner. Each appointment is for one pet with one vet on a given date and time; a vet sees many appointments.

Entities: Owner, Pet, Vet, Appointment
Relationships: Owner 1:M Pet; Pet 1:M Appointment; Vet 1:M Appointment (no M:M to resolve)

Owner(OwnerID, OwnerName, OwnerPhone)
Pet(PetID, PetName, Species, OwnerID(fk))
Vet(VetID, VetName)
Appointment(AppointmentID, AppDate, AppTime, PetID(fk), VetID(fk))

Give three limitations of a file-based approach.

fragments.label: Give three limitations of a file-based approach.
fragments.text: Any three of: data redundancy; data inconsistency; no built-in validation so poor data integrity; data dependency (programs must be rewritten if file structure changes); no control over access to part of a file; hard to combine data for new uses.
What is the difference between a candidate key and a secondary key?

fragments.label: What is the difference between a candidate key and a secondary key?
fragments.text: A candidate key is any attribute (or minimal combination) that could be the primary key; a secondary key is a candidate key that was not chosen as the primary key.
What is referential integrity?

fragments.label: What is referential integrity?
fragments.text: The rule, enforced by a foreign key, that a value can only be entered in the foreign key if the same value exists as a primary key in the referenced table.
What does an index contain and why is it used?

fragments.label: What does an index contain and why is it used?
fragments.text: The values of one key attribute in order, each with a pointer to the matching tuple; it makes searching on that attribute much faster than scanning the whole table.
How is a many-to-many relationship implemented in a relational database?

fragments.label: How is a many-to-many relationship implemented in a relational database?
fragments.text: With a link table containing a foreign key to each of the two tables, usually combined as its composite primary key, creating two one-to-many relationships.
What must be true for a table to be in 2NF?

fragments.label: What must be true for a table to be in 2NF?
fragments.text: It is in 1NF and every non-key attribute depends on the whole primary key, so there are no partial dependencies on part of a composite key.
What does 3NF remove?

fragments.label: What does 3NF remove?
fragments.text: Non-key dependencies: a non-key attribute that depends on another non-key attribute is moved to a new table keyed by that attribute, which stays behind as a foreign key.
Is Student(StudentID, StudentName, TutorID, TutorName) in 3NF?

fragments.label: Is Student(StudentID, StudentName, TutorID, TutorName) in 3NF?
fragments.text: No. TutorName depends on TutorID, which is a non-key attribute; split into Student(StudentID, StudentName, TutorID(fk)) and Tutor(TutorID, TutorName).

A DBMS is the software through which every user and program reaches a database. This topic covers the DBMS features that fix the problems of a file-based approach (data management through a data dictionary, data modelling, the logical schema, data integrity, and data security through backup procedures and access rights for individuals and groups) and the software tools a DBMS provides in practice: the developer interface and the query processor. Paper 1 questions typically ask you to name a feature and explain the file-based problem it solves, describe what a data dictionary holds, or explain how access rights and backups protect the data in a given scenario.

fragments.label: Database management system (DBMS)
fragments.text: Software that controls all access to the data in a database: it creates and maintains the structure, stores and retrieves data on request, and enforces integrity and security rules.

fragments.label: Database administrator (DBA)
fragments.text: The person who uses the DBMS to set up and customise the database for its users, including defining views and access rights and organising backups.

fragments.label: Data dictionary
fragments.text: A part of the database, maintained by the DBMS and visible only to the DBA, holding metadata (data about the data): table and attribute names, data types, keys, relationships, validation rules, indexes, access rights and physical storage details.

fragments.label: Data modelling
fragments.text: Analysing an organisation's data to identify its entities, attributes and relationships, typically as an E-R diagram, so the structure can be defined in the DBMS.

fragments.label: Logical schema
fragments.text: The overall description of how the database is organised as seen by users and programmers (its tables, attributes, keys, relationships and constraints), independent of how the data is physically stored. Also called the conceptual schema.

fragments.label: Data integrity
fragments.text: The accuracy, completeness and consistency of the stored data, maintained by the DBMS through keys, referential integrity, validation rules and controlled updates.

fragments.label: Access rights
fragments.text: Permissions assigned by the DBA to an individual user or a group of users stating which tables or views they can reach and whether they can read, insert, update or delete data.

fragments.label: Backup
fragments.text: A copy of the database made at regular, planned intervals and stored separately from the live data, so the database can be restored if the original is lost or corrupted.

fragments.label: Developer interface
fragments.text: The part of a DBMS giving developers access to tools for creating tables, defining attributes, data types and keys, and building forms, queries and reports.

fragments.label: Query processor
fragments.text: The DBMS software that accepts a query, checks it against the data dictionary, turns it into an efficient plan and executes it to retrieve or change the data.
The DBMS and the problems it solves

fragments.label: The DBMS and the problems it solves
fragments.text: A database is more than a collection of files: it is data organised according to a model (for AS, the relational model) and managed by a database management system. Programs and users never read or write the stored data directly; they send requests to the DBMS, which carries out the operation and applies the same rules every time. This single controlling layer is what solves the problems of the file-based approach. Data is held once and shared by every department instead of each department keeping its own copy, which removes redundancy and inconsistency. Structure is defined once, centrally, in the data dictionary, instead of inside each program. Validation, key and relationship rules are enforced whoever enters the data. Access is controlled per user or group rather than being all-or-nothing for a file. Backups are organised centrally by the database administrator (DBA) instead of being left to chance. The syllabus groups these features as data management, data modelling, the logical schema, data integrity and data security.

fragments.label: The DBMS and the problems it solves
fragments.text: Every create, read, update and delete request passes through the DBMS, so rules are applied consistently.

fragments.label: The DBMS and the problems it solves
fragments.text: The DBA is the person who uses the DBMS to set up the database, user views, access rights and backup routines.

fragments.label: The DBMS and the problems it solves
fragments.text: Examples of relational DBMS software include MySQL, PostgreSQL, Microsoft Access and Microsoft SQL Server.
Data modelling

fragments.label: Data modelling
fragments.text: Before a database is built its data must be modelled: the designer identifies the entities the organisation needs to store data about, their attributes and the relationships between them, usually drawn as an E-R diagram (see 8.1). The first model is conceptual, describing the data without reference to any particular technology. It is then turned into a logical model for a relational database, where each entity becomes a table, many-to-many relationships are resolved with link tables, and primary and foreign keys are chosen. Many DBMSs include modelling tools that let the designer draw tables and relationship lines, and then generate the table definitions directly from the diagram, or show the relationships between existing tables. This is a feature a file-based approach lacks: there, the structure of each file is decided separately by each program's author, with no overall model of how the data fits together.

fragments.label: Data modelling
fragments.text: Data modelling produces the entities, attributes, relationships and keys that the logical schema records.

fragments.label: Data modelling
fragments.text: A good model is what makes normalised, non-redundant tables possible.

fragments.label: Data modelling
fragments.text: DBMS relationship tools let the designer declare foreign keys so that referential integrity is then enforced automatically.
The logical schema and data independence

fragments.label: The logical schema and data independence
fragments.text: A DBMS describes a database at three levels. At the internal level, the internal schema records how the data is physically stored on disk; only the DBMS software deals with this. At the conceptual level there is a single logical schema: the complete description of the database as users and programmers understand it, meaning every table, attribute, data type, key, relationship and constraint, with no mention of physical storage. The DBA controls this level. At the external level, each user group or program has its own view (external schema) showing only the part of the database it needs; for example, a finance view might include member payments but not coaching notes. Separating the levels gives data independence. If the physical storage is reorganised or moved to new hardware, the logical schema is unchanged, so programs keep working. If a new attribute or table is added to the logical schema, existing views and the programs that use them are unaffected, and only new programs that need the new data have to be written. This is the direct fix for the data dependency problem of file-based systems.

fragments.label: The logical schema and data independence
fragments.text: Logical schema = what data is held and how it is organised; internal schema = how it is stored physically.

fragments.label: The logical schema and data independence
fragments.text: External views are also a security mechanism, because a user can only reach the data in their view.

fragments.label: The logical schema and data independence
fragments.text: Data independence means changes at one level do not force changes to programs working at a higher level.
Data security: access rights for individuals and groups

fragments.label: Data security: access rights for individuals and groups
fragments.text: In a file-based system anyone who can open a file can read all of it. A DBMS lets the DBA control access at a much finer level. Each person logs in with their own user account, authenticated by a password or similar, so the DBMS knows who is making every request. The DBA then assigns access rights, which state which tables or views the account can use and which operations are allowed on each: read (SELECT), insert, update or delete. Rather than setting rights one person at a time, users with the same job are usually placed in a group (or role), such as Reception, Finance or Coaches, and the rights are granted to the group; a new employee then only needs to be added to the right group, and a change of job means moving them to another group. Individual rights can still be added or removed where one person needs something different, such as a manager who can delete records. Following the principle of least privilege, each user or group receives only the access their work requires, which protects confidential data and limits the damage from mistakes or a compromised account.

fragments.label: Data security: access rights for individuals and groups
fragments.text: Authentication (user ID and password) establishes who the user is; access rights then decide what that user may do.

fragments.label: Data security: access rights for individuals and groups
fragments.text: Rights can be limited to particular tables, to views that hide some attributes, and to particular operations.

fragments.label: Data security: access rights for individuals and groups
fragments.text: Group rights make administration simpler and more consistent than setting every user's rights separately.

fragments.label: Data security: access rights for individuals and groups
fragments.text: The DBMS can also keep an audit log of who accessed or changed which data.

fragments.label: Data security: access rights for individuals and groups
fragments.text:
Group | Member | ClassMember | Payment | Instructor
Reception | read, insert, update | read, insert, delete | none | read
Finance | read | read | read, insert, update | none
Coaches | read (view without phone numbers) | read | none | read
DBA | full | full | full | full

A receptionist can enrol a member in a class but cannot see or alter payment records; a coach sees who is in a class without seeing members' contact details.
Software tools: the developer interface

fragments.label: Software tools: the developer interface
fragments.text: The developer interface is the part of the DBMS that gives developers the tools to build and change a database. Through it a developer creates tables, names each attribute and sets its data type and size, declares the primary key and foreign keys (which records the relationships and switches on referential integrity), adds validation rules such as a range check or a required field, and creates indexes. The same interface is used to build the parts that end users see: data-entry forms, saved queries and formatted reports, which can be combined into a user interface so staff can work with the data without knowing SQL. Most DBMSs offer both a graphical way of doing this (design grids, drag-and-drop form designers, query-by-example) and a way to type SQL commands directly. Graphical tools are quicker for simple tasks, while writing SQL gives the developer precise control and is needed for more complex queries; in either case the DBMS ultimately carries out the work using its DDL and DML (see 8.3).

fragments.label: Software tools: the developer interface
fragments.text: Used for: creating and altering tables, attributes, data types, keys, validation rules and indexes.

fragments.label: Software tools: the developer interface
fragments.text: Also used for: designing forms for data entry, queries for retrieving data and reports for presenting output.

fragments.label: Software tools: the developer interface
fragments.text: Every change to the structure made here is recorded in the data dictionary.
Software tools: the query processor

fragments.label: Software tools: the query processor
fragments.text: A query is a request to select data that meets stated conditions, or to change data. The query processor is the DBMS software that accepts a query, whether typed in SQL or built with a graphical query tool, and carries it out. It first checks the query: that it is correctly formed, that every table and attribute named exists (by looking them up in the data dictionary) and that the user has the access rights needed. It then works out an efficient way of executing it, for example deciding to use an index on a key attribute rather than scanning a whole table, or choosing the order in which to join tables. Finally it executes the plan against the stored data and returns the result, such as a table of matching rows, or makes the requested changes. Structure-changing (DDL) statements are handled by updating the data dictionary; data-handling (DML) statements are compiled and run against the tables. Because users only describe what data they want, not how to find it, the same query keeps working even if the physical storage or indexes change.

fragments.label: Software tools: the query processor
fragments.text: Purpose: allow queries to be created and executed so data can be extracted or updated.

fragments.label: Software tools: the query processor
fragments.text: Steps: check syntax and names against the data dictionary, check access rights, optimise, execute, return the result.

fragments.label: Software tools: the query processor
fragments.text: Query results can be used directly, fed into a report, or built into a form in the user interface.

fragments.label: Software tools: the query processor
fragments.text:
Query from a receptionist:
SELECT MemberName FROM Member WHERE MemberID = 'M104';

1. Parse: the statement is valid SQL.
2. Check names: the data dictionary confirms table Member and attributes MemberName, MemberID exist, and MemberID is VARCHAR so 'M104' is a valid comparison.
3. Check rights: the Reception group has read access to Member.
4. Optimise: MemberID is the primary key and has an index, so use the index instead of reading every row.
5. Execute: follow the index pointer to the M104 row.
6. Return: MemberName = O. Haddad.
Data management: the data dictionary

fragments.label: Data management: the data dictionary
fragments.text: Data management in a DBMS is centred on the data dictionary: a part of the database, maintained by the DBMS and normally hidden from everyone except the DBA, that holds metadata, meaning data about the data rather than the data itself. It stores the name of every table, the name, data type and size of every attribute, primary and foreign keys and the relationships they form, validation rules and default values, indexes, user views and access rights, and details of how the data is physically stored. The DBMS keeps it up to date automatically whenever the structure is changed through the developer interface or a DDL command, and consults it constantly: the query processor uses it to check that names in a query exist and to find indexes, and the data-entry process uses it to check each new value against its data type and validation rule. In a file-based system this information is scattered inside each program; in a DBMS it is held once and shared, so every program works to the same definitions.

fragments.label: Data management: the data dictionary
fragments.text: Metadata examples to quote: table names, attribute names, data types, field lengths, primary/foreign keys, validation rules, relationships, access rights.

fragments.label: Data management: the data dictionary
fragments.text: The data dictionary does not contain the records themselves (for example, not a member's actual phone number).

fragments.label: Data management: the data dictionary
fragments.text: Because definitions are central, a change such as lengthening an attribute is made once and applies to every program.

fragments.label: Data management: the data dictionary
fragments.text:
Table: Member
Attribute | Data type | Size | Key | Validation
MemberID | VARCHAR | 4 | Primary key | Format: letter M followed by 3 digits
MemberName | VARCHAR | 40 | - | Required
MemberPhone | VARCHAR | 15 | - | -
EmailAddress | VARCHAR | 60 | Secondary key (indexed) | Must be unique
Indexes: MemberID, EmailAddress
Referenced by: ClassMember.MemberID (foreign key)
Data integrity

fragments.label: Data integrity
fragments.text: Data integrity means the stored data is accurate, complete and consistent. A DBMS maintains it with several features that a file-based approach lacks. Entity integrity: every table has a primary key and the DBMS rejects a missing or duplicate key value, so no tuple is recorded twice. Referential integrity: a foreign key value is accepted only if it matches an existing primary key in the referenced table, and a referenced tuple cannot be deleted while others still depend on it. Validation: each value is checked against the data type, size and any rule held in the data dictionary (a range check on a price, a format check on an ID, a presence check on a required attribute). Single storage: because each fact is held once, there are no copies to fall out of step. Controlled updates: a transaction that is interrupted part way, for example by a power failure, is either completed or fully undone, so the database is never left half-updated, and when several users update at the same time the DBMS uses record locking so one user's change cannot silently overwrite another's.

fragments.label: Data integrity
fragments.text: Validation reduces errors but cannot guarantee correctness: a valid but wrong phone number will still be accepted.

fragments.label: Data integrity
fragments.text: Keys and referential integrity are declared once in the DBMS and then enforced for every program and user.

fragments.label: Data integrity
fragments.text: Record locking stops two users updating the same tuple at once, preventing a lost update.
Data security: backup procedures

fragments.label: Data security: backup procedures
fragments.text: Access rights protect data from people who should not see or change it, but they do not protect against hardware failure, accidental deletion, corruption, malware or a fire in the server room. For that, the DBA sets up a backup procedure, and the DBMS provides tools to run it, often automatically. A good procedure states what is copied, how often, where the copies are kept, how long they are kept and how they are tested. A common pattern is a full backup of the whole database at regular intervals (for example, every night when few users are working) with incremental backups of only the changes in between. Copies are stored off-site or in the cloud, and often encrypted, so that the event that damages the live system cannot also destroy the backups, and several generations are kept in case the most recent copy is itself corrupted. Many DBMSs also keep a transaction log of every change since the last backup. To recover, the latest backup is restored and the logged transactions are reapplied, bringing the database back to its state just before the failure. Restores should be tested regularly, because a backup that cannot be restored gives no protection.

fragments.label: Data security: backup procedures
fragments.text: Backup frequency is set by how much data the organisation can afford to lose: data changed since the last backup (and not in a log) is lost.

fragments.label: Data security: backup procedures
fragments.text: Store backups away from the live database, for example off-site or in the cloud.

fragments.label: Data security: backup procedures
fragments.text: Keep several generations of backups, and test that they can actually be restored.

fragments.label: Data security: backup procedures
fragments.text: A transaction log lets recovery go beyond the last backup up to the point of failure.

fragments.label: Data security: backup procedures
fragments.text:
Procedure: full backup every night at 01:00 to an encrypted cloud store; 14 nightly copies kept; transaction log kept on a separate disk.

The server disk fails at 15:30 on Thursday.
1. Replace the disk and restore Thursday's 01:00 full backup: the database is now as it was at 01:00.
2. Reapply the transaction log from 01:00 to 15:30: all changes made during Thursday are restored.
3. Only transactions still in progress at 15:30 are lost.
Without the log, every change made between 01:00 and 15:30 would have been lost.
What is a data dictionary? Give two items it holds.

fragments.label: What is a data dictionary? Give two items it holds.
fragments.text: A part of the database holding metadata (data about the data). Any two of: table names, attribute names, data types, field lengths, primary/foreign keys, validation rules, relationships, indexes, access rights.
What is the logical schema?

fragments.label: What is the logical schema?
fragments.text: The overall description of the database as seen by users and programmers: its tables, attributes, keys, relationships and constraints, independent of physical storage.
How does a DBMS maintain data integrity?

fragments.label: How does a DBMS maintain data integrity?
fragments.text: Through primary keys (no duplicate or missing keys), referential integrity on foreign keys, validation rules from the data dictionary, storing each fact once, and controlled updates such as record locking.
Why are access rights often given to groups rather than individuals?

fragments.label: Why are access rights often given to groups rather than individuals?
fragments.text: Users with the same job need the same access, so granting rights to a group is quicker and more consistent; new or moving staff just join the appropriate group.
Give three features of a good backup procedure.

fragments.label: Give three features of a good backup procedure.
fragments.text: Any three of: regular scheduled backups (full and incremental), stored off-site or in the cloud, encrypted, several generations kept, restores tested, transaction log kept to recover up to the failure.
What is the developer interface used for?

fragments.label: What is the developer interface used for?
fragments.text: Creating and altering tables, attributes, data types, keys, validation rules and indexes, and building forms, queries and reports for the user interface.
What does the query processor do?

fragments.label: What does the query processor do?
fragments.text: Accepts a query, checks it against the data dictionary and the user's rights, works out an efficient way to run it (for example using an index) and executes it to return or change data.

A DBMS never changes a database by magic: every table it builds is described in its Data Definition Language (DDL), and every look-up, insertion, correction or removal of data is written in its Data Manipulation Language (DML). SQL is the standard language for both. At AS level you must read a given SQL statement and say exactly what it does, write DDL that creates a database and its tables with suitable data types and keys, and write DML scripts over at most two tables using SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, INNER JOIN, SUM, COUNT and AVG, plus INSERT INTO, UPDATE and DELETE FROM. This note uses one small sports-centre database (a Member table and a Booking table, continuing the example from 8.1 and 8.2) so that every query can be checked row by row against the data shown.

fragments.label: Structured Query Language (SQL)
fragments.text: The industry-standard language that relational DBMSs accept for both defining a database's structure (DDL) and querying or maintaining the data in it (DML). Keywords are not case sensitive and each statement ends with a semicolon.

fragments.label: Data Definition Language (DDL)
fragments.text: The part of SQL the DBMS uses to create or change the structure of a database: the database itself, its tables, attributes, data types and keys (CREATE DATABASE, CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE). DDL puts no data into the tables.

fragments.label: Data Manipulation Language (DML)
fragments.text: The part of SQL the DBMS uses to work with the data held inside existing tables: reading it with SELECT queries and maintaining it with INSERT INTO, UPDATE and DELETE FROM.

fragments.label: VARCHAR(n) and CHARACTER
fragments.text: Two text data types. VARCHAR(n) holds a string of any length up to n characters; CHARACTER holds a single character, or with a size such as CHARACTER(4), a string of exactly that fixed length.

fragments.label: PRIMARY KEY (field)
fragments.text: The DDL clause, written inside CREATE TABLE or added with ALTER TABLE, that names the attribute whose value must be unique for every record of the table.

fragments.label: FOREIGN KEY (field) REFERENCES Table (Field)
fragments.text: The DDL clause that makes an attribute a foreign key, linking it to the primary key of another table, so the DBMS rejects any value that does not already exist in that table.

fragments.label: WHERE clause
fragments.text: Part of a SELECT, UPDATE or DELETE FROM statement that gives a condition; only records for which the condition is true are returned, changed or removed.

fragments.label: Aggregate function
fragments.text: A function such as SUM, COUNT or AVG that takes the values of one attribute from many records and returns a single value, either for the whole set of selected records or for each group formed by GROUP BY.

fragments.label: GROUP BY
fragments.text: A clause that collects together records having the same value in the named attribute(s) so that one output row is produced per group; used with aggregate functions, or on its own to list each value once.

fragments.label: INNER JOIN
fragments.text: A way of combining two tables in one query: each record in one table is paired with every record in the other whose linking attributes match the ON condition (normally foreign key = primary key); records with no match are left out.
SQL: the DBMS's language for structure (DDL) and data (DML)

fragments.label: SQL: the DBMS's language for structure (DDL) and data (DML)
fragments.text: Whatever tools a DBMS shows the user, the work underneath is done through two sets of commands. Anything that creates or alters the structure of the database (the database itself, the tables, the attributes and their data types, and the primary and foreign keys) is carried out by the DBMS using its Data Definition Language. Anything that looks up data, or keeps the stored data up to date by adding, amending or removing records, is carried out using its Data Manipulation Language.

fragments.label: SQL: the DBMS's language for structure (DDL) and data (DML)
fragments.text: Structured Query Language (SQL) is the industry standard for both. Even when a developer builds a table by clicking in a graphical developer interface, or a user builds a query with a form, the DBMS turns this into SQL. Knowing SQL therefore lets you work with almost any relational DBMS. A few general rules apply to every statement: a script is a sequence of statements; each statement ends with a semicolon and may be spread over several lines; keywords are not case sensitive, though writing them in capitals makes them easy to spot; items in a list are separated by commas.

fragments.label: SQL: the DBMS's language for structure (DDL) and data (DML)
fragments.text: DDL = structure: CREATE DATABASE, CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY ... REFERENCES.

fragments.label: SQL: the DBMS's language for structure (DDL) and data (DML)
fragments.text: DML = data: SELECT queries, and maintenance with INSERT INTO, UPDATE and DELETE FROM.

fragments.label: SQL: the DBMS's language for structure (DDL) and data (DML)
fragments.text: Quick test: does the statement change which attributes/keys exist (DDL) or which records exist or are returned (DML)?

fragments.label: SQL: the DBMS's language for structure (DDL) and data (DML)
fragments.text: SQL is the standard for both, so the same statements work, with small dialect differences, across relational DBMSs.
CREATE DATABASE and the SQL data types

fragments.label: CREATE DATABASE and the SQL data types
fragments.text: The first DDL statement in a script creates the empty database that the tables will belong to, for example CREATE DATABASE SportsCentre; Nothing else about the structure exists yet.

fragments.label: CREATE DATABASE and the SQL data types
fragments.text: Each attribute defined later must be given a data type, which tells the DBMS how to store it and which values are allowed. The syllabus uses seven types. Choose the type by what the data really is: a membership code such as M104 is text even though it contains digits, and a telephone number is text because it can start with 0 and is never used in arithmetic.

fragments.label: CREATE DATABASE and the SQL data types
fragments.text: Text types: VARCHAR(n) for names and descriptions that vary in length; CHARACTER for one character, or CHARACTER(n) for codes of a fixed length.

fragments.label: CREATE DATABASE and the SQL data types
fragments.text: Number types: INTEGER for whole numbers (counts, quantities); REAL for numbers with a fractional part (prices, measurements).

fragments.label: CREATE DATABASE and the SQL data types
fragments.text: BOOLEAN for yes/no facts such as Junior or Paid.

fragments.label: CREATE DATABASE and the SQL data types
fragments.text: DATE for a calendar date and TIME for a time of day; keep them separate from text so they sort and compare correctly.

fragments.label: CREATE DATABASE and the SQL data types
fragments.text:
Data type  | Holds                                   | Sports-centre example
CHARACTER  | one character, or a fixed-length string | MemberID CHARACTER(4)  e.g. M104
VARCHAR(n) | text of up to n characters              | MemberName VARCHAR(30)
BOOLEAN    | TRUE or FALSE                           | Junior BOOLEAN
INTEGER    | whole number                            | BookingNo INTEGER
REAL       | number with a fractional part           | Fee REAL  e.g. 6.00
DATE       | calendar date                           | DateJoined DATE
TIME       | time of day                             | StartTime TIME
CREATE TABLE: attributes, data types and keys

fragments.label: CREATE TABLE: attributes, data types and keys
fragments.text: CREATE TABLE is followed by the table name and then, inside one pair of brackets, a comma-separated list of attribute definitions, each an attribute name followed by its data type. The keys can be declared inside the same brackets: PRIMARY KEY (field) names the identifying attribute, and FOREIGN KEY (field) REFERENCES Table (Field) links an attribute to the primary key of another table.

fragments.label: CREATE TABLE: attributes, data types and keys
fragments.text: In the sports centre, one member can make many bookings, but each booking is for one member. The foreign key MemberID therefore goes in Booking (the 'many' side) and refers to Member's primary key. Member must be created first, because a foreign key can only refer to a table that already exists. Once the tables exist, the DBMS enforces the link: a booking cannot be added for a MemberID that is not in Member.

fragments.label: CREATE TABLE: attributes, data types and keys
fragments.text: Syntax: CREATE TABLE Name ( attribute TYPE, attribute TYPE, ... , PRIMARY KEY (attribute) );

fragments.label: CREATE TABLE: attributes, data types and keys
fragments.text: The foreign key goes in the table on the 'many' side and names the table and attribute it refers to.

fragments.label: CREATE TABLE: attributes, data types and keys
fragments.text: Create the referenced ('one' side) table before the table holding the foreign key.

fragments.label: CREATE TABLE: attributes, data types and keys
fragments.text: DDL only defines the structure: after CREATE TABLE the tables are empty.

fragments.label: CREATE TABLE: attributes, data types and keys
fragments.text:
CREATE DATABASE SportsCentre;

CREATE TABLE Member (
  MemberID   CHARACTER(4),
  MemberName VARCHAR(30),
  Junior     BOOLEAN,
  DateJoined DATE,
  PRIMARY KEY (MemberID)
);

CREATE TABLE Booking (
  BookingNo  INTEGER,
  MemberID   CHARACTER(4),
  ClassName  VARCHAR(20),
  ClassDate  DATE,
  StartTime  TIME,
  Fee        REAL,
  PRIMARY KEY (BookingNo),
  FOREIGN KEY (MemberID) REFERENCES Member(MemberID)
);
ALTER TABLE: changing a table definition and adding keys

fragments.label: ALTER TABLE: changing a table definition and adding keys
fragments.text: ALTER TABLE changes the definition of a table that already exists, so the table does not have to be deleted and rebuilt. It is used to add a new attribute, and it is also a second way of declaring keys: a table can be created with its attributes only, and the primary and foreign keys added afterwards. Exam questions use both styles, so be ready to write either.

fragments.label: ALTER TABLE: changing a table definition and adding keys
fragments.text: A new attribute added with ALTER TABLE exists for every existing record but holds no value until one is supplied, for example by an UPDATE statement.

fragments.label: ALTER TABLE: changing a table definition and adding keys
fragments.text: Add an attribute: ALTER TABLE Member ADD Phone VARCHAR(15);

fragments.label: ALTER TABLE: changing a table definition and adding keys
fragments.text: Add a primary key: ALTER TABLE Member ADD PRIMARY KEY (MemberID);

fragments.label: ALTER TABLE: changing a table definition and adding keys
fragments.text: Add a foreign key: ALTER TABLE Booking ADD FOREIGN KEY (MemberID) REFERENCES Member(MemberID);

fragments.label: ALTER TABLE: changing a table definition and adding keys
fragments.text: ALTER TABLE is DDL: it changes the table's structure, not the data values stored in it.

fragments.label: ALTER TABLE: changing a table definition and adding keys

fragments.text: INSERT INTO: putting data into the tables

fragments.label: INSERT INTO: putting data into the tables
fragments.text: DML covers three jobs: loading data into the new tables, maintaining it (changing or removing records) and reading it with queries. Loading is done with INSERT INTO, one statement per record. The safer form lists the attribute names and then the matching values, so the statement still works if the column order is not what you expected; the short form gives only the values and relies on them being in the same order as the attributes in the table definition.

fragments.label: INSERT INTO: putting data into the tables
fragments.text: Text, date and time values are written inside single quotes; numbers and TRUE/FALSE are not. The syllabus does not fix a date format; this note writes dates as 'YYYY-MM-DD', which cannot be misread and sorts correctly. The eight INSERT INTO statements for Booking, plus four for Member, give the sample data below, which every query in the rest of this note uses. Notice that S. Mensah (M123) has made no bookings.

fragments.label: INSERT INTO: putting data into the tables
fragments.text: Full form: INSERT INTO Table (attr1, attr2, ...) VALUES (value1, value2, ...);

fragments.label: INSERT INTO: putting data into the tables
fragments.text: Short form: INSERT INTO Table VALUES (value1, value2, ...); with a value for every attribute in table order.

fragments.label: INSERT INTO: putting data into the tables
fragments.text: One INSERT INTO adds one record; the order records were inserted in has no meaning later, so use ORDER BY when order matters.

fragments.label: INSERT INTO: putting data into the tables
fragments.text: Insert into the 'one' table (Member) before the 'many' table (Booking), or the foreign key check fails.

fragments.label: INSERT INTO: putting data into the tables
INSERT INTO: putting data into the tables

fragments.text: SELECT ... FROM with WHERE and ORDER BY

fragments.label: SELECT ... FROM with WHERE and ORDER BY
fragments.text: A query always begins with SELECT, followed by the attributes to output, then FROM and the table to read. SELECT * outputs every attribute. A WHERE clause adds a condition, so only records for which it is true are output; conditions can use =, <>, <, >, <=, >= and be combined with AND and OR. ORDER BY sorts the output by the named attribute, ascending (ASC) unless DESC is written.

fragments.label: SELECT ... FROM with WHERE and ORDER BY
fragments.text: WHERE decides which records appear; ORDER BY only decides the order they appear in. Comparisons on DATE and TIME values work in time order, so WHERE DateJoined < '2025-01-01' means 'joined before 2025'.

fragments.label: SELECT ... FROM with WHERE and ORDER BY
fragments.text: Attributes in the SELECT list are separated by commas, with no brackets.

fragments.label: SELECT ... FROM with WHERE and ORDER BY
fragments.text: Text literals in quotes ('Yoga'); numbers without (7.00); BOOLEAN values as TRUE or FALSE.

fragments.label: SELECT ... FROM with WHERE and ORDER BY
fragments.text: ORDER BY attribute DESC gives largest/latest first; ASC (the default) gives smallest/earliest or A to Z first.

fragments.label: SELECT ... FROM with WHERE and ORDER BY
fragments.text: Only the attributes listed after SELECT are output, even if WHERE tests a different attribute.

fragments.label: SELECT ... FROM with WHERE and ORDER BY
fragments.text:
Query A
SELECT MemberID, MemberName
FROM Member
WHERE Junior = TRUE
ORDER BY MemberName;

Junior is TRUE for M117 and M123. Sorted A to Z by name:
MemberID | MemberName
M117     | L. Ortiz
M123     | S. Mensah

Query B
SELECT MemberName, DateJoined
FROM Member
WHERE DateJoined < '2025-01-01'
ORDER BY DateJoined;

Joined before 2025: M104 (2024-03-15) and M120 (2023-11-20). Earliest first:
MemberName | DateJoined
T. Reyes   | 2023-11-20
O. Haddad  | 2024-03-15

Query C
SELECT BookingNo, ClassName, Fee
FROM Booking
WHERE MemberID = 'M104' AND Fee >= 7.00
ORDER BY Fee DESC;

M104's bookings are 1 (6.00), 2 (8.00), 5 (7.00), 8 (6.00); only 2 and 5 have Fee >= 7.00:
BookingNo | ClassName | Fee
2         | Spin      | 8.00
5         | Pilates   | 7.00
GROUP BY and the aggregate functions SUM, COUNT and AVG

fragments.label: GROUP BY and the aggregate functions SUM, COUNT and AVG
fragments.text: SUM, COUNT and AVG each take many records and return one value. COUNT(*) counts records; SUM(attribute) adds up a numeric attribute; AVG(attribute) gives its mean. Without GROUP BY, the function works over every record that passes the WHERE clause and the query outputs a single row.

fragments.label: GROUP BY and the aggregate functions SUM, COUNT and AVG
fragments.text: GROUP BY puts records with the same value of the named attribute into one group and outputs one row per group, so an aggregate function is worked out separately for each group. Any attribute in the SELECT list that is not inside an aggregate function must also appear in GROUP BY, because it has to have one value per group. GROUP BY can also be used with no aggregate at all to list each value once, for example the members who have made at least one booking. The WHERE clause is applied first, to individual records, before the groups are formed.

fragments.label: GROUP BY and the aggregate functions SUM, COUNT and AVG
fragments.text: COUNT(*) counts records; SUM(Fee) totals; AVG(Fee) = SUM(Fee) / COUNT of the records used.

fragments.label: GROUP BY and the aggregate functions SUM, COUNT and AVG
fragments.text: Order of work: FROM, then WHERE removes records, then GROUP BY forms groups, then each aggregate is calculated per group, then ORDER BY sorts the output rows.

fragments.label: GROUP BY and the aggregate functions SUM, COUNT and AVG
fragments.text: Every non-aggregated attribute in SELECT must be listed in GROUP BY.

fragments.label: GROUP BY and the aggregate functions SUM, COUNT and AVG
fragments.text: SELECT MemberID FROM Booking GROUP BY MemberID; lists each member with a booking once, instead of once per booking.

fragments.label: GROUP BY and the aggregate functions SUM, COUNT and AVG
fragments.text:
Query D (whole table, no GROUP BY)
SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(Fee), AVG(Fee)
FROM Booking;

COUNT = 8 records
SUM   = 6.00 + 8.00 + 6.00 + 7.00 + 7.00 + 8.00 + 6.00 + 6.00 = 54.00
AVG   = 54.00 / 8 = 6.75
COUNT(*) | SUM(Fee) | AVG(Fee)
8        | 54.00    | 6.75

Query E (one row per class)
SELECT ClassName, COUNT(*), SUM(Fee)
FROM Booking
GROUP BY ClassName
ORDER BY ClassName;

Pilates: bookings 4, 5        -> 2 records, 7.00 + 7.00 = 14.00
Spin:    bookings 2, 6        -> 2 records, 8.00 + 8.00 = 16.00
Yoga:    bookings 1, 3, 7, 8  -> 4 records, 4 x 6.00   = 24.00
ClassName | COUNT(*) | SUM(Fee)
Pilates   | 2        | 14.00
Spin      | 2        | 16.00
Yoga      | 4        | 24.00

Query F (WHERE before GROUP BY)
SELECT MemberID, AVG(Fee)
FROM Booking
WHERE ClassName <> 'Yoga'
GROUP BY MemberID
ORDER BY MemberID;

WHERE keeps bookings 2, 4, 5, 6 only.
M104: bookings 2, 5 -> (8.00 + 7.00) / 2 = 7.50
M117: booking 6     -> 8.00 / 1 = 8.00
M120: booking 4     -> 7.00 / 1 = 7.00
MemberID | AVG(Fee)
M104     | 7.50
M117     | 8.00
M120     | 7.00

Query G (GROUP BY to list each value once)
SELECT MemberID FROM Booking GROUP BY MemberID ORDER BY MemberID;
MemberID
M104
M117
M120
(M123 has no bookings, so it cannot appear.)
INNER JOIN: a query over two tables

fragments.label: INNER JOIN: a query over two tables
fragments.text: When the output needs attributes from both tables, such as a member's name (in Member) next to the class booked (in Booking), the tables are combined with INNER JOIN. The ON condition says which records belong together: the foreign key in one table must equal the primary key it refers to in the other, here Member.MemberID = Booking.MemberID. Each Booking record is paired with the one Member record that has the same MemberID.

fragments.label: INNER JOIN: a query over two tables
fragments.text: Because both tables contain an attribute called MemberID, attributes are written in full as Table.Attribute to make clear which table each comes from. An inner join only outputs pairs that match, so a member with no bookings (S. Mensah) never appears in a joined result. WHERE, GROUP BY, the aggregate functions and ORDER BY can all be used on the joined records exactly as on a single table. Some texts write the join condition in the WHERE clause instead of using INNER JOIN ... ON; the result is the same, but the INNER JOIN form is the one the syllabus names.

fragments.label: INNER JOIN: a query over two tables
fragments.text: Syntax: SELECT T1.a, T2.b FROM T1 INNER JOIN T2 ON T1.key = T2.key;

fragments.label: INNER JOIN: a query over two tables
fragments.text: The ON condition matches the foreign key to the primary key it references, not any two attributes that happen to look alike.

fragments.label: INNER JOIN: a query over two tables
fragments.text: Unmatched records (a member with no bookings) are left out of an inner join.

fragments.label: INNER JOIN: a query over two tables
fragments.text: The syllabus limits queries to at most two tables, so one INNER JOIN is the most you will need.

fragments.label: INNER JOIN: a query over two tables
fragments.text:
Query H
SELECT Member.MemberName, Booking.ClassName, Booking.ClassDate
FROM Member
INNER JOIN Booking ON Member.MemberID = Booking.MemberID
WHERE Member.Junior = TRUE
ORDER BY Booking.ClassDate;

Junior members: M117 and M123. M117 matches bookings 3 and 6; M123 matches none.
MemberName | ClassName | ClassDate
L. Ortiz   | Yoga      | 2026-10-05
L. Ortiz   | Spin      | 2026-10-06

Query I (join + GROUP BY + COUNT)
SELECT Member.MemberName, COUNT(*)
FROM Member
INNER JOIN Booking ON Member.MemberID = Booking.MemberID
GROUP BY Member.MemberName
ORDER BY Member.MemberName;

O. Haddad (M104): bookings 1, 2, 5, 8 -> 4
L. Ortiz  (M117): bookings 3, 6       -> 2
T. Reyes  (M120): bookings 4, 7       -> 2
S. Mensah (M123): no matching booking -> no row
MemberName | COUNT(*)
L. Ortiz   | 2
O. Haddad  | 4
T. Reyes   | 2
UPDATE and DELETE FROM: maintaining the data

fragments.label: UPDATE and DELETE FROM: maintaining the data
fragments.text: UPDATE changes values in records that already exist: the table name, then SET with the new value(s), then a WHERE clause picking out the records to change. DELETE FROM removes whole records that match a WHERE clause; the table and its structure remain. In both, the WHERE clause is what limits the change. Leave it out and every record in the table is updated or deleted.

fragments.label: UPDATE and DELETE FROM: maintaining the data
fragments.text: Referential integrity affects the order of deletions. A member cannot be removed while Booking still holds records whose foreign key refers to that member, so the DBMS rejects the delete. Remove the member's bookings first, then the member.

fragments.label: UPDATE and DELETE FROM: maintaining the data
fragments.text: UPDATE Table SET attribute = value WHERE condition;  (several changes: SET a = 1, b = 2)

fragments.label: UPDATE and DELETE FROM: maintaining the data
fragments.text: DELETE FROM Table WHERE condition;  removes whole records, never single attribute values.

fragments.label: UPDATE and DELETE FROM: maintaining the data
fragments.text: No WHERE clause means every record is affected.

fragments.label: UPDATE and DELETE FROM: maintaining the data
fragments.text: Delete from the 'many' table before the 'one' table when removing linked data.

fragments.label: UPDATE and DELETE FROM: maintaining the data

fragments.text: Understanding a given SQL statement

fragments.label: Understanding a given SQL statement
fragments.text: Many questions give you a statement and ask what it does or what it outputs. First decide whether it is DDL (it creates or changes structure: say which table, attributes, types or keys) or DML. For a query, work through the clauses in the order the DBMS applies them rather than the order they are written: FROM and any INNER JOIN say which records are available; WHERE removes records; GROUP BY forms groups; SUM, COUNT or AVG are worked out per group; SELECT picks the attributes to output; ORDER BY sorts.

fragments.label: Understanding a given SQL statement
fragments.text: When sample data is given, list the records that survive each step, write the output as a table with the column headings, and check the number of rows. Describing the output in words, when the question asks for the result, will not earn the marks.

fragments.label: Understanding a given SQL statement
fragments.text: DDL question: name the table, each attribute with its type, and each key and what it references.

fragments.label: Understanding a given SQL statement
fragments.text: Query question: FROM/JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, aggregates, SELECT, ORDER BY.

fragments.label: Understanding a given SQL statement
fragments.text: Write the result as rows with headings, in the order ORDER BY gives.

fragments.label: Understanding a given SQL statement
fragments.text: Check for traps: an inner join drops unmatched records; WHERE on text is an exact match; a missing WHERE affects every record.

fragments.label: Understanding a given SQL statement
fragments.text:
SELECT Member.MemberName, SUM(Booking.Fee)
FROM Member
INNER JOIN Booking ON Member.MemberID = Booking.MemberID
WHERE Member.Junior = FALSE
GROUP BY Member.MemberName
ORDER BY SUM(Booking.Fee) DESC;

1. FROM/JOIN: each of the 8 bookings is paired with its member (M123 has none).
2. WHERE: keep non-junior members only: M104 (bookings 1, 2, 5, 8) and M120 (bookings 4, 7).
3. GROUP BY: two groups, O. Haddad and T. Reyes.
4. SUM: O. Haddad 6.00 + 8.00 + 7.00 + 6.00 = 27.00; T. Reyes 7.00 + 6.00 = 13.00.
5. ORDER BY ... DESC: largest total first.

MemberName | SUM(Booking.Fee)
O. Haddad  | 27.00
T. Reyes   | 13.00

In words: the total spent on bookings by each adult (non-junior) member, highest spender first.
Which part of the DBMS's language creates or changes the database structure, and which queries and maintains the data?

fragments.label: Which part of the DBMS's language creates or changes the database structure, and which queries and maintains the data?
fragments.text: DDL creates/modifies the structure (CREATE DATABASE, CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, keys); DML queries and maintains data (SELECT, INSERT INTO, UPDATE, DELETE FROM).
What is the industry standard language for both DDL and DML?

fragments.label: What is the industry standard language for both DDL and DML?
fragments.text: Structured Query Language (SQL).
Name the seven data types listed in the syllabus.

fragments.label: Name the seven data types listed in the syllabus.
fragments.text: CHARACTER, VARCHAR(n), BOOLEAN, INTEGER, REAL, DATE, TIME.
Write the DDL to make MemberID in Booking a foreign key to Member.

fragments.label: Write the DDL to make MemberID in Booking a foreign key to Member.
fragments.text: ALTER TABLE Booking ADD FOREIGN KEY (MemberID) REFERENCES Member(MemberID); (or the FOREIGN KEY clause inside CREATE TABLE Booking).
Using the sample Booking data, what does SELECT ClassName, COUNT(*) FROM Booking GROUP BY ClassName ORDER BY ClassName; output?

fragments.label: Using the sample Booking data, what does SELECT ClassName, COUNT(*) FROM Booking GROUP BY ClassName ORDER BY ClassName; output?
fragments.text: Pilates 2, Spin 2, Yoga 4.
What is output by SELECT AVG(Fee) FROM Booking; on the sample data?

fragments.label: What is output by SELECT AVG(Fee) FROM Booking; on the sample data?

fragments.text: Why does S. Mensah never appear in a query that uses Member INNER JOIN Booking?

fragments.label: Why does S. Mensah never appear in a query that uses Member INNER JOIN Booking?
fragments.text: She has no Booking records, and an inner join only outputs records whose ON condition finds a match.
What happens if UPDATE Booking SET Fee = 7.50; is run without a WHERE clause?

fragments.label: What happens if UPDATE Booking SET Fee = 7.50; is run without a WHERE clause?
fragments.text: Every booking's Fee becomes 7.50, not just the intended records.

Topic 9.1 is about two thinking skills used before any code is written. Abstraction strips a problem down to the details that actually affect the result, giving a simpler model to design against. Decomposition splits the problem into sub-problems small enough to solve one at a time, and each sub-problem becomes a program module: a procedure or a function. Paper 2 questions give a short scenario and expect you to apply both skills to it: name the details you would keep and drop, and name the modules you would write and what each one does.

fragments.label: Computational thinking
fragments.text: A logical way of analysing a problem and building a solution that a person can follow and a computer can carry out; it draws on abstraction, decomposition, data modelling, pattern recognition and algorithm design.

fragments.label: Abstraction
fragments.text: Filtering out the details of a problem that do not affect the solution, so that attention stays on the information that does.

fragments.label: Abstract model
fragments.text: A simplified representation of a real system that keeps only the essential data and behaviour needed for the task, such as a route map that shows stations and connections but not streets.

fragments.label: Decomposition
fragments.text: Breaking a problem into smaller sub-problems, each of which can be understood, solved and tested separately; the sub-problems lead to program modules.

fragments.label: Program module
fragments.text: A named, self-contained block of steps that carries out one sub-task and can be called from elsewhere in the program; in 9618 pseudocode a module is a procedure or a function.

fragments.label: Procedure
fragments.text: A module given an identifier that performs a sub-task when it is called with a CALL statement; it does not itself return a value to an expression.

fragments.label: Function
fragments.text: A module given an identifier that returns a single value of a stated data type; a function call is written inside an expression, for example Total ← Total + VAT(Price).

fragments.label: Pattern recognition
fragments.text: Spotting that a problem, or part of one, matches a problem already solved, so a known method or standard algorithm can be reused.

fragments.label: Top-down design
fragments.text: Designing a solution by starting from the whole problem and repeatedly splitting each part into smaller parts until every part is simple enough to program.
What computational thinking is

fragments.label: What computational thinking is
fragments.text: Computational thinking is the set of habits a programmer uses to turn a vague real-world problem into something a computer can solve. The emphasis is on analysis before code: working out what the problem really is, what data matters, and what steps will produce the answer. The coursebook groups the skills into strands: abstraction, decomposition, data modelling, pattern recognition and algorithm design.

fragments.label: What computational thinking is
fragments.text: The 9618 AS syllabus examines two of these directly, abstraction and decomposition, and uses the others as supporting ideas. Algorithm design itself is developed in 9.2, where the steps are written as structured English, flowcharts and pseudocode.

fragments.label: What computational thinking is
fragments.text: Abstraction answers 'what do I need to know?'; decomposition answers 'what are the separate jobs?'.

fragments.label: What computational thinking is
fragments.text: Both are applied before writing pseudocode, which is why exam questions on them usually come with an unfamiliar scenario.

fragments.label: What computational thinking is
fragments.text: The skills feed into each other: an abstract model shows which data exists, and decomposition decides which module handles which part of it.
Abstraction and its purpose

fragments.label: Abstraction and its purpose
fragments.text: Abstraction means deliberately leaving out detail that has no effect on the result you need. A real situation always contains far more information than a program could or should hold. The purpose of abstraction is to reduce that situation to a model containing only what the solution depends on, so the designer can concentrate on the parts that matter.

fragments.label: Abstraction and its purpose
fragments.text: A familiar example is a metro or bus network map. The real routes curve through streets, tunnels and hills, yet a passenger planning a journey only needs to know which stops exist, which lines join them and the order of the stops. The map keeps exactly that and drops distances, geography and street names. It is less 'accurate' than an aerial photograph, but far more useful for the task.

fragments.label: Abstraction and its purpose
fragments.text: Abstraction also appears inside programming itself. An algorithm is an abstraction of a process: it states the inputs, steps and outputs and ignores how the hardware carries them out. Calling a module such as CALL PrintReceipt hides the detail of how the receipt is laid out, so the caller only needs to know what the module does.

fragments.label: Abstraction and its purpose
fragments.text: The test for a detail is: would changing it change the output? If not, it can be abstracted away.

fragments.label: Abstraction and its purpose
fragments.text: What counts as essential depends on the task. A car's colour is irrelevant to a parking charge but essential to a paint shop's stock system.

fragments.label: Abstraction and its purpose
fragments.text: A game or simulator uses abstraction too: it keeps what the player must see and control and hides the complex rules running underneath.
The need for abstraction and its benefits

fragments.label: The need for abstraction and its benefits
fragments.text: Abstraction is needed because a computer system cannot model the whole of reality, and trying to include everything makes a design unmanageable. Every extra data item has to be input, validated, stored and tested. Removing what the problem does not need keeps the program focused on its actual requirements.

fragments.label: The need for abstraction and its benefits
fragments.text: The benefits appear throughout development. Design is quicker because there is less to think about. The program is smaller, so it takes less time to write and test and uses less memory and storage. The customer gets a system that does what was asked without clutter, and the solution is easier for other programmers to read and maintain later.

fragments.label: The need for abstraction and its benefits
fragments.text: Less data to collect and store: fewer inputs, smaller files, less validation code.

fragments.label: The need for abstraction and its benefits
fragments.text: Simpler, shorter programs that are faster to develop, test and debug.

fragments.label: The need for abstraction and its benefits
fragments.text: Reduced complexity lets the designer see the core problem and spot when it matches a known solution.

fragments.label: The need for abstraction and its benefits
fragments.text: Hiding the inner detail of a module means it can be reused without the user needing to understand how it works.

fragments.label: The need for abstraction and its benefits
fragments.text: Risk to manage: removing a detail that turns out to matter gives a model that produces wrong results, so each omission must be justified.
Producing an abstract model of a system

fragments.label: Producing an abstract model of a system
fragments.text: To produce an abstract model, start from the scenario, list every piece of information it mentions, then keep only the items the required outputs depend on. What remains becomes the data your program will hold (later, the fields of a record or the columns of a table) plus the operations the system must carry out on that data.

fragments.label: Producing an abstract model of a system
fragments.text: Worked scenario: a school library wants a system that records loans and reminds students when a book is overdue. The scenario describes the building, the shelves, each book's cover, page count and price, and each student's name, form, photo and date of birth. The model needs far less than that.

fragments.label: Producing an abstract model of a system
fragments.text: State each item you keep and say which output or operation needs it.

fragments.label: Producing an abstract model of a system
fragments.text: State each item you drop and give the reason it does not affect the outputs.

fragments.label: Producing an abstract model of a system
fragments.text: An abstract model includes behaviour as well as data: here, 'lend', 'return' and 'check overdue'.

fragments.label: Producing an abstract model of a system
fragments.text:
Required outputs: record a loan, record a return, list overdue loans with the student to remind.

Kept (essential)            | Why it is needed
BookID                      | identifies which copy is on loan
Title                       | shown on the reminder so the student knows which book
StudentID                   | links the loan to one borrower
StudentName, TutorGroup     | needed to deliver the reminder
DateBorrowed, DateDue       | DateDue decides whether a loan is overdue
DateReturned (empty if out) | shows whether the book is still on loan

Dropped (not essential)     | Why it can go
Cover colour, page count    | no output depends on them
Shelf layout of the library | not needed to lend or remind
Student photo, date of birth| the reminder does not use them
Price of the book           | not needed unless the school charges for lost books

Operations in the model: LendBook, ReturnBook, ListOverdue.
If the requirement later adds charging for lost books, Price moves into the 'kept' list: essential always means essential for the stated task.
Decomposition

fragments.label: Decomposition
fragments.text: Decomposition breaks a large problem into sub-problems. Each sub-problem is smaller, so it is easier to understand, to solve and to test on its own. If a sub-problem is still too large, it is decomposed again, giving a hierarchy that goes from the whole problem at the top down to small tasks at the bottom. Working in this direction is called top-down design.

fragments.label: Decomposition
fragments.text: Decomposition helps a team as well as an individual. Separate sub-problems can be given to different programmers, finished in parallel and tested independently before being put together. It also makes errors easier to find, because a fault can be traced to one sub-problem rather than hunted for across the whole program, and it shows up tasks that repeat so they can be written once and reused.

fragments.label: Decomposition
fragments.text: Stop decomposing when each task is small enough to write as one short module.

fragments.label: Decomposition
fragments.text: Good sub-problems have one clear job and a clear set of inputs and outputs.

fragments.label: Decomposition
fragments.text: Testing each part alone is not enough: the parts must also be tested together to check they pass data correctly.

fragments.label: Decomposition
fragments.text:
Quiz program
|-- 1 Set up the quiz
|     |-- 1.1 Read the questions and answers from a file
|     |-- 1.2 Ask the player for their name
|-- 2 Run the quiz (repeat for each question)
|     |-- 2.1 Display the question
|     |-- 2.2 Input the player's answer
|     |-- 2.3 Check whether the answer is correct
|     |-- 2.4 Update the score
|-- 3 Finish
      |-- 3.1 Output the final score
      |-- 3.2 Save the score if it is a new high score

Each bottom-level box is small enough to become one module, e.g. 2.3 becomes
FUNCTION IsCorrect(Given : STRING, Expected : STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN
Pattern recognition, data modelling and algorithm design

fragments.label: Pattern recognition, data modelling and algorithm design
fragments.text: The other strands of computational thinking support abstraction and decomposition. Pattern recognition notices that a sub-problem has the same shape as one already solved. Finding the highest score, the most expensive product and the hottest day are all 'keep the largest value seen so far'. Recognising that lets you reuse a tested method, or a standard algorithm such as a linear search or bubble sort.

fragments.label: Pattern recognition, data modelling and algorithm design
fragments.text: Data modelling decides how the data kept by abstraction will be organised: records, arrays, files or abstract data types such as stacks and queues (topic 10). Algorithm design turns each sub-problem into a precise sequence of steps (topic 9.2).

fragments.label: Pattern recognition, data modelling and algorithm design
fragments.text: Patterns only become visible after abstraction has removed the scenario-specific detail.

fragments.label: Pattern recognition, data modelling and algorithm design
fragments.text: Reusing a known pattern saves design and testing time.

fragments.label: Pattern recognition, data modelling and algorithm design
fragments.text: Data modelling links 9.1 to records and abstract data types in 10.1 and 10.4.
From sub-problems to program modules

fragments.label: From sub-problems to program modules
fragments.text: When a problem has been decomposed, each sub-task can be written as a module: a named group of steps that is written once and called whenever that sub-task is needed. In 9618 pseudocode there are two kinds. A procedure performs a task and is run with a CALL statement. A function performs a task and returns one value, so its call is placed inside an expression, and its header states the data type of the value it returns.

fragments.label: From sub-problems to program modules
fragments.text: The main program then reads like the top level of the decomposition: a short list of calls. Modules should be self-contained. They receive the data they need through parameters and use local variables for their own working, rather than relying on global variables. This makes each module independent, easy to test alone and reusable in other programs.

fragments.label: From sub-problems to program modules
fragments.text: Use a function when the sub-task produces one value to be used in a calculation or condition; use a procedure otherwise.

fragments.label: From sub-problems to program modules
fragments.text: Module identifiers follow the same naming rules as variable identifiers.

fragments.label: From sub-problems to program modules
fragments.text: A module can call other modules, mirroring lower levels of the decomposition.

fragments.label: From sub-problems to program modules
fragments.text: Parameters and local variables are covered in detail in 11.3.

fragments.label: From sub-problems to program modules
fragments.text:
FUNCTION ToFahrenheit(Celsius : REAL) RETURNS REAL
   RETURN Celsius * 9 / 5 + 32
ENDFUNCTION

PROCEDURE ShowConversion(Celsius : REAL)
   OUTPUT Celsius, " C = ", ToFahrenheit(Celsius), " F"
ENDPROCEDURE

// main program
DECLARE Reading : REAL
DECLARE Count : INTEGER
FOR Count ← 1 TO 3
   INPUT Reading
   CALL ShowConversion(Reading)
NEXT Count

fragments.label: From sub-problems to program modules
fragments.text:
Count | Reading | ToFahrenheit(Reading)  | OUTPUT
1     | 0       | 0 * 9 / 5 + 32 = 32    | 0 C = 32 F
2     | 100     | 900 / 5 + 32 = 212     | 100 C = 212 F
3     | -40     | -360 / 5 + 32 = -40    | -40 C = -40 F

The loop ends after Count = 3. The main program never repeats the formula: it is written once in the function and reached through the procedure.
What is the purpose of abstraction?

fragments.label: What is the purpose of abstraction?
fragments.text: To remove details that do not affect the solution so the designer can concentrate on the essential information, giving a simpler model of the problem.
Give three benefits of using abstraction.

fragments.label: Give three benefits of using abstraction.
fragments.text: Less data to input and store; smaller, simpler programs that are quicker to write and test; a solution focused on what the customer actually needs.
How do you decide whether a detail belongs in an abstract model?

fragments.label: How do you decide whether a detail belongs in an abstract model?
fragments.text: Keep it only if a required output or operation of the system depends on it.
What is decomposition?

fragments.label: What is decomposition?
fragments.text: Breaking a problem into smaller sub-problems that can be solved and tested separately.
What does decomposition lead to in a program?

fragments.label: What does decomposition lead to in a program?
fragments.text: Program modules: each sub-problem becomes a procedure or a function.
State the difference between a procedure and a function.

fragments.label: State the difference between a procedure and a function.
fragments.text: A procedure is called with CALL to perform a task; a function returns one value of a stated type and is called inside an expression.
Why should modules use parameters and local variables?

fragments.label: Why should modules use parameters and local variables?
fragments.text: So each module is self-contained, can be tested on its own and can be reused in other programs.

Topic 9.2 is about designing an algorithm and writing it down precisely before it is programmed. It covers choosing identifiers and recording them in an identifier table; writing pseudocode with input, processing and output; the three basic constructs of sequence, selection and iteration; documenting an algorithm as structured English, a flowchart or pseudocode, and converting between those forms; logic statements that define conditions; and stepwise refinement, which breaks an outline into steps detailed enough to code. Paper 2 marks depend on correct Cambridge pseudocode keywords, sensible identifiers and logic that works for every input, so each example here is dry-run with a trace table.

fragments.label: Algorithm
fragments.text: A solution to a problem written as a finite sequence of defined, unambiguous steps carried out in a set order.

fragments.label: Identifier
fragments.text: The name given to a variable, constant, array or module so that it can be referred to in an algorithm.

fragments.label: Identifier table
fragments.text: A table listing each identifier used in a solution with its data type and an explanation of what it stores or does.

fragments.label: Structured English
fragments.text: A restricted form of English made of short command statements (INPUT, SET, IF, REPEAT, OUTPUT) used to describe the steps of an algorithm.

fragments.label: Pseudocode
fragments.text: A notation that uses keywords and identifiers to describe an algorithm like program code but without the syntax of any one programming language.

fragments.label: Flowchart
fragments.text: A diagram of an algorithm made of standard shapes (terminator, process, input/output, decision) joined by flow lines showing the order of steps.

fragments.label: Sequence / selection / iteration
fragments.text: The three basic constructs: steps run one after another; a condition chooses which steps run; a group of steps is repeated.

fragments.label: Logic statement
fragments.text: A condition built from relational operators (=, <>, <, >, <=, >=) and logical operators (AND, OR, NOT) that evaluates to TRUE or FALSE.

fragments.label: Rogue value
fragments.text: A value of the correct data type but outside the normal range, used only to mark the end of a sequence of inputs (e.g. -1 for marks).

fragments.label: Stepwise refinement
fragments.text: Repeatedly breaking each step of an outline solution into smaller, more detailed steps until every step can be written directly as program code.
What an algorithm is

fragments.label: What an algorithm is
fragments.text: An algorithm is a solution to a problem written as a sequence of defined steps. 'Defined' is the key word: each step must be exact, so anyone (or any computer) following it does the same thing and gets the same result. A good algorithm finishes after a finite number of steps for every valid input, and its steps are carried out in a fixed order.

fragments.label: What an algorithm is
fragments.text: Everyday instructions are algorithms too. Withdrawing cash at an ATM is: insert card; enter PIN; if the PIN is wrong, allow another try, up to three; choose an amount; if the balance is high enough, dispense the cash, otherwise show a message; return the card. Swap two of those steps, such as dispensing cash before checking the balance, and the process fails. The same instructions also show the three building blocks every algorithm uses: steps in order, choices and repetition.

fragments.label: What an algorithm is
