fragments.text: Most computer algorithms take data in, process it and output a result. A problem can often be solved by several different algorithms; a better one gives correct results, is easy to follow, and uses less time and memory.

fragments.label: What an algorithm is
fragments.text: Every step must be unambiguous: 'add a bit of tax' is not a defined step; 'Tax ← Price * 0.2' is.

fragments.label: What an algorithm is
fragments.text: Order matters: the same steps in a different sequence can give a different or no result.

fragments.label: What an algorithm is
fragments.text: An algorithm is language-independent; it is designed first and then coded in any programming language.
Documenting an algorithm: structured English, flowcharts and pseudocode

fragments.label: Documenting an algorithm: structured English, flowcharts and pseudocode
fragments.text: The syllabus names three ways to document an algorithm. Structured English uses a small set of English command words, such as INPUT, SET, IF, REPEAT, OUTPUT, written as short numbered or indented statements. It is quick to write and easy for a non-programmer to read, but it is not precise enough to code from without further work.

fragments.label: Documenting an algorithm: structured English, flowcharts and pseudocode
fragments.text: A flowchart draws the algorithm as a set of standard shapes joined by arrows. It makes the paths through selections and loops easy to see at a glance, but becomes hard to follow for long algorithms. Pseudocode uses the keywords and layout of the Cambridge pseudocode guide (DECLARE, ←, IF … THEN … ELSE … ENDIF, FOR … NEXT and so on) and is the closest of the three to real program code. A flowchart and its pseudocode should contain the same level of detail.

fragments.label: Documenting an algorithm: structured English, flowcharts and pseudocode
fragments.text: In pseudocode, ← means assignment and = means 'is equal to' in a condition; never swap them.

fragments.label: Documenting an algorithm: structured English, flowcharts and pseudocode
fragments.text: Indent the body of every IF, CASE and loop so that its extent is clear.

fragments.label: Documenting an algorithm: structured English, flowcharts and pseudocode
fragments.text: Every decision diamond needs exactly two labelled exits (Yes/No or TRUE/FALSE).

fragments.label: Documenting an algorithm: structured English, flowcharts and pseudocode
fragments.text: Flowcharts in exams are drawn with shapes; in these notes they are shown in a text form using the key below.

fragments.label: Documenting an algorithm: structured English, flowcharts and pseudocode
fragments.text:
Symbol (shape)                 | Used for                         | Text form used in these notes
Terminator (rounded / oval)    | START and END of the algorithm   | ( START )
Process (rectangle)            | assignment or calculation        | [ Total ← Total + Mark ]
Input/output (parallelogram)   | INPUT and OUTPUT                 | / INPUT Mark /
Decision (diamond)             | a condition with two exits       | < Mark > 50 ? >  with Yes / No labels
Subroutine (rectangle with     | CALL to a procedure              | [[ CALL PrintReport ]]
  double side lines)           |                                  |
Flow line (arrow)              | order of execution; a line that  | |  v  -->
                               | goes back up forms a loop        |
The three basic constructs: sequence, selection, iteration

fragments.label: The three basic constructs: sequence, selection, iteration
fragments.text: Any algorithm can be built from three constructs. Sequence means statements are executed one after another in the order written. Selection means a condition is tested and the result decides which group of statements runs; in pseudocode it is written with IF … THEN … ELSE … ENDIF for one or two choices, or CASE OF … OTHERWISE … ENDCASE when one value is compared with several options. Iteration (repetition) means a group of statements is executed more than once, using a FOR, REPEAT or WHILE loop.

fragments.label: The three basic constructs: sequence, selection, iteration
fragments.text: Assignment, giving a variable a value with ←, is the basic statement placed inside these constructs; the coursebook lists it as a fourth construct. Input and output statements let the algorithm receive data and report results. Constructs can be nested: a selection inside a loop, a loop inside a selection, or one IF inside another (a nested IF).

fragments.label: The three basic constructs: sequence, selection, iteration
fragments.text: Sequence: order of steps; selection: choose a path; iteration: repeat a block.

fragments.label: The three basic constructs: sequence, selection, iteration
fragments.text: CASE is tidier than a long chain of nested IFs when one variable is tested against many values or ranges.

fragments.label: The three basic constructs: sequence, selection, iteration
fragments.text: The same construct can be written in all three notations; the comparison table shows how.

fragments.label: The three basic constructs: sequence, selection, iteration
fragments.text:
// sequence
INPUT Width
INPUT Height
Area ← Width * Height

// selection: IF
IF Area > 100
   THEN
      OUTPUT "Large"
   ELSE
      OUTPUT "Small"
ENDIF

// selection: CASE
CASE OF Direction
   "N" : OUTPUT "North"
   "S" : OUTPUT "South"
   OTHERWISE : OUTPUT "Unknown"
ENDCASE

// iteration
FOR Row ← 1 TO 3
   OUTPUT Row
NEXT Row
Pseudocode with input, process and output

fragments.label: Pseudocode with input, process and output
fragments.text: Most algorithms follow the pattern input → process → output. Inputs are the data supplied from outside, typed by a user, read from a file or taken from a sensor, and are written with INPUT. Processing is everything done to the data: calculations, comparisons, validation, counting and totalling. Outputs are the results displayed or stored, written with OUTPUT; several items can be output in one statement separated by commas.

fragments.label: Pseudocode with input, process and output
fragments.text: Before writing pseudocode it helps to list the three parts separately. Every input should be used by some process, and every output should be produced by one; if not, something is missing. The worked example below reads marks until a rogue value is entered, rejects any out of range, and outputs how many were valid and their mean.

fragments.label: Pseudocode with input, process and output
fragments.text: Initialise totals and counters (usually to 0) before a loop that adds to them.

fragments.label: Pseudocode with input, process and output
fragments.text: Guard against division by zero when an average could be taken of no values.

fragments.label: Pseudocode with input, process and output
fragments.text: Choose a rogue value that can never be a genuine input; here -1, because marks are 0 to 100.

fragments.label: Pseudocode with input, process and output
fragments.text:
Input   | Mark, entered repeatedly; -1 ends the input (rogue value)
Process | reject a mark outside 0 to 100; add each valid mark to Total and add 1 to Count;
        | after the loop, Average ← Total / Count
Output  | a message for each rejected mark; the number of valid marks and their average,
        | or a message if no valid marks were entered

fragments.label: Pseudocode with input, process and output
fragments.text:
DECLARE Mark : INTEGER
DECLARE Total : INTEGER
DECLARE Count : INTEGER
DECLARE Average : REAL
Total ← 0
Count ← 0
INPUT Mark
WHILE Mark <> -1
   IF Mark >= 0 AND Mark <= 100
      THEN
         Total ← Total + Mark
         Count ← Count + 1
      ELSE
         OUTPUT "Mark rejected: ", Mark
   ENDIF
   INPUT Mark
ENDWHILE
IF Count > 0
   THEN
      Average ← Total / Count
      OUTPUT Count, " marks, average ", Average
   ELSE
      OUTPUT "No valid marks"
ENDIF

fragments.label: Pseudocode with input, process and output
fragments.text:
Mark | Total | Count | Average | OUTPUT
     | 0     | 0     |         |
64   | 64    | 1     |         |
105  |       |       |         | Mark rejected: 105
80   | 144   | 2     |         |
-1   |       |       | 72      | 2 marks, average 72

-1 makes the WHILE condition FALSE, so the loop ends; 144 / 2 = 72. If -1 were the first input, the loop body would never run and "No valid marks" would be output.
Identifiers, identifier tables and assignment

fragments.label: Identifiers, identifier tables and assignment
fragments.text: A variable is a named memory location holding a value that can change; its name is its identifier. Good identifiers describe their contents, such as NumberOfGuesses or TotalCost rather than N or X, which makes an algorithm self-documenting. The pseudocode guide's rules: an identifier starts with a letter and contains only letters, digits and the underscore, with no spaces; keywords such as INPUT or ENDIF cannot be used; and identifiers should be treated as case-insensitive, so never use two names that differ only in capital letters. Joining words with capitals (CamelCase) keeps long names readable.

fragments.label: Identifiers, identifier tables and assignment
fragments.text: An identifier table lists every identifier a solution needs, with its data type and a short explanation. Building it before writing pseudocode forces you to decide what data the problem really involves, and exam questions often ask for one.

fragments.label: Identifiers, identifier tables and assignment
fragments.text: Assignment uses ←: the expression on the right is evaluated and the result stored in the variable on the left. Count ← Count + 1 updates a variable using its own old value. Copying (B ← A) leaves A unchanged. Swapping two variables needs a third, temporary variable; otherwise the first copy overwrites a value that is still needed.

fragments.label: Identifiers, identifier tables and assignment
fragments.text: Explain each identifier's purpose, not just its type: 'Count: number of valid marks entered so far'.

fragments.label: Identifiers, identifier tables and assignment
fragments.text: Use constants for fixed values, e.g. CONSTANT VATRate ← 0.2, so the value is changed in one place.

fragments.label: Identifiers, identifier tables and assignment
fragments.text: Declare variables with DECLARE <identifier> : <data type> (INTEGER, REAL, CHAR, STRING, BOOLEAN, DATE).

fragments.label: Identifiers, identifier tables and assignment
fragments.text:
Identifier | Data type | Explanation
Mark       | INTEGER   | the mark just input; -1 ends the input
Total      | INTEGER   | running total of the valid marks
Count      | INTEGER   | how many valid marks have been input
Average    | REAL      | Total / Count, calculated after the loop

fragments.label: Identifiers, identifier tables and assignment
fragments.text:
Pseudocode:            Trace (Left = 8, Right = 3 at the start):
Temp ← Left            Left | Right | Temp
Left ← Right           8    | 3     |
Right ← Temp                |       | 8
                       3    |       |
                            | 8     |

Result: Left = 3, Right = 8. Without Temp, Left ← Right followed by Right ← Left would leave both variables holding 3.
Logic statements and selection

fragments.label: Logic statements and selection
fragments.text: A logic statement is a condition that is either TRUE or FALSE. Simple conditions compare two values with a relational operator: = equal to, <> not equal to, <, >, <= and >=. More complex conditions combine simple ones with the logical operators AND (both must be true), OR (at least one must be true) and NOT (reverses the result); brackets make the order of evaluation clear.

fragments.label: Logic statements and selection
fragments.text: Writing the rules of a problem as logic statements first is a reliable way to define the selection part of an algorithm. Each statement then becomes a branch of an IF or CASE. Check that the statements cover every possible value exactly once and pay special attention to the boundaries.

fragments.label: Logic statements and selection
fragments.text: 'Between 5 and 15 inclusive' is Age >= 5 AND Age <= 15; a range can never be written 5 <= Age <= 15 in pseudocode.

fragments.label: Logic statements and selection
fragments.text: In a nested IF, earlier conditions have already filtered values, so later tests can be simpler (Age <= 15 in the ELSE branch of Age < 5).

fragments.label: Logic statements and selection
fragments.text: CASE ranges are written 5 TO 15 : and OTHERWISE catches anything not listed.

fragments.label: Logic statements and selection
fragments.text: Test data should include each boundary value and the values either side of it.

fragments.label: Logic statements and selection
fragments.text:
Age < 5                   → Price is 0
Age >= 5 AND Age <= 15    → Price is 4
Age >= 16 AND Age <= 64   → Price is 9
Age >= 65                 → Price is 5
Each whole-number age satisfies exactly one statement.

fragments.label: Logic statements and selection
fragments.text:
INPUT Age
IF Age < 5
   THEN
      Price ← 0
   ELSE
      IF Age <= 15
         THEN
            Price ← 4
         ELSE
            IF Age <= 64
               THEN
                  Price ← 9
               ELSE
                  Price ← 5
            ENDIF
      ENDIF
ENDIF

// equivalent CASE (assumes Age has already been validated as >= 0)
CASE OF Age
   0 TO 4   : Price ← 0
   5 TO 15  : Price ← 4
   16 TO 64 : Price ← 9
   OTHERWISE : Price ← 5
ENDCASE
OUTPUT "Price: ", Price

fragments.label: Logic statements and selection
fragments.text:
Age | Branch taken            | Price
4   | Age < 5                 | 0
5   | Age <= 15               | 4
15  | Age <= 15               | 4
16  | Age <= 64               | 9
64  | Age <= 64               | 9
65  | final ELSE / OTHERWISE  | 5
Iteration: FOR, REPEAT and WHILE loops

fragments.label: Iteration: FOR, REPEAT and WHILE loops
fragments.text: Pseudocode has three loops. A count-controlled loop, FOR Counter ← Start TO End … NEXT Counter, runs a known number of times; the counter goes up by 1 automatically, or by another amount with STEP. A post-condition loop, REPEAT … UNTIL condition, tests at the end, so its body always runs at least once, and it stops when the condition becomes TRUE. A pre-condition loop, WHILE condition … ENDWHILE, tests before each pass, so its body may run zero times, and it continues while the condition is TRUE.

fragments.label: Iteration: FOR, REPEAT and WHILE loops
fragments.text: Choose FOR when the number of repetitions is known before the loop starts; REPEAT when the body must run at least once, as in input validation or a password prompt; WHILE when the body might not need to run at all, as with a rogue value that could be the first input. Loops can be nested, with the inner loop completing all its passes for each pass of the outer loop.

fragments.label: Iteration: FOR, REPEAT and WHILE loops
fragments.text: A trace table is the standard way to check a loop by hand. It has a column for each variable and for output, and a new row each time values change. Dry-running with carefully chosen data shows whether the loop stops at the right point.

fragments.label: Iteration: FOR, REPEAT and WHILE loops
fragments.text: REPEAT … UNTIL stops when its condition is TRUE; WHILE continues while its condition is TRUE: the conditions are opposites.

fragments.label: Iteration: FOR, REPEAT and WHILE loops
fragments.text: Do not change the FOR counter inside the loop body.

fragments.label: Iteration: FOR, REPEAT and WHILE loops
fragments.text: Make sure something inside a REPEAT or WHILE loop can change the condition, or the loop never ends.

fragments.label: Iteration: FOR, REPEAT and WHILE loops
fragments.text: A combined condition such as UNTIL Correct OR Tries = 3 gives a loop two ways to stop.

fragments.label: Iteration: FOR, REPEAT and WHILE loops
fragments.text:
// FOR: sum of the squares of 1 to 4
Total ← 0
FOR Index ← 1 TO 4
   Total ← Total + Index * Index
NEXT Index
OUTPUT Total

// REPEAT: up to three password attempts
Tries ← 0
REPEAT
   INPUT Attempt
   Tries ← Tries + 1
UNTIL Attempt = "Orange7" OR Tries = 3
IF Attempt = "Orange7"
   THEN
      OUTPUT "Access granted"
   ELSE
      OUTPUT "Locked"
ENDIF

// WHILE: years for 1000 to reach 2000 at 20% growth a year
Balance ← 1000
Years ← 0
WHILE Balance < 2000
   Balance ← Balance * 1.2
   Years ← Years + 1
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT Years

fragments.label: Iteration: FOR, REPEAT and WHILE loops
fragments.text:
FOR loop                 REPEAT loop (inputs "apple", "Orange7")
Index | Total            Attempt   | Tries | OUTPUT
      | 0                          | 0     |
1     | 1                "apple"   | 1     |
2     | 5                "Orange7" | 2     | Access granted
3     | 14
4     | 30               With inputs "a", "b", "c" the loop stops
OUTPUT 30                because Tries = 3, and "Locked" is output.

WHILE loop
Balance | Years | Balance < 2000?
1000    | 0     | TRUE
1200    | 1     | TRUE
1440    | 2     | TRUE
1728    | 3     | TRUE
2073.6  | 4     | FALSE → loop ends, OUTPUT 4

fragments.label: Iteration: FOR, REPEAT and WHILE loops
fragments.text:
INPUT Number
Digits ← 0
REPEAT
   Number ← Number DIV 10
   Digits ← Digits + 1
UNTIL Number = 0
OUTPUT Digits

Number | Digits
4072   | 0
407    | 1
40     | 2
4      | 3
0      | 4      → OUTPUT 4

Written as WHILE Number > 0 instead, an input of 0 would skip the loop and output 0 digits; REPEAT guarantees one pass and correctly gives 1.
Writing pseudocode from structured English and from a flowchart

fragments.label: Writing pseudocode from structured English and from a flowchart
fragments.text: To turn structured English into pseudocode, first build an identifier table from the nouns in the description (the data), then translate each statement into the matching construct: INPUT and OUTPUT stay as they are, calculations become assignments, 'if' becomes IF … ENDIF, and 'repeat' becomes whichever loop fits how the repetition ends. Add anything the English leaves implicit, such as setting a total to zero before the loop.

fragments.label: Writing pseudocode from structured English and from a flowchart
fragments.text: To turn a flowchart into pseudocode, follow the arrows from START. Parallelograms become INPUT or OUTPUT, rectangles become assignments and diamonds become conditions. A diamond whose arrow goes back up the chart is a loop: if the test comes before the body it is a WHILE loop; if the body comes first and the test is at the bottom it is a REPEAT … UNTIL loop. A diamond whose two paths rejoin further down is an IF.

fragments.label: Writing pseudocode from structured English and from a flowchart
fragments.text: Check the loop condition's direction: a flowchart that loops back on 'No' to 'Count = 9?' becomes UNTIL Count = 9.

fragments.label: Writing pseudocode from structured English and from a flowchart
fragments.text: Keep the flowchart's identifiers exactly; examiners check they are used consistently.

fragments.label: Writing pseudocode from structured English and from a flowchart
fragments.text: Dry-run the pseudocode with the same data as the flowchart to confirm they agree.

fragments.label: Writing pseudocode from structured English and from a flowchart
fragments.text:
Structured English:
SET total points to zero
INPUT amount spent
WHILE amount is not zero
   CALCULATE points as the number of whole tens in the amount
   IF amount is 100 or more THEN DOUBLE the points
   ADD points to total points
   INPUT next amount
OUTPUT total points

Identifier table:
Identifier  | Data type | Explanation
Amount      | INTEGER   | amount spent on one purchase; 0 ends the input
Points      | INTEGER   | points for the current purchase
TotalPoints | INTEGER   | running total of points

fragments.label: Writing pseudocode from structured English and from a flowchart
fragments.text:
DECLARE Amount : INTEGER
DECLARE Points : INTEGER
DECLARE TotalPoints : INTEGER
TotalPoints ← 0
INPUT Amount
WHILE Amount <> 0
   Points ← Amount DIV 10
   IF Amount >= 100
      THEN
         Points ← Points * 2
   ENDIF
   TotalPoints ← TotalPoints + Points
   INPUT Amount
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT "Points earned: ", TotalPoints

fragments.label: Writing pseudocode from structured English and from a flowchart
fragments.text:
Amount | Points | TotalPoints | OUTPUT
       |        | 0           |
45     | 4      | 4           |
120    | 24     | 28          |   (120 DIV 10 = 12, doubled)
9      | 0      | 28          |
0      |        |             | Points earned: 28

fragments.label: Writing pseudocode from structured English and from a flowchart
fragments.text:
( START )
              |
         / INPUT N /
              |
      [ Result ← 1  ]
      [ Counter ← 1 ]
              |
   +--------->|
   |          v
   |   < Counter <= N ? > --No--> / OUTPUT Result / --> ( END )
   |          | Yes
   |  [ Result ← Result * Counter ]
   |  [ Counter ← Counter + 1     ]
   |          |
   +----------+

The test comes before the body and the arrow returns above it, so this is a pre-condition (WHILE) loop.

fragments.label: Writing pseudocode from structured English and from a flowchart
fragments.text:
DECLARE N : INTEGER
DECLARE Result : INTEGER
DECLARE Counter : INTEGER
INPUT N
Result ← 1
Counter ← 1
WHILE Counter <= N
   Result ← Result * Counter
   Counter ← Counter + 1
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT Result

fragments.label: Writing pseudocode from structured English and from a flowchart
fragments.text:
N | Counter | Result | Counter <= N? | OUTPUT
4 | 1       | 1      | TRUE          |
  | 2       | 1      | TRUE          |
  | 3       | 2      | TRUE          |
  | 4       | 6      | TRUE          |
  | 5       | 24     | FALSE         | 24

4! = 1 × 2 × 3 × 4 = 24.
Drawing a flowchart from structured English and from pseudocode

fragments.label: Drawing a flowchart from structured English and from pseudocode
fragments.text: Drawing a flowchart is the reverse process: give each statement its standard shape and join them in execution order. Start and finish with terminators. Each INPUT or OUTPUT becomes a parallelogram and each assignment a rectangle. Each IF becomes a diamond whose Yes and No paths rejoin after the ENDIF. A CALL becomes a subroutine box.

fragments.label: Drawing a flowchart from structured English and from pseudocode
fragments.text: Loops are drawn with a decision and an arrow going back. For WHILE, the diamond sits before the body and the 'continue' exit leads into the body. For REPEAT … UNTIL, the body comes first and the diamond sits after it, with the exit for 'condition FALSE' going back to the top of the body. For FOR, draw the counter being set, a diamond testing whether it has passed the end value, and a rectangle adding 1 at the end of the body.

fragments.label: Drawing a flowchart from structured English and from pseudocode
fragments.text: Label both exits of every diamond.

fragments.label: Drawing a flowchart from structured English and from pseudocode
fragments.text: One START and one END; every path must reach END.

fragments.label: Drawing a flowchart from structured English and from pseudocode
fragments.text: Keep the same identifiers and conditions as the source so the two versions can be checked against each other.

fragments.label: Drawing a flowchart from structured English and from pseudocode
fragments.text:
Structured English:
INPUT the room temperature
IF the temperature is below 18 THEN switch the heater on
OTHERWISE switch the heater off

              ( START )
                  |
            / INPUT Temp /
                  |
            < Temp < 18 ? >
           Yes |        | No
   [ Heater ← TRUE ]  [ Heater ← FALSE ]
               |        |
               +---+----+
                   |
                ( END )

Tests: Temp = 17 gives Heater TRUE; Temp = 18 gives Heater FALSE (18 is not below 18).

fragments.label: Drawing a flowchart from structured English and from pseudocode
fragments.text:
( START )
                  |
           [ Tries ← 0 ]
                  |
   +------------->|
   |              v
   |       / INPUT Attempt /
   |              |
   |      [ Tries ← Tries + 1 ]
   |              |
   |  < Attempt = "Orange7" OR Tries = 3 ? >
   +------No------+
                  | Yes
        < Attempt = "Orange7" ? >
        Yes |              | No
 / OUTPUT "Access granted" /  / OUTPUT "Locked" /
            |              |
            +------+-------+
                   |
                ( END )

The body is drawn before the test, which is what makes this a post-condition loop.
Stepwise refinement

fragments.label: Stepwise refinement
fragments.text: Stepwise refinement takes an outline solution, a handful of broad steps, and repeatedly rewrites each step as a list of smaller, more exact steps. It stops when every step is a single input, output, assignment, selection or loop, so the result can be typed straight into a programming language. Numbering the levels (1, then 1.1, 1.2, then 1.2.1 …) shows which step each detail came from.

fragments.label: Stepwise refinement
fragments.text: It is the algorithm-level version of decomposition from 9.1. Decomposition splits the problem into modules; stepwise refinement adds detail to the steps inside them. The refinements also reveal decisions the outline hid, such as how invalid input is handled or when a loop ends.

fragments.label: Stepwise refinement
fragments.text: Refine one step at a time and keep the higher-level step as a comment, so the design remains readable.

fragments.label: Stepwise refinement
fragments.text: A step is detailed enough when it maps to one pseudocode construct without further explanation.

fragments.label: Stepwise refinement
fragments.text: Refinement often uncovers extra identifiers; add them to the identifier table as they appear.

fragments.label: Stepwise refinement
fragments.text:
Level 1 (outline):
1 Set up: input the class size, set the pass count to 0
2 For each student: get a mark, grade it, output the grade, update the pass count
3 Output the number of passes

Level 2 (refining step 2):
2.1 Input a mark, repeating until it is between 0 and 100
2.2 Decide the grade: 70 or more is Distinction, 40 to 69 is Pass, below 40 is Fail
2.3 Output the student number and grade
2.4 If the mark is 40 or more, add 1 to the pass count

Level 3 (refining 2.1 and 2.2 into constructs):
2.1.1 REPEAT INPUT Mark UNTIL Mark >= 0 AND Mark <= 100
2.2.1 IF Mark >= 70 THEN Distinction
2.2.2 ELSE IF Mark >= 40 THEN Pass
2.2.3 ELSE Fail

fragments.label: Stepwise refinement
fragments.text:
DECLARE ClassSize : INTEGER
DECLARE Student : INTEGER
DECLARE Mark : INTEGER
DECLARE Passes : INTEGER
DECLARE Grade : STRING
// 1 set up
Passes ← 0
INPUT ClassSize
// 2 each student
FOR Student ← 1 TO ClassSize
   REPEAT                                 // 2.1
      INPUT Mark
   UNTIL Mark >= 0 AND Mark <= 100
   IF Mark >= 70                          // 2.2
      THEN
         Grade ← "Distinction"
      ELSE
         IF Mark >= 40
            THEN
               Grade ← "Pass"
            ELSE
               Grade ← "Fail"
         ENDIF
   ENDIF
   OUTPUT Student, ": ", Grade             // 2.3
   IF Mark >= 40                          // 2.4
      THEN
         Passes ← Passes + 1
   ENDIF
NEXT Student
// 3 report
OUTPUT "Passes: ", Passes

fragments.label: Stepwise refinement
fragments.text:
ClassSize | Student | Mark | Grade       | Passes | OUTPUT
3         |         |      |             | 0      |
          | 1       | 72   | Distinction | 1      | 1: Distinction
          | 2       | 150  |             |        |   (UNTIL is FALSE, input again)
          |         | 45   | Pass        | 2      | 2: Pass
          | 3       | 38   | Fail        | 2      | 3: Fail
          |         |      |             |        | Passes: 2
What is an algorithm?

fragments.label: What is an algorithm?
fragments.text: A finite set of exact steps, carried out in a fixed order, that solves a problem.
What three things does an identifier table record?

fragments.label: What three things does an identifier table record?
fragments.text: Each identifier's name, its data type and an explanation of what it stores or does.
Name the three basic constructs.

fragments.label: Name the three basic constructs.
fragments.text: Sequence, selection and iteration (repetition).
Which loop always runs its body at least once?

fragments.label: Which loop always runs its body at least once?
fragments.text: REPEAT … UNTIL (a post-condition loop).
When should you use a FOR loop?

fragments.label: When should you use a FOR loop?
fragments.text: When the number of repetitions is known before the loop starts.
How is 'between 13 and 19 inclusive' written as a logic statement?

fragments.label: How is 'between 13 and 19 inclusive' written as a logic statement?
fragments.text: Age >= 13 AND Age <= 19
What is a rogue value?

fragments.label: What is a rogue value?
fragments.text: A value of the right data type but outside the normal range, used only to mark the end of input, such as -1 for marks.
What is stepwise refinement?

fragments.label: What is stepwise refinement?
fragments.text: Repeatedly breaking each step of an outline solution into smaller steps until each can be programmed directly.

Topic 10.1 is about choosing how each item of data is stored. At AS level the pseudocode types are INTEGER, REAL, CHAR, STRING, BOOLEAN and DATE, plus ARRAY and FILE for collections and stored files. Exam questions ask for the type of each variable in an identifier table, with a reason tied to what the value is and how it will be used. The second half covers the record: a user-defined type that keeps several fields of different types together under one identifier. You need to be able to write the TYPE … ENDTYPE definition, declare a variable or an array of that type, and put data into fields and read it back out with dot notation.

fragments.label: Data type
fragments.text: The kind of value an identifier can hold. It fixes which values are allowed, how much memory is set aside and which operations make sense, such as arithmetic on numbers or joining on strings.

fragments.label: Primitive (atomic) data type
fragments.text: A type built into the language that holds a single value and cannot be split into smaller parts, such as INTEGER, REAL, CHAR or BOOLEAN.

fragments.label: INTEGER
fragments.text: A signed whole number with no fractional part, for example -3, 0 or 250.

fragments.label: REAL
fragments.text: A signed number that can have a fractional part; in pseudocode a REAL literal is written with a decimal point and a digit on each side, for example 4.0 or -0.75.

fragments.label: CHAR
fragments.text: Exactly one character, written in single quotes, for example 'Y' or '7'.

fragments.label: STRING
fragments.text: A sequence of zero or more characters, written in double quotes; "" is the empty string.

fragments.label: BOOLEAN
fragments.text: A type with only two values, TRUE and FALSE, used for flags and the results of conditions.

fragments.label: DATE
fragments.text: A calendar date (day, month and year), written in pseudocode as dd/mm/yyyy, which the language can compare and calculate with.

fragments.label: Record (composite, user-defined type)
fragments.text: A type the programmer defines that groups a fixed set of named fields, possibly of different data types, so that all the data about one item is held under one identifier.

fragments.label: Field
fragments.text: One named, typed part of a record, reached with dot notation such as Student.Name.
Primitive data types: INTEGER, REAL, CHAR and BOOLEAN

fragments.label: Primitive data types: INTEGER, REAL, CHAR and BOOLEAN
fragments.text: When you plan an algorithm, each identifier in the identifier table needs a data type as well as a name and a purpose. The simplest types are the primitive (also called atomic) types, which the language provides directly and which each hold one indivisible value.

fragments.label: Primitive data types: INTEGER, REAL, CHAR and BOOLEAN
fragments.text: INTEGER holds signed whole numbers, so it suits anything that is counted rather than measured: loop counters, array indexes, the number of items in stock, a year. REAL holds numbers that may have a fractional part, so it suits measurements and results of division, such as a height in metres, a price or an average. CHAR holds exactly one character, for instance a menu choice 'A' to 'D' or a grade. BOOLEAN holds TRUE or FALSE and is the natural type for any yes/no fact or flag, such as whether a value has been found.

fragments.label: Primitive data types: INTEGER, REAL, CHAR and BOOLEAN
fragments.text: Cambridge pseudocode also fixes how literal values of each type are written. An INTEGER literal is plain digits, optionally with a minus sign. A REAL literal always has a decimal point with at least one digit on each side, so 5.0 not 5. or .5. A CHAR literal goes in single quotes and a STRING literal in double quotes. TRUE and FALSE are written in capitals without quotes.

fragments.label: Primitive data types: INTEGER, REAL, CHAR and BOOLEAN
fragments.text: Counted values (how many, which position) are INTEGER; measured or calculated values that may not be whole are REAL.

fragments.label: Primitive data types: INTEGER, REAL, CHAR and BOOLEAN
fragments.text: Any value produced by '/' division should be stored as REAL, even when the inputs are integers.

fragments.label: Primitive data types: INTEGER, REAL, CHAR and BOOLEAN
fragments.text: CHAR is for one character only; 'Y' is a CHAR but "Yes" must be a STRING.

fragments.label: Primitive data types: INTEGER, REAL, CHAR and BOOLEAN
fragments.text: Use BOOLEAN for two-state data rather than an INTEGER 0/1 or a STRING "yes"/"no"; it can be tested directly in a condition.

fragments.label: Primitive data types: INTEGER, REAL, CHAR and BOOLEAN
fragments.text:
DECLARE ItemsInBasket : INTEGER
DECLARE MeanSpeed : REAL
DECLARE MenuChoice : CHAR
DECLARE IsMember : BOOLEAN

ItemsInBasket ← 12
MeanSpeed ← 48.5          // REAL: decimal point with digits both sides
MenuChoice ← 'C'          // CHAR: single quotes, one character
IsMember ← FALSE          // BOOLEAN: no quotes
STRING, DATE, ARRAY and FILE

fragments.label: STRING, DATE, ARRAY and FILE
fragments.text: A STRING is a sequence of characters, so it is a structured rather than atomic type: you can take its length or pick out part of it. It may hold no characters at all (the empty string ""), which is useful as a starting value when a string is built up in a loop. The number 12 and the string "12" are different values: 12 can be used in arithmetic, while "12" is two characters and "12" & "3" gives "123".

fragments.label: STRING, DATE, ARRAY and FILE
fragments.text: A DATE holds a day, month and year. It exists as a separate type because programs often need to compare dates or work out the gap between them, and a date held as text cannot do this reliably: compared as strings, "09/05/2025" counts as earlier than "10/01/2024" because the first characters, '0' and '1', settle the comparison, even though the 2025 date is really the later one. In pseudocode a date literal is written dd/mm/yyyy, for example 21/06/2008.

fragments.label: STRING, DATE, ARRAY and FILE
fragments.text: The syllabus list also contains ARRAY and FILE. ARRAY is used when many values of the same type are kept under one identifier, for example DECLARE Marks : ARRAY[1:30] OF INTEGER (see 10.2). FILE is the type of data stored outside the program, for example a text file opened with OPENFILE and read line by line (see 10.3). In an identifier table these appear in the data type column just like the primitive types.

fragments.label: STRING, DATE, ARRAY and FILE
fragments.text: STRING is for text and for codes that are never used in arithmetic, even if they contain only digits.

fragments.label: STRING, DATE, ARRAY and FILE
fragments.text: The empty string "" is a valid STRING value with length 0.

fragments.label: STRING, DATE, ARRAY and FILE
fragments.text: DATE lets dates be compared and subtracted correctly; STRING dates only compare character by character.

fragments.label: STRING, DATE, ARRAY and FILE
fragments.text: ARRAY and FILE are also pseudocode data types: an identifier table may show ARRAY[1:30] OF INTEGER or FILE as the type.

fragments.label: STRING, DATE, ARRAY and FILE
fragments.text:
DECLARE FullName : STRING
DECLARE Initials : STRING
DECLARE JoinDate : DATE
DECLARE Marks : ARRAY[1:30] OF INTEGER

FullName ← "Leila Haddad"
Initials ← ""                // empty string, filled in later
JoinDate ← 04/09/2025        // DATE literal dd/mm/yyyy
Initials ← Initials & 'L' & 'H'
OUTPUT Initials                 // LH
Selecting and justifying a data type

fragments.label: Selecting and justifying a data type
fragments.text: In Paper 2 you are often given a scenario and asked to complete an identifier table or to state and justify the data type of a variable. The type should follow from two questions: what values can this item take, and what will the program do with it? A justification earns the mark when it names the property that decides the choice, for instance 'always a whole number', 'may contain a fractional part', 'only ever one of two values' or 'contains a leading zero and is not used in calculations'.

fragments.label: Selecting and justifying a data type
fragments.text: The commonest trap is data that looks numeric but is really an identifier: telephone numbers, ISBNs, postcodes, product codes and candidate numbers. These are STRING because they may start with 0 or contain spaces, letters or '+', and nobody adds or averages them. On the other side, choose REAL, not INTEGER, whenever the value could legitimately be non-whole, and INTEGER, not REAL, for anything used as a counter or an array index.

fragments.label: Selecting and justifying a data type
fragments.text: State the type, then give a reason based on the data (whole number, fractional part, one character, two states, calendar date, text).

fragments.label: Selecting and justifying a data type
fragments.text: Numeric-looking codes that are never used in arithmetic are STRING, which also keeps leading zeros.

fragments.label: Selecting and justifying a data type
fragments.text: Money is usually REAL (for example 14.99); a quantity or count is INTEGER.

fragments.label: Selecting and justifying a data type
fragments.text: A single-letter code such as a size 'S', 'M', 'L' is CHAR; a value that is sometimes more than one character is STRING.

fragments.label: Selecting and justifying a data type
fragments.text:
Identifier     | Data type | Justification
MemberCode     | STRING    | e.g. "0041-B": leading zero and a letter, never used in arithmetic
Surname        | STRING    | text of varying length
DateJoined     | DATE      | a calendar date that is compared with today's date
VisitsThisYear | INTEGER   | a count, always a whole number
MonthlyFee     | REAL      | money, e.g. 27.50, has a fractional part
AgeBand        | CHAR      | one letter: 'J' junior, 'A' adult, 'S' senior
IsActive       | BOOLEAN   | only two possible states, active or not
Phone          | STRING    | starts with 0 or +, may contain spaces
The purpose of a record structure

fragments.label: The purpose of a record structure
fragments.text: Some data items belong together because they all describe one thing. A library book has a title (STRING), an ISBN (STRING), a year of publication (INTEGER), a price (REAL) and a flag for whether it is on loan (BOOLEAN). These values have different types, so they cannot share an array, which needs every element to be the same type.

fragments.label: The purpose of a record structure
fragments.text: A record solves this. The programmer defines a new record type that lists the fields and their types; the language does not supply it, which is why a record is called a user-defined type, and because it is built from other types it is also called a composite type. A variable of that type then holds one complete set of field values under a single identifier, so everything about one book travels together: it can be assigned, passed to a procedure or stored in an array as one unit.

fragments.label: The purpose of a record structure
fragments.text: Be careful not to confuse this with a record in a database table (topic 8). A record data structure is a type inside a program; a database record is a row in a table. The idea is similar, one set of values about one entity, but the exam context tells you which is meant.

fragments.label: The purpose of a record structure
fragments.text: Purpose: to hold a set of related data of different data types under one identifier.

fragments.label: The purpose of a record structure
fragments.text: Each field has its own name and its own data type; the set of fields is fixed when the type is defined.

fragments.label: The purpose of a record structure
fragments.text: A record is user-defined (the programmer declares it) and composite (made of other types).

fragments.label: The purpose of a record structure
fragments.text: An array holds many values of one type; a record holds several named values of possibly different types.
Defining a record type and declaring record variables

fragments.label: Defining a record type and declaring record variables
fragments.text: A record type is defined with TYPE, the type name, one DECLARE line per field, and ENDTYPE. The definition only describes the layout: no data exists yet, in the same way that the word INTEGER on its own stores nothing. A separate DECLARE statement then creates a variable of the new type, and every such variable gets its own copy of every field.

fragments.label: Defining a record type and declaring record variables
fragments.text: Choose each field's type using the same rules as for ordinary variables (see the section on justifying a data type), and give the type a name that makes clear it is a type, such as StudentRecord or BookType, so it is not mistaken for a variable.

fragments.label: Defining a record type and declaring record variables
fragments.text: TYPE … ENDTYPE defines the structure; DECLARE Variable : TypeName creates storage.

fragments.label: Defining a record type and declaring record variables
fragments.text: Every field line inside the TYPE block has the form DECLARE FieldName : DataType.

fragments.label: Defining a record type and declaring record variables
fragments.text: Two variables of the same record type have independent fields: changing Student1.Name leaves Student2.Name alone.

fragments.label: Defining a record type and declaring record variables
fragments.text: A field can itself be an ARRAY or another record type, but at AS level fields are usually primitive types, STRING or DATE.

fragments.label: Defining a record type and declaring record variables
fragments.text:
TYPE StudentRecord
   DECLARE StudentID : STRING
   DECLARE Name : STRING
   DECLARE DateOfBirth : DATE
   DECLARE TestMark : INTEGER
   DECLARE FeesPaid : BOOLEAN
ENDTYPE

DECLARE Student : StudentRecord
DECLARE Prefect : StudentRecord
Saving data to and reading data from a record

fragments.label: Saving data to and reading data from a record
fragments.text: Each field is reached with dot notation: the variable identifier, a full stop, then the field identifier, as in Student.TestMark. A field used this way behaves exactly like an ordinary variable of the field's type. To save data to a record you assign to its fields, either from literals, from calculations or directly from INPUT. To read data from a record you use the fields in expressions, conditions or OUTPUT statements.

fragments.label: Saving data to and reading data from a record
fragments.text: You cannot assign a single value to the whole record variable (Student ← "Aisha" is wrong, because Student is not a STRING). The one whole-record operation allowed is copying one record variable into another of the same type, for example Prefect ← Student, which copies every field at once.

fragments.label: Saving data to and reading data from a record
fragments.text: Write: Student.Name ← "Aisha" or INPUT Student.Name.

fragments.label: Saving data to and reading data from a record
fragments.text: Read: OUTPUT Student.Name or IF Student.FeesPaid = FALSE THEN …

fragments.label: Saving data to and reading data from a record
fragments.text: A field has the type given in the TYPE block, so Student.TestMark + 5 is INTEGER arithmetic.

fragments.label: Saving data to and reading data from a record
fragments.text: Record ← Record of the same type copies all fields; Record ← single value is an error.

fragments.label: Saving data to and reading data from a record
fragments.text:
// save data to the record
Student.StudentID ← "S1042"
Student.Name ← "Aisha"
Student.DateOfBirth ← 14/03/2008
INPUT Student.TestMark                // user types 72
Student.FeesPaid ← FALSE

// read data from the record
IF Student.FeesPaid = FALSE
   THEN
      OUTPUT Student.Name, " has fees outstanding"
ENDIF
Student.TestMark ← Student.TestMark + 3   // moderation adds 3 marks
OUTPUT Student.Name, ": ", Student.TestMark

Output:
Aisha has fees outstanding
Aisha: 75

Only TestMark changes (72 to 75); StudentID, DateOfBirth and FeesPaid keep the values saved at the start.
Arrays of records

fragments.label: Arrays of records
fragments.text: One record variable holds one item. To hold a whole class or a whole stock list, declare an array whose element type is the record type. Each element is then a complete record, and a field of one element is written with the index first and the field second: Class[3].Name is the Name field of the third student.

fragments.label: Arrays of records
fragments.text: Because the element number can be a loop counter, the same few lines can save data into, or read data out of, every record in turn. This is the main practical reason for records: without them you would need a separate parallel 1D array for each field (IDs, names, dates, marks, flags) and would have to keep the same index lined up across all of them.

fragments.label: Arrays of records
fragments.text: DECLARE Class : ARRAY[1:30] OF StudentRecord creates 30 records.

fragments.label: Arrays of records
fragments.text: Syntax order: ArrayName[Index].FieldName.

fragments.label: Arrays of records
fragments.text: A FOR loop over the index processes every record; inside it, each field is used like a normal variable.

fragments.label: Arrays of records
fragments.text: An array of records replaces several parallel arrays and keeps each item's data together.

fragments.label: Arrays of records
fragments.text:
DECLARE Class : ARRAY[1:4] OF StudentRecord
DECLARE Index : INTEGER
DECLARE Total : INTEGER

// save: fill every record from input
FOR Index ← 1 TO 4
   INPUT Class[Index].StudentID
   INPUT Class[Index].Name
   INPUT Class[Index].DateOfBirth
   INPUT Class[Index].TestMark
   INPUT Class[Index].FeesPaid
NEXT Index

// read: average mark and names of students who still owe fees
Total ← 0
FOR Index ← 1 TO 4
   Total ← Total + Class[Index].TestMark
   IF Class[Index].FeesPaid = FALSE
      THEN
         OUTPUT Class[Index].Name
   ENDIF
NEXT Index
OUTPUT "Average: ", Total / 4

fragments.label: Arrays of records
fragments.text:
Data stored:
Index | StudentID | Name  | DateOfBirth | TestMark | FeesPaid
1     | "S1042"   | Aisha | 14/03/2008  | 72       | TRUE
2     | "S1043"   | Ben   | 02/11/2007  | 58       | FALSE
3     | "S1044"   | Chen  | 21/06/2008  | 85       | TRUE
4     | "S1045"   | Dara  | 09/01/2008  | 41       | FALSE

Second loop:
Index | Class[Index].TestMark | Total | FeesPaid | OUTPUT
1     | 72                    | 72    | TRUE     |
2     | 58                    | 130   | FALSE    | Ben
3     | 85                    | 215   | TRUE     |
4     | 41                    | 256   | FALSE    | Dara
after loop                                       | Average: 64.0

256 / 4 = 64.0 (the result of '/' is REAL). Checked with an equivalent Python run.
Justifying a record over separate variables or parallel arrays

fragments.label: Justifying a record over separate variables or parallel arrays
fragments.text: When a question asks why a record is suitable, link the answer to the data. The fields all describe one entity (one student, one book, one parcel) and they have different data types, so no single array can hold them, but a record type can. Keeping them under one identifier means the program cannot accidentally pair the name of one student with the mark of another, which is a real risk with parallel arrays if one array is sorted and the others are not.

fragments.label: Justifying a record over separate variables or parallel arrays
fragments.text: Records also make code shorter and clearer. A whole record can be passed to a procedure as one parameter, copied in one assignment, or swapped in one step during a sort, instead of handling five separate values. When the collection grows, an array of records scales with a single declaration, whereas separate variables would need new names for every extra item.

fragments.label: Justifying a record over separate variables or parallel arrays
fragments.text: A record is not the right choice for everything. Many values of the same type that are processed together, such as 52 weekly rainfall readings, belong in an array. A record fits the attributes of one item; an array fits a list of similar items; an array of records fits a list of items that each have several attributes.

fragments.label: Justifying a record over separate variables or parallel arrays
fragments.text: Purpose answer: groups related data of different types about one item under one identifier.

fragments.label: Justifying a record over separate variables or parallel arrays
fragments.text: Benefit: fields stay together, so data for one item cannot become misaligned as it can across parallel arrays.

fragments.label: Justifying a record over separate variables or parallel arrays
fragments.text: Benefit: one record can be passed, copied or swapped as a single unit.

fragments.label: Justifying a record over separate variables or parallel arrays
fragments.text: Same-type lists belong in an array; mixed-type attributes of one item belong in a record.
List the eight pseudocode data types named in the syllabus.

fragments.label: List the eight pseudocode data types named in the syllabus.
fragments.text: INTEGER, REAL, CHAR, STRING, BOOLEAN, DATE, ARRAY and FILE.
Why should a telephone number be stored as STRING?

fragments.label: Why should a telephone number be stored as STRING?
fragments.text: It may start with 0 or contain spaces or '+', and it is never used in arithmetic; an INTEGER would drop the leading zero and could not hold the other characters.
How is a REAL literal written in Cambridge pseudocode?

fragments.label: How is a REAL literal written in Cambridge pseudocode?
fragments.text: With a decimal point and at least one digit on each side, for example 7.0 or 0.5.
What is the purpose of a record structure?

fragments.label: What is the purpose of a record structure?
fragments.text: To hold a set of related data items, which may be of different data types, under one identifier.
Why is a record called a user-defined or composite type?

fragments.label: Why is a record called a user-defined or composite type?
fragments.text: User-defined because the programmer declares its fields rather than the language supplying it; composite because it is built from other data types.
Write the statement that sets the mark of the second student in array Class to 64.

fragments.label: Write the statement that sets the mark of the second student in array Class to 64.
fragments.text: Class[2].TestMark ← 64
What does TYPE BookType … ENDTYPE create on its own?

fragments.label: What does TYPE BookType … ENDTYPE create on its own?
fragments.text: Only a definition of the layout; no storage exists until a variable such as DECLARE Book : BookType is declared.

Topic 10.2 covers arrays: a list (1D array) or a table (2D array) of values of one data type, stored under one identifier and reached by an index. You need the vocabulary (element, index, lower bound, upper bound), the Cambridge declarations such as DECLARE Marks : ARRAY[1:10] OF INTEGER and DECLARE Sales : ARRAY[1:3, 1:4] OF INTEGER, and the loop patterns that process them: filling, totalling, finding the largest value, and nested loops over rows and columns. The syllabus also places two standard algorithms here: a linear search that stops when the item is found, and a bubble sort, including the efficient version that shortens each pass and stops as soon as a pass makes no swaps. Paper 2 expects these to be written from memory and dry-run with a trace table.

fragments.label: Array
fragments.text: An ordered, fixed-size collection of elements that all have the same data type, stored under one identifier and accessed by index.

fragments.label: Element
fragments.text: One item stored in an array, such as Marks[4] or Sales[2, 3].

fragments.label: Index
fragments.text: The position number used to select an element; a 1D array uses one index and a 2D array uses a row index and a column index.

fragments.label: Lower bound
fragments.text: The smallest valid index of an array dimension, fixed in the declaration (often 1, sometimes 0).

fragments.label: Upper bound
fragments.text: The largest valid index of an array dimension; the number of elements in that dimension is upper bound - lower bound + 1.

fragments.label: 1D array
fragments.text: An array with one dimension, used like a numbered list, for example ARRAY[1:10] OF INTEGER.

fragments.label: 2D array
fragments.text: An array with two dimensions, used like a table of rows and columns; the row index is written first, for example Grid[Row, Column].

fragments.label: Linear search
fragments.text: A search that compares the target with each element in turn from the first, stopping when it is found or when every element has been checked.

fragments.label: Bubble sort
fragments.text: A sort that repeatedly passes through an array comparing adjacent elements and swapping any pair that is in the wrong order, until a pass makes no swaps.

fragments.label: Pass
fragments.text: One run of a bubble sort's inner loop along the unsorted part of the array; after each pass the largest remaining value has reached its final position.
Array terms: element, index, lower bound and upper bound

fragments.label: Array terms: element, index, lower bound and upper bound
fragments.text: An array lets a program keep many values of the same type under one name instead of inventing a separate variable for each. Thirty test marks stored as Mark1, Mark2 … Mark30 would need thirty INPUT statements; stored as Marks[1] to Marks[30] they can be handled by one loop whose counter supplies the position.

fragments.label: Array terms: element, index, lower bound and upper bound
fragments.text: The position is the index. The declaration fixes the lowest index (the lower bound) and the highest index (the upper bound) for each dimension, and the array keeps that size while the program runs, so it is a static structure. Cambridge pseudocode lets you choose the bounds: many exam questions start at 1, which matches how people number a list, while Python, Java and VB.NET start their arrays at 0. Always read the bounds from the declaration rather than assuming.

fragments.label: Array terms: element, index, lower bound and upper bound
fragments.text: The number of elements in a dimension is upper bound - lower bound + 1, so ARRAY[1:10] has 10 elements and ARRAY[0:25] has 26. An index outside the bounds refers to an element that does not exist; running such a statement causes a run-time error (an 'index out of range' or array bound error). A loop that stops one short of the upper bound does not crash but silently misses the last element, which is a logic error.

fragments.label: Array terms: element, index, lower bound and upper bound
fragments.text: Index: the position of an element. Lower bound: smallest index. Upper bound: largest index.

fragments.label: Array terms: element, index, lower bound and upper bound
fragments.text: Number of elements = upper bound - lower bound + 1.

fragments.label: Array terms: element, index, lower bound and upper bound
fragments.text: Every element has the same data type; the size is fixed at declaration.

fragments.label: Array terms: element, index, lower bound and upper bound
fragments.text: Index beyond a bound = run-time error; loop bound one too small = logic error (element skipped).

fragments.label: Array terms: element, index, lower bound and upper bound
fragments.text:
Declaration                              | Lower | Upper | Elements
DECLARE Letters : ARRAY[0:25] OF CHAR    | 0     | 25    | 26
DECLARE Marks : ARRAY[1:30] OF INTEGER   | 1     | 30    | 30
DECLARE Temps : ARRAY[1:7] OF REAL       | 1     | 7     | 7
DECLARE Sales : ARRAY[1:3, 1:4] OF INTEGER | rows 1-3, columns 1-4 | 3 x 4 = 12

Marks[31] ← 50 would fail at run time: 31 is above the upper bound 30.
Declaring and using a 1D array

fragments.label: Declaring and using a 1D array
fragments.text: A 1D array is declared with DECLARE, the identifier, the bounds in square brackets separated by a colon, and the element type after OF. An element is then written as the identifier followed by an index in square brackets, and that element can be used anywhere an ordinary variable of the element type could be: on the left of an assignment, in an INPUT statement, in a condition or in an OUTPUT.

fragments.label: Declaring and using a 1D array
fragments.text: The index does not have to be a literal. Any INTEGER expression works, which is what makes arrays powerful: inside FOR Index ← 1 TO 7 the element Temps[Index] means a different element on each iteration. Before an array's values are used they must be given values, typically by an initialisation loop that sets every element to a starting value such as 0, or by a loop of INPUT statements. Cambridge pseudocode also allows one array to be copied into another of the same size and type in a single assignment.

fragments.label: Declaring and using a 1D array
fragments.text: DECLARE Temps : ARRAY[1:7] OF REAL gives Temps[1] to Temps[7].

fragments.label: Declaring and using a 1D array
fragments.text: Temps[3] ← 18.5 saves a value; OUTPUT Temps[3] reads it.

fragments.label: Declaring and using a 1D array
fragments.text: The index can be a variable or expression, such as Temps[Day] or Values[J + 1].

fragments.label: Declaring and using a 1D array
fragments.text: Initialise every element (with a loop) before relying on its value.

fragments.label: Declaring and using a 1D array
fragments.text:
DECLARE Temps : ARRAY[1:7] OF REAL
DECLARE Day : INTEGER

// initialise every element
FOR Day ← 1 TO 7
   Temps[Day] ← 0.0
NEXT Day

// fill from input, one reading per day
FOR Day ← 1 TO 7
   OUTPUT "Temperature for day ", Day
   INPUT Temps[Day]
NEXT Day

OUTPUT "Wednesday: ", Temps[3]
Processing a 1D array: totals, averages and the largest value

fragments.label: Processing a 1D array: totals, averages and the largest value
fragments.text: Most array processing is one FOR loop from the lower bound to the upper bound with the loop counter used as the index. A total needs a variable set to 0 before the loop and increased by each element inside it; an average is the total divided by the number of elements after the loop, and should be REAL.

fragments.label: Processing a 1D array: totals, averages and the largest value
fragments.text: To find the largest value, start by assuming the first element is the largest, then compare each later element with the current largest and replace it when a bigger one appears. Starting from the first element, rather than from 0, means the method also works when every value is negative. Storing the index of the largest value as well as the value lets the program report where it is.

fragments.label: Processing a 1D array: totals, averages and the largest value
fragments.text: Total: set to 0 before the loop, add each element inside the loop.

fragments.label: Processing a 1D array: totals, averages and the largest value
fragments.text: Average: Total / number of elements, calculated after the loop and stored as REAL.

fragments.label: Processing a 1D array: totals, averages and the largest value
fragments.text: Maximum: start with the first element, replace when a larger element is found; also track its index.

fragments.label: Processing a 1D array: totals, averages and the largest value
fragments.text: Loop bounds must match the declaration exactly: FOR Index ← 1 TO 6 for ARRAY[1:6].

fragments.label: Processing a 1D array: totals, averages and the largest value
fragments.text:
DECLARE Marks : ARRAY[1:6] OF INTEGER
DECLARE Index, Total, Highest, HighPos : INTEGER
DECLARE Average : REAL

// Marks holds 54, 71, 38, 90, 66, 47
Total ← 0
Highest ← Marks[1]
HighPos ← 1
FOR Index ← 1 TO 6
   Total ← Total + Marks[Index]
   IF Marks[Index] > Highest
      THEN
         Highest ← Marks[Index]
         HighPos ← Index
   ENDIF
NEXT Index
Average ← Total / 6
OUTPUT "Total ", Total, ", average ", Average
OUTPUT "Highest ", Highest, " at position ", HighPos

fragments.label: Processing a 1D array: totals, averages and the largest value
fragments.text:
Index | Marks[Index] | Total | Highest | HighPos
      |              | 0     | 54      | 1
1     | 54           | 54    |         |
2     | 71           | 125   | 71      | 2
3     | 38           | 163   |         |
4     | 90           | 253   | 90      | 4
5     | 66           | 319   |         |
6     | 47           | 366   |         |

Average = 366 / 6 = 61.0
Output: Total 366, average 61.0
        Highest 90 at position 4
(An equivalent Python run gives the same total, average and position.)
Linear search

fragments.label: Linear search
fragments.text: A linear search looks for a target value by checking the elements one after another, starting at the lower bound. It needs no preparation: the data does not have to be sorted, which is why it is the standard search for an unordered array. Each check either finds the target, in which case the search can stop, or moves on to the next index. If the index passes the upper bound without a match, the target is not in the array.

fragments.label: Linear search
fragments.text: A good linear search stops as soon as the item is found, so it uses a conditional loop (WHILE or REPEAT) controlled by a BOOLEAN flag such as Found and by the index reaching the end. A FOR loop over the whole array also gives the right answer but always makes every comparison, even when the target is in the first position. In the worst case (the item is last, or absent) a linear search on n elements makes n comparisons; on average it makes about half that when the item is present.

fragments.label: Linear search
fragments.text: Works on unsorted data; compares elements in index order from the lower bound.

fragments.label: Linear search
fragments.text: Two stopping conditions: target found, or no elements left to check.

fragments.label: Linear search
fragments.text: Use a BOOLEAN Found flag and a WHILE/REPEAT loop so the search stops early.

fragments.label: Linear search
fragments.text: After the loop, test Found to decide between reporting the position and reporting 'not found'.

fragments.label: Linear search
fragments.text: Worst case n comparisons for n elements.

fragments.label: Linear search
fragments.text:
DECLARE Names : ARRAY[1:6] OF STRING
DECLARE SearchName : STRING
DECLARE Index : INTEGER
DECLARE Found : BOOLEAN

// Names holds "Ravi", "Mei", "Tomas", "Leila", "Owen", "Grace"
INPUT SearchName
Found ← FALSE
Index ← 1
WHILE Found = FALSE AND Index <= 6
   IF Names[Index] = SearchName
      THEN
         Found ← TRUE
      ELSE
         Index ← Index + 1
   ENDIF
ENDWHILE

IF Found = FALSE
   THEN
      OUTPUT SearchName, " is not in the list"
   ELSE
      OUTPUT SearchName, " is at position ", Index
ENDIF

fragments.label: Linear search
fragments.text:
Search 1: SearchName = "Leila"
Index | Names[Index] | Match? | Found
1     | "Ravi"       | no     | FALSE
2     | "Mei"        | no     | FALSE
3     | "Tomas"      | no     | FALSE
4     | "Leila"      | yes    | TRUE
Loop ends because Found = TRUE (4 comparisons).
Output: Leila is at position 4

Search 2: SearchName = "Sam"
Index | Names[Index] | Match? | Found
1     | "Ravi"       | no     | FALSE
2     | "Mei"        | no     | FALSE
3     | "Tomas"      | no     | FALSE
4     | "Leila"      | no     | FALSE
5     | "Owen"       | no     | FALSE
6     | "Grace"      | no     | FALSE
7     | (not read)   |        | FALSE
Loop ends because Index <= 6 is FALSE (6 comparisons). Names[7] is never accessed.
Output: Sam is not in the list

(An equivalent Python search returns position 4 after 4 comparisons and not found after 6.)
Bubble sort

fragments.label: Bubble sort
fragments.text: A bubble sort puts an array into order by comparing neighbouring elements. Starting at the lower bound, it compares elements 1 and 2 and swaps them if the first is larger, then compares 2 and 3, and so on to the end. That complete run is one pass. During a pass the largest value keeps being swapped forward, so at the end of the first pass it sits in the last element, which is now final. The next pass does the same for the rest of the array, placing the second largest value, and so on.

fragments.label: Bubble sort
fragments.text: Swapping two elements needs a temporary variable: copy the first element to Temp, copy the second into the first, then copy Temp into the second. Without Temp, the first value would be overwritten and lost.

fragments.label: Bubble sort
fragments.text: For an array of n elements, n - 1 passes are always enough. Because the end of the array fills up with finished values, each pass can stop one position earlier than the last; a variable (here Boundary) holds the last index to compare and is reduced by 1 after every pass. The algorithm uses nested loops: the outer loop counts passes and the inner loop moves along the array comparing pairs. To sort into descending order, change the comparison from > to <.

fragments.label: Bubble sort
fragments.text: Compare adjacent pairs; swap if Values[J] > Values[J + 1] (ascending).

fragments.label: Bubble sort
fragments.text: A swap uses Temp: Temp ← a, a ← b, b ← Temp.

fragments.label: Bubble sort
fragments.text: After pass k the largest k values are in their final positions at the end of the array.

fragments.label: Bubble sort
fragments.text: At most n - 1 passes; the inner loop's end can be reduced by 1 after each pass.

fragments.label: Bubble sort
fragments.text: Descending order: use < in the comparison.

fragments.label: Bubble sort
fragments.text:
DECLARE Values : ARRAY[1:5] OF INTEGER
DECLARE Pass, J, Boundary, Temp : INTEGER

// Values holds 7, 3, 9, 1, 5
Boundary ← 4                       // last J to compare: upper bound - 1
FOR Pass ← 1 TO 4                  // n - 1 passes
   FOR J ← 1 TO Boundary
      IF Values[J] > Values[J + 1]
         THEN
            Temp ← Values[J]
            Values[J] ← Values[J + 1]
            Values[J + 1] ← Temp
      ENDIF
   NEXT J
   Boundary ← Boundary - 1         // last element of this pass is now final
NEXT Pass

fragments.label: Bubble sort
fragments.text:
Pass 1 (J = 1 to 4)
  J=1: 7 > 3 swap  -> 3 7 9 1 5
  J=2: 7 > 9 no    -> 3 7 9 1 5
  J=3: 9 > 1 swap  -> 3 7 1 9 5
  J=4: 9 > 5 swap  -> 3 7 1 5 9     9 is now final
Pass 2 (J = 1 to 3)
  J=1: 3 > 7 no    -> 3 7 1 5 9
  J=2: 7 > 1 swap  -> 3 1 7 5 9
  J=3: 7 > 5 swap  -> 3 1 5 7 9     7 is now final
Pass 3 (J = 1 to 2)
  J=1: 3 > 1 swap  -> 1 3 5 7 9
  J=2: 3 > 5 no    -> 1 3 5 7 9
Pass 4 (J = 1 to 1)
  J=1: 1 > 3 no    -> 1 3 5 7 9

After pass: 1: 3 7 1 5 9 | 2: 3 1 5 7 9 | 3: 1 3 5 7 9 | 4: 1 3 5 7 9
Comparisons: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10. Pass 4 changes nothing: the array was already sorted after pass 3.
(An equivalent Python run produces the same four states and 10 comparisons.)
Efficient bubble sort: a swap flag and shorter passes

fragments.label: Efficient bubble sort: a swap flag and shorter passes
fragments.text: The fixed-pass version keeps going even after the data is in order. The improvement rests on one observation: if a whole pass makes no swaps, every adjacent pair is already in order, so the array is sorted and the algorithm can stop. A BOOLEAN flag records this. It is set to TRUE (no swaps yet) at the start of each pass and set to FALSE whenever a swap happens; the outer loop becomes a REPEAT … UNTIL that ends when a pass finishes with the flag still TRUE.

fragments.label: Efficient bubble sort: a swap flag and shorter passes
fragments.text: Keeping the reducing boundary as well gives the efficient bubble sort that mark schemes look for: a conditional outer loop, the flag reset at the start of each pass, the flag changed inside the swap, and the inner loop's end reduced after each pass. On nearly sorted data it can finish after one or two passes; on already sorted data it needs just one pass of n - 1 comparisons. Its worst case (data in reverse order) is still about n²/2 comparisons, which is why bubble sort is only used for small arrays.

fragments.label: Efficient bubble sort: a swap flag and shorter passes
fragments.text: The same idea works on a 2D array or an array of records. When sorting rows of a table by one column, compare that column and swap the entire row (every column), or with an array of records swap whole records, so that each item's data stays together.

fragments.label: Efficient bubble sort: a swap flag and shorter passes
fragments.text: NoSwaps ← TRUE at the start of each pass; NoSwaps ← FALSE inside the swap.

fragments.label: Efficient bubble sort: a swap flag and shorter passes
fragments.text: Outer loop: REPEAT … UNTIL NoSwaps = TRUE (stops early once sorted).

fragments.label: Efficient bubble sort: a swap flag and shorter passes
fragments.text: Boundary ← Boundary - 1 after each pass so finished values are not compared again.

fragments.label: Efficient bubble sort: a swap flag and shorter passes
fragments.text: Best case (already sorted): one pass. Worst case (reverse order): n - 1 passes.

fragments.label: Efficient bubble sort: a swap flag and shorter passes
fragments.text: When sorting a table by one column, swap the whole row, not just the compared value.

fragments.label: Efficient bubble sort: a swap flag and shorter passes
fragments.text:
DECLARE Values : ARRAY[1:6] OF INTEGER
DECLARE J, Boundary, Temp : INTEGER
DECLARE NoSwaps : BOOLEAN

Boundary ← 5                       // upper bound - 1
REPEAT
   NoSwaps ← TRUE
   FOR J ← 1 TO Boundary
      IF Values[J] > Values[J + 1]
         THEN
            Temp ← Values[J]
            Values[J] ← Values[J + 1]
            Values[J + 1] ← Temp
            NoSwaps ← FALSE
      ENDIF
   NEXT J
   Boundary ← Boundary - 1
UNTIL NoSwaps = TRUE

fragments.label: Efficient bubble sort: a swap flag and shorter passes
fragments.text:
Pass 1 (Boundary = 5), NoSwaps starts TRUE
  J=1: 3 > 1 swap -> 1 3 4 6 5 8   NoSwaps = FALSE
  J=2: 3 > 4 no
  J=3: 4 > 6 no
  J=4: 6 > 5 swap -> 1 3 4 5 6 8   NoSwaps = FALSE
  J=5: 6 > 8 no
  end of pass: 1 3 4 5 6 8, Boundary becomes 4, NoSwaps = FALSE so repeat
Pass 2 (Boundary = 4), NoSwaps starts TRUE
  J=1..4: 1>3, 3>4, 4>5, 5>6 all no
  end of pass: 1 3 4 5 6 8, NoSwaps = TRUE so UNTIL ends the sort

Efficient version: 2 passes, 5 + 4 = 9 comparisons.
Fixed-pass version on the same data: 5 passes, 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15 comparisons.
For 7, 3, 9, 1, 5 the flag version still needs 4 passes (10 comparisons), because pass 3 made a swap.
(Checked with an equivalent Python run.)

fragments.label: Efficient bubble sort: a swap flag and shorter passes

fragments.text: Declaring and using a 2D array

fragments.label: Declaring and using a 2D array
fragments.text: A 2D array stores a table. Its declaration gives two pairs of bounds separated by a comma: the first pair is for the rows and the second for the columns, following the usual convention of naming the row first when you describe a cell of a table. DECLARE Sales : ARRAY[1:3, 1:4] OF INTEGER creates 3 rows and 4 columns, 12 elements in all, and every element must be an INTEGER.

fragments.label: Declaring and using a 2D array
fragments.text: An element is reached with two indexes in the same order: Sales[2, 3] is row 2, column 3. Mixing up the order is one of the most frequent errors; with a non-square table it may even produce an out-of-range index. As with 1D arrays the bounds are chosen by the programmer: rows and columns starting at 1 often match the problem (shop 1 to 3, quarter 1 to 4, a game board of rows 1 to 6).

fragments.label: Declaring and using a 2D array
fragments.text: DECLARE Name : ARRAY[RowLower:RowUpper, ColLower:ColUpper] OF Type.

fragments.label: Declaring and using a 2D array
fragments.text: Element count = rows x columns, e.g. 3 x 4 = 12.

fragments.label: Declaring and using a 2D array
fragments.text: Access as Name[Row, Column], row index first.

fragments.label: Declaring and using a 2D array
fragments.text: All elements share one data type.

fragments.label: Declaring and using a 2D array
fragments.text:
DECLARE Sales : ARRAY[1:3, 1:4] OF INTEGER   // 3 shops (rows), 4 quarters (columns)

Sales[1, 1] ← 12      // shop 1, quarter 1
Sales[2, 3] ← 14      // shop 2, quarter 3
OUTPUT Sales[2, 3]     // 14
Processing a 2D array with nested loops

fragments.label: Processing a 2D array with nested loops
fragments.text: Visiting every element of a table needs a loop inside a loop. The outer loop selects a row; for each row the inner loop runs through all the columns before the outer loop moves on, so the elements are visited row by row. The same pattern initialises a table, outputs it one row per line, or totals it.

fragments.label: Processing a 2D array with nested loops
fragments.text: Where a total is set matters. A total for each row is reset to 0 inside the outer loop but before the inner loop, and output after the inner loop finishes. A grand total is set to 0 once, before both loops. A column total swaps the roles: the outer loop runs over columns and the inner loop over rows.

fragments.label: Processing a 2D array with nested loops
fragments.text: Outer loop = rows, inner loop = columns, element = Table[Row, Column].

fragments.label: Processing a 2D array with nested loops
fragments.text: Row total: reset inside the outer loop, before the inner loop; output after the inner loop.

fragments.label: Processing a 2D array with nested loops
fragments.text: Grand total: reset once before both loops.

fragments.label: Processing a 2D array with nested loops
fragments.text: Column totals: make the column the outer loop.

fragments.label: Processing a 2D array with nested loops
fragments.text:
DECLARE Sales : ARRAY[1:3, 1:4] OF INTEGER
DECLARE Shop, Quarter, ShopTotal, GrandTotal : INTEGER

// Sales holds  row 1: 12 15  9 20
//              row 2:  8 11 14  6
//              row 3: 17  5 10 13
GrandTotal ← 0
FOR Shop ← 1 TO 3
   ShopTotal ← 0
   FOR Quarter ← 1 TO 4
      ShopTotal ← ShopTotal + Sales[Shop, Quarter]
   NEXT Quarter
   OUTPUT "Shop ", Shop, ": ", ShopTotal
   GrandTotal ← GrandTotal + ShopTotal
NEXT Shop
OUTPUT "All shops: ", GrandTotal

fragments.label: Processing a 2D array with nested loops
fragments.text:
Shop | Quarter values added   | ShopTotal | GrandTotal | OUTPUT
     |                        |           | 0          |
1    | 12, 15, 9, 20          | 56        | 56         | Shop 1: 56
2    | 8, 11, 14, 6           | 39        | 95         | Shop 2: 39
3    | 17, 5, 10, 13          | 45        | 140        | Shop 3: 45
                                                      | All shops: 140

Inside row 1 the running ShopTotal is 12, 27, 36, 56.
Column (quarter) totals, with Quarter as the outer loop: 37, 31, 33, 39, which also sum to 140.
(An equivalent Python run with nested lists gives the same row, column and grand totals.)
Selecting a 1D or 2D array for a task

fragments.label: Selecting a 1D or 2D array for a task
fragments.text: Choose a 1D array when the data is a single list of values of one type identified by one number: the daily rainfall for a month, the names in a register, a list of scores to sort. Choose a 2D array when each value is identified by two things at once and all the values have the same type: sales by shop and quarter, marks by student and test, the cells of a game board or a seating plan.

fragments.label: Selecting a 1D or 2D array for a task
fragments.text: Parallel 1D arrays (for example Names[1:30] and Marks[1:30] matched by index) can hold related data of different types, but they must be kept in step by hand, which is fragile when sorting. A 2D array cannot help here because all its elements must share one type; if a table would mix types, such as a name column and a mark column, use an array of records instead (see 10.1).

fragments.label: Selecting a 1D or 2D array for a task
fragments.text: One list, one index: 1D array.

fragments.label: Selecting a 1D or 2D array for a task
fragments.text: Values located by two coordinates (row and column), all the same type: 2D array.

fragments.label: Selecting a 1D or 2D array for a task
fragments.text: Related values of different types per item: array of records, or parallel 1D arrays kept in step.

fragments.label: Selecting a 1D or 2D array for a task
fragments.text: Justify the choice from the data: how many indexes identify a value, and are the types the same?

fragments.label: Selecting a 1D or 2D array for a task
fragments.text:
Task                                               | Structure                              | Reason
Rainfall for each day of June                      | ARRAY[1:30] OF REAL                    | one list, one index (day)
Marks of 25 students in 6 tests                    | ARRAY[1:25, 1:6] OF INTEGER            | two indexes (student, test), all INTEGER
Noughts and crosses board                          | ARRAY[1:3, 1:3] OF CHAR                | cell found by row and column
Names to be sorted into order                      | ARRAY[1:40] OF STRING                  | one list
Name, form and date of birth for each student      | ARRAY[1:40] OF StudentRecord           | different types per student, so not a 2D array
Checking loops against bounds

fragments.label: Checking loops against bounds
fragments.text: Every loop over an array should be checked against the declaration. For ARRAY[1:6], FOR Index ← 0 TO 6 reads the non-existent element 0 and FOR Index ← 1 TO 7 reads element 7: both stop the program with a run-time error when that line executes. FOR Index ← 1 TO 5 runs without error but never processes element 6, which gives a wrong answer and is a logic error.

fragments.label: Checking loops against bounds
fragments.text: Bubble sort needs particular care, because the comparison uses Values[J + 1]. The inner loop must stop at the upper bound minus 1 (then minus the number of passes completed), otherwise J + 1 goes past the upper bound. In a linear search with a WHILE loop, test the index before using it, so that the loop ends when the index passes the upper bound rather than trying to read a missing element.

fragments.label: Checking loops against bounds
fragments.text: Loop from exactly the lower bound to exactly the upper bound for a full traversal.

fragments.label: Checking loops against bounds
fragments.text: In comparisons using J + 1, the loop must end one before the upper bound.

fragments.label: Checking loops against bounds
fragments.text: Out-of-range index: run-time error. Missing an element: logic error.

fragments.label: Checking loops against bounds
fragments.text:
