fragments.text: A construct in which a condition is evaluated and its result decides which block of statements is executed next; written with IF or CASE.

fragments.label: Nested IF
fragments.text: An IF statement placed inside the THEN or ELSE part of another IF, so that a second condition is tested only after the first has been decided.

fragments.label: CASE structure
fragments.text: A selection construct that compares one expression with a list of values or ranges, executes the statements of the first clause that matches, and uses OTHERWISE for any value that matches none.

fragments.label: Iteration
fragments.text: Repeating a block of statements, either a set number of times or until a condition is met.

fragments.label: Count-controlled loop
fragments.text: A loop, FOR … NEXT, whose number of repetitions is fixed by a start value, an end value and an optional STEP before the loop begins; the loop variable is updated automatically.

fragments.label: Post-condition loop
fragments.text: A loop, REPEAT … UNTIL, whose condition is tested after the body, so the body always runs at least once; it stops when the condition becomes TRUE.

fragments.label: Pre-condition loop
fragments.text: A loop, WHILE … ENDWHILE, whose condition is tested before each pass, so the body may run zero times; it continues while the condition is TRUE.

fragments.label: Infinite loop
fragments.text: A loop whose ending condition can never be reached, usually because nothing inside the body changes the variables the condition tests.
IF … THEN … ELSE … ENDIF

fragments.label: IF … THEN … ELSE … ENDIF
fragments.text: The simplest selection is IF <condition> THEN <statements> ENDIF. If the condition is TRUE, the statements after THEN run; if it is FALSE they are skipped and execution carries on after ENDIF. Adding an ELSE clause gives a two-way choice: exactly one of the two blocks runs, never both and never neither. The pseudocode guide lays the keywords out on separate lines, with THEN and ELSE indented under IF and the statements indented again; THEN on the same line as the condition is also accepted. Whatever the layout, every IF needs its own ENDIF.

fragments.label: IF … THEN … ELSE … ENDIF
fragments.text: The condition can be any Boolean expression from 11.1: a comparison, a BOOLEAN variable, or a combination joined with AND, OR and NOT. In Python the structure becomes if condition: with an indented block and else: lined up under if, and there is no ENDIF because the indentation ends the block. VB.NET writes If … Then … Else … End If, and Java writes if (condition) { … } else { … }.

fragments.label: IF … THEN … ELSE … ENDIF
fragments.text: IF … THEN … ENDIF: do something or nothing. IF … THEN … ELSE … ENDIF: choose between two actions.

fragments.label: IF … THEN … ELSE … ENDIF
fragments.text: Every IF is closed by its own ENDIF, at the same indentation as the IF.

fragments.label: IF … THEN … ELSE … ENDIF
fragments.text: Test a BOOLEAN directly: IF Finished, not IF Finished = TRUE (both are correct, the first is neater).

fragments.label: IF … THEN … ELSE … ENDIF
fragments.text: Python: if … : / else: ; VB.NET: If … Then / Else / End If; Java: if ( … ) { } else { }.

fragments.label: IF … THEN … ELSE … ENDIF
fragments.text:
// one-way: nothing happens when the condition is FALSE
IF Temperature > 30
   THEN
      OUTPUT "Heat warning"
ENDIF

// two-way: exactly one branch runs
IF Balance >= Price
   THEN
      Balance ← Balance - Price
      OUTPUT "Purchase complete"
   ELSE
      OUTPUT "Insufficient funds"
ENDIF
Nested IF statements

fragments.label: Nested IF statements
fragments.text: An IF can be placed inside the THEN or the ELSE block of another IF. The inner test is only reached when the outer test has already gone a particular way, so the inner condition can rely on what the outer one has established. A login check is a natural case: there is no point testing the password until the username has been found, and the two failures need different messages. Each inner IF must be completely closed with its own ENDIF before the outer IF continues, so an IF nested twice ends with two ENDIFs.

fragments.label: Nested IF statements
fragments.text: Nesting in the ELSE branch builds a chain of tests on the same value, such as 'if negative … else if zero … else …'. Here the order of the tests matters: the first condition that is TRUE wins, so tests must go from the most specific or most extreme case outward. Python shortens an ELSE-then-IF into elif, and VB.NET into ElseIf, each needing only one closing keyword; in pseudocode you still write the full ELSE, IF and ENDIF. When every branch compares the same single variable with fixed values or ranges, a CASE structure is usually clearer.

fragments.label: Nested IF statements
fragments.text: The inner IF runs only on one path of the outer IF.

fragments.label: Nested IF statements
fragments.text: Count your ENDIFs: one per IF, closed innermost first.

fragments.label: Nested IF statements
fragments.text: In an ELSE-IF chain, test the most restrictive condition first, or later branches become unreachable.

fragments.label: Nested IF statements
fragments.text: Use nested IF when different conditions or different variables are involved; use CASE for one variable against many values.

fragments.label: Nested IF statements
fragments.text:
IF Username = StoredName
   THEN
      IF Password = StoredPassword
         THEN
            OUTPUT "Welcome ", Username
         ELSE
            OUTPUT "Wrong password"
      ENDIF
   ELSE
      OUTPUT "Unknown user"
ENDIF

// StoredName "kim", StoredPassword "Tr33top"
// Username "kim", Password "Tr33top"  → Welcome kim
// Username "kim", Password "treetop"  → Wrong password
// Username "sam", any password        → Unknown user (the password is never tested)
CASE OF … OTHERWISE … ENDCASE

fragments.label: CASE OF … OTHERWISE … ENDCASE
fragments.text: A CASE structure compares the value of one expression, usually a single variable, with a list of clauses. Each clause is a value, or a range written <low> TO <high>, followed by a colon and the statement to run. The clauses are checked from the top, and only the first clause that matches is executed; after that, control jumps past ENDCASE. The optional final clause, OTHERWISE, runs when nothing above it matched, which makes it the natural place for an error message about invalid data. The coursebook also shows several values separated by commas in one clause, which VB.NET supports directly.

fragments.label: CASE OF … OTHERWISE … ENDCASE
fragments.text: Ranges suit INTEGER and CHAR values, for example 70 TO 100 or 'A' TO 'Z'. Because the first match wins, overlapping ranges are legal but the later part of an overlap is never reached, so ranges should normally be written so that they do not overlap. A REAL value such as 69.5 would fall between two whole-number ranges, so either round it first or use nested IF with < and >= tests instead. Python has no CASE statement in older versions and is normally translated into if … elif … else; Python 3.10's match statement handles single values but not ranges. VB.NET uses Select Case with Case 70 To 100 and Case Else, and Java uses switch with case labels, break and default.

fragments.label: CASE OF … OTHERWISE … ENDCASE
fragments.text: CASE OF <identifier> … ENDCASE; each clause is <value> : <statement> or <low> TO <high> : <statement>.

fragments.label: CASE OF … OTHERWISE … ENDCASE
fragments.text: Only the first matching clause runs, so clause order matters when values could match more than one.

fragments.label: CASE OF … OTHERWISE … ENDCASE
fragments.text: OTHERWISE catches every unlisted value; use it to reject invalid input.

fragments.label: CASE OF … OTHERWISE … ENDCASE
fragments.text: A CASE tests one expression only; conditions on different variables need IF.

fragments.label: CASE OF … OTHERWISE … ENDCASE
fragments.text:
DECLARE Mark : INTEGER
DECLARE Grade : STRING
INPUT Mark
CASE OF Mark
   70 TO 100 : Grade ← "Distinction"
   50 TO 69  : Grade ← "Merit"
   40 TO 49  : Grade ← "Pass"
   0 TO 39   : Grade ← "Fail"
   OTHERWISE : Grade ← "Invalid mark"
ENDCASE
OUTPUT Grade

Test data (normal, boundary and erroneous)
Mark | Clause matched | OUTPUT
73   | 70 TO 100      | Distinction
70   | 70 TO 100      | Distinction
69   | 50 TO 69       | Merit
40   | 40 TO 49       | Pass
39   | 0 TO 39        | Fail
105  | OTHERWISE      | Invalid mark
-3   | OTHERWISE      | Invalid mark

fragments.label: CASE OF … OTHERWISE … ENDCASE
fragments.text:
INPUT Choice
CASE OF UCASE(Choice)
   'A' : OUTPUT "Adding a record"
   'D' : OUTPUT "Deleting a record"
   'S' : OUTPUT "Searching"
   OTHERWISE : OUTPUT "Not a menu option"
ENDCASE

// Choice 'd' → UCASE gives 'D' → Deleting a record
// Choice 'x' → Not a menu option
Count-controlled loop: FOR … TO … STEP … NEXT

fragments.label: Count-controlled loop: FOR … TO … STEP … NEXT
fragments.text: A FOR loop repeats its body a number of times that is fixed before the first pass. It is written FOR <identifier> ← <start> TO <end>, followed by the body and then NEXT <identifier>. The loop variable is given the start value, the body runs, the variable is increased by 1, and this repeats until the pass with the end value has been completed. FOR Count ← 1 TO 5 therefore runs five times, with Count taking 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. For a start of 1, the number of passes is simply the end value; in general, with the default step it is End - Start + 1.

fragments.label: Count-controlled loop: FOR … TO … STEP … NEXT
fragments.text: STEP changes the amount added each time: FOR X ← 2 TO 14 STEP 4 gives 2, 6, 10 and 14, and a negative step counts down, so FOR X ← 10 TO 1 STEP -3 gives 10, 7, 4 and 1. The loop stops once the next value would pass the end value, so the end value itself is only used if the steps land on it exactly. The pseudocode guide requires the step to be a whole number, and the body must not assign to the loop variable. Python's range excludes its end value, which is the usual source of off-by-one errors when translating: FOR X ← 1 TO 5 becomes for x in range(1, 6), and FOR X ← 10 TO 1 STEP -3 becomes range(10, 0, -3). A FOR loop is also the natural way to visit every element of an array or every character of a string, as in FOR Position ← 1 TO LENGTH(Word).

fragments.label: Count-controlled loop: FOR … TO … STEP … NEXT
fragments.text: FOR … NEXT for a known number of passes; NEXT names the same loop variable as FOR.

fragments.label: Count-controlled loop: FOR … TO … STEP … NEXT
fragments.text: Default step is +1; STEP -1 counts down; the step must be an integer.

fragments.label: Count-controlled loop: FOR … TO … STEP … NEXT
fragments.text: Never change the loop variable inside the body.

fragments.label: Count-controlled loop: FOR … TO … STEP … NEXT
fragments.text: Python: range(start, end + 1, step) for a counting-up loop, because range stops before its end value.

fragments.label: Count-controlled loop: FOR … TO … STEP … NEXT
fragments.text:
Total ← 0
FOR N ← 2 TO 10 STEP 2
   Total ← Total + N
NEXT N
OUTPUT Total

N  | Total
   | 0
2  | 2
4  | 6
6  | 12
8  | 20
10 | 30      → OUTPUT 30 (5 passes: the even numbers 2 to 10)

FOR X ← 10 TO 1 STEP -3
   OUTPUT X
NEXT X

X  | OUTPUT
10 | 10
7  | 7
4  | 4
1  | 1       → next value would be -2, which is past 1, so the loop ends

Python check: sum(range(2, 11, 2)) = 30 and list(range(10, 0, -3)) = [10, 7, 4, 1].
Post-condition loop: REPEAT … UNTIL

fragments.label: Post-condition loop: REPEAT … UNTIL
fragments.text: A REPEAT loop runs its body first and tests the condition afterwards: REPEAT <statements> UNTIL <condition>. If the condition is FALSE, the body runs again; as soon as it is TRUE, the loop ends. Because the test comes at the end, the body always runs at least once. This makes REPEAT the natural choice for input validation, where a value has to be read before there is anything to check, and for menus that must be shown at least once.

fragments.label: Post-condition loop: REPEAT … UNTIL
fragments.text: The condition describes when to stop, so it is the opposite of a WHILE condition for the same task: UNTIL LENGTH(Code) = 4 means the same as WHILE LENGTH(Code) <> 4. Something inside the body must be able to make the condition TRUE, usually an INPUT or an update to a counter, or the loop will never end. Python has no post-condition loop; the usual translation is while True: with the body followed by if condition: break. VB.NET writes Do … Loop Until condition and Java writes do { … } while (!condition);, where Java's condition is reversed because it says when to continue.

fragments.label: Post-condition loop: REPEAT … UNTIL
fragments.text: Body first, test last: at least one pass is guaranteed.

fragments.label: Post-condition loop: REPEAT … UNTIL
fragments.text: UNTIL gives the stopping condition; the loop repeats while it is FALSE.

fragments.label: Post-condition loop: REPEAT … UNTIL
fragments.text: No variable in the condition needs a value before the loop, as long as the body sets it.

fragments.label: Post-condition loop: REPEAT … UNTIL
fragments.text: Python: while True: … if condition: break.

fragments.label: Post-condition loop: REPEAT … UNTIL
fragments.text:
DECLARE Code : STRING
REPEAT
   OUTPUT "Enter a 4-character code: "
   INPUT Code
UNTIL LENGTH(Code) = 4
OUTPUT "Code accepted: ", Code

Inputs: "12", "12345", "7a9b"
Pass | Code    | LENGTH(Code) | LENGTH(Code) = 4 ? | Action
1    | "12"    | 2            | FALSE              | repeat
2    | "12345" | 5            | FALSE              | repeat
3    | "7a9b"  | 4            | TRUE               | leave loop
OUTPUT: the prompt three times, then Code accepted: 7a9b
Pre-condition loop: WHILE … ENDWHILE

fragments.label: Pre-condition loop: WHILE … ENDWHILE
fragments.text: A WHILE loop tests its condition before every pass: WHILE <condition> <statements> ENDWHILE. If the condition is TRUE the body runs and the test is made again; as soon as it is FALSE, execution continues after ENDWHILE. If the condition is already FALSE the first time, the body is skipped completely, so a WHILE loop can run zero times. The current pseudocode guide writes WHILE <condition> on its own; the coursebook adds DO at the end of the line, and either is understood.

fragments.label: Pre-condition loop: WHILE … ENDWHILE
fragments.text: Every variable in the condition must already have a value when the loop is first reached, so a WHILE loop is usually preceded by an initialising assignment or a first INPUT. As with REPEAT, the body must change something the condition depends on. WHILE suits problems where the loop may legitimately not be needed at all, such as processing data that might be empty, or repeating a calculation until a target is reached when the target might already be met. Python, VB.NET and Java all have this loop directly: while condition:, Do While … Loop and while (condition) { }.

fragments.label: Pre-condition loop: WHILE … ENDWHILE
fragments.text: Test first, body second: zero or more passes.

fragments.label: Pre-condition loop: WHILE … ENDWHILE
fragments.text: WHILE gives the condition to carry on; the loop ends when it becomes FALSE.

fragments.label: Pre-condition loop: WHILE … ENDWHILE
fragments.text: Initialise the condition's variables before the loop.

fragments.label: Pre-condition loop: WHILE … ENDWHILE
fragments.text: Make sure the body can eventually make the condition FALSE.

fragments.label: Pre-condition loop: WHILE … ENDWHILE
fragments.text:
DECLARE N, Power, Doublings : INTEGER
INPUT N
Power ← 1
Doublings ← 0
WHILE Power < N
   Power ← Power * 2
   Doublings ← Doublings + 1
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT Power, " after ", Doublings, " doublings"

N = 37
Power | Doublings | Power < 37 ?
1     | 0         | TRUE
2     | 1         | TRUE
4     | 2         | TRUE
8     | 3         | TRUE
16    | 4         | TRUE
32    | 5         | TRUE
64    | 6         | FALSE → OUTPUT 64 after 6 doublings

N = 1
Power | Doublings | Power < 1 ?
1     | 0         | FALSE → body never runs, OUTPUT 1 after 0 doublings

A REPEAT version would double at least once and wrongly output 2 for N = 1.
Justifying the choice of loop

fragments.label: Justifying the choice of loop
fragments.text: Any loop can be rewritten using either of the others, so the question is which fits the problem best. Ask two things. First, is the number of passes known when the loop is reached, even if it is held in a variable such as ClassSize or LENGTH(Word)? If so, use FOR: the counting is built in, so there is no counter to initialise or increment and no condition to get wrong. Second, if the number is not known, must the body run at least once? If yes, use REPEAT … UNTIL; if the body might not be needed at all, use WHILE … ENDWHILE.

fragments.label: Justifying the choice of loop
fragments.text: A justification earns marks when it links the property of the loop to the specific problem, not when it just names the loop. 'REPEAT, because the password has to be entered before it can be checked, so the body must run at least once' scores; 'REPEAT, because it is a condition-controlled loop' does not. For a FOR loop the key phrase is 'the number of iterations is known before the loop starts'; for WHILE it is 'the condition is tested first, so the loop can be skipped when it is not needed'.

fragments.label: Justifying the choice of loop
fragments.text: Known number of passes → FOR (count-controlled).

fragments.label: Justifying the choice of loop
fragments.text: Unknown, but at least one pass needed → REPEAT … UNTIL (post-condition).

fragments.label: Justifying the choice of loop
fragments.text: Unknown, and zero passes possible → WHILE … ENDWHILE (pre-condition).

fragments.label: Justifying the choice of loop
fragments.text: Always tie the justification to the scenario, not just to the definition.

fragments.label: Justifying the choice of loop
fragments.text:
Output the numbers 1 to 5

FOR Count ← 1 TO 5         Count ← 1                  Count ← 1
   OUTPUT Count            REPEAT                     WHILE Count <= 5
NEXT Count                    OUTPUT Count               OUTPUT Count
                              Count ← Count + 1          Count ← Count + 1
                           UNTIL Count > 5            ENDWHILE

All three output 1 2 3 4 5, but FOR needs no manual initialise-and-increment, so it is the best fit.
Note the conditions: WHILE Count <= 5 (carry on) is the opposite of UNTIL Count > 5 (stop).

Scenario                                              Best loop and justification
Total the marks of the 30 students in a class         FOR: the number of iterations (30) is known
                                                      before the loop starts.
Keep asking for a PIN until it is 4 digits long       REPEAT: a PIN must be input before it can
                                                      be checked, so the body must run at least once.
Print every line of a file, which may be empty        WHILE NOT EOF(…): the test comes first, so an
                                                      empty file is handled with zero passes.
Combining and nesting constructs

fragments.label: Combining and nesting constructs
fragments.text: Real programs place constructs inside one another: an IF or CASE inside a loop to treat each value differently, a loop inside a loop to cover rows and columns, or a validation loop inside a counting loop. The inner construct runs completely on every pass of the outer one, and each construct keeps its own closing keyword at the matching indentation: ENDIF, ENDCASE, NEXT, UNTIL or ENDWHILE. Closing keywords must be nested properly, so an ENDIF that belongs inside a FOR loop has to appear before that loop's NEXT.

fragments.label: Combining and nesting constructs
fragments.text: To trace nested constructs, add a column for every variable and for the output, and work through the inner construct fully for each value of the outer loop variable before moving on. The example below uses a FOR loop containing a nested IF chain. It also shows why order matters: a number divisible by 15 is also divisible by 3 and by 5, so the MOD 15 test has to come first or that branch would never run.

fragments.label: Combining and nesting constructs
fragments.text: Inner constructs complete on every pass of the outer loop.

fragments.label: Combining and nesting constructs
fragments.text: Close constructs innermost first: an inner ENDIF comes before the outer NEXT.

fragments.label: Combining and nesting constructs
fragments.text: Indent each level consistently so the structure can be checked by eye.

fragments.label: Combining and nesting constructs
fragments.text: In an IF chain inside a loop, put the most specific test first.

fragments.label: Combining and nesting constructs
fragments.text:
FOR Number ← 9 TO 15
   IF Number MOD 15 = 0
      THEN
         OUTPUT "FizzBuzz"
      ELSE
         IF Number MOD 3 = 0
            THEN
               OUTPUT "Fizz"
            ELSE
               IF Number MOD 5 = 0
                  THEN
                     OUTPUT "Buzz"
                  ELSE
                     OUTPUT Number
               ENDIF
         ENDIF
   ENDIF
NEXT Number

Number | MOD 15 | MOD 3 | MOD 5 | OUTPUT
9      | 9      | 0     | –     | Fizz
10     | 10     | 1     | 0     | Buzz
11     | 11     | 2     | 1     | 11
12     | 12     | 0     | –     | Fizz
13     | 13     | 1     | 3     | 13
14     | 14     | 2     | 4     | 14
15     | 0      | –     | –     | FizzBuzz
(– means the test is not reached)

fragments.label: Combining and nesting constructs

fragments.text: Write the skeleton of a two-way selection in Cambridge pseudocode.

fragments.label: Write the skeleton of a two-way selection in Cambridge pseudocode.
fragments.text: IF <condition> THEN <statements> ELSE <statements> ENDIF, with THEN and ELSE on their own indented lines.
In a CASE structure, what happens when a value matches two clauses, and what is OTHERWISE for?

fragments.label: In a CASE structure, what happens when a value matches two clauses, and what is OTHERWISE for?
fragments.text: Only the first matching clause runs. OTHERWISE runs when no clause matches, typically to report invalid data.
What values does FOR X ← 10 TO 1 STEP -3 give X, and what is the Python equivalent?

fragments.label: What values does FOR X ← 10 TO 1 STEP -3 give X, and what is the Python equivalent?

fragments.text: What is the minimum number of times the body of a REPEAT loop and of a WHILE loop can run?

fragments.label: What is the minimum number of times the body of a REPEAT loop and of a WHILE loop can run?
fragments.text: REPEAT at least once (condition tested after the body); WHILE zero times (condition tested before the body).
Rewrite WHILE Total < 100 … ENDWHILE as a post-condition loop condition.

fragments.label: Rewrite WHILE Total < 100 … ENDWHILE as a post-condition loop condition.
fragments.text: REPEAT … UNTIL Total >= 100 (the condition is reversed, and the body now runs at least once).
When is a FOR loop the best choice?

fragments.label: When is a FOR loop the best choice?
fragments.text: When the number of iterations is known when the loop is reached, for example the size of an array or a value already input.
Justify using REPEAT … UNTIL to validate an input.

fragments.label: Justify using REPEAT … UNTIL to validate an input.
fragments.text: The value has to be input before it can be checked, so the body must execute at least once; REPEAT tests its condition after the body, guaranteeing that first pass.
Why must an inner IF inside a FOR loop have its ENDIF before the loop's NEXT?

fragments.label: Why must an inner IF inside a FOR loop have its ENDIF before the loop's NEXT?
fragments.text: Constructs must be closed innermost first; the IF is part of the loop body, so it has to finish before the loop does.

Topic 9.1 showed how decomposition turns a problem into modules; this topic is about writing those modules in Cambridge pseudocode. Paper 2 expects a procedure written as PROCEDURE … ENDPROCEDURE and run with CALL, taking none, one or several parameters; a function written as FUNCTION … RETURNS <type> … ENDFUNCTION whose RETURN value takes the place of the call inside an expression; and parameters marked BYVAL or BYREF, with a trace showing whether the caller's variable has changed after the call. Candidates must also explain when a procedure or a function is the right choice, use the words header, interface, parameter, argument and return value accurately, and write pseudocode that does not waste work. Marks are lost for putting CALL in front of a function, for a function with no RETURN on some path, for passing a constant to a BYREF parameter, and for assuming a BYVAL change reaches the caller.

fragments.label: Procedure
fragments.text: A named block of statements that carries out a task and is run with a CALL statement. It does not hand a value back to the point of call, although it can change the caller's variables through BYREF parameters.

fragments.label: Function
fragments.text: A named block of statements that works out and returns exactly one value of a stated data type. It is called inside an expression, never with CALL, and the returned value takes the place of the call when the expression is evaluated.

fragments.label: Procedure/function header
fragments.text: The first line of a procedure or function definition: the keyword, the identifier, the parameter list with each parameter's data type (and BYVAL/BYREF), and for a function the RETURNS data type.

fragments.label: Procedure/function interface
fragments.text: What the rest of the program needs to know to use a subroutine: the number, order, data types and passing method of its parameters, and for a function the type of value it returns.

fragments.label: Parameter
fragments.text: An identifier listed in the subroutine header that acts as a variable inside the subroutine and receives a value (or, BYREF, access to a variable) when the subroutine is called.

fragments.label: Argument
fragments.text: The actual value, variable or expression written in the brackets of a call, matched by position to the corresponding parameter.

fragments.label: Return value
fragments.text: The single value a function sends back with RETURN; it replaces the function call in the expression that called it.

fragments.label: BYVAL (by value)
fragments.text: The parameter receives a copy of the argument's value, so changes made inside the subroutine do not affect the caller's variable. It is the default when no method is stated.

fragments.label: BYREF (by reference)
fragments.text: The parameter receives the address of the caller's variable, so the parameter and the argument are the same memory location and any change made inside the procedure is still there after the call. The argument must be a variable.
Subroutines: giving a block of code a name

fragments.label: Subroutines: giving a block of code a name
fragments.text: A subroutine is a set of statements that has been given an identifier so it can be run by name from anywhere in the program. Cambridge pseudocode has two kinds: procedures and functions. Both are written out once, above the main program that uses them, and are then run by calling them. When the subroutine finishes, control goes back to the statement just after the point of call.

fragments.label: Subroutines: giving a block of code a name
fragments.text: Subroutines are how the modules found by decomposition (9.1) and drawn on a structure chart (12.2) turn into code. Because each one has a single job and receives its data through parameters, it can be written, tested and corrected on its own, and then used again wherever the same job is needed.

fragments.label: Subroutines: giving a block of code a name
fragments.text: Two kinds of subroutine: a procedure (run with CALL) and a function (used inside an expression, returns one value).

fragments.label: Subroutines: giving a block of code a name
fragments.text: Definitions come before the main program; a call jumps into the subroutine and control returns to the line after the call.

fragments.label: Subroutines: giving a block of code a name
fragments.text: Data goes in through parameters; a function sends one value back with RETURN.
Defining and calling a procedure

fragments.label: Defining and calling a procedure
fragments.text: A procedure is written PROCEDURE <identifier>(<parameter list>), then its statements, then ENDPROCEDURE. The brackets may be empty, or hold one or more parameters, each written <identifier> : <data type> and separated by commas. The parameters behave as variables inside the procedure body. Any variable the procedure needs just for its own work is declared inside it, so it is local.

fragments.label: Defining and calling a procedure
fragments.text: A procedure is run with CALL <identifier>(<arguments>), and this is a complete statement on its own line. The arguments must match the parameters in number, order and data type: the first argument goes to the first parameter, and so on. A procedure with no parameters is still called with empty brackets, CALL <identifier>(). Unless BYREF is written, parameters are passed by value.

fragments.label: Defining and calling a procedure
fragments.text: Syntax: PROCEDURE Name(P1 : TYPE, P2 : TYPE) … ENDPROCEDURE; with no parameters, PROCEDURE Name() … ENDPROCEDURE.

fragments.label: Defining and calling a procedure
fragments.text: Call: CALL Name(arg1, arg2) as a statement by itself; CALL Name() when there are no parameters.

fragments.label: Defining and calling a procedure
fragments.text: Arguments are matched to parameters by position, so the order and data types must agree.

fragments.label: Defining and calling a procedure
fragments.text: Variables declared inside the procedure are local to it.

fragments.label: Defining and calling a procedure
fragments.text:
PROCEDURE ShowRule()
   OUTPUT "----------"
ENDPROCEDURE

PROCEDURE ShowTitle(Title : STRING)
   OUTPUT "== ", Title, " =="
ENDPROCEDURE

PROCEDURE ShowRow(Symbol : STRING, Count : INTEGER)
   DECLARE Line : STRING
   DECLARE Index : INTEGER
   Line ← ""
   FOR Index ← 1 TO Count
      Line ← Line & Symbol
   NEXT Index
   OUTPUT Line
ENDPROCEDURE

// main program
CALL ShowTitle("Pattern")
CALL ShowRule()
CALL ShowRow("*", 3)
CALL ShowRow("#", 5)
CALL ShowRule()

Output:
== Pattern ==
----------
***
#####
----------

ShowRow is called twice with different arguments: "*" and 3 the first time, "#" and 5 the second. Line and Index are local, so each call starts with its own fresh copies.
Where a procedure is appropriate

fragments.label: Where a procedure is appropriate
fragments.text: Use a procedure when a part of the algorithm is an action rather than a calculation of one answer: displaying a menu or a report, writing records to a file, sorting an array, or reading and validating several inputs. It is also the right choice when a task has to change more than one of the caller's variables, since a procedure can do this through BYREF parameters, whereas a function returns only one value.

fragments.label: Where a procedure is appropriate
fragments.text: In practice a procedure is worth writing whenever the same group of steps appears in more than one place, or whenever a step of the design is big enough to be its own sub-task. Writing it once removes duplicated code, gives the main program a short, readable outline of calls, allows the procedure to be tested by itself, and means a later fix is made in one place only.

fragments.label: Where a procedure is appropriate
fragments.text: Choose a procedure for an action with no single result: output, file handling, updating an array, input with validation.

fragments.label: Where a procedure is appropriate
fragments.text: Choose a procedure (with BYREF parameters) when several of the caller's variables must be updated.

fragments.label: Where a procedure is appropriate
fragments.text: Any repeated group of steps is a candidate: write once, call many times, fix in one place.

fragments.label: Where a procedure is appropriate
fragments.text: Each procedure can be tested on its own before it is joined to the rest of the program.
Defining and using a function

fragments.label: Defining and using a function
fragments.text: A function is written FUNCTION <identifier>(<parameter list>) RETURNS <data type>, then its statements, then ENDFUNCTION. The body must contain a RETURN <expression> statement on every path through it, and the value returned must be of the type named after RETURNS. RETURN takes effect at once: the function stops, and any statements after it are skipped. This allows a function to have more than one RETURN, for example one in each branch of an IF.

fragments.label: Defining and using a function
fragments.text: A function call is not a statement by itself, so it is never preceded by CALL. It is written where a value is needed: on the right of an assignment, in an OUTPUT list, in a condition, or as an argument to another call. When the function reaches RETURN, the returned value replaces the call and the rest of the expression is then evaluated. The pseudocode guide also says parameters should not be passed BYREF to a function, so a function's only effect on the caller is its return value.

fragments.label: Defining and using a function
fragments.text: Syntax: FUNCTION Name(P1 : TYPE) RETURNS TYPE … RETURN value … ENDFUNCTION.

fragments.label: Defining and using a function
fragments.text: Every path through the body must reach a RETURN; RETURN ends the function immediately.

fragments.label: Defining and using a function
fragments.text: Call it inside an expression, never with CALL; the return value replaces the call.

fragments.label: Defining and using a function
fragments.text: Function parameters are passed by value.

fragments.label: Defining and using a function
fragments.text:
FUNCTION Square(N : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
   RETURN N * N
ENDFUNCTION

FUNCTION Larger(A : INTEGER, B : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
   IF A > B THEN
      RETURN A
   ENDIF
   RETURN B
ENDFUNCTION

DECLARE Result : INTEGER
Result ← 50 + Square(3) * 2
OUTPUT Larger(Result, Square(8))
OUTPUT Larger(4, 7)

Step-by-step:
Result ← 50 + Square(3) * 2
   Square(3) returns 9     → 50 + 9 * 2
   * before +              → 50 + 18 = 68, so Result = 68
OUTPUT Larger(Result, Square(8))
   Square(8) returns 64    → Larger(68, 64)
   68 > 64 is TRUE         → RETURN 68; the final RETURN B is never reached
   Output: 68
OUTPUT Larger(4, 7)
   4 > 7 is FALSE          → skip the IF, reach RETURN 7
   Output: 7

Writing CALL Square(3) would be wrong: the 9 it returns would have nowhere to go.
Where a function is appropriate: procedure or function?

fragments.label: Where a function is appropriate: procedure or function?
fragments.text: Use a function when a part of the algorithm works out one answer that the caller then uses: a total, an average, the larger of two values, the position of an item in an array, or a TRUE/FALSE result from a validation check such as IsValidDate(Day, Month, Year). Because the answer comes back as a value, it can go straight into an expression or a condition, for example IF IsValidDate(D, M, Y) THEN … . The built-in routines such as LENGTH, MID and INT are functions for exactly this reason.

fragments.label: Where a function is appropriate: procedure or function?
fragments.text: The quick test is to ask what the caller needs back. If the answer is one value, write a function. If the answer is nothing, or several values, write a procedure (using BYREF for values that must come back). Converting one into the other changes the call as well as the header: a procedure call is a CALL statement, while a function call sits inside an expression.

fragments.label: Where a function is appropriate: procedure or function?
fragments.text: Function: exactly one value is needed back, often used in a calculation or condition.

fragments.label: Where a function is appropriate: procedure or function?
fragments.text: Procedure: an action with no value back, or several values back through BYREF.

fragments.label: Where a function is appropriate: procedure or function?
fragments.text: Validation checks are often written as BOOLEAN functions so they can be used directly in IF or WHILE conditions.
Local and global variables

fragments.label: Local and global variables
fragments.text: A variable declared inside a procedure or function is local: it exists only while that call is running and cannot be seen from the main program or from other subroutines. Parameters behave the same way. Each new call creates fresh local variables, so no value is carried over from a previous call. A variable declared in the main program, outside every subroutine, is global and can be read or changed from anywhere.

fragments.label: Local and global variables
fragments.text: Good practice is to keep any variable that a subroutine alone needs as a local, and to pass data in through parameters rather than relying on globals. A subroutine that quietly reads or alters a global is harder to reuse and to test, because its behaviour depends on something not shown in its header. Exam questions sometimes state that an array is global to keep the answer short; otherwise, use parameters.

fragments.label: Local and global variables
fragments.text: Local: declared inside a subroutine, exists only during that call, invisible outside it.

fragments.label: Local and global variables
fragments.text: Global: declared outside all subroutines, visible everywhere.

fragments.label: Local and global variables
fragments.text: Prefer locals and parameters; hidden use of globals makes subroutines harder to test and reuse.
Terminology: header, interface, parameter, argument, return value

fragments.label: Terminology: header, interface, parameter, argument, return value
fragments.text: The header is the first line of a definition. It names the subroutine and lists its parameters with their data types, and for a function it ends with RETURNS and a type. A parameter is one of the identifiers in that list; inside the body it is used like a variable. An argument is what is actually supplied in the brackets when the subroutine is called; it can be a literal, a variable or a whole expression (except that a BYREF argument must be a variable). Arguments are matched to parameters by position, not by name, so the names do not need to agree.

fragments.label: Terminology: header, interface, parameter, argument, return value
fragments.text: The interface is everything a programmer needs to know to use the subroutine without reading its body: how many parameters there are, their order, data types and passing method, and the type of value a function returns. The return value is the single value that a function's RETURN statement sends back. Because callers depend only on the interface, the body can later be rewritten, for instance to make it faster, without changing a single call.

fragments.label: Terminology: header, interface, parameter, argument, return value
fragments.text: Header: the first line, with identifier, parameter list and (for a function) RETURNS type.

fragments.label: Terminology: header, interface, parameter, argument, return value
fragments.text: Parameter: an identifier in the header. Argument: the value or variable given in the call.

fragments.label: Terminology: header, interface, parameter, argument, return value
fragments.text: Interface: number, order, types and passing method of the parameters, plus the return type.

fragments.label: Terminology: header, interface, parameter, argument, return value
fragments.text: Return value: the one value sent back by RETURN, which replaces the function call.

fragments.label: Terminology: header, interface, parameter, argument, return value
fragments.text:
FUNCTION CountChar(Word : STRING, Target : STRING) RETURNS INTEGER   // header
   DECLARE Index, Total : INTEGER                                   // local variables
   Total ← 0
   FOR Index ← 1 TO LENGTH(Word)
      IF MID(Word, Index, 1) = Target THEN
         Total ← Total + 1
      ENDIF
   NEXT Index
   RETURN Total                                                     // return value
ENDFUNCTION

DECLARE Place : STRING
DECLARE Count : INTEGER
Place ← "Mississippi"
Count ← CountChar("banana", "a") + CountChar(Place, "s")

Parameters:  Word, Target
Arguments:   "banana" and "a" in the first call; Place and "s" in the second
Interface:   two STRING parameters (by value, the default), returns an INTEGER
Trace:       CountChar("banana", "a") returns 3 (positions 2, 4, 6)
             CountChar("Mississippi", "s") returns 4 (positions 3, 4, 6, 7)
             Count ← 3 + 4, so Count = 7
Passing parameters BYVAL and BYREF

fragments.label: Passing parameters BYVAL and BYREF
fragments.text: Writing BYVAL or BYREF in front of a parameter in the header states how it is passed. BYVAL copies the argument's current value into the parameter; the procedure works on that copy, and the caller's variable is exactly as it was when the call ends. The argument may therefore be a literal or an expression. BYREF passes the address of the caller's variable, so inside the procedure the parameter is just another name for that same memory location. Every assignment to the parameter changes the caller's variable, and the argument must be a variable, not a constant or an expression.

fragments.label: Passing parameters BYVAL and BYREF
fragments.text: If neither keyword is written, BYVAL is assumed. A keyword also carries on to the parameters that follow it until the other keyword appears, so in PROCEDURE Swap(BYREF X : INTEGER, Y : INTEGER) both X and Y are passed by reference. BYREF is used with procedures only; functions take BYVAL parameters and send their result back with RETURN. Choose BYREF when the purpose of the procedure is to update the caller's variables, and BYVAL whenever the caller's data should be protected.

fragments.label: Passing parameters BYVAL and BYREF
fragments.text: BYVAL: a copy is passed; the caller's variable cannot be changed; argument may be any expression. Default.

fragments.label: Passing parameters BYVAL and BYREF
fragments.text: BYREF: the variable's address is passed; changes inside the procedure remain after the call; argument must be a variable.

fragments.label: Passing parameters BYVAL and BYREF
fragments.text: A BYVAL/BYREF keyword applies to the following parameters too, until the other keyword is written.

fragments.label: Passing parameters BYVAL and BYREF
fragments.text: Do not use BYREF with a function: a function returns its result with RETURN.
Worked traces: BYVAL and BYREF side by side

fragments.label: Worked traces: BYVAL and BYREF side by side
fragments.text: To decide what a call does to the caller, trace the caller's variables before and after each call, not just the parameters. In the first trace, Step is BYVAL and Total is BYREF. Doubling Step changes only the copy, so P stays 3 however many times the procedure is called, while every change to Total is made directly to Q.

fragments.label: Worked traces: BYVAL and BYREF side by side
fragments.text: The second trace uses the same swap body twice. With BYREF applying to both parameters, the values are exchanged. With Y marked BYVAL, the assignment Y ← Temp changes only a copy, so the caller ends with the same value in both variables. That half-working swap is a classic exam trace.

fragments.label: Worked traces: BYVAL and BYREF side by side
fragments.text: Always record the caller's variables after the call returns: that is where BYVAL and BYREF differ.

fragments.label: Worked traces: BYVAL and BYREF side by side
fragments.text: A BYVAL parameter can be changed inside the procedure; the change is simply thrown away at the end.

fragments.label: Worked traces: BYVAL and BYREF side by side
fragments.text: A swap needs both parameters BYREF; with one BYVAL, both variables end up holding the same value.

fragments.label: Worked traces: BYVAL and BYREF side by side
fragments.text:
PROCEDURE Update(BYVAL Step : INTEGER, BYREF Total : INTEGER)
   Step ← Step * 2
   Total ← Total + Step
ENDPROCEDURE

DECLARE P, Q : INTEGER
P ← 3
Q ← 4
CALL Update(P, Q)
OUTPUT P, " ", Q
CALL Update(P, Q)
OUTPUT P, " ", Q

Statement             | Step | Total (= Q) | P | Q  | OUTPUT
P ← 3, Q ← 4          |      |             | 3 | 4  |
CALL Update: enter    | 3    | 4           | 3 | 4  |
Step ← Step * 2       | 6    | 4           | 3 | 4  |
Total ← Total + Step  | 6    | 10          | 3 | 10 |
return, OUTPUT        |      |             | 3 | 10 | 3 10
CALL Update: enter    | 3    | 10          | 3 | 10 |
Step ← Step * 2       | 6    | 10          | 3 | 10 |
Total ← Total + Step  | 6    | 16          | 3 | 16 |
return, OUTPUT        |      |             | 3 | 16 | 3 16

Step starts at 3 on each call because it is a fresh copy of P; Q keeps growing because Total is Q.

fragments.label: Worked traces: BYVAL and BYREF side by side
fragments.text:
PROCEDURE SwapBoth(BYREF X : INTEGER, Y : INTEGER)     // BYREF covers X and Y
   DECLARE Temp : INTEGER
   Temp ← X
   X ← Y
   Y ← Temp
ENDPROCEDURE

PROCEDURE SwapOne(BYREF X : INTEGER, BYVAL Y : INTEGER) // only X is BYREF
   DECLARE Temp : INTEGER
   Temp ← X
   X ← Y
   Y ← Temp
ENDPROCEDURE

First ← 1
Second ← 2
CALL SwapBoth(First, Second)
   Temp ← 1; X ← 2 (First = 2); Y ← 1 (Second = 1)
   After the call: First = 2, Second = 1   → swapped

First ← 1
Second ← 2
CALL SwapOne(First, Second)
   Temp ← 1; X ← 2 (First = 2); Y ← 1 changes only the copy
   After the call: First = 2, Second = 2   → not swapped

fragments.label: Worked traces: BYVAL and BYREF side by side
fragments.text:
# Assigning to an int parameter in Python never changes the caller's
# variable, so it behaves like BYVAL. To imitate BYREF, pass a one-item
# list and change item [0], which the caller can see.

def update(step, total_ref):        # BYVAL Step, BYREF Total
    step = step * 2
    total_ref[0] = total_ref[0] + step

p, q = 3, [4]
update(p, q)
print(p, q[0])                      # 3 10
update(p, q)
print(p, q[0])                      # 3 16

def swap_one(x_ref, y):              # BYREF X, BYVAL Y
    temp = x_ref[0]
    x_ref[0] = y
    y = temp                         # only the local copy changes

first, second = [1], 2
swap_one(first, second)
print(first[0], second)             # 2 2
Writing efficient pseudocode

fragments.label: Writing efficient pseudocode
fragments.text: Efficient pseudocode reaches the correct result without doing unnecessary work. Three habits cover most exam questions. First, do not repeat a calculation whose answer does not change: work it out once before a loop, or store a function's return value in a variable instead of calling the function twice. Second, stop a loop as soon as the answer is known: a search that has found its item should not keep checking the rest of the array, so a WHILE or REPEAT loop with a flag suits it better than a FOR loop over every element. Third, reuse modules: one procedure with parameters is better than several near-identical copies.

fragments.label: Writing efficient pseudocode
fragments.text: Choosing the right structure is part of efficiency as well: a CASE instead of a long chain of separate IFs that are all tested, a FOR loop when the number of passes is fixed, and a condition-controlled loop when it is not. Efficient code is also usually shorter and clearer, which reduces the chance of errors.

fragments.label: Writing efficient pseudocode
fragments.text: Move calculations that do not change out of the loop; store a return value rather than calling the same function again.

fragments.label: Writing efficient pseudocode
fragments.text: Exit early: use a condition-controlled loop with a flag when the job can finish before the end of the data.

fragments.label: Writing efficient pseudocode
fragments.text: Reuse one parameterised subroutine rather than writing several similar ones.

fragments.label: Writing efficient pseudocode
fragments.text: Use IF … ELSE or CASE so that once one branch is chosen the other tests are skipped.

fragments.label: Writing efficient pseudocode
fragments.text:
// 1. Repeated calculation
// Wasteful: Average(Marks) is worked out twice
IF Average(Marks) >= 50 THEN
   OUTPUT "Pass, mean ", Average(Marks)
ENDIF
// Better: call once, keep the return value
Mean ← Average(Marks)
IF Mean >= 50 THEN
   OUTPUT "Pass, mean ", Mean
ENDIF

// 2. Exiting a loop early (Names has 1000 elements, SearchName is in Names[3])
// Wasteful: always checks all 1000 elements
Found ← FALSE
FOR Index ← 1 TO 1000
   IF Names[Index] = SearchName THEN
      Found ← TRUE
   ENDIF
NEXT Index
// Better: stops as soon as the name is found
Found ← FALSE
Index ← 1
WHILE Index <= 1000 AND NOT Found
   IF Names[Index] = SearchName THEN
      Found ← TRUE
   ELSE
      Index ← Index + 1
   ENDIF
ENDWHILE

Comparisons of Names[Index] with SearchName:
   FOR version:   1000 (every element)
   WHILE version: 3 (Index 1 no, 2 no, 3 yes; Found = TRUE ends the loop, Index = 3)
How is a procedure with no parameters defined and called?

fragments.label: How is a procedure with no parameters defined and called?
fragments.text: PROCEDURE Name() … ENDPROCEDURE, called with the statement CALL Name().
Give the general form of a function header.

fragments.label: Give the general form of a function header.
fragments.text: FUNCTION Name(P1 : TYPE, P2 : TYPE) RETURNS TYPE.
What happens to a function call when RETURN is executed?

fragments.label: What happens to a function call when RETURN is executed?
fragments.text: The function ends immediately and the returned value replaces the call in the expression, which is then evaluated.
What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?

fragments.label: What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?
fragments.text: A parameter is the identifier listed in the subroutine header; an argument is the actual value, variable or expression supplied in the call.
What does a subroutine's interface consist of?

fragments.label: What does a subroutine's interface consist of?
fragments.text: The number, order, data types and passing method of its parameters, and for a function the data type returned.
After PROCEDURE Update(BYVAL Step : INTEGER, BYREF Total : INTEGER) with Step ← Step * 2 and Total ← Total + Step, what are P and Q after CALL Update(P, Q) with P = 3, Q = 4?

fragments.label: After PROCEDURE Update(BYVAL Step : INTEGER, BYREF Total : INTEGER) with Step ← Step * 2 and Total ← Total + Step, what are P and Q after CALL Update(P, Q) with P = 3, Q = 4?
fragments.text: P = 3 (only a copy was doubled) and Q = 10 (4 + 6, changed through BYREF).
If no BYVAL or BYREF is written, how is a parameter passed?

fragments.label: If no BYVAL or BYREF is written, how is a parameter passed?
fragments.text: By value; BYVAL is the default.
When is a function more appropriate than a procedure?

fragments.label: When is a function more appropriate than a procedure?
fragments.text: When the task produces exactly one value that the caller uses, for example in a calculation or as a condition.

A program development life cycle is the planned route a piece of software takes from an idea to a working, maintained product. Paper 2 asks why such a life cycle is used, why one model does not suit every project, and for the principles, benefits and drawbacks of the waterfall, iterative and rapid application development (RAD) models. It also asks what happens in the analysis, design, coding, testing and maintenance stages. Answers score when each stage is described by what it produces (for example a requirements specification from analysis), when a model's benefit or drawback is tied to how that model works rather than listed from memory, and when a recommended model is justified against the details of the scenario given: how stable the requirements are, the size of the project, how available the client is and how quickly the software is needed.

fragments.label: Program development life cycle
fragments.text: The ordered set of stages that software passes through during its development and use: analysis, design, coding, testing and maintenance. When maintenance can no longer keep the program fit for purpose, a new cycle begins.

fragments.label: Requirements specification
fragments.text: The document produced by analysis that states precisely what the new system must do and any constraints on it; later stages design, build and test against it.

fragments.label: Waterfall model
fragments.text: A linear life cycle in which each stage is finished and signed off before the next begins, with the output of one stage becoming the input to the next.

fragments.label: Iterative model
fragments.text: A life cycle that begins by building a small part of the requirements and then repeats cycles of planning, building, testing and review, each adding to a working version, until the whole system is complete.

fragments.label: Rapid application development (RAD)
fragments.text: A life cycle with minimal up-front planning in which modules are built as prototypes, often in parallel, refined through short cycles with frequent user feedback, and joined together for fast delivery.

fragments.label: Prototype
fragments.text: A working model of part of a system, built quickly so that users can try it and say what should change.

fragments.label: Maintenance
fragments.text: Changes made to a program after it is in use: corrective (fixing faults found later), adaptive (responding to a new environment or new requirements) and perfective (improving performance or usability).
The purpose of a development life cycle

fragments.label: The purpose of a development life cycle
fragments.text: A small program for your own use can be written by thinking for a few minutes and then typing. Commercial software is different: it is larger, involves a team, and is paid for by a client who expects particular results. A development life cycle gives that work a defined structure. The job is divided into stages (analysis, design, coding, testing and maintenance), each with a clear purpose and a clear output, so that progress can be planned, checked and managed.

fragments.label: The purpose of a development life cycle
fragments.text: Working to a life cycle means the problem is understood before anything is built, the solution is planned before it is coded, and the product is tested against what the client actually asked for. It also makes it easier to estimate time and cost, to share the work between team members, and to produce documentation along the way. The stages form a cycle because, when a program can no longer be maintained to meet its users' needs, the process starts again with a fresh analysis.

fragments.label: The purpose of a development life cycle
fragments.text: Purpose: give development a structured, manageable sequence of stages with defined outputs.

fragments.label: The purpose of a development life cycle
fragments.text: Benefits: the problem is understood first, work can be planned and costed, progress can be measured, the product is checked against the requirements.

fragments.label: The purpose of a development life cycle
fragments.text: Stages: analysis → design → coding → testing → maintenance, and back to analysis when the system is no longer fit for purpose.
Analysis

fragments.label: Analysis
fragments.text: Analysis is about understanding the problem, not solving it yet. The analyst investigates the current system if there is one, for example by interviewing users, observing how they work and examining existing documents, and uses abstraction to concentrate on what matters. The problem is then defined clearly and precisely: the inputs, the outputs, the processing needed between them and any constraints, such as hardware, budget, deadlines or rules on the data.

fragments.label: Analysis
fragments.text: The result is a requirements specification that the client can agree to. Possible solutions may be compared at this stage and the most suitable one chosen. Everything later is judged against this document, so a requirement missed here tends to surface much later, when it is expensive to fix.

fragments.label: Analysis
fragments.text: Investigate the problem and any existing system (interviews, observation, documents).

fragments.label: Analysis
fragments.text: Define inputs, outputs, processing and constraints precisely.

fragments.label: Analysis
fragments.text: Output: an agreed requirements specification; possible solutions compared and one chosen.

fragments.label: Analysis
fragments.text: A requirement missed in analysis usually shows up only in testing or after release.

fragments.label: Analysis
fragments.text:
A program works out a student's grade from three test scores. The requirements said "average three scores" and never considered a student who was absent for one test.

Testing: a tester enters 0 for the missed test. The average falls from 70 (marks 68 and 72) to 46.7, and the grade drops sharply.

Where is the fault?
   Coding? No. The code averages three numbers, exactly as designed.
   Design? No. The design follows the specification it was given.
   Analysis? Yes. "A score may be missing" was never identified as a requirement.

Fix: go back to analysis and add the requirement (e.g. average only the tests actually taken), then update the design, then the code, then re-test.
Patching the code alone (e.g. ignoring every 0) would wrongly discard a genuine mark of 0.
Design

fragments.label: Design
fragments.text: Design decides how the requirements will be met, in enough detail that a programmer could build the solution from it. A useful starting point is an identifier table listing the data the program needs. From that the designer chooses data structures (a 1D or 2D array, a record) and decides whether data must be kept permanently in a file. The program is decomposed into modules, shown on a structure chart, and each algorithm is planned as a flowchart or in pseudocode (see 12.2). Test data can also be planned here.

fragments.label: Design
fragments.text: Design mistakes are much cheaper to correct on paper than after the code has been written, which is why it comes before coding.

fragments.label: Design
fragments.text: Plan data: identifier table, data structures, files.

fragments.label: Design
fragments.text: Plan structure: decomposition into modules on a structure chart.

fragments.label: Design
fragments.text: Plan logic: flowcharts or pseudocode for each module; plan test data.
Coding (implementation)

fragments.label: Coding (implementation)
fragments.text: In coding, often called implementation, the design is turned into program code. A suitable high-level language has to be chosen, taking into account what the problem needs and what the team knows well. The pseudocode is then translated into that language, module by module.

fragments.label: Coding (implementation)
fragments.text: Code rarely works first time. Syntax errors stop it compiling, and once it runs it may crash or give wrong output, so the programmer debugs as they go. Each module is normally tested on its own as it is written, and tested again after every change, so that fixing one thing does not break another.

fragments.label: Coding (implementation)
fragments.text: Choose a suitable programming language; translate the design into code.

fragments.label: Coding (implementation)
fragments.text: Remove syntax errors so it translates, then debug crashes and wrong output.

fragments.label: Coding (implementation)
fragments.text: Test each module as it is written and again after each change.
Testing

fragments.label: Testing
fragments.text: Getting some output is not the same as the program being correct. Testing checks, in a planned and thorough way, that the whole program meets every requirement in the specification, accepts valid input, rejects invalid input sensibly and behaves reliably in all situations. Normal, boundary and erroneous test data and methods such as white-box, black-box, alpha and beta testing are covered in 12.3.

fragments.label: Testing
fragments.text: When a test fails, the cause is traced back to the stage where it began, which may be coding, design or even analysis. Testing can show that errors are present but can never prove that none are left, which is one reason maintenance is needed later.

fragments.label: Testing
fragments.text: Check the whole program against the requirements specification.

fragments.label: Testing
fragments.text: Use planned test data covering valid, boundary and invalid input (details in 12.3).

fragments.label: Testing
fragments.text: A failed test is traced back to the stage that caused it; testing cannot prove a program is error-free.
Maintenance

fragments.label: Maintenance
fragments.text: Once the software is in use, maintenance keeps it useful. Corrective maintenance fixes faults that testing missed. Adaptive maintenance changes the program because its environment or the requirements have changed, for example new hardware, a new operating system or a new law. Perfective maintenance makes the program better without changing what it does, such as making it faster or easier to use. The three types are covered fully in 12.3.

fragments.label: Maintenance
fragments.text: Maintenance can carry on for years, and it relies on the documentation produced in earlier stages. When changes can no longer keep the system fit for purpose, a new analysis begins, which is what makes the process a cycle rather than a straight line.

fragments.label: Maintenance
fragments.text: Corrective: fix faults found after release.

fragments.label: Maintenance
fragments.text: Adaptive: respond to a changed environment or changed requirements.

fragments.label: Maintenance
fragments.text: Perfective: improve performance or usability.

fragments.label: Maintenance
fragments.text: When maintenance is no longer enough, the cycle restarts with analysis.
The waterfall model

fragments.label: The waterfall model
fragments.text: Principles: the stages are carried out one after another, like water falling down steps. Each stage is completed, and its output (the specification, the design, the code) is passed down as the input to the next. All requirements are fixed at the start. Arrows back up to the previous stage allow for going back when more work is found to be needed, but the model assumes this is rare. Nothing usable is delivered until the end.

fragments.label: The waterfall model
fragments.text: Benefits: it is simple to understand and easy to manage, because every stage has a defined output and a clear end point; one stage is handled at a time; and it suits smaller projects whose requirements are well understood and fixed. Drawbacks: working software appears only late in the project; changing requirements cannot easily be accommodated; progress inside a stage is hard to measure; modules are brought together only at the end, so integration problems are found late; and it is a poor choice for complex, long-running or ongoing projects.

fragments.label: The waterfall model
fragments.text: Principle: strictly sequential stages, each finished before the next; requirements fixed at the start.

fragments.label: The waterfall model
fragments.text: Benefits: simple, easy to manage, clear milestones and outputs; good for small, well-understood projects.

fragments.label: The waterfall model
fragments.text: Drawbacks: no working product until late, cannot cope with changing requirements, late integration, poor for large or long projects.
The iterative model

fragments.label: The iterative model
fragments.text: Principles: development does not wait for a complete specification. A small subset of the requirements is built first, giving a working, if limited, version. It is then reviewed, more requirements are identified, and another cycle of design, coding and testing adds to it. The cycles repeat until the whole system is complete, often tackling the highest-risk parts first.

fragments.label: The iterative model
fragments.text: Benefits: a working model exists early, so design or functional flaws are spotted and corrected quickly; the client can try each version and give feedback; progress is visible after each cycle; changing the scope costs less; each increment is small, so it is easier to test and debug; and lessons from one cycle improve the next. It suits large and mission-critical projects. Drawbacks: it needs more resources and management; a small system may be hard to split into useful increments; because not all requirements are known at the start, the overall design may need reworking later; and planning the increments may require a view of the complete system anyway.

fragments.label: The iterative model
fragments.text: Principle: build a small part, review, then add more in repeated cycles until complete.

fragments.label: The iterative model
fragments.text: Benefits: early working versions, early fault detection, regular client feedback, measurable progress, lower cost of change, risks tackled early.

fragments.label: The iterative model
fragments.text: Drawbacks: more resources, hard to divide small systems, design issues from requirements that arrive late.
Rapid application development (RAD)

fragments.label: Rapid application development (RAD)
fragments.text: Principles: RAD replaces detailed up-front planning with prototyping. Modules are built as prototypes, often by separate small teams at the same time, and users try them and suggest changes. Analysis, design, coding and testing are squeezed into a series of short, repeated cycles, requirements are allowed to change as the work proceeds, and the finished prototypes are joined together to give the complete product quickly.

fragments.label: Rapid application development (RAD)
fragments.text: Benefits: much shorter development time; changing requirements are welcomed rather than resisted; users give feedback from the first review, so the product matches what they need; integrating from the start avoids a big integration problem at the end; progress is measurable; and components are often reused. Drawbacks: the system must be one that can be split into modules; it needs highly skilled developers and designers; users must be available and involved throughout; and it is best suited to component-based projects that need a short development time. Speed can also mean less formal documentation.

fragments.label: Rapid application development (RAD)
fragments.text: Principle: minimal planning, prototypes built in parallel, short feedback cycles, prototypes integrated into the final product.

fragments.label: Rapid application development (RAD)
fragments.text: Benefits: fast delivery, flexible requirements, strong user feedback, early integration, component reuse.

fragments.label: Rapid application development (RAD)
fragments.text: Drawbacks: needs modular systems, skilled staff and constant user involvement; documentation may be thin.
Why different programs need different life cycles

fragments.label: Why different programs need different life cycles
fragments.text: No single model suits every program. The right choice depends on how clearly the requirements are known and whether they will change, the size and complexity of the system, how much risk is involved, how quickly something usable is needed, how skilled the team is, and whether the client can take part throughout.

fragments.label: Why different programs need different life cycles
fragments.text: Waterfall fits a small or well-understood job with fixed, agreed requirements, such as software that must follow a fixed standard. The iterative model fits a large or critical system where the full requirements emerge over time and early working versions reduce risk. RAD fits a system that has to be delivered quickly, can be split into components and has users available to test prototypes, such as a business app whose screens need regular user input.

fragments.label: Why different programs need different life cycles
fragments.text: Deciding factors: stability of requirements, size and complexity, risk, deadline, team skill, client availability.

fragments.label: Why different programs need different life cycles
fragments.text: Fixed, clear requirements and a small project → waterfall.

fragments.label: Why different programs need different life cycles
fragments.text: Large or critical project with evolving requirements → iterative.

fragments.label: Why different programs need different life cycles
fragments.text: Short deadline, modular system, users available throughout → RAD.

fragments.label: Why different programs need different life cycles
fragments.text:
Scenario A: a program to calculate payroll deductions to a tax rule that is fully published and will not change this year. Small team, fixed deadline.
   → Waterfall. Requirements are complete and stable, so each stage can be finished and signed off in order; the clear milestones make it easy to manage.

Scenario B: a hospital system for patient records, scheduling and prescriptions, to be used for many years; staff are not yet sure of every feature they need.
   → Iterative. Build the high-risk records core first, deliver working versions, and add features as requirements become clear; each increment is tested on its own.

Scenario C: a shop needs a customer ordering app in eight weeks. The manager can meet the developers every week to try screens.
   → RAD. Tight deadline, the app splits into separate screens/modules built in parallel as prototypes, and the available user gives constant feedback.
What is the purpose of a program development life cycle?

fragments.label: What is the purpose of a program development life cycle?
fragments.text: To give development a structured sequence of stages with defined outputs, so the work can be planned, managed and checked against the requirements.
Name the stages of the program development life cycle.

fragments.label: Name the stages of the program development life cycle.
fragments.text: Analysis, design, coding (implementation), testing and maintenance.
What is the main output of the analysis stage?

fragments.label: What is the main output of the analysis stage?
fragments.text: A requirements specification defining what the system must do and any constraints.
State one benefit and one drawback of the waterfall model.

fragments.label: State one benefit and one drawback of the waterfall model.
fragments.text: Benefit: simple and easy to manage, with clear stages and outputs. Drawback: no working software until late, and changing requirements are hard to accommodate.
How does the iterative model begin?

fragments.label: How does the iterative model begin?
fragments.text: By building a small subset of the requirements, then adding to it through repeated cycles of review, design, coding and testing.
What is a prototype, and why does RAD use them?

fragments.label: What is a prototype, and why does RAD use them?
fragments.text: A working model of part of a system; RAD uses prototypes so users can give feedback quickly instead of relying on detailed up-front planning.
Give two conditions a project needs for RAD to be suitable.

fragments.label: Give two conditions a project needs for RAD to be suitable.
fragments.text: Any two of: the system can be split into modules; skilled developers are available; users can be involved throughout; a short development time is required.
Why is it called a life cycle?

fragments.label: Why is it called a life cycle?
fragments.text: Because when maintenance can no longer keep the program fit for purpose, development begins again with a new analysis.

Program design turns a problem into a plan that can be coded. This topic covers two design tools. A structure chart breaks a problem into modules and shows the parameters passed between them. A state-transition diagram documents an algorithm that behaves as a finite state machine. Paper 2 asks candidates to describe the purpose of a structure chart, to complete or draw one for a given problem, to write the pseudocode a chart describes, and to read a state-transition diagram, usually by completing a state-transition table or tracing a sequence of inputs. Answers score when every parameter on a chart is named and points the right way, when each module in the pseudocode becomes a procedure or function whose parameters match the arrows, and when a trace follows the arrows exactly, starting from the start state.

fragments.label: Structure chart
fragments.text: A diagram of the modular structure of a solution. Each box is a module, each level refines the level above it, and labelled arrows show the parameters passed between modules.

fragments.label: Module
fragments.text: A self-contained part of a solution that carries out one sub-task. On a structure chart it is a box; in the program it becomes a procedure or a function.

fragments.label: Parameter
fragments.text: A value passed between modules. On a structure chart a downward arrow supplies a value to the module being called, and an upward arrow returns a value to the calling module.

fragments.label: Interface
fragments.text: The parameters that pass between a calling module and the module it calls. A structure chart shows each module's interface as the named arrows on the line joining the two boxes.

fragments.label: Flag
fragments.text: A Boolean parameter that reports a condition, such as whether an input was valid. On a structure chart its arrow has a solid (filled) circle at the tail.

fragments.label: Finite state machine (FSM)
fragments.text: A machine with a fixed set of possible states, a start state, a set of inputs that move it from one state to another, and possibly a set of outputs.

fragments.label: State-transition table
fragments.text: A table that gives, for each current state and each input, the next state the FSM moves to and any output it produces.

fragments.label: State-transition diagram
fragments.text: A diagram that describes the behaviour of an FSM. States are circles and each transition is an arrow labelled with the input that causes it, written input | output when the transition also produces an output.
The purpose of a structure chart

fragments.label: The purpose of a structure chart
fragments.text: A structure chart is a design tool for modular programs. The problem is decomposed into sub-tasks, and each sub-task becomes a module drawn as a box. The top box (level 0) names the whole program. The boxes below it (level 1) are the sub-tasks it calls, and any of those can be refined again into its own lower level. This is top-down design with stepwise refinement: each level adds detail to the level above it.

fragments.label: The purpose of a structure chart
fragments.text: Lines join each module to the modules it calls, and the calls on one level are normally read from left to right. A structure chart shows what the program does and how its modules fit together. It does not show how a module does its job. The detailed logic of each module is written separately in pseudocode or drawn as a flowchart.

fragments.label: The purpose of a structure chart
fragments.text: A structure chart also shows the interface between modules: the parameters passed each time one module calls another. This lets several programmers each write a module, knowing exactly what data it receives and what it must return, and it shows which modules can be tested or reused on their own.

fragments.label: The purpose of a structure chart
fragments.text: Purpose: decompose a problem into sub-tasks (modules), showing the hierarchy of modules and the parameters passed between them.

fragments.label: The purpose of a structure chart
fragments.text: Each box is a module; each level is a refinement of the level above (top-down design, stepwise refinement).

fragments.label: The purpose of a structure chart
fragments.text: It shows which module calls which and the interface, not the logic inside a module.

fragments.label: The purpose of a structure chart
fragments.text: Benefits: helps programmers see how modules are related, lets modules be shared out, written and tested separately, and shows the parameters each module needs.
Showing parameters on a structure chart

fragments.label: Showing parameters on a structure chart
fragments.text: Every parameter is drawn as a short arrow beside the line joining two modules, labelled with the parameter's identifier. The direction of the arrow shows which way the value travels. A downward arrow supplies a value from the calling module to the module it calls. An upward arrow returns a new value from the called module to the module above it. A double-headed arrow shows a value that is passed down, updated inside the lower module, and passed back up.

fragments.label: Showing parameters on a structure chart
fragments.text: Two arrow styles are commonly used. A data parameter is often drawn with an open (hollow) circle at its tail. A flag, a Boolean value that reports a condition such as Valid or GameFinished, is drawn with a solid circle at its tail.

fragments.label: Showing parameters on a structure chart
fragments.text: A value produced by one module and needed by another is passed up to their common parent and then down again. Modules on the same level never pass values to each other directly. The structure chart does not state whether a parameter is passed by value or by reference; that decision is made when the pseudocode is written.

fragments.label: Showing parameters on a structure chart
fragments.text: Downward arrow: a value supplied to the lower-level (called) module.

fragments.label: Showing parameters on a structure chart
fragments.text: Upward arrow: a value returned to the higher-level (calling) module.

fragments.label: Showing parameters on a structure chart
fragments.text: Double-headed arrow: a value passed down, changed inside the module, and passed back up.

fragments.label: Showing parameters on a structure chart
fragments.text: Solid circle at the tail: a flag (Boolean); open circle: a data value.

fragments.label: Showing parameters on a structure chart
fragments.text: Sibling modules exchange data only through their parent; the chart does not say BYVAL or BYREF.
Selection and repetition on a structure chart

fragments.label: Selection and repetition on a structure chart
fragments.text: A structure chart can also show control information. Selection is drawn as a diamond on the line below a module, with the condition written beside it. The branches are labelled True and False, and only one of the modules below the diamond is called each time. For example, a CheckLogin module might test PasswordCorrect and call either OutputWelcome (True) or OutputWarning (False).

fragments.label: Selection and repetition on a structure chart
fragments.text: Repetition is drawn as a semi-circular (curved) arrow across the lines to the modules that are repeated, labelled with the condition that controls the loop, such as UNTIL Valid or WHILE game not finished. Every module under the arrow is called again on each pass.

fragments.label: Selection and repetition on a structure chart
fragments.text: Diamond with a condition: selection; one of the True / False branches is called.

fragments.label: Selection and repetition on a structure chart
fragments.text: Semi-circular arrow with a label: repetition of the modules beneath it; the label gives the loop condition.

fragments.label: Selection and repetition on a structure chart
fragments.text: In pseudocode a diamond becomes an IF statement and a semi-circular arrow becomes a loop (REPEAT, WHILE or FOR).

fragments.label: Selection and repetition on a structure chart
fragments.text:
