PROCEDURE CheckLogin(PasswordCorrect : BOOLEAN)
   IF PasswordCorrect = TRUE THEN
      CALL OutputWelcome()
   ELSE
      CALL OutputWarning()
   ENDIF
ENDPROCEDURE
Constructing a structure chart for a given problem

fragments.label: Constructing a structure chart for a given problem
fragments.text: Start with one box naming the whole problem. Split it into the main sub-tasks, usually input, processing and output, and draw them left to right in the order they are carried out. Refine any sub-task that is still too large into a lower level. Then, for each line, decide what data the called module needs (downward arrows) and what it produces for its caller (upward arrows), and name each arrow with a meaningful identifier. Finally, add a diamond for any module that is only called under a condition and a semi-circular arrow for any modules that repeat.

fragments.label: Constructing a structure chart for a given problem
fragments.text: The worked example designs a program that reads a journey distance, repeating the input until it is a positive number, then works out the fuel cost and the travel time and outputs both.

fragments.label: Constructing a structure chart for a given problem
fragments.text: Top box: the whole problem; level 1: the main sub-tasks in order, left to right.

fragments.label: Constructing a structure chart for a given problem
fragments.text: Refine large sub-tasks into a further level until each box is one clear task.

fragments.label: Constructing a structure chart for a given problem
fragments.text: Add a named arrow for every value a module needs (down) or produces (up).

fragments.label: Constructing a structure chart for a given problem
fragments.text: Add diamonds for conditional calls and semi-circular arrows for repeated calls.

fragments.label: Constructing a structure chart for a given problem
fragments.text:
Level 0:  JourneyCost

Level 1 (called by JourneyCost, left to right):
  InputDistance      up:   Distance
  CalculateJourney   down: Distance        up: Cost, Hours
  OutputResults      down: Cost, Hours

Level 2 (called by InputDistance, under a semi-circular arrow labelled UNTIL Valid):
  GetNumber          up:   Distance
  CheckPositive      down: Distance        up: Valid  (flag, solid circle)

Reading the interface:
- Distance goes up from InputDistance to JourneyCost, then down into CalculateJourney.
  The two level-1 modules do not pass it to each other directly.
- CalculateJourney returns two values (Cost and Hours), so both arrows point up.
- Valid is a Boolean, so it is drawn as a flag.
- The semi-circular arrow means GetNumber and CheckPositive are called again
  until Valid is TRUE.
Deriving pseudocode from a structure chart

fragments.label: Deriving pseudocode from a structure chart
fragments.text: Each box below the top becomes a subroutine, and the top box becomes the main program that calls the level-1 modules in order. Use local variables and parameters rather than global variables, so each module is self-contained and a change inside one module cannot accidentally alter a variable elsewhere.

fragments.label: Deriving pseudocode from a structure chart
fragments.text: The arrows decide the header. A module that sends exactly one value up can be written as a FUNCTION that RETURNS that value. A module that sends no value up is a PROCEDURE called with CALL, with its downward values as BYVAL parameters. A module that sends two or more values up, or has a double-headed arrow, is a PROCEDURE whose upward values are BYREF parameters, so the changes reach the caller. A diamond becomes an IF statement, and a semi-circular arrow becomes a loop whose condition matches the label.

fragments.label: Deriving pseudocode from a structure chart
fragments.text: Because the chart does not say how parameters are passed, choose BYVAL for values that only travel down and BYREF for values that must come back up in a procedure.

fragments.label: Deriving pseudocode from a structure chart
fragments.text: Top box: main program; every other box: a procedure or function with the same identifier.

fragments.label: Deriving pseudocode from a structure chart
fragments.text: One upward value: FUNCTION ... RETURNS; no upward value: PROCEDURE with BYVAL parameters.

fragments.label: Deriving pseudocode from a structure chart
fragments.text: Several upward values or a double-headed arrow: PROCEDURE with BYREF parameters.

fragments.label: Deriving pseudocode from a structure chart
fragments.text: Diamond → IF ... THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF; semi-circular arrow → REPEAT ... UNTIL, WHILE ... ENDWHILE or FOR ... NEXT.

fragments.label: Deriving pseudocode from a structure chart
fragments.text:
CONSTANT CostPerKm = 0.25        // dollars per km
CONSTANT AverageSpeed = 50      // km per hour

FUNCTION GetNumber() RETURNS REAL          // one value up: Distance
   DECLARE Value : REAL
   OUTPUT "Enter the distance in km: "
   INPUT Value
   RETURN Value
ENDFUNCTION

FUNCTION CheckPositive(Distance : REAL) RETURNS BOOLEAN   // flag up: Valid
   RETURN Distance > 0
ENDFUNCTION

FUNCTION InputDistance() RETURNS REAL      // one value up: Distance
   DECLARE Distance : REAL
   DECLARE Valid : BOOLEAN
   REPEAT                                  // the semi-circular arrow
      Distance ← GetNumber()
      Valid ← CheckPositive(Distance)
   UNTIL Valid = TRUE
   RETURN Distance
ENDFUNCTION

// two values up, so a procedure with BYREF parameters
PROCEDURE CalculateJourney(BYVAL Distance : REAL, BYREF Cost : REAL, BYREF Hours : REAL)
   Cost ← Distance * CostPerKm
   Hours ← Distance / AverageSpeed
ENDPROCEDURE

PROCEDURE OutputResults(Cost : REAL, Hours : REAL)   // values only come down
   OUTPUT "Fuel cost: $", Cost
   OUTPUT "Travel time: ", Hours, " hours"
ENDPROCEDURE

// main program: the JourneyCost box
DECLARE Distance, Cost, Hours : REAL
Distance ← InputDistance()
CALL CalculateJourney(Distance, Cost, Hours)
CALL OutputResults(Cost, Hours)

// Test run: inputs -40 then 120
// -40 fails CheckPositive, so the loop asks again; 120 passes.
// Cost = 120 * 0.25 = 30, Hours = 120 / 50 = 2.4
// Output: Fuel cost: $30   Travel time: 2.4 hours
Finite state machines and state-transition tables

fragments.label: Finite state machines and state-transition tables
fragments.text: Some algorithms are best described by the states they can be in rather than by a sequence of steps: a burglar alarm, a door lock or a vending machine. Each can be modelled as a finite state machine (FSM). An FSM has a fixed set of states and one start state. Each input moves it from its current state to a next state, which may be the same state. It may also produce an output.

fragments.label: Finite state machines and state-transition tables
fragments.text: A state-transition table lists this behaviour. Each row gives a current state, an input (event), the next state and, if there is one, the output. Building the table from a written description is usually the first step, because it forces every combination of state and input to be considered. Any combination the description does not mention shows a gap in the specification that must be resolved.

fragments.label: Finite state machines and state-transition tables
fragments.text: FSM: a fixed set of states, a start state, inputs that change the state, and possibly outputs.

fragments.label: Finite state machines and state-transition tables
fragments.text: An input can leave the FSM in the same state (no change of state).

fragments.label: Finite state machines and state-transition tables
fragments.text: State-transition table columns: current state, input, (output), next state.

fragments.label: Finite state machines and state-transition tables
fragments.text: Purpose: documents an algorithm precisely, including what each input does in every state, before it is coded.

fragments.label: Finite state machines and state-transition tables
fragments.text:
Description: A locker starts Locked. Entering the correct code unlocks it. One wrong
code gives a Warning; a correct code from Warning still unlocks it, but a second wrong
code Blocks the locker until a member of staff resets it. Closing the door of an
unlocked locker locks it again.

Current state | Input         | Next state
--------------+---------------+-----------
Locked        | Correct code  | Unlocked
Locked        | Wrong code    | Warning
Warning       | Correct code  | Unlocked
Warning       | Wrong code    | Blocked
Unlocked      | Door closed   | Locked
Blocked       | Staff reset   | Locked

Trace the input sequence: Wrong, Correct, Door closed, Wrong, Wrong
Locked -> Warning -> Unlocked -> Locked -> Warning -> Blocked

Note: the FSM counts wrong attempts by being in a different state (Warning),
not by using a variable. The description does not say what a code does while
Blocked; a designer would add a row such as Blocked | any code | Blocked.
Drawing and reading state-transition diagrams

fragments.label: Drawing and reading state-transition diagrams
fragments.text: A state-transition diagram shows the same information as the table. Each state is a circle labelled with its name. The start state has an arrow pointing into it from nowhere, often labelled start. Each transition is an arrow from the current state to the next state, labelled with the input that causes it. An input that causes no change of state is drawn as an arrow that loops back to the same circle. A final (halting) state, if the FSM has one, is drawn as a double circle.

fragments.label: Drawing and reading state-transition diagrams
fragments.text: When a transition also produces an output, the arrow's label is written input | output. For example, 1 | 0 means an input of 1 produces an output of 0 as the FSM follows that arrow. An FSM with outputs is also called a Mealy machine. If there is no output for a transition, exam tables often write none in the output column.

fragments.label: Drawing and reading state-transition diagrams
fragments.text: To trace an input sequence, start in the start state. For each input, find the arrow leaving the current state that carries that input, record the output on its label, and move to the state it points to. The next input is always taken from this new state.

fragments.label: Drawing and reading state-transition diagrams
fragments.text: Circle: a state; double circle: a final (halting) state; arrow from nowhere into a state: the start state.

fragments.label: Drawing and reading state-transition diagrams
fragments.text: Arrow labelled with an input: a transition; a loop back to the same circle: no change of state.

fragments.label: Drawing and reading state-transition diagrams
fragments.text: Label input | output: the output produced by that transition (Mealy machine).

fragments.label: Drawing and reading state-transition diagrams
fragments.text: Tracing: always begin in the start state, and take each new input from the state reached by the previous one.

fragments.label: Drawing and reading state-transition diagrams
fragments.text:
An FSM reads a bit stream one bit at a time and outputs 1 whenever the bit just read
is the second (or later) of consecutive 1s; otherwise it outputs 0.
Start state: S1 (the last bit was 0, or nothing has been read yet).

Transitions (diagram labels):
  S1 --0|0--> S1   (loop back to S1)
  S1 --1|0--> S2
  S2 --1|1--> S2   (loop back to S2)
  S2 --0|0--> S1

Trace for the input 0 1 1 1 0 1 1:
Current state | Input | Output | Next state
S1            | 0     | 0      | S1
S1            | 1     | 0      | S2
S2            | 1     | 1      | S2
S2            | 1     | 1      | S2
S2            | 0     | 0      | S1
S1            | 1     | 0      | S2
S2            | 1     | 1      | S2

Output stream: 0 0 1 1 0 0 1   Final state: S2

Each row's current state is the previous row's next state.
State two purposes of a structure chart.

fragments.label: State two purposes of a structure chart.
fragments.text: It shows how a problem is decomposed into modules and which module calls which, and it shows the parameters passed between modules (the interface).
What does a downward arrow on a structure chart show, and what does an upward arrow show?

fragments.label: What does a downward arrow on a structure chart show, and what does an upward arrow show?
fragments.text: A downward arrow is a value supplied to the called (lower) module; an upward arrow is a value returned to the calling (higher) module.
How is a flag shown on a structure chart?

fragments.label: How is a flag shown on a structure chart?
fragments.text: As an arrow with a solid (filled) circle at its tail; it carries a Boolean value.
How are selection and repetition shown on a structure chart?

fragments.label: How are selection and repetition shown on a structure chart?
fragments.text: Selection by a diamond with a condition and True / False branches; repetition by a semi-circular arrow labelled with the loop condition.
A module on a chart returns one value upward. How is it usually written in pseudocode?

fragments.label: A module on a chart returns one value upward. How is it usually written in pseudocode?
fragments.text: As a FUNCTION with RETURNS, taking its downward values as parameters.
What does a structure chart not tell you about parameters?

fragments.label: What does a structure chart not tell you about parameters?
fragments.text: Whether they are passed by value or by reference; that is decided when the pseudocode is written.
What is a finite state machine?

fragments.label: What is a finite state machine?
fragments.text: A machine with a fixed set of states, a start state, inputs that change it from one state to another, and possibly outputs.
What does the label b | c on a state-transition diagram mean?

fragments.label: What does the label b | c on a state-transition diagram mean?
fragments.text: An input of b causes this transition and produces an output of c.
How are the start state and a final (halting) state shown on a state-transition diagram?

fragments.label: How are the start state and a final (halting) state shown on a state-transition diagram?
fragments.text: The start state has an arrow pointing into it from nowhere; a final state is drawn as a double circle.

This topic covers finding faults in a program, testing it methodically and keeping it useful after release. Paper 2 asks candidates to identify syntax, logic and run-time errors in given pseudocode and correct them, to dry-run an algorithm with a trace table, to name and describe testing methods (dry run, walkthrough, white-box, black-box, integration, alpha, beta, acceptance and stub), to choose normal, abnormal, extreme and boundary test data for a test plan, and to identify or carry out corrective, adaptive and perfective maintenance, often by amending a given program. Answers score when an error is classified by its effect (will not translate, wrong result, or crash), when each testing method is described by who tests and what they can see, when test data comes with its expected result, and when a maintenance type is matched to the reason for the change.

fragments.label: Syntax error
fragments.text: An error in which a statement does not follow the grammar rules of the programming language, so the program cannot be translated. It is reported by the compiler or interpreter.

fragments.label: Logic error
fragments.text: An error in the logic of the solution: the program runs, but it does not behave as intended and produces an incorrect result.

fragments.label: Run-time error
fragments.text: An error that occurs while the program is running and causes it to crash (stop unexpectedly) or freeze, for example dividing by zero or an infinite loop.

fragments.label: Dry run
fragments.text: Working through an algorithm or program by hand, without a computer, recording the value of each variable and condition at each step in a trace table.

fragments.label: Trace table
fragments.text: A table with a column for each variable (and for conditions and output) that records how their values change as an algorithm is dry-run.

fragments.label: White-box testing
fragments.text: Testing that uses knowledge of the program code, choosing test data so that every path through the code is executed and its results checked.

fragments.label: Black-box testing
fragments.text: Testing that compares the actual results with the expected results for chosen inputs, worked out from the specification, without looking at the program code.

fragments.label: Stub testing
fragments.text: Testing the structure of a program before all modules are written, by using stubs: dummy modules whose body only outputs a message (or returns a fixed value) to show they were called.

fragments.label: Integration testing
fragments.text: Testing that individually tested modules work correctly together once they are combined into one program, usually adding one module at a time.

fragments.label: Alpha, beta and acceptance testing
fragments.text: Alpha testing is done in-house by the developer's own testers. Beta testing is done by a limited number of chosen external users, in their own environments, before general release. Acceptance testing is done by the client, to check that bespoke software meets the requirements before they sign it off.

fragments.label: Test plan
fragments.text: A detailed list of the tests to be carried out, giving for each test its purpose, the test data, the type of test data and the expected result, with space to record the actual result.

fragments.label: Corrective, adaptive and perfective maintenance
fragments.text: Corrective maintenance corrects errors found after the program is in use. Adaptive maintenance amends a program to enhance its functionality or respond to changed requirements or a changed environment. Perfective maintenance improves a program's performance or maintainability without changing what it does.
Why faults occur, and ways of exposing and avoiding them

fragments.label: Why faults occur, and ways of exposing and avoiding them
fragments.text: Software may not behave as expected for several reasons: a programmer makes a coding mistake, the requirements specification was drawn up wrongly, the designer makes a design error, a poorly designed interface leads users into mistakes, or the hardware fails. A fault that reaches the end user harms the developer's reputation, and the later a fault is found the more expensive it is to fix. So testing must happen throughout development, not only at the end.

fragments.label: Why faults occur, and ways of exposing and avoiding them
fragments.text: Faults are exposed by testing: dry-running algorithms, reviewing code in walkthroughs, and running the program with carefully chosen test data. Testing can show that faults are present but can never prove that none remain, because a program cannot be tested with every possible input.

fragments.label: Why faults occur, and ways of exposing and avoiding them
fragments.text: The best approach is to avoid faults in the first place. Most faults come from not fully understanding the problem, so a careful requirements analysis is essential. Faults are also reduced by using tried and tested design methods such as structured programming (small modules with clear interfaces, local variables and parameters), by following conventions such as meaningful identifiers, identifier tables and standard algorithms, and by reusing library modules that have already been tested.

fragments.label: Why faults occur, and ways of exposing and avoiding them
fragments.text: Causes: coding mistakes, a wrong requirements specification, design errors, a poor user interface, hardware failure.

fragments.label: Why faults occur, and ways of exposing and avoiding them
fragments.text: Expose faults: dry runs, walkthroughs, testing with chosen test data at every stage.

fragments.label: Why faults occur, and ways of exposing and avoiding them
fragments.text: Avoid faults: thorough analysis, structured/modular design, conventions (meaningful identifiers, identifier tables), tested library modules.

fragments.label: Why faults occur, and ways of exposing and avoiding them
fragments.text: Testing shows the presence of faults, never their absence; the earlier a fault is found, the cheaper it is to fix.
Types of error: syntax, logic and run-time

fragments.label: Types of error: syntax, logic and run-time
fragments.text: A syntax error breaks the grammar rules of the language: a misspelt keyword, a missing bracket or quote, a missing ENDIF, or = used where the assignment arrow is needed. Syntax errors are the easiest to find because the translator reports them. Many editors underline them as the code is typed. A compiler checks the whole program, so a program that compiles has no syntax errors left. An interpreter only checks each statement as it is about to be executed, so a syntax error in a part of the program that has not yet been run can remain hidden. The error is sometimes reported on the line after the real mistake, because the translator only notices a problem when the next token is unexpected.

fragments.label: Types of error: syntax, logic and run-time
fragments.text: A logic error lets the program run but gives the wrong result: the wrong operator (< instead of <=, AND instead of OR), a loop that runs one time too many or too few, a variable initialised to the wrong value, or a calculation in the wrong order. The translator cannot detect these because the code is valid.

fragments.label: Types of error: syntax, logic and run-time
fragments.text: A run-time error happens while the program is executing and makes it crash or freeze: dividing by zero, using an array index outside the array's bounds, reading a file that does not exist, or an infinite loop. Logic and run-time errors can only be found by careful testing, and they are dangerous because they may only appear for particular data, so a program can seem to work for a long time before failing.

fragments.label: Types of error: syntax, logic and run-time
fragments.text: Syntax error: breaks the language rules; found by the compiler/interpreter; the program cannot be translated.

fragments.label: Types of error: syntax, logic and run-time
fragments.text: Logic error: the program runs but gives an incorrect result; found by testing and dry runs.

fragments.label: Types of error: syntax, logic and run-time
fragments.text: Run-time error: the program crashes or freezes during execution (division by zero, index out of range, missing file, infinite loop).

fragments.label: Types of error: syntax, logic and run-time
fragments.text: A compiled program has no syntax errors left; an interpreted one can still contain them in code that has not been run.
Locating and correcting errors

fragments.label: Locating and correcting errors
fragments.text: To correct an error, first classify it by its effect, then find the line responsible. A syntax error message points close to the line. A logic error is found by comparing actual results with expected ones and then dry-running the code, or by using a debugger, to find where the values first go wrong. A run-time error is found by identifying the data that caused the crash and the statement being executed at the time.

fragments.label: Locating and correcting errors
fragments.text: When writing a correction in an exam, give the corrected line of code in full, not just a description, and check that the fix does not break anything else. The worked example has one error of each type.

fragments.label: Locating and correcting errors
fragments.text: Classify the error first: will not translate (syntax), wrong answer (logic), crash or freeze (run-time).

fragments.label: Locating and correcting errors
fragments.text: Locate: translator message for syntax; expected-versus-actual results plus a dry run for logic; the failing data for run-time.

fragments.label: Locating and correcting errors
fragments.text: Correct: rewrite the whole line, then re-test with the data that exposed the error.

fragments.label: Locating and correcting errors
fragments.text:
Intended: read marks until -1 is entered, then output the average mark.

01  DECLARE Total, Count, Mark : INTEGER
02  Total ← 0
03  Count ← 1
04  INPUT Mark
05  WHILE Mark <> -1
06     Total ← Total + Mark
07     Count ← Count + 1
08     INPUT Mark
09  ENDWHILE
10  OUTPUT "Average: , Total / Count

Syntax error, line 10: the closing quote is missing, so the string never ends.
   Correction: OUTPUT "Average: ", Total / Count

Logic error, line 03: Count starts at 1, so it ends one higher than the number
   of marks and the average is too small (see the trace in the dry-run section).
   Correction: Count ← 0

Run-time error, line 10 (after correcting line 03): if -1 is the first input,
   Count is 0 and the program divides by zero and crashes.
   Correction: replace line 10 with
      IF Count > 0 THEN
         OUTPUT "Average: ", Total / Count
      ELSE
         OUTPUT "No marks entered"
      ENDIF
Stub testing

fragments.label: Stub testing
fragments.text: Stub testing lets the top-level structure of a program, such as a menu, be tested before all the modules it calls have been written. Each unfinished module is replaced by a stub: a procedure with the correct identifier whose body only outputs a message showing it was called, or a function that returns a fixed, known value.

fragments.label: Stub testing
fragments.text: Running the program then shows whether each menu choice or condition calls the right module in the right order. Each stub is later replaced by the real module and tested. Stub testing fits top-down development and the structure chart from 12.2: the upper levels are tested first, with stubs standing in for the lower levels.

fragments.label: Stub testing
fragments.text: A stub is a dummy module: it has the right identifier (and parameters) but only outputs a message or returns a fixed value.

fragments.label: Stub testing
fragments.text: Purpose: test the flow of control (which module is called when) before the modules are finished.

fragments.label: Stub testing
fragments.text: Stubs are replaced one at a time by the real, tested modules.

fragments.label: Stub testing
fragments.text:
PROCEDURE AddStudent()
   OUTPUT "AddStudent called"          // stub
ENDPROCEDURE

PROCEDURE FindStudent()
   OUTPUT "FindStudent called"         // stub
ENDPROCEDURE

FUNCTION CountStudents() RETURNS INTEGER
   RETURN 3                            // stub returns a fixed value
ENDFUNCTION

DECLARE Choice : INTEGER
OUTPUT "1 Add  2 Find  3 Count"
INPUT Choice
CASE OF Choice
   1 : CALL AddStudent()
   2 : CALL FindStudent()
   3 : OUTPUT "Students: ", CountStudents()
   OTHERWISE : OUTPUT "Not a menu option"
ENDCASE

// Test: input 2 should output "FindStudent called";
// input 3 should output "Students: 3"; input 7 should output "Not a menu option".
Black-box and white-box testing

fragments.label: Black-box and white-box testing
fragments.text: In black-box testing the tester cannot see the code, and it is often someone other than the programmer. Test data and expected results are worked out from the specification: what the program is supposed to do. The program is run, the actual results are recorded and compared with the expected ones. A difference shows a fault exists, but not where; a dry run or a debugger is then used to find the lines that need correcting.

fragments.label: Black-box and white-box testing
fragments.text: In white-box testing the tester uses knowledge of the code to choose test data that makes every path through it run: both branches of every IF, every CASE clause, and each loop run zero times, once and several times. The exact values do not matter as long as together they reach every path. White-box testing is usually done by the programmer while modules are being written; black-box testing checks the program against its requirements.

fragments.label: Black-box and white-box testing
fragments.text: The worked example shows the minimum white-box test data for a nested IF with three paths.

fragments.label: Black-box and white-box testing
fragments.text: Black-box: code not visible; test data and expected results come from the specification; compares expected with actual results.

fragments.label: Black-box and white-box testing
fragments.text: White-box: code visible; test data chosen so that every path (every branch and loop) is executed.

fragments.label: Black-box and white-box testing
fragments.text: Black-box shows that a fault exists; white-box, dry runs and debuggers help locate it.

fragments.label: Black-box and white-box testing
fragments.text:
IF Age < 16 THEN
   Price ← 5
ELSE
   IF Age >= 65 THEN
      Price ← 6
   ELSE
      Price ← 10
   ENDIF
ENDIF

There are three paths, so at least three tests are needed:

Test | Age | Age < 16 | Age >= 65 | Expected Price
1    | 10  | TRUE     | (not tested) | 5
2    | 70  | FALSE    | TRUE      | 6
3    | 30  | FALSE    | FALSE     | 10

Any values giving these condition results would do. To check the comparisons
themselves (< rather than <=, >= rather than >), add the values at each edge:
15 → 5, 16 → 10, 64 → 10, 65 → 6.
Dry runs, trace tables and walkthroughs

fragments.label: Dry runs, trace tables and walkthroughs
fragments.text: A dry run checks an algorithm by hand. Draw a trace table with a column for every variable, one for each condition being tested and one for output. Work through the algorithm one statement at a time, writing a value only when it changes (a blank cell means the value is unchanged) and starting a new row for each pass of a loop. Numbering the lines, with a column for the line being executed, helps you follow the exact order. Comparing the final output with the expected result shows whether the algorithm is correct, and the rows show where it first goes wrong.

fragments.label: Dry runs, trace tables and walkthroughs
fragments.text: A walkthrough is a review in which the programmer steps through the algorithm or code, often with other people such as colleagues, explaining what each part does. The coursebook treats walking through with a trace table as another name for a dry run. Both are used early, while modules are being written, and they can be done before the program even exists as code.

fragments.label: Dry runs, trace tables and walkthroughs
fragments.text: Trace table: one column per variable, condition and output; enter a value only when it changes; one row per loop pass.

fragments.label: Dry runs, trace tables and walkthroughs
fragments.text: Dry run: find the expected output by hand and see where the actual values first go wrong.

fragments.label: Dry runs, trace tables and walkthroughs
fragments.text: Walkthrough: stepping through the code, often explaining it to others, to spot errors before or during coding.

fragments.label: Dry runs, trace tables and walkthroughs
fragments.text:
Dry run of the original average program (Count ← 1 on line 03)
with the inputs 10, 20, -1. Expected output: Average: 15

Mark | Total | Count | Mark <> -1 | OUTPUT
     | 0     | 1     |            |
10   |       |       | TRUE       |
     | 10    | 2     |            |
20   |       |       | TRUE       |
     | 30    | 3     |            |
-1   |       |       | FALSE      |
     |       |       |            | Average: 10

Actual output 10 ≠ expected 15. Only two marks were entered but Count is 3,
and the table shows Count was already 1 before any mark was read: line 03
is the fault. With Count ← 0 the final row gives 30 / 2 = 15.
Integration, alpha, beta and acceptance testing

fragments.label: Integration, alpha, beta and acceptance testing
fragments.text: Programs are usually made of many modules, sometimes written by different programmers. Each module can pass its own tests and still fail when combined, for example if the modules disagree about the order or type of parameters. Integration testing tests the modules together once they are joined, usually adding one module at a time and testing again before the next is added, so any new fault can be traced to the module just added.

fragments.label: Integration, alpha, beta and acceptance testing
fragments.text: Before release, software is alpha tested in-house by the developer's own testers, who try to find faults before anyone outside sees it. What happens next depends on who the software is for. Bespoke software, written for a particular client, goes to acceptance testing: the client tests it, often with real data, to confirm it does everything in the requirements specification. When it passes, the client signs it off as part of the hand-over. Software written for general sale has no single client, so after alpha testing a beta version is given to a limited number of chosen users, who use it in their own environments with their own hardware and data and report faults back so they can be fixed before general release.

fragments.label: Integration, alpha, beta and acceptance testing
fragments.text: Integration: combine separately tested modules and check they work together; add one module at a time.

fragments.label: Integration, alpha, beta and acceptance testing
fragments.text: Alpha: in-house testers at the developer, before anyone outside sees the software.

fragments.label: Integration, alpha, beta and acceptance testing
fragments.text: Beta: a limited number of chosen external users, in real environments, before general release; they report faults back.

fragments.label: Integration, alpha, beta and acceptance testing
fragments.text: Acceptance: the client checks bespoke software against the requirements before signing it off.
Test strategy and test plan

fragments.label: Test strategy and test plan
fragments.text: A test strategy is decided during design. It sets out how the software will be tested: which testing methods suit the project, in what order they happen, and who carries them out. Planning this early means testing is rigorous from the start rather than improvised at the end.

fragments.label: Test strategy and test plan
fragments.text: Large programs cannot be tested exhaustively, so testing has to be systematic to find as many faults as possible. An outline test plan lists what needs checking: does each menu choice go to the correct module, is input validated, do loops and decisions work correctly, is data saved to the correct files, and are the results correct? This is then expanded into a detailed test plan, where each test has a number, a description of what it tests, the test data, the type of test data, the expected result and a column for the actual result. Writing the expected result before the test is run keeps the comparison honest, and a completed plan is a record of what has and has not been checked.

fragments.label: Test strategy and test plan
fragments.text: Test strategy: the overall approach (which methods, when, by whom), decided during design.

fragments.label: Test strategy and test plan
fragments.text: Test plan contents: test number, what is being tested, test data, type of data, expected result, actual result (and any action taken).

fragments.label: Test strategy and test plan
fragments.text: Need: programs cannot be tested exhaustively, so testing must be planned and systematic, and the results recorded.
Choosing test data: normal, abnormal, extreme and boundary

fragments.label: Choosing test data: normal, abnormal, extreme and boundary
fragments.text: Test data is chosen deliberately, unlike real data, so that each test checks a particular possibility. Normal (valid) data is typical data the program should accept and process correctly. Abnormal (erroneous) data is data the program should reject: values outside the allowed range, the wrong data type, or missing input. Extreme data is the largest and smallest values that are still valid, at each end of the normal range. Boundary data tests each edge of the range from both sides: the value just within the limit, which must be accepted, and the value just outside it, which must be rejected.

fragments.label: Choosing test data: normal, abnormal, extreme and boundary
fragments.text: Use a separate test for each kind of abnormal value. A single value that is wrong in two ways, such as a negative decimal, does not show which check is working. Boundary tests matter because the most common logic error in validation is a comparison off by one, such as < where <= was needed, and only values at the edge reveal it.

fragments.label: Choosing test data: normal, abnormal, extreme and boundary
fragments.text: Always give the expected result with each item of test data. The worked example is a test plan for a ticket-booking input where the number of tickets must be a whole number from 1 to 10 inclusive.

fragments.label: Choosing test data: normal, abnormal, extreme and boundary
fragments.text: Normal: typical valid data, should be accepted.

fragments.label: Choosing test data: normal, abnormal, extreme and boundary
fragments.text: Abnormal (erroneous): invalid data such as out of range, wrong type or missing, should be rejected.

fragments.label: Choosing test data: normal, abnormal, extreme and boundary
fragments.text: Extreme: the largest and smallest valid values, should be accepted.

fragments.label: Choosing test data: normal, abnormal, extreme and boundary
fragments.text: Boundary: values on either side of each limit: just inside (accept) and just outside (reject).

fragments.label: Choosing test data: normal, abnormal, extreme and boundary
fragments.text: Test one kind of invalid value at a time, and state the expected result for every test.

fragments.label: Choosing test data: normal, abnormal, extreme and boundary
fragments.text:
Rule: the number of tickets must be a whole number from 1 to 10 inclusive.

No. | Test data | Type                  | Expected result | Actual result
1   | 4         | Normal                | Accepted        | Accepted
2   | 7         | Normal                | Accepted        | Accepted
3   | 1         | Extreme / boundary    | Accepted        | Accepted
4   | 10        | Extreme / boundary    | Accepted        | Rejected  ← fault
5   | 0         | Boundary (just below) | Rejected        | Rejected
6   | 11        | Boundary (just above) | Rejected        | Rejected
7   | -5        | Abnormal              | Rejected        | Rejected
8   | 2.5       | Abnormal (not whole)  | Rejected        | Rejected
9   | "three"   | Abnormal (not number) | Rejected        | Rejected
10  | (blank)   | Abnormal (missing)    | Rejected        | Rejected

Test 4 fails: 10 is valid but was rejected. The upper check was most likely
written Tickets < 10 instead of Tickets <= 10. Only a test at the edge could
reveal this: 4 and 7 pass either way. After correcting the line, test 4
(and test 6, to check 11 is still rejected) must be run again.
The need for continuing maintenance and its three types

fragments.label: The need for continuing maintenance and its three types
fragments.text: A program does not wear out like a machine, but it still needs changing after it has been released. Faults appear that testing missed, often because a rarely used part of the program is finally run or unusual data is entered. Users' needs change, the law changes, or the program must run on new hardware or a new operating system. And a working program can often be made faster or easier to maintain. Maintenance keeps the program correct and useful for as long as it is in use.

fragments.label: The need for continuing maintenance and its three types
fragments.text: Corrective maintenance corrects errors, logic or run-time, that come to light while the program is in use. The programmer uses a trace table or debugging software to find the cause. A correction can introduce a new error, so the program must be tested again afterwards.

fragments.label: The need for continuing maintenance and its three types
fragments.text: Adaptive maintenance amends a program to enhance its functionality or to respond to changes in the specification, for example adding a new feature the users now need, changing it for a new tax law, or making it work on a new platform. Perfective maintenance improves a program that already works correctly, making it faster or more efficient (for example changing file access from sequential to direct) or easier to maintain (clearer identifiers, comments, repeated code moved into a subroutine), without changing what it does.

fragments.label: The need for continuing maintenance and its three types
fragments.text: Why maintenance is needed: faults missed in testing, changing requirements or laws, new hardware or software, room for improvement.

fragments.label: The need for continuing maintenance and its three types
fragments.text: Corrective: fix errors found during use.

fragments.label: The need for continuing maintenance and its three types
fragments.text: Adaptive: change what the program does, to enhance functionality or meet new or changed requirements.

fragments.label: The need for continuing maintenance and its three types
fragments.text: Perfective: improve performance or maintainability without changing what the program does.

fragments.label: The need for continuing maintenance and its three types
fragments.text: Classify by the reason for the change, not by how big the change is; re-test after any maintenance.
Analysing an existing program and making amendments

fragments.label: Analysing an existing program and making amendments
fragments.text: To amend an existing program, first read and dry-run it until you understand what each variable holds and what each part does. Then decide exactly what the new requirement changes, make the smallest set of changes that meets it (new variables declared, conditions added, outputs extended), and keep the existing style and identifiers. Finally, test again with test data that checks both the new behaviour and the old behaviour, which must not have been broken.

fragments.label: Analysing an existing program and making amendments
fragments.text: The worked example is adaptive maintenance on the corrected average program. Two new requirements are added: marks outside 0 to 100 must be rejected with a message, and the highest mark must be output as well as the average.

fragments.label: Analysing an existing program and making amendments
fragments.text: Understand first: read and dry-run the existing code.

fragments.label: Analysing an existing program and making amendments
fragments.text: Change only what the new requirement needs, and declare any new variables.

fragments.label: Analysing an existing program and making amendments
fragments.text: Re-test the new behaviour and the original behaviour.

fragments.label: Analysing an existing program and making amendments
fragments.text:
DECLARE Total, Count, Mark, Highest : INTEGER     // Highest is new
Total ← 0
Count ← 0
Highest ← -1                                      // new: below any valid mark
INPUT Mark
WHILE Mark <> -1
   IF Mark >= 0 AND Mark <= 100 THEN              // new: validation
      Total ← Total + Mark
      Count ← Count + 1
      IF Mark > Highest THEN                      // new: track the highest
         Highest ← Mark
      ENDIF
   ELSE
      OUTPUT "Mark rejected: must be 0 to 100"   // new
   ENDIF
   INPUT Mark
ENDWHILE
IF Count > 0 THEN
   OUTPUT "Average: ", Total / Count
   OUTPUT "Highest: ", Highest                   // new
ELSE
   OUTPUT "No marks entered"
ENDIF

// Test: inputs 40, 150, 70, -1
// 150 is rejected with the message; Total = 110, Count = 2
// Output: Average: 55   Highest: 70
// Test: input -1 only → No marks entered (the original behaviour still works)
Name the three types of error and how each shows itself.

fragments.label: Name the three types of error and how each shows itself.
fragments.text: Syntax error: breaks the language rules, so the program will not translate. Logic error: runs but gives a wrong result. Run-time error: crashes or freezes during execution.
Why can a syntax error remain in an interpreted program but not a compiled one?

fragments.label: Why can a syntax error remain in an interpreted program but not a compiled one?
fragments.text: A compiler checks every statement before running, whereas an interpreter only checks a statement when it is about to execute it, so errors in code that has not been run stay hidden.
Give three ways of avoiding faults in programs.

fragments.label: Give three ways of avoiding faults in programs.
fragments.text: Thorough requirements analysis; tried and tested design methods such as structured/modular programming; conventions such as meaningful identifiers and identifier tables; reusing tested library modules.
What is a stub and why is it used?

fragments.label: What is a stub and why is it used?
fragments.text: A dummy module with the correct identifier whose body only outputs a message or returns a fixed value; it lets the program's structure and flow of control be tested before all modules are written.
Distinguish white-box from black-box testing.

fragments.label: Distinguish white-box from black-box testing.
fragments.text: White-box uses the code and chooses data to test every path; black-box does not look at the code and compares actual with expected results worked out from the specification.
What is integration testing?

fragments.label: What is integration testing?
fragments.text: Testing that separately tested modules work correctly together when combined, usually adding one module at a time.
Who carries out alpha, beta and acceptance testing?

fragments.label: Who carries out alpha, beta and acceptance testing?
fragments.text: Alpha: in-house testers at the developer. Beta: a limited number of chosen external users before general release. Acceptance: the client, for bespoke software, before sign-off.
What does a test plan contain?

fragments.label: What does a test plan contain?
fragments.text: For each test: a number, what is being tested, the test data, the type of test data, the expected result and the actual result.
For whole numbers 1 to 10 inclusive, give extreme and boundary test data.

fragments.label: For whole numbers 1 to 10 inclusive, give extreme and boundary test data.
fragments.text: Extreme: 1 and 10 (accepted). Boundary: 1 and 0 at the lower limit, 10 and 11 at the upper limit; 0 and 11 must be rejected.
Define corrective, adaptive and perfective maintenance.

fragments.label: Define corrective, adaptive and perfective maintenance.
fragments.text: Corrective: fixing errors found in use. Adaptive: amending the program to enhance functionality or meet changed requirements. Perfective: improving performance or maintainability without changing what it does.

Topic 13.1 is about data types that the programmer writes into the program, rather than ones the language supplies. You need to explain why they are needed, then define and use the two non-composite kinds (enumerated and pointer) and the three composite kinds (record, set and class/object) in Cambridge pseudocode: TYPE Name = (value1, value2) for an enumeration, TYPE Name = ^INTEGER for a pointer, TYPE Name ... ENDTYPE for a record, TYPE Name = SET OF CHAR with DEFINE for a set, and CLASS ... ENDCLASS for a class. Paper 3 and Paper 4 questions usually give a scenario and ask you to write the type declarations, to use them (dot notation, dereferencing with ^), or to choose and justify the most suitable type. Marks come from exact syntax and from reasons tied to the data in the scenario.

fragments.label: Built-in data type
fragments.text: A type supplied by the programming language, such as INTEGER, REAL, CHAR, STRING, BOOLEAN or DATE, for which the language already fixes the range of values and the operations allowed.

fragments.label: User-defined data type
fragments.text: A data type whose definition the programmer writes in the program (with TYPE in pseudocode); variables can then be declared with it like any built-in type.

fragments.label: Non-composite data type
fragments.text: A data type that can be defined without referencing another data type and contains only one data type; it can be primitive (INTEGER, BOOLEAN) or user-defined (enumerated, pointer).

fragments.label: Composite data type
fragments.text: A collection of data items, of different (or the same) data types, grouped under a single identifier; it can be user-defined (record, set, class) or built in (array, string).

fragments.label: Enumerated data type
fragments.text: A non-composite user-defined type whose definition lists every value a variable of that type may take; the values are ordered.

fragments.label: Pointer data type
fragments.text: A non-composite user-defined type used to reference a memory location: its variables store an address, and the definition indicates the type of data stored at that address.

fragments.label: Dereferencing
fragments.text: Following a pointer to reach the value stored at the address it holds, written PointerName^ in Cambridge pseudocode.

fragments.label: Record data type
fragments.text: A composite user-defined type made of a fixed number of named fields, which may have different data types, declared with TYPE ... ENDTYPE.

fragments.label: Set data type
fragments.text: A composite type holding an unordered collection of values of one data type, with no duplicates and no index, on which set operations such as membership, union and intersection can be carried out.

fragments.label: Class
fragments.text: A composite user-defined type that combines attributes (data) with the methods that act on them; it is the blueprint from which objects are created.

fragments.label: Object
fragments.text: An instance of a class, created in pseudocode with NEW, holding its own values for the class attributes.
Built-in types, user-defined types and why they are needed

fragments.label: Built-in types, user-defined types and why they are needed
fragments.text: Built-in types (INTEGER, REAL, CHAR, STRING, BOOLEAN, DATE) have values and operations fixed by the language. A user-defined type is constructed by the programmer, with TYPE in pseudocode, and can then be used in DECLARE statements like any built-in type.

fragments.label: Built-in types, user-defined types and why they are needed
fragments.text: They are needed because real problems involve data the language designer could not predict: an order that can only be at one of four stages, or a book with a title, a price and a loan status. Defining the type extends the flexibility of the language, keeps related data under one identifier and restricts variables to valid values.

fragments.label: Built-in types, user-defined types and why they are needed
fragments.text: Every type is either composite or non-composite. A composite type is a collection of several data items, of different (or the same) data types, grouped under a single identifier; its definition refers to other data types. A non-composite type can be defined without referencing another data type and holds a single value; it can be a primitive (built-in) type or a user-defined one. Do not confuse user-defined types with abstract data types such as stacks, which are defined by their operations.

fragments.label: Built-in types, user-defined types and why they are needed
fragments.text: Purpose: to create a new data type that is not available in the language (it extends the flexibility of the language).

fragments.label: Built-in types, user-defined types and why they are needed
fragments.text: User-defined types are constructed by the programmer, not supplied by the language.

fragments.label: Built-in types, user-defined types and why they are needed
fragments.text: They model the problem's data, make code easier to read and allow only valid values.

fragments.label: Built-in types, user-defined types and why they are needed
fragments.text: Composite: multiple elements, of different or the same data types, grouped under a single identifier; its definition refers to other data types. Examples: record, set, class/object.

fragments.label: Built-in types, user-defined types and why they are needed
fragments.text: Composite types can be user-defined (record, class) or built in (array, string).

fragments.label: Built-in types, user-defined types and why they are needed
fragments.text: Non-composite: defined without referencing another data type; contains only one data type. Examples: any primitive type, enumerated, pointer.

fragments.label: Built-in types, user-defined types and why they are needed
fragments.text: Non-composite types can be primitive (INTEGER, BOOLEAN) or user-defined (enumerated, pointer).

fragments.label: Built-in types, user-defined types and why they are needed
fragments.text:
Type        | Category      | Pseudocode definition
Enumerated  | non-composite | TYPE TStage = (Placed, Packed, Dispatched, Delivered)
Pointer     | non-composite | TYPE TRealPointer = ^REAL
Record      | composite     | TYPE TBook ... ENDTYPE (fields declared inside)
Set         | composite     | TYPE TNameSet = SET OF STRING, then DEFINE
Class       | composite     | CLASS Ticket ... ENDCLASS

Test: does the definition group several items of other types under one name? Yes = composite.
A pointer mentions a type (^REAL) but still holds just one value, an address, so it is non-composite.
Enumerated types

fragments.label: Enumerated types
fragments.text: An enumerated type is defined by listing every value a variable of the type can take: TYPE <identifier> = (value1, value2, ...). The values are identifiers, not strings, so they are written without quotes. Because they form an ordered list, they can be compared with < and >, and adding 1 gives the next value (check for the last value first).

fragments.label: Enumerated types
fragments.text: Enumerated type: a non-composite type with an ordered list of all possible values.

fragments.label: Enumerated types
fragments.text: Syntax: TYPE TStage = (Placed, Packed, Dispatched, Delivered).

fragments.label: Enumerated types
fragments.text: Declare: DECLARE Stage : TStage. Assign: Stage ← Packed (no quotes).

fragments.label: Enumerated types
fragments.text: Values are ordinal: Stage >= Dispatched and Stage + 1 are valid.

fragments.label: Enumerated types
fragments.text: Benefits: readable code; only the listed values can be stored; comparisons follow the list order.

fragments.label: Enumerated types
fragments.text:
TYPE TStage = (Placed, Packed, Dispatched, Delivered)

DECLARE Stage : TStage

Stage ← Packed
IF Stage < Delivered THEN
   Stage ← Stage + 1               // move on to the next stage
ENDIF
IF Stage >= Dispatched THEN
   OUTPUT "Your parcel is on its way"
ELSE
   OUTPUT "Your parcel is still in the warehouse"
ENDIF

fragments.label: Enumerated types
fragments.text:
Position of each value: Placed 1, Packed 2, Dispatched 3, Delivered 4

Statement                  | Stage       | Notes
Stage ← Packed            | Packed      | position 2
Stage < Delivered?         |             | 2 < 4, TRUE
Stage ← Stage + 1         | Dispatched  | position 3
Stage >= Dispatched?       |             | 3 >= 3, TRUE
Output: Your parcel is on its way

Had Stage been a STRING, the comparison "Dispatched" >= "Packed" would compare letters
(D comes before P), giving FALSE: alphabetical order is not the order of the stages.
(Checked with a Python IntEnum: Stage(Packed + 1) is Dispatched.)
Records

fragments.label: Records
fragments.text: A record type groups a fixed number of named fields, which can have different data types, under one identifier. It is defined with TYPE Name, one DECLARE line per field, and ENDTYPE. Fields are reached with dot notation, and an array of records holds a table whose columns have different types, keeping each item's data together when sorting or searching. Python has no record type, so a class or dataclass is used instead.

fragments.label: Records
fragments.text: Record: composite; a fixed number of named fields, possibly of different data types.

fragments.label: Records
fragments.text: TYPE TBook ... DECLARE Field : Type ... ENDTYPE.

fragments.label: Records
fragments.text: Field access with dot notation: ThisBook.Title, Library[Index].OnLoan.

fragments.label: Records
fragments.text: A field can be of another user-defined type (e.g. an enumerated type) or an array.

fragments.label: Records
fragments.text: Whole records can be assigned in one statement: Copy ← Library[2].

fragments.label: Records
fragments.text: An array of records replaces parallel arrays and keeps each item's fields together.

fragments.label: Records
fragments.text:
TYPE TGenre = (Fiction, History, Science)

TYPE TBook
   DECLARE Title : STRING
   DECLARE Price : REAL
   DECLARE OnLoan : BOOLEAN
   DECLARE Genre : TGenre
ENDTYPE

DECLARE Library : ARRAY[1:5] OF TBook
DECLARE Index, LoanCount : INTEGER
DECLARE LoanValue : REAL

Library[1].Title ← "Tide Maps"
Library[1].Price ← 12.50
Library[1].OnLoan ← TRUE
Library[1].Genre ← Fiction
// ... books 2 to 5 set up in the same way

LoanCount ← 0
LoanValue ← 0.0
FOR Index ← 1 TO 5
   IF Library[Index].OnLoan = TRUE THEN
      LoanCount ← LoanCount + 1
      LoanValue ← LoanValue + Library[Index].Price
   ENDIF
NEXT Index
OUTPUT LoanCount, " books on loan, worth ", LoanValue

fragments.label: Records
fragments.text:
Index | Title           | Price | OnLoan | Genre   | LoanCount | LoanValue
      |                 |       |        |         | 0         | 0.00
1     | Tide Maps       | 12.50 | TRUE   | Fiction | 1         | 12.50
2     | Quiet Engines   | 8.99  | FALSE  | Science | 1         | 12.50
3     | Salt Roads      | 15.00 | TRUE   | History | 2         | 27.50
4     | Glass Harbour   | 9.75  | FALSE  | Fiction | 2         | 27.50
5     | Small Moons     | 11.20 | TRUE   | Science | 3         | 38.70

Output: 3 books on loan, worth 38.7
(Recalculated with a Python list of records: 3 on loan, total 38.70.)
Classes and objects as user-defined types

fragments.label: Classes and objects as user-defined types
fragments.text: A class is a composite user-defined type that holds attributes (data) and the methods that act on them. Attributes are normally PRIVATE and reached only through PUBLIC methods (encapsulation). In pseudocode: CLASS Name ... ENDCLASS, a constructor PROCEDURE NEW, and ObjectName ← NEW ClassName(parameters). Inheritance and polymorphism belong to 20.1.

fragments.label: Classes and objects as user-defined types
fragments.text: Class = attributes + methods; record = fields only.

fragments.label: Classes and objects as user-defined types
fragments.text: Object = an instance of a class, created with NEW.

fragments.label: Classes and objects as user-defined types
fragments.text: PRIVATE attributes are accessed through PUBLIC methods (encapsulation).

fragments.label: Classes and objects as user-defined types
fragments.text:
CLASS Ticket
   PRIVATE Band : STRING
   PRIVATE BasePrice : REAL

   PUBLIC PROCEDURE NEW(GivenBand : STRING, GivenPrice : REAL)
      Band ← GivenBand
      BasePrice ← GivenPrice
   ENDPROCEDURE

   PUBLIC FUNCTION GetPrice() RETURNS REAL
      IF Band = "VIP" THEN
         RETURN BasePrice * 2
      ELSE
         RETURN BasePrice
      ENDIF
   ENDFUNCTION
ENDCLASS

DECLARE MyTicket : Ticket
MyTicket ← NEW Ticket("VIP", 18.50)
OUTPUT MyTicket.GetPrice()        // 18.50 * 2 = 37.0
Pointer types and dereferencing

fragments.label: Pointer types and dereferencing
fragments.text: A pointer variable stores the memory address of another data item, not the data itself. The pointer type names the type of data found at that address: TYPE TRealPointer = ^REAL. A variable of that type is declared without a caret.

fragments.label: Pointer types and dereferencing
fragments.text: ^Price (caret before) means 'the address of Price'. PricePtr^ (caret after) means 'the value at the address held in PricePtr' (dereferencing); assigning to PricePtr^ changes Price itself. Use the 2026 guide's ^ form, not the coursebook's @. The guide defines no null value; a question will say what to use.

fragments.label: Pointer types and dereferencing
fragments.text: Pointers let dynamic data structures (linked lists, trees) grow and shrink at run time. Python has no pointer type; it handles references automatically.

fragments.label: Pointer types and dereferencing
fragments.text: Pointer type: non-composite; used to reference a memory location.

fragments.label: Pointer types and dereferencing
fragments.text: It stores an address, and its definition indicates the type of data stored at that address.

fragments.label: Pointer types and dereferencing
fragments.text: Define: TYPE TRealPointer = ^REAL. Declare: DECLARE PricePtr : TRealPointer (no caret).

fragments.label: Pointer types and dereferencing
fragments.text: Address of a variable: ^Price. Dereference: PricePtr^.

fragments.label: Pointer types and dereferencing
fragments.text: Changing PricePtr^ changes the variable pointed to.

fragments.label: Pointer types and dereferencing
fragments.text: Used to build dynamic structures (linked lists, trees) that change size at run time.

fragments.label: Pointer types and dereferencing
fragments.text:
TYPE TRealPointer = ^REAL

DECLARE PricePtr : TRealPointer
DECLARE Price, Discounted : REAL

Price ← 40.0
PricePtr ← ^Price                  // PricePtr now holds the address of Price
Discounted ← PricePtr^ * 0.75      // dereference: 40.0 * 0.75
PricePtr^ ← 52.0                   // writes 52.0 into Price
OUTPUT Discounted, " ", Price

fragments.label: Pointer types and dereferencing
fragments.text:
Address | Identifier | After line 3 | After line 4 | After line 6
3012    | Price      | 40.0         | 40.0         | 52.0
3020    | Discounted | ?            | ?            | 30.0
3028    | PricePtr   | ?            | 3012         | 3012

Line 5: PricePtr^ looks in address 3012 and finds 40.0; 40.0 * 0.75 = 30.0.
Line 6: PricePtr^ ← 52.0 writes into address 3012, so Price becomes 52.0.
Output: 30.0 52.0
PricePtr itself never changes from 3012.
(Checked with a Python ctypes pointer: dereferenced value * 0.75 = 30.0, then the target reads 52.0.)
Set types

fragments.label: Set types
fragments.text: A set holds values of one data type with no order, no index and no duplicates. The guide defines it in two steps: TYPE TNameSet = SET OF STRING, then DEFINE Chess ("Ana", "Ben") : TNameSet. Set operations (membership, union, intersection, difference) have no keywords in the 2026 guide, so describe them in words or use the notation a question gives.

fragments.label: Set types
fragments.text: Set: composite; unordered values of one type, no index, no duplicates.

fragments.label: Set types
fragments.text: TYPE TNameSet = SET OF STRING, then DEFINE SetName (values) : TNameSet.

fragments.label: Set types
fragments.text: Operations: membership, add, remove, union, intersection, difference.

fragments.label: Set types
fragments.text: Loading values into a set removes duplicates automatically.

fragments.label: Set types
fragments.text: No operator syntax in the 2026 guide: describe set operations in words.

fragments.label: Set types
Set types

fragments.text: User-defined types in a real language

fragments.label: User-defined types in a real language
fragments.text: Paper 4 uses a real language. In Python an enumeration comes from the enum module (IntEnum keeps values ordered), a record is a class or dataclass, a set is built in, and there is no pointer type because every variable already holds a reference.

fragments.label: User-defined types in a real language
fragments.text: Enumerated: class Stage(IntEnum) in Python; Enum in Java and VB.NET.

fragments.label: User-defined types in a real language
fragments.text: Record: dataclass or class in Python; Structure in VB.NET; class in Java.

fragments.label: User-defined types in a real language
fragments.text: Set: built-in set in Python; HashSet in Java and VB.NET.

fragments.label: User-defined types in a real language
fragments.text: Pointer: no pointer syntax in Python or Java; references are automatic.

fragments.label: User-defined types in a real language
fragments.text:
from dataclasses import dataclass
from enum import IntEnum


class Stage(IntEnum):          # enumerated type: every value listed, in order
    PLACED = 1
    PACKED = 2
    DISPATCHED = 3
    DELIVERED = 4


@dataclass
class Book:                    # record type: named fields of different types
    isbn: str
    title: str
    price: float
    on_loan: bool


stage = Stage.PACKED
stage = Stage(stage + 1)       # ordinal: the next value in the list
assert stage is Stage.DISPATCHED and stage >= Stage.DISPATCHED

shelf = [
    Book("978-0001", "Tide Maps", 12.50, True),
    Book("978-0002", "Quiet Engines", 8.99, False),
    Book("978-0003", "Salt Roads", 15.00, True),
]
on_loan = sum(1 for book in shelf if book.on_loan)
assert on_loan == 2

chess = {"Ana", "Ben", "Chen", "Dev", "Eli"}      # set type: no order, no duplicates
robotics = {"Chen", "Eli", "Farah", "Gus"}
assert chess & robotics == {"Chen", "Eli"}         # intersection
assert len(chess | robotics) == 7                  # union
assert chess - robotics == {"Ana", "Ben", "Dev"}   # difference
assert "Gus" in robotics                           # membership
assert set(["Ben", "Ana", "Ben", "Chen"]) == {"Ana", "Ben", "Chen"}
