fragments.label: Choosing and designing a user-defined type for a problem
fragments.text: Match each part of the scenario's data to a type and justify the match with a feature of that data. Then write the full declaration: define enumerated and set types before the record that uses them, and give every field a suitable data type (an ID with leading zeros is a STRING, a yes/no fact is BOOLEAN).

fragments.label: Choosing and designing a user-defined type for a problem
fragments.text: Fixed list of named values: enumerated.

fragments.label: Choosing and designing a user-defined type for a problem
fragments.text: Several related values of different types about one thing: record (array of records for many).

fragments.label: Choosing and designing a user-defined type for a problem
fragments.text: Membership only, no duplicates, no order: set.

fragments.label: Choosing and designing a user-defined type for a problem
fragments.text: Data plus the operations on it, with protected attributes: class.

fragments.label: Choosing and designing a user-defined type for a problem
fragments.text: Links between items, size changing at run time: pointer.

fragments.label: Choosing and designing a user-defined type for a problem

fragments.text: Why are user-defined data types necessary?

fragments.label: Why are user-defined data types necessary?
fragments.text: The built-in types cannot model the specific values or groups of fields a problem needs, and the language cannot know them in advance, so the programmer defines them; this improves readability and restricts data to valid values.
Name the two non-composite and three composite user-defined types.

fragments.label: Name the two non-composite and three composite user-defined types.
fragments.text: Non-composite: enumerated and pointer. Composite: record, set and class/object.
Write a Cambridge definition of an enumerated type for the stages of a traffic-light sequence: Red, RedAmber, Green, Amber.

fragments.label: Write a Cambridge definition of an enumerated type for the stages of a traffic-light sequence: Red, RedAmber, Green, Amber.
fragments.text: TYPE TLight = (Red, RedAmber, Green, Amber)
What does 'ordinal' mean for an enumerated type?

fragments.label: What does 'ordinal' mean for an enumerated type?
fragments.text: The values have an order given by the definition, so they can be compared and the next value found.
Given TYPE TIntPointer = ^INTEGER, DECLARE P : TIntPointer and a variable Count, how do you make P point to Count and then output Count's value through P?

fragments.label: Given TYPE TIntPointer = ^INTEGER, DECLARE P : TIntPointer and a variable Count, how do you make P point to Count and then output Count's value through P?
fragments.text: P ← ^Count, then OUTPUT P^ (dereferencing).
Give two differences between a record and an array.

fragments.label: Give two differences between a record and an array.
fragments.text: Record fields can have different data types, array elements share one type; record fields are reached by name with dot notation, array elements by index.
State three properties of a set.

fragments.label: State three properties of a set.
fragments.text: Its values have no order, it has no index, and it contains no duplicates (all values are of one type).
How does a class differ from a record?

fragments.label: How does a class differ from a record?
fragments.text: A class holds methods as well as data, and its attributes are usually private, reached only through its methods; a record holds only fields.
Which type would you choose for a list of permitted file extensions that is only ever checked for membership?

fragments.label: Which type would you choose for a list of permitted file extensions that is only ever checked for membership?
fragments.text: A set, because only membership matters, order is irrelevant and duplicates must not appear.

Topic 13.2 is about how the records of a file are arranged on backing storage (organisation) and how a program reaches a particular record (access). There are three organisations: serial (records in the order they arrived), sequential (records in order of a key field) and random (each record at an address worked out from its record key). There are two access methods: sequential access, which reads from the start of the file and works for serial and sequential files, and direct access, which goes straight to a record, using an index for a sequential file or a hash function for a random file. Hashing gets the most exam attention: calculate addresses with a hash function such as Key MOD 13, explain collisions, and show how linear probing, an overflow area or chaining handles them when writing and reading.

fragments.label: Record
fragments.text: A collection of related fields about one item, such as one customer; a data file is made of many records with the same fields.

fragments.label: Key field
fragments.text: A field whose value identifies a record, such as a customer number, used to order a sequential file or to calculate the address in a random file.

fragments.label: Serial file
fragments.text: A file in which records are stored one after another in chronological order, each new record appended to the end, with no ordering by key.

fragments.label: Sequential file
fragments.text: A file in which the records are stored in order of a key field (ascending or descending).

fragments.label: Random file
fragments.text: A file in which records are stored in no particular order; each record's location is calculated from its record key by a hashing algorithm, so it can be read or written directly.

fragments.label: Sequential access
fragments.text: Reading records one after another from the start of the file until the required record is found or the end of the file is reached.

fragments.label: Direct access
fragments.text: Going straight to the location of a required record without reading the records before it, using an index or a hash function.

fragments.label: Index
fragments.text: A separate table of key values, each with the position of its record in the main file, searched to find where a record is stored.

fragments.label: Hash function
fragments.text: A calculation (hashing algorithm) applied to a record key whose result is the address where that record is stored or should be found.

fragments.label: Collision
fragments.text: The situation where two different record keys produce the same hash value, so the location may already be in use; two records cannot occupy the same address.

fragments.label: Overflow area
fragments.text: A separate part of the file where records whose home address is already occupied are stored, usually one after another.
Data files, records and the difference between organisation and access

fragments.label: Data files, records and the difference between organisation and access
fragments.text: A binary data file is made of records, and each record of fields. When every record has the same fields and fixed-length strings, all records are the same size, so the position of record n can be calculated; that is what makes direct access possible.

fragments.label: Data files, records and the difference between organisation and access
fragments.text: File organisation is how the records are arranged (arrival order, key order or calculated addresses). File access is how a program reaches a record (read through from the start, or go straight to it). Keep the two ideas separate in answers.

fragments.label: Data files, records and the difference between organisation and access
fragments.text: File = records; record = fields; key field = the field that uniquely identifies a record.

fragments.label: Data files, records and the difference between organisation and access
fragments.text: Fixed-length records let the position of any record be calculated.

fragments.label: Data files, records and the difference between organisation and access
fragments.text: Organisation: serial, sequential, random. Access: sequential or direct.
Serial file organisation

fragments.label: Serial file organisation
fragments.text: In a serial file records are stored one after another in chronological order: each new record goes into the next available space at the end of the file. Adding is fast; finding a record is slow because every record may have to be checked. Suits data collected as it happens and processed later as a whole.

fragments.label: Serial file organisation
fragments.text: Records are stored one after the other, in chronological order (order of arrival).

fragments.label: Serial file organisation
fragments.text: New records are appended to the end of the file (next available space).

fragments.label: Serial file organisation
fragments.text: Searching: every record is checked until the record is found or all records have been checked.

fragments.label: Serial file organisation
fragments.text: Uses: transaction files, logs, audit trails, backups.
Sequential file organisation (using a key field)

fragments.label: Sequential file organisation (using a key field)
fragments.text: A sequential file stores its records one after another in order of a key field (e.g. ascending customer number). Keys are unique and in order but need not be consecutive. To insert, delete or amend a record, the old file is copied record by record to a new version of the file, making the change at the correct position; the new file replaces the old one.

fragments.label: Sequential file organisation (using a key field)
fragments.text: Records are stored in order of the key field.

fragments.label: Sequential file organisation (using a key field)
fragments.text: New records are inserted in the correct position, so a new version of the file has to be created to update it.

fragments.label: Sequential file organisation (using a key field)
fragments.text: Searching: compare key fields record by record until the record is found or the current key is greater than the key being searched for.

fragments.label: Sequential file organisation (using a key field)
fragments.text: Uses: master files updated in batches, payroll, billing.

fragments.label: Sequential file organisation (using a key field)
fragments.text:
Old file keys: 1012 1188 2045 2960 3071 4420 5503 6019

Read 1012: less than 2500, copy to new file
Read 1188: less than 2500, copy
Read 2045: less than 2500, copy
Read 2960: greater than 2500, so write the new record 2500 first, then copy 2960
Copy the remaining records 3071 4420 5503 6019 unchanged

New file keys: 1012 1188 2045 2500 2960 3071 4420 5503 6019
Every one of the 8 old records is rewritten, even though only one was added.
(Merge checked by script.)
Random file organisation (using a record key)

fragments.label: Random file organisation (using a record key)
fragments.text: In a random (direct-access) file the location of each record is found from its record key by a hashing algorithm. Writing and reading both put the key through the same algorithm, so the program jumps straight to the record. Seen from start to finish the records are in no particular order, but every address is calculated, not chosen haphazardly. Records can be updated directly, in place, with no new file.

fragments.label: Random file organisation (using a record key)
fragments.text: Records are stored in no particular order within the file (no sequencing).

fragments.label: Random file organisation (using a record key)
fragments.text: There is a relationship between the record key and its location: the location is found with a hashing algorithm.

fragments.label: Random file organisation (using a record key)
fragments.text: Same key + same algorithm = same address, when writing and when reading.

fragments.label: Random file organisation (using a record key)
fragments.text: Updates to the file can be carried out directly (in place).
Hashing algorithms: the hash function

fragments.label: Hashing algorithms: the hash function
fragments.text: A hash function (hashing algorithm) is a calculation on the key field whose result is the record's address. The usual one is Address = Key MOD N, where N is the number of record positions (0 to N - 1). N is best a prime close to the expected number of records, which spreads patterned keys more evenly. A text key can be converted first (sum of ASCII codes, then MOD N); folding splits a long key into parts, adds them and takes MOD N.

fragments.label: Hashing algorithms: the hash function
fragments.text: There are more possible keys than addresses, so different keys can give the same address: a collision.

fragments.label: Hashing algorithms: the hash function
fragments.text: Hash function: a calculation on the record key that gives the address of the record.

fragments.label: Hashing algorithms: the hash function
fragments.text: Modulo division: Address = Key MOD N (addresses 0 to N - 1); a prime N spreads keys best.

fragments.label: Hashing algorithms: the hash function
fragments.text: Text key: sum the ASCII codes, then MOD N. Folding: split the key into parts, add, then MOD N.

fragments.label: Hashing algorithms: the hash function
fragments.text: Good hash function: quick to calculate, always in range, spreads keys evenly, few collisions.

fragments.label: Hashing algorithms: the hash function
fragments.text:
ASCII sum, file of 13 positions:
LIM    = 76 + 73 + 77 = 226        226 MOD 13 = 5
DAVIS  = 68 + 65 + 86 + 73 + 83 = 375   375 MOD 13 = 11
OKAFOR = 79 + 75 + 65 + 70 + 79 + 82 = 450   450 MOD 13 = 8
MAY, AMY and YAM all sum to 231, so all hash to 231 MOD 13 = 10:
an ASCII sum ignores letter order, so anagrams always collide.

Folding, file of 100 positions (00 to 99):
Key 350712 -> parts 35, 07, 12 -> 35 + 7 + 12 = 54 -> 54 MOD 100 = 54

Choosing the divisor, keys that are all multiples of 5 (105, 110, ... 155):
MOD 10 gives only addresses 0 and 5 (8 of 10 addresses never used).
MOD 11 gives 6, 0, 5, 10, 4, 9, 3, 8, 2, 7, 1: all 11 addresses, no collisions.
(All sums and remainders checked by script.)
Collisions and how they are handled

fragments.label: Collisions and how they are handled
fragments.text: A collision occurs when two different key values produce the same hash value, so the storage location may already be in use by another record; two records cannot occupy the same address. The same collision rule must be used when reading as when writing.

fragments.label: Collisions and how they are handled
fragments.text: Linear probing: from the original hashed slot, search the file linearly for the next available space (wrap round from the last address to 0). Overflow area: put the record in the first free slot of a separate area and search that area linearly when reading. Chaining: each address holds a linked list of the records that hash to it. Clustering makes probing slower as the file fills.

fragments.label: Collisions and how they are handled
fragments.text: Collision: two different key values produce the same hash value (synonyms).

fragments.label: Collisions and how they are handled
fragments.text: The location may already be in use, and two records cannot occupy the same address.

fragments.label: Collisions and how they are handled
fragments.text: Storing: search linearly from the original hashed slot (or through the overflow area) and store the record in the first available slot.

fragments.label: Collisions and how they are handled
fragments.text: Finding: start at the hashed address, then search linearly (or the overflow area) until the matching key is found; if it is not found, the record is not in the file.

fragments.label: Collisions and how they are handled
fragments.text: Chaining: a linked list from each address holds all records with that hash value.

fragments.label: Collisions and how they are handled
fragments.text: Reading must follow the same collision rule as writing.

Writing to and reading from a random file

fragments.label: Writing to and reading from a random file
fragments.text: Cambridge pseudocode uses OPENFILE ... FOR RANDOM, SEEK to move to an address, GETRECORD to read a record and PUTRECORD to write one. The code below uses Key MOD 13 with linear probing, on a file of 13 records where CustomerID 0 means never used and -1 means deleted. GETRECORD moves the file pointer on, so SEEK back before PUTRECORD. The search stops at an empty record but steps over deleted ones.

fragments.label: Writing to and reading from a random file
fragments.text: OPENFILE "Customers.dat" FOR RANDOM; SEEK file, address; GETRECORD / PUTRECORD file, variable.

fragments.label: Writing to and reading from a random file
fragments.text: Writing: hash the key, probe until an empty or deleted record, SEEK back, PUTRECORD.

fragments.label: Writing to and reading from a random file
fragments.text: Reading: hash the key, probe until the key or an empty record is found.

fragments.label: Writing to and reading from a random file
fragments.text: Count the probes so a full file cannot cause an infinite loop.

fragments.label: Writing to and reading from a random file
fragments.text:
CONSTANT FileSize = 13

TYPE TCustomer
   DECLARE CustomerID : INTEGER      // 0 = never used, -1 = deleted
   DECLARE Name : STRING
   DECLARE Balance : REAL
ENDTYPE

FUNCTION Hash(Key : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
   RETURN Key MOD FileSize
ENDFUNCTION

PROCEDURE WriteCustomer(NewCustomer : TCustomer)
   DECLARE Address, Tries : INTEGER
   DECLARE Slot : TCustomer
   DECLARE Placed : BOOLEAN
   Address ← Hash(NewCustomer.CustomerID)
   Placed ← FALSE
   Tries ← 0
   OPENFILE "Customers.dat" FOR RANDOM
   WHILE Placed = FALSE AND Tries < FileSize
      SEEK "Customers.dat", Address
      GETRECORD "Customers.dat", Slot
      IF Slot.CustomerID <= 0 THEN
         SEEK "Customers.dat", Address       // GETRECORD moved the pointer on
         PUTRECORD "Customers.dat", NewCustomer
         Placed ← TRUE
      ELSE
         Address ← (Address + 1) MOD FileSize   // linear probing with wrap-round
         Tries ← Tries + 1
      ENDIF
   ENDWHILE
   CLOSEFILE "Customers.dat"
   IF Placed = FALSE THEN
      OUTPUT "File is full"
   ENDIF
ENDPROCEDURE

FUNCTION FindCustomer(SearchID : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Address, Tries, Result : INTEGER
   DECLARE Slot : TCustomer
   Address ← Hash(SearchID)
   Tries ← 0
   Result ← -2                        // -2 = still searching
   OPENFILE "Customers.dat" FOR RANDOM
   WHILE Result = -2 AND Tries < FileSize
      SEEK "Customers.dat", Address
      GETRECORD "Customers.dat", Slot
      IF Slot.CustomerID = SearchID THEN
         Result ← Address
      ELSE
         IF Slot.CustomerID = 0 THEN
            Result ← -1                 // empty position: key not in file
         ELSE
            Address ← (Address + 1) MOD FileSize
            Tries ← Tries + 1
         ENDIF
      ENDIF
   ENDWHILE
   CLOSEFILE "Customers.dat"
   IF Result = -2 THEN
      Result ← -1                       // every position checked
   ENDIF
   RETURN Result
ENDFUNCTION

fragments.text:
FILE_SIZE = 13
EMPTY, DELETED = 0, -1


def hash_address(key):
    return key % FILE_SIZE              # hash function: modulo division


def write_record(slots, key):
    address = hash_address(key)
    for _ in range(FILE_SIZE):
        if slots[address] in (EMPTY, DELETED):
            slots[address] = key
            return address
        address = (address + 1) % FILE_SIZE   # linear probing, wraps to 0
    raise OverflowError("file full")


def find_record(slots, key):
    address = hash_address(key)
    for _ in range(FILE_SIZE):
        if slots[address] == key:
            return address
        if slots[address] == EMPTY:       # a never-used slot ends the search
            return None
        address = (address + 1) % FILE_SIZE
    return None


slots = [EMPTY] * FILE_SIZE
keys = [20417, 47208, 31562, 20430, 58311, 64007, 15014, 52024, 39019]
placed = [write_record(slots, key) for key in keys]
assert placed == [7, 5, 11, 8, 6, 9, 12, 0, 10]
assert find_record(slots, 39019) == 10 and find_record(slots, 33009) is None
slots[9] = DELETED                        # delete 64007 with a flag, not a blank
assert find_record(slots, 39019) == 10
File access: sequential access and direct access

fragments.label: File access: sequential access and direct access
fragments.text: Sequential access starts at the physical start of the file and checks records one after another until the record is found or the end of file is reached. It is used for serial and sequential files and suits data stored in order of a field, e.g. a bank processing records in ascending account number. In a sequential file the search can stop early once a larger key is read.

fragments.label: File access: sequential access and direct access
fragments.text: Direct access finds a record without reading other records, using its key field; it suits records referenced by a unique address. For a sequential file an index of all key fields is kept and searched for the address of the record. For a random file the hashing algorithm is applied to the key to calculate the expected address; if the record is not there, linear probing or a search of the overflow area finds it.

fragments.label: File access: sequential access and direct access
fragments.text: Sequential access (serial and sequential files): records checked linearly from the physical start of the file until the record is found or end of file is reached.

fragments.label: File access: sequential access and direct access
fragments.text: Most suitable when records are stored in order of a field, e.g. accounts in ascending account number.

fragments.label: File access: sequential access and direct access
fragments.text: Direct access (sequential and random files): a record is found using its key field without other records being read; suits records referenced by a unique address.

fragments.label: File access: sequential access and direct access
fragments.text: Sequential file: an index of all key fields is searched for the address of the target record.

fragments.label: File access: sequential access and direct access
fragments.text: Random file: the hashing algorithm on the key field calculates the address; linear probing or an overflow search finds a record not at that address.

fragments.label: File access: sequential access and direct access
fragments.text: An index costs extra storage and must be updated when records are added or removed.

Editing and deleting records

fragments.label: Editing and deleting records
fragments.text: A sequential file is edited by copying to a new file, changing the record on the way. A random file is edited in place at the hashed address. Deleting from a probed random file uses a 'deleted' flag, not a blank, because a search stops at an empty position and would miss records stored further along.

fragments.label: Editing and deleting records
fragments.text: Sequential file: copy to a new file, making the change on the way.

fragments.label: Editing and deleting records
fragments.text: Random file: edit in place at the hashed address.

fragments.label: Editing and deleting records
fragments.text: Random file deletion: set a 'deleted' flag, do not blank the position.

fragments.label: Editing and deleting records
fragments.text:
Linear-probing file: 6:58311 7:20417 8:20430 9:64007 10:39019
Delete 64007 by blanking address 9, then search for 39019 (hash 6):
  reads 6, 7, 8, then 9 is empty, so the search reports 'not found' after 4 reads. Wrong.
Delete 64007 by setting a deleted flag at address 9 instead:
  reads 6, 7, 8, 9 (flagged, keep going), 10: found after 5 reads. Correct.
A later write may reuse address 9, because a flagged position counts as free for writing.

Choosing file organisation and access for a problem

fragments.label: Choosing file organisation and access for a problem
fragments.text: Base the choice on how the file is used, and name the cost: sequential files must be rewritten to insert, indexes need storage and upkeep, hashed files need spare space and a collision rule.

fragments.label: Choosing file organisation and access for a problem
fragments.text: Transaction log, audit trail, backup: serial, sequential access.

fragments.label: Choosing file organisation and access for a problem
fragments.text: Payroll or monthly billing of every customer in key order: sequential, sequential access.

fragments.label: Choosing file organisation and access for a problem
fragments.text: Same file also needing single-record lookups: sequential with an index for direct access.

fragments.label: Choosing file organisation and access for a problem
fragments.text: Login passwords, stock lookup, booking systems: random, direct access by hashing.

Scenario                                          | Organisation | Access  | Reason
Gym entry barrier logs each swipe                 | Serial       | Seq.    | records only appended, processed later as a batch
Water company bills every customer each quarter   | Sequential   | Seq.    | every record processed in customer-number order
Airline checks one passenger's booking at a desk  | Random       | Direct  | one record needed immediately from a large file

Describe serial file organisation.

fragments.label: Describe serial file organisation.
fragments.text: Records are stored in the order they arrive, each new record appended to the end of the file, with no key order.
What does a sequential file need that a serial file does not?

fragments.label: What does a sequential file need that a serial file does not?
fragments.text: A key field, with the records stored in order of that key.
Which access methods can be used with each organisation?

fragments.label: Which access methods can be used with each organisation?
fragments.text: Serial: sequential access. Sequential: sequential access, or direct access through an index. Random: direct access through a hash function.
What is a hash function?

fragments.label: What is a hash function?
fragments.text: A calculation applied to a record's key whose result is the address where the record is stored or found, for example Key MOD 13.

fragments.text: What is a collision, and name three ways of handling one.

fragments.label: What is a collision, and name three ways of handling one.
fragments.text: Two different keys give the same address. Linear probing to the next free address, storing the record in an overflow area, or chaining records in a linked list from the address.
Why is a prime number a good choice for N in Key MOD N?

fragments.label: Why is a prime number a good choice for N in Key MOD N?
fragments.text: It spreads keys more evenly across the addresses, especially when the keys share a pattern, so there are fewer collisions.
How can a sequential file be accessed directly?

fragments.label: How can a sequential file be accessed directly?
fragments.text: Through an index file of key values with the position of each record; search the index, then go straight to that position.
Why is a deleted record in a hashed file flagged rather than cleared?

fragments.label: Why is a deleted record in a hashed file flagged rather than cleared?
fragments.text: A search stops at an empty position, so clearing one would hide any record placed beyond it by linear probing.

Topic 13.3 is about storing real numbers in binary as a mantissa multiplied by 2 to the power of an exponent. In the Cambridge format both parts are two's complement, and the mantissa has its binary point straight after the sign bit, so it is a fraction between -1 and just under 1. You need to convert floating-point binary to denary and back for positive and negative mantissas and exponents, normalise a number (a positive mantissa starts 01, a negative one starts 10) and explain why, and explain how moving bits between mantissa and exponent trades precision for range. You also need to explain why many values, such as 0.1, can only be approximated, how rounding errors build up, and how overflow and underflow occur.

fragments.label: Fixed-point representation
fragments.text: A binary representation of a real number in which a set number of bits is used for the whole-number part and the rest for the fractional part, so the binary point never moves.

fragments.label: Floating-point representation
fragments.text: A representation of a real number that stores a mantissa and an exponent, the value being mantissa x 2^exponent; the base 2 is implied and not stored.

fragments.label: Mantissa
fragments.text: The part of a floating-point number that holds its significant bits; in the Cambridge format a two's complement fraction with the binary point after the sign bit.

fragments.label: Exponent
fragments.text: The two's complement integer power of 2 that the mantissa is multiplied by; it sets how far, and in which direction, the binary point moves.

fragments.label: Normalised floating-point number
fragments.text: A floating-point number whose mantissa has the largest possible magnitude, recognised by its first two bits differing: 01 for positive, 10 for negative.

fragments.label: Precision
fragments.text: How accurately a value can be stored, set by the number of mantissa bits: more bits keep more significant binary digits.

fragments.label: Range
fragments.text: The span from the smallest to the largest magnitude that can be stored, set mainly by the number of exponent bits.

fragments.label: Rounding error
fragments.text: The difference between a real number and the approximation actually stored, caused by the mantissa having too few bits to hold its exact binary value.

fragments.label: Overflow
fragments.text: An error that occurs when the result of an arithmetic operation is too large to be represented in the available bits, because it needs an exponent larger than the maximum.

fragments.label: Underflow
fragments.text: An error that occurs when the result of an arithmetic operation is too small (too close to zero) to be represented, because it needs an exponent more negative than the minimum.
Real numbers: fixed-point and floating-point

fragments.label: Real numbers: fixed-point and floating-point
fragments.text: A real number has a fractional part. In fixed-point binary the binary point is in a fixed place (a set number of whole-number and fraction bits), so values are evenly spaced but the range is small. Floating-point binary stores a mantissa (the significant bits) and an exponent (how far the point moves); the value is mantissa x 2^exponent, and the base 2 is not stored. Moving the point lets the same number of bits cover a far wider range.

fragments.label: Real numbers: fixed-point and floating-point
fragments.text: Real number: a number with a fractional part.

fragments.label: Real numbers: fixed-point and floating-point
fragments.text: Fixed point: binary point in a fixed position; even spacing, limited range.

fragments.label: Real numbers: fixed-point and floating-point
fragments.text: Floating point: value = M x 2^E; M = mantissa, E = exponent; base 2 implied, not stored.

fragments.label: Real numbers: fixed-point and floating-point
fragments.text: Negative fixed-point values use two's complement, as for integers.

fragments.label: Real numbers: fixed-point and floating-point

-6.375: flip the bits of 0110.0110 -> 1001.1001, add 1 in the last place -> 1001.1010

A 12-bit float (8-bit mantissa, 4-bit exponent) reaches 127 but gets down to 1/512 (section 4).

The Cambridge floating-point format

fragments.label: The Cambridge floating-point format
fragments.text: For 9618 both mantissa and exponent are two's complement. The mantissa has its binary point straight after the first bit, which is the sign bit worth -1, so it lies between -1 and just under +1. The exponent is a two's complement integer: positive moves the point right, negative moves it left. The question always states the format, e.g. an 8-bit mantissa and a 4-bit exponent.

fragments.label: The Cambridge floating-point format
fragments.text: Mantissa: two's complement fraction, point after the sign bit (place values -1, 1/2, 1/4, ...).

fragments.label: The Cambridge floating-point format
fragments.text: Exponent: two's complement integer (place values -8, 4, 2, 1 for 4 bits).

fragments.label: The Cambridge floating-point format
fragments.text: First mantissa bit 0 = positive number; 1 = negative number.

fragments.label: The Cambridge floating-point format
fragments.text: The exponent's sign only says whether the magnitude is large or small, not the number's sign.

Mantissa (8 bits, point after the sign bit):
  -1 . 1/2  1/4  1/8  1/16  1/32  1/64  1/128
Exponent (4 bits, two's complement integer):
  -8   4   2   1

Mantissa range: 1.0000000 = -1  up to  0.1111111 = 127/128
Exponent range: 1000 = -8  up to  0111 = +7
Converting floating-point binary to denary

fragments.label: Converting floating-point binary to denary
fragments.text: Decode the mantissa by adding place values (the sign bit is worth -1), or, for a negative mantissa, take the two's complement to find the magnitude and put a minus sign in front. Decode the exponent as a two's complement integer. Then calculate M x 2^E, or move the point E places (right for positive, left for negative).

fragments.label: Converting floating-point binary to denary
fragments.text: Step 1: convert the mantissa to denary using two's complement (-1, 1/2, 1/4, ...).

fragments.label: Converting floating-point binary to denary
fragments.text: Step 2: convert the exponent to denary (two's complement).

fragments.label: Converting floating-point binary to denary
fragments.text: Step 3: value = M x 2^E (move the point right for positive E, left for negative E).

fragments.label: Converting floating-point binary to denary

Exponent 1101 = -8 + 4 + 1 = -3
Mantissa 1.0100000 = -1 + 1/4 = -3/4
Value = -3/4 x 2^-3 = -3/32 = -0.09375

fragments.text: Each extreme value combines an extreme mantissa with an extreme exponent. Questions normally say 'normalised' for the smallest positive value, because an unnormalised 000...01 mantissa would be smaller but have only one significant bit.

Allocating bits: precision against range

fragments.label: Allocating bits: precision against range
fragments.text: The total number of bits is fixed, so a bit given to the mantissa is taken from the exponent. More mantissa bits keep more significant digits (precision); more exponent bits let the point move further (range). To store large numbers accurately, with all their significant digits, the mantissa needs enough bits; the exponent decides only how large a magnitude can be reached. Increasing the total size (double precision) improves both.

fragments.label: Allocating bits: precision against range
fragments.text: More mantissa bits: precision/accuracy increases; fewer mantissa bits: accuracy is reduced.

fragments.label: Allocating bits: precision against range
fragments.text: More exponent bits: the range of numbers that can be represented increases; fewer: the range decreases.

fragments.label: Allocating bits: precision against range
fragments.text: With a fixed total, gaining precision loses range and vice versa.

fragments.label: Allocating bits: precision against range
fragments.text: A large number with many significant digits needs more mantissa bits to be stored accurately.

fragments.label: Allocating bits: precision against range
fragments.text: More bits in total (double precision) improves both.

Normalisation: what it is and why it is done

fragments.label: Normalisation: what it is and why it is done
fragments.text: One value can have many mantissa/exponent pairs: 5.5 is 01011000 0011, 00101100 0100 or 00010110 0101. The normalised form has no redundant leading 0s (positive) or 1s (negative), so its mantissa starts 01 or 10. A mantissa starting 00 or 11 is not normalised.

fragments.label: Normalisation: what it is and why it is done
fragments.text: To normalise, shift the mantissa left until the first two bits differ, filling with 0s on the right, and subtract 1 from the exponent for each place shifted, so the value is unchanged. If the exponent would go below its minimum, the number cannot be normalised in that format. A negative power of two such as -0.5 is normalised as 1.0000000 x 2^-1.

fragments.label: Normalisation: what it is and why it is done
fragments.text: Normalised mantissa: positive starts 01, negative starts 10.

fragments.label: Normalisation: what it is and why it is done
fragments.text: Normalisation minimises the number of leading 0s/1s stored.

fragments.label: Normalisation: what it is and why it is done
fragments.text: It maximises the number of significant bits, so precision/accuracy is as high as possible for very large and very small numbers.

fragments.label: Normalisation: what it is and why it is done
fragments.text: It stores the maximum range of numbers in the minimum number of bits.

fragments.label: Normalisation: what it is and why it is done
fragments.text: It avoids multiple representations of the same number (each value has one unique form).

fragments.label: Normalisation: what it is and why it is done
fragments.text: Method: shift left n places, subtract n from the exponent.

fragments.label: Normalisation: what it is and why it is done
fragments.text: Normalised mantissa ranges: positive 1/2 to just under 1; negative -1 to just under -1/2.

fragments.label: Normalisation: what it is and why it is done
fragments.text:
Value before: 0.0010110 x 2^5 = 11/64 x 32 = 5.5
The mantissa starts 00, so shift left until it starts 01: 2 places
Mantissa 00010110 -> 01011000
Exponent 0101 (+5) - 2 = +3 -> 0011
Normalised: 01011000 0011 = 0.1011 x 2^3 = 101.1 = 5.5  (value unchanged)

fragments.label: Normalisation: what it is and why it is done
fragments.text:
Value before: 1.1101000 = -1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/16 = -3/16, x 2^4 = -3
The mantissa starts 11, so shift left until it starts 10: 2 places
Mantissa 11101000 -> 10100000
Exponent 0100 (+4) - 2 = +2 -> 0010
Normalised: 10100000 0010 = -3/4 x 2^2 = -3  (value unchanged)

fragments.label: Normalisation: what it is and why it is done
fragments.text:
Value before: 0.0001100 x 2^1 = 3/32 x 2 = 0.1875
Shift left 3 places: 00001100 -> 01100000
Exponent +1 - 3 = -2 -> 1110
Normalised: 01100000 1110 = 3/4 x 2^-2 = 0.1875
(All three normalisations performed and value-checked by script.)

fragments.label: Normalisation: what it is and why it is done
fragments.text:
5.40625 = 101.01101 = 0.10101101 x 2^3 (8 significant bits; only 7 fit after the sign bit)
Normalised:           01010110 0011 = 0.1010110 x 2^3 = 5.375
Exponent forced to 5: 00010101 0101 = 0.0010101 x 2^5 = 5.25
The two wasted leading 0s pushed two more significant bits off the end.
(Checked by script.)
Converting denary to floating-point binary

fragments.label: Converting denary to floating-point binary
fragments.text: Method 1 (binary point): write the value in binary (fraction by repeated x2), move the point to give 0.1xxx, and the number of places moved is the exponent. The mantissa is 0 followed by the bits after the point, padded with 0s.

fragments.label: Converting denary to floating-point binary
fragments.text: Method 2 (fractions): write the value as a fraction and divide by 2 until the denominator is larger than the numerator (for values below 1/2, multiply by 2 until the fraction is at least 1/2, giving a negative exponent). The number of divisions is the exponent. Then split the fraction into 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, ... to read off the mantissa bits.

fragments.label: Converting denary to floating-point binary
fragments.text: For a negative value, find the positive mantissa first, then take its two's complement (flip all bits, add 1); the exponent is unchanged. Changing only the sign bit is sign and magnitude and scores nothing. If the fraction has more bits than the mantissa holds, the extra bits are truncated and the stored value is an approximation. Always decode the answer to check it.

fragments.label: Converting denary to floating-point binary
fragments.text: Write the value in binary, or as a fraction.

fragments.label: Converting denary to floating-point binary
fragments.text: Move the point (or divide by 2) until the form is 0.1xxx; places moved (divisions) = exponent.

fragments.label: Converting denary to floating-point binary
fragments.text: Mantissa = 0 + bits after the point, padded with 0s.

fragments.label: Converting denary to floating-point binary
fragments.text: Negative: two's complement the whole mantissa; exponent unchanged.

fragments.label: Converting denary to floating-point binary
fragments.text: Exponent in two's complement; check by converting back.

fragments.label: Converting denary to floating-point binary
fragments.text:
6.75 = 27/4
Divide by 2 until denominator > numerator: 27/8, 27/16, 27/32  -> 3 divisions, exponent +3
27/32 = 16/32 + 8/32 + 2/32 + 1/32 = 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/16 + 1/32 -> 0.1101100
Answer: 01101100 0011   Check: 27/32 x 2^3 = 6.75

0.1875 = 3/16 (below 1/2, so multiply by 2 instead): 3/8, 3/4  -> 2 multiplications, exponent -2
3/4 = 1/2 + 1/4 -> 0.1100000
Answer: 01100000 1110   Check: 3/4 x 2^-2 = 0.1875
(Both checked by script with exact fractions.)

fragments.label: Converting denary to floating-point binary
fragments.text:
0.3125 = 0.0101 = 0.101 x 2^-1
Positive mantissa: 01010000
Two's complement:  flip -> 10101111, add 1 -> 10110000
Exponent: -1 -> 1111
Answer: 10110000 1111
Check: (-1 + 1/4 + 1/8) x 2^-1 = -5/8 x 1/2 = -0.3125
(All four encodings produced by the encode function and decoded back exactly.)
Approximation and rounding errors

fragments.label: Approximation and rounding errors
fragments.text: Real numbers can have a fractional part, but a binary fraction can only be built from powers of 2 (1/2, 1/4, 1/8, ...). A value such as 0.1 recurs for ever in binary (0.000110011...), and the fixed length of the mantissa means the extra digits are cut off. So it is not possible to store every fraction with full precision, and very large or very small numbers cannot be stored at all: the stored value is an approximation.

fragments.label: Approximation and rounding errors
fragments.text: The difference is a rounding error. Each is tiny, but repeated calculations add a new error each time, so errors accumulate: a loop such as WHILE Total <> 1.0 may never end. Reduce the problem with more mantissa bits, comparison against a tolerance, and integers (cents) for money.

fragments.label: Approximation and rounding errors
fragments.text: Real numbers can have a fractional part; binary can only represent fractions made of powers of 2.

fragments.label: Approximation and rounding errors
fragments.text: The fixed length of storage means digits beyond the mantissa are truncated: the stored value is an approximation, with a loss of precision.

fragments.label: Approximation and rounding errors
fragments.text: Fixed-length storage cannot hold very large or very small numbers.

fragments.label: Approximation and rounding errors
fragments.text: Rounding errors accumulate over repeated calculations.

fragments.label: Approximation and rounding errors
fragments.text: Remedies: more mantissa bits, tolerance comparisons, integers for money.

fragments.label: Approximation and rounding errors
fragments.text:
0.1 = 0.0001100110011001100... = 0.110011001100... x 2^-3
8-bit mantissa, 4-bit exponent:  01100110 1101   = 51/512    = 0.099609375     (error 0.000390625)
10-bit mantissa, 6-bit exponent: 0110011001 111101 = 409/4096 = 0.099853515625  (error 0.000146484375)
Two more mantissa bits cut the error but can never remove it.
(Checked by script.)

fragments.label: Approximation and rounding errors
fragments.text:
After 1: 0.099853515625
After 2: 0.19970703125
After 3: 0.298828125
After 5: 0.498046875
After 10: 0.99609375
The total should be 1.0 but is short by 0.00390625, about 27 times the error in one 0.1.
(Simulated by script: every sum re-encoded in 10/6 before the next addition.)

fragments.label: Approximation and rounding errors

fragments.text: Overflow and underflow

fragments.label: Overflow and underflow
fragments.text: Overflow occurs following an arithmetic operation when the result is too large to be represented in the available bits: it would need an exponent above the maximum. In the 8/4 format the largest value is 127, so 100 + 50 overflows.

fragments.label: Overflow and underflow
fragments.text: Underflow occurs following an arithmetic operation when a non-zero result is too small (too close to zero) to be represented: it would need an exponent below the minimum, so there are not enough bits. In the 8/4 format 1/256 divided by 4 underflows. The result may be set to 0, which is risky if it is later divided by.

fragments.label: Overflow and underflow
fragments.text: In both cases the number cannot be stored accurately because it needs more bits than are available: digits are truncated and precision is lost.

fragments.label: Overflow and underflow
fragments.text: Overflow: after an arithmetic operation, the result is too large to be represented; the exponent would exceed its maximum.

fragments.label: Overflow and underflow
fragments.text: Underflow: after an arithmetic operation, the result is too small (too close to zero) to be represented; the exponent would be below its minimum.

fragments.label: Overflow and underflow
fragments.text: Always state the consequence: the number needs more bits than are available, digits are truncated and precision is lost.

fragments.label: Overflow and underflow
fragments.text: Underflow often leads to the value being stored as 0.

fragments.label: Overflow and underflow
fragments.text: Range problems (overflow, underflow) need more exponent bits; precision problems need more mantissa bits.

fragments.label: Overflow and underflow
fragments.text:
1/256 = 01000000 1001 (1/2 x 2^-7)
1/256 / 4 = 1/1024 = 0.1 x 2^-9
Exponent -9 does not fit in 4 bits (minimum 1000 = -8), and 1/1024 < 1/512: underflow.
(The encode function refuses both results: 'exponent 8 / -9 does not fit in 4 bits'.)
Where is the binary point in a Cambridge floating-point mantissa, and what is the sign bit worth?

fragments.label: Where is the binary point in a Cambridge floating-point mantissa, and what is the sign bit worth?
fragments.text: Straight after the first bit; that sign bit has a place value of -1.
Convert 10100000 1101 (8-bit mantissa, 4-bit exponent) to denary.
How do you recognise a normalised floating-point number?

fragments.label: How do you recognise a normalised floating-point number?
fragments.text: The first two bits of the mantissa differ: 01 for a positive number, 10 for a negative number.
Give two reasons for normalising floating-point numbers.

fragments.label: Give two reasons for normalising floating-point numbers.
fragments.text: It gives the maximum precision for the number of mantissa bits, and it gives each value a unique representation.
Represent -13.625 with a 10-bit mantissa and 6-bit exponent.

fragments.label: Represent -13.625 with a 10-bit mantissa and 6-bit exponent.
fragments.text: 13.625 = 0.1101101 x 2^4; positive mantissa 0110110100, two's complement 1001001100; exponent 000100.
What are the largest positive and most negative values with an 8-bit mantissa and 4-bit exponent?

fragments.label: What are the largest positive and most negative values with an 8-bit mantissa and 4-bit exponent?

fragments.text: What is the effect of moving bits from the exponent to the mantissa?

fragments.label: What is the effect of moving bits from the exponent to the mantissa?
fragments.text: Precision increases, but the range of values that can be represented decreases.
Why can 0.1 not be stored exactly in binary floating point?

fragments.label: Why can 0.1 not be stored exactly in binary floating point?
fragments.text: Its binary fraction 0.000110011... recurs for ever, so a finite mantissa must cut it off, leaving an approximation.
Distinguish overflow from underflow.

fragments.label: Distinguish overflow from underflow.
fragments.text: Overflow: a result too large to store (exponent above its maximum). Underflow: a non-zero result too close to zero to store (exponent below its minimum).

Protocols let computers from different manufacturers, running different software, exchange data: both ends follow the same agreed rules. Networking needs many protocols, so they are organised as a stack of layers, each with one job, serving the layer above. The internet uses the TCP/IP suite with four layers: Application, Transport, Internet and Link. You must describe the purpose and function of each layer and trace a message from one host to another across the internet: headers added down the sender's stack (encapsulation), routers working up to the Internet layer, headers removed up the receiver's stack (decapsulation). The topic ends with the purposes of HTTP, FTP, SMTP, POP3, IMAP and the peer-to-peer BitTorrent protocol.

fragments.label: Protocol
fragments.text: A set of rules for data transmission that the sender and receiver both agree to follow, covering things such as message format, addressing, timing, error checking and the order of exchanges.

fragments.label: Protocol stack
fragments.text: The protocols of a suite arranged as layers, where each layer has one area of responsibility, uses the services of the layer below and provides services to the layer above through a defined interface.

fragments.label: TCP/IP
fragments.text: The protocol suite that the internet runs on, named after its two central protocols (Transmission Control Protocol and Internet Protocol) and organised into Application, Transport, Internet and Link layers.

fragments.label: Encapsulation
fragments.text: Wrapping the data received from the layer above inside a new unit that carries this layer's header (and, at the Link layer, a trailer) as data moves down the stack.

fragments.label: Decapsulation
fragments.text: Removing and acting on each layer's header as data moves up the receiver's stack, until only the original message reaches the application.

fragments.label: Port number
fragments.text: A 16-bit number in the transport header that identifies which application or service on a host the data belongs to, for example 80 for an HTTP web server.

fragments.label: MAC address
fragments.text: The physical address that uniquely identifies a network interface card, usually 48 bits written as six hexadecimal pairs; the Link layer uses it to deliver a frame across one local network.

fragments.label: Peer-to-peer (P2P)
fragments.text: A network model with no central server holding the content, in which every peer can act as both a client (downloading) and a server (uploading).
Why a protocol is essential

fragments.label: Why a protocol is essential
fragments.text: Two computers may have different hardware, operating systems and makers. A stream of bits means nothing unless both ends agree where a message starts, which bits are addresses, how errors are detected and what reply is expected. A protocol fixes these rules in advance, so any two devices that follow it can communicate. If two devices used different protocols, they could not communicate properly.

fragments.label: Why a protocol is essential
fragments.text: Security protocols add to this. SSL and its successor TLS provide communication security over a network by encrypting the data, and let the two parties identify and authenticate each other, so they communicate with confidentiality and integrity (HTTPS is HTTP over TLS; the detail is in 17.1).

fragments.label: Why a protocol is essential
fragments.text: Protocol: a standard set of rules that enables successful data transfer.

fragments.label: Why a protocol is essential
fragments.text: Enables communication/compatibility between devices from different manufacturers or platforms.

fragments.label: Why a protocol is essential
fragments.text: Makes communication independent of the software and hardware used.

fragments.label: Why a protocol is essential
fragments.text: Devices using different protocols would not be able to communicate properly.

fragments.label: Why a protocol is essential
fragments.text: Rules cover format, addressing, timing/order of messages and error handling.

fragments.label: Why a protocol is essential
fragments.text: SSL/TLS: provide communication security (encryption) and let the two parties identify and authenticate each other, giving confidentiality and integrity.
Protocol implementation viewed as a stack

fragments.label: Protocol implementation viewed as a stack
fragments.text: Networking involves many separate jobs, so a protocol suite splits them into layers stacked on top of each other, each with its own function and protocols. The protocols in the stack determine the interconnectivity rules for a layered network model such as TCP/IP. A layer only talks to the layers directly above and below through a defined interface, so one layer (e.g. Wi-Fi replacing cable) can be changed without changing the others.

fragments.label: Protocol implementation viewed as a stack
fragments.text: The protocols in a stack determine the interconnectivity rules for a layered network model such as TCP/IP.

fragments.label: Protocol implementation viewed as a stack
fragments.text: Each layer has its own functionality and accepts input only from the layer directly above or below.

fragments.label: Protocol implementation viewed as a stack
fragments.text: A layer is serviced by the layer beneath it and provides a service to the layer above.

fragments.label: Protocol implementation viewed as a stack
fragments.text: The user interacts only with the top (Application) layer; only the bottom (Link) layer accesses the hardware.

fragments.label: Protocol implementation viewed as a stack
fragments.text: A layer can be replaced without redesigning the others, as long as its interface stays the same.
The TCP/IP protocol suite and its four layers

fragments.label: The TCP/IP protocol suite and its four layers
fragments.text: TCP/IP is the protocol suite of the internet, with four layers from the top: Application, Transport, Internet and Link. Other sources use other names (the coursebook's Network layer is the Internet layer; the Link layer is also called the Network access or Network interface layer), but use the syllabus names in answers.

fragments.label: The TCP/IP protocol suite and its four layers
fragments.text: Application: network services for applications (HTTP(S), FTP, SMTP, POP3, IMAP, BitTorrent).

fragments.label: The TCP/IP protocol suite and its four layers
fragments.text: Transport: delivery of data from source host to destination host; segmentation, sequencing, flow and error control (TCP).

fragments.label: The TCP/IP protocol suite and its four layers
fragments.text: Internet: IP addressing and routing of packets across networks (IP).

fragments.label: The TCP/IP protocol suite and its four layers
fragments.text: Link: transmits frames across the physical network (Ethernet, Wi-Fi).
Application layer

fragments.label: Application layer
fragments.text: Application-layer protocols are used by software such as browsers and email clients. They define the messages and the request/response rules (an HTTP client sends a request and the server replies) and put data into a format the other end understands. They pass the message to the Transport layer; DNS is used first to find the destination IP address.

fragments.label: Application layer
fragments.text: Purpose: provides network services to applications and the user.

fragments.label: Application layer
fragments.text: Formats application messages and follows the protocol's request/response rules.

fragments.label: Application layer
fragments.text: Passes data to the Transport layer and presents received data to the application.
Transport layer

fragments.label: Transport layer
fragments.text: TCP gives end-to-end delivery between applications on two hosts. It breaks the data into manageable packets (segments), adds a header with source and destination port numbers and a sequence number, and passes them to the Internet layer. It sets up a connection (handshake), and the receiver acknowledges segments; unacknowledged segments are resent after a timeout, and a checksum detects corruption. At the receiver TCP reorders segments by sequence number and hands the data to the application given by the port. UDP is the connectionless alternative with no sequencing or acknowledgements.

fragments.label: Transport layer
fragments.text: Responsible for delivery of data from the source host to the destination host.

fragments.label: Transport layer
fragments.text: Breaks data into manageable packets (segmentation) and sends them to the Internet layer.

fragments.label: Transport layer
fragments.text: Adds a packet header containing port numbers and a sequence number (sequences the packets).

fragments.label: Transport layer
fragments.text: Controls the flow of packets.

fragments.label: Transport layer
fragments.text: Handles packet loss/corruption (acknowledgements, retransmission, checksum) so data arrives error free.

fragments.label: Transport layer
fragments.text: Receiver: reorders by sequence number and passes data to the correct application (port).
Internet layer

fragments.label: Internet layer
fragments.text: IP adds a header with the source and destination IP addresses (and a TTL) to each segment to form a packet, identifying the intended network and host. Each packet is routed independently along the best available route; at every router the destination IP address is looked up in the routing table to choose the next hop. The IP address together with the port number forms a socket, which identifies one application on one host. IP is connectionless best-effort delivery: reliability is left to TCP.

fragments.label: Internet layer
fragments.text: Identifies the intended network and host.

fragments.label: Internet layer
fragments.text: Addresses packets with their source and destination IP addresses.

fragments.label: Internet layer
fragments.text: Routes packets independently, through the optimum route, using routers' routing tables.

fragments.label: Internet layer
fragments.text: Transmits packets to the Link layer.

fragments.label: Internet layer
fragments.text: IP address + port number form a socket.

fragments.label: Internet layer
fragments.text: Connectionless 'best effort': packets can be lost or arrive out of order.
Link layer

fragments.label: Link layer
fragments.text: The Link layer carries data across one physical network: host to router, router to router, router to host. It formats each packet into a frame with the source and destination MAC addresses and an error-check trailer, maps the next device's IP address to its MAC address (ARP), and converts the bits into signals on the medium, following that network's protocols (Ethernet, Wi-Fi). A new frame is built for every hop; IP addresses stay the same. A switch works at this layer, a router up to the Internet layer.

fragments.label: Link layer
fragments.text: Enables the upper layers to access the physical medium; handles how data is physically sent.

fragments.label: Link layer
fragments.text: Ensures the correct network protocols (e.g. Ethernet, Wi-Fi) are followed.

fragments.label: Link layer
fragments.text: Transports data within the network by formatting it into frames for transmission.

fragments.label: Link layer
fragments.text: Maps IP addresses to MAC addresses.

fragments.label: Link layer
fragments.text: Frame header holds source and destination MAC addresses; trailer holds an error check.

fragments.label: Link layer
fragments.text: A new frame is made on every hop; MAC addresses change, IP addresses do not.
What each layer does when a message is sent across the internet

fragments.label: What each layer does when a message is sent across the internet
fragments.text: Down the sender's stack each layer encapsulates what it receives: HTTP request, then TCP header, IP header and frame. Each router removes the frame, reads the destination IP address, decreases the TTL, chooses the next hop and sends the packet in a new frame; it never reads the TCP header. Up the receiver's stack each layer checks and removes its header, and TCP uses the port to hand the complete message to the application.

fragments.label: What each layer does when a message is sent across the internet
fragments.text: Sender: Application creates the message, then Transport, Internet and Link each add a header (encapsulation).

fragments.label: What each layer does when a message is sent across the internet
fragments.text: Each router: Link up to Internet layer only; read destination IP, decrease TTL, choose next hop, new frame.

fragments.label: What each layer does when a message is sent across the internet
fragments.text: Receiver: Link, Internet and Transport each check and remove their header (decapsulation); the port selects the application.

fragments.label: What each layer does when a message is sent across the internet
fragments.text: The same layers on the two end hosts have a logical peer-to-peer relationship: the receiving TCP sees exactly what the sending TCP produced.

fragments.label: What each layer does when a message is sent across the internet
fragments.text:
SENDING HOST (laptop)
Application : HTTP request line  'GET /timetable.html HTTP/1.1'
Transport   : + TCP header  src port 51200, dst port 80, seq 1
Internet    : + IP header   src 192.0.2.15, dst 203.0.113.8, TTL 64
Link        : + frame header  src MAC 02:00:00:AA:01:0F, dst MAC of home router
              + trailer (frame check sequence); sent as signals

EACH ROUTER
Link        : check and remove the frame
Internet    : read dst 203.0.113.8, TTL 64 -> 63, routing table gives next hop
Link        : new frame with this router's MAC and the next hop's MAC

RECEIVING HOST (web server)
Link        : check frame, remove header and trailer
Internet    : dst IP matches this host, remove IP header
Transport   : reorder by sequence number, send ACK, remove TCP header,
              dst port 80 -> hand to web server software
Application : web server reads 'GET /timetable.html' and prepares a response

fragments.label: What each layer does when a message is sent across the internet
fragments.text:
# Each layer wraps what it receives from the layer above in its own header
def send(message):
    segment = {"src_port": 51200, "dst_port": 80, "seq": 1, "data": message}      # Transport
    packet = {"src_ip": "192.0.2.15", "dst_ip": "203.0.113.8", "ttl": 64,
              "data": segment}                                                    # Internet
    frame = {"src_mac": "02:00:00:AA:01:0F", "dst_mac": "02:00:00:BB:02:01",
             "data": packet, "fcs": "checksum"}                                   # Link
    return frame

def receive(frame):
    packet = frame["data"]      # Link layer checks the frame, removes its header and trailer
    segment = packet["data"]    # Internet layer checks the IP address, removes the IP header
    port = segment["dst_port"]  # Transport layer uses the port to pick the application
    return port, segment["data"]

frame = send("GET /timetable.html HTTP/1.1")
print(frame)
print(receive(frame))

# Output (last line): (80, 'GET /timetable.html HTTP/1.1')

fragments.label: What each layer does when a message is sent across the internet
fragments.text:
Ethernet carries at most 1,500 bytes of IP packet per frame.
Minimum IP header = 20 bytes, minimum TCP header = 20 bytes
Maximum data per segment = 1500 - 20 - 20 = 1460 bytes

3,500 bytes of HTTP data -> segments of 1460, 1460 and 580 bytes (3 segments)
Each frame adds 20 (TCP) + 20 (IP) + 14 (Ethernet header) + 4 (trailer) = 58 bytes
Frame sizes: 1518, 1518 and 638 bytes; total sent = 3,674 bytes
Overhead = 3,674 - 3,500 = 174 bytes, about 4.7% of what is transmitted

(Segment sizes, totals and percentage checked by script.)
HTTP: HyperText Transfer Protocol

fragments.label: HTTP: HyperText Transfer Protocol
fragments.text: HTTP is the client-server, request-response protocol of the web: the browser requests a resource by URL (GET to fetch, POST to send form data) and the server returns a status code and the resource. HTTP is not encrypted; HTTPS is HTTP over TLS and is used for personal or financial data. Do not confuse HTTP with HTML.

fragments.label: HTTP: HyperText Transfer Protocol
fragments.text: HTTP(S): sending, receiving and transfer of web pages and hypertext documents between server and browser.

fragments.label: HTTP: HyperText Transfer Protocol
fragments.text: Client sends a request; server returns a response with a status code (200 OK, 404 Not Found).

fragments.label: HTTP: HyperText Transfer Protocol
fragments.text: HTTP is not encrypted; HTTPS encrypts using TLS.
Email protocols: SMTP, POP3 and IMAP

fragments.label: Email protocols: SMTP, POP3 and IMAP
fragments.text: The sender's client pushes the email to its mail server with SMTP, and that server pushes it with SMTP to the recipient's mail server. The recipient's client pulls it with POP3 or IMAP. POP3 downloads the email to one device and normally deletes it from the server. IMAP keeps the original on the server, so the server and all clients stay in sync. Webmail uses HTTPS between browser and server, but SMTP still moves mail between servers.

fragments.label: Email protocols: SMTP, POP3 and IMAP
fragments.text: SMTP: handles sending/uploading email, client to server and server to server (push protocol).

fragments.label: Email protocols: SMTP, POP3 and IMAP
fragments.text: POP3: retrieves email from the mail server to one client, normally deleting it from the server (pull protocol).

fragments.label: Email protocols: SMTP, POP3 and IMAP
fragments.text: IMAP: retrieves email but keeps the original on the server, so server and clients stay in sync (pull protocol).

fragments.label: Email protocols: SMTP, POP3 and IMAP
fragments.text: Webmail: browser uses HTTP(S); server to server is still SMTP.

fragments.label: Email protocols: SMTP, POP3 and IMAP
fragments.text:
1 Priya's phone (email client)   --SMTP-->  Priya's mail server      push
2 Priya's mail server            --SMTP-->  Tomas's mail server      push (server acts as client)
3 Tomas's laptop (email client)  <--IMAP--  Tomas's mail server      pull, copy stays on server

If Tomas used POP3 at stage 3, the email would be downloaded to the laptop and removed
from the server, so it would not appear on his phone afterwards.
If Priya wrote the email in a webmail page, stage 1 would use HTTPS instead of SMTP.
FTP: File Transfer Protocol

fragments.label: FTP: File Transfer Protocol
fragments.text: FTP transfers whole files between a client and a server, e.g. uploading a website's files to a web server. It uses a control connection for commands (login, list, rename, delete) and a separate data connection for the file itself. Plain FTP is unencrypted; SFTP or FTPS is used when security matters.

fragments.label: FTP: File Transfer Protocol
fragments.text: FTP: sending and receiving files over a network, between a client and a server.

fragments.label: FTP: File Transfer Protocol
fragments.text: Separate control connection (commands) and data connection (file contents).

fragments.label: FTP: File Transfer Protocol
fragments.text: Needs a login (or anonymous access); plain FTP is not encrypted.
BitTorrent: peer-to-peer file sharing

fragments.label: BitTorrent: peer-to-peer file sharing
fragments.text: BitTorrent is a peer-to-peer file-sharing protocol. There is no central web server holding the file: users share files directly with each other, and all peers have equal status. The file is split into small pieces; each peer downloads pieces it lacks from many peers at once and uploads the pieces it has, so every new downloader adds upload capacity and far more users can share a file than a single server, or a simple peer-to-peer network, could support.

fragments.label: BitTorrent: peer-to-peer file sharing
fragments.text: A user opens a small torrent file that names the tracker and holds a hash of every piece. The tracker lists the peers in the swarm but does not store the file. A seed has the complete file and uploads; a leecher is still downloading (or downloads without uploading). Pieces are requested rarest first, checked against their hashes, then assembled.

fragments.label: BitTorrent: peer-to-peer file sharing
fragments.text: BitTorrent: provides peer-to-peer file sharing between many users connected over the internet.

fragments.label: BitTorrent: peer-to-peer file sharing
fragments.text: Users share files directly with each other; there is no web server and all peers have equal status.

fragments.label: BitTorrent: peer-to-peer file sharing
fragments.text: Allows more users to share a file efficiently, because every downloader also uploads pieces.

fragments.label: BitTorrent: peer-to-peer file sharing
fragments.text: Torrent file: names the tracker and describes the pieces (with a hash of each).

fragments.label: BitTorrent: peer-to-peer file sharing
fragments.text: Tracker: lists the peers in the swarm; it does not store the content.

fragments.label: BitTorrent: peer-to-peer file sharing
fragments.text: Swarm: all peers sharing a torrent. Seed: has the whole file and uploads. Leecher: still downloading.

fragments.label: BitTorrent: peer-to-peer file sharing
fragments.text: Pieces are downloaded from many peers at once, rarest first, and checked by hash.

fragments.label: BitTorrent: peer-to-peer file sharing
fragments.text:
Client-server: the college server uploads 200 full copies
  200 x 700 MiB = 140,000 MiB (about 136.7 GiB) from one server.

BitTorrent with 512 KiB pieces:
  700 MiB / 512 KiB = 1,400 pieces.
  1 Student opens the torrent file -> learns the tracker's address and the 1,400 piece hashes.
  2 Tracker returns a list of peers in the swarm (one seed: the college; many leechers).
  3 The client asks peers which pieces they hold and requests the rarest ones first,
    from several peers at once.
  4 Each finished piece is checked against its hash and immediately offered to other peers.
  5 After all 1,400 pieces pass the check, the file is assembled; the student can stay on as a seed.
  The college still uploads, but most of the 140,000 MiB now flows between students.

(Piece count and totals checked by script.)
Why is a protocol essential for communication between computers?

fragments.label: Why is a protocol essential for communication between computers?
fragments.text: Sender and receiver must agree the rules for format, addressing, timing and error handling so that data sent by one device is correctly interpreted by another, whatever their make.
Give three features of a layered protocol stack.

fragments.label: Give three features of a layered protocol stack.
fragments.text: Each layer has its own function; each layer only communicates with the layers directly above and below through a defined interface; a layer can be replaced without changing the others (only the bottom layer touches hardware, only the top layer the user).
Name the four TCP/IP layers from top to bottom.

fragments.label: Name the four TCP/IP layers from top to bottom.
fragments.text: Application, Transport, Internet, Link.
State two functions of the Transport layer.

fragments.label: State two functions of the Transport layer.
fragments.text: Splits data into segments with sequence numbers and port numbers; with TCP, acknowledges receipt, retransmits lost segments and reassembles them in order for the correct application.
What does the Internet layer add, and why?

fragments.label: What does the Internet layer add, and why?
fragments.text: An IP header with the source and destination IP addresses (and TTL), so that routers can route the packet across networks to the destination host.
What is the function of the Link layer?

fragments.label: What is the function of the Link layer?
fragments.text: It puts the packet in a frame with source and destination MAC addresses and an error-check trailer, and transmits it as signals to the next device on the same physical network.
What is encapsulation?

fragments.label: What is encapsulation?
fragments.text: Each layer on the sending host wraps the data from the layer above with its own header (and a trailer at the Link layer); the receiver removes them in reverse order (decapsulation).
What are a tracker, a seed and a swarm in BitTorrent?

fragments.label: What are a tracker, a seed and a swarm in BitTorrent?
fragments.text: The tracker is a server listing the peers sharing a file; a seed is a peer with the complete file that uploads it; the swarm is all the peers sharing that file.

Topic 14.2 compares the two ways of carrying data across a network made of many linked switching nodes. Circuit switching sets up a dedicated path between sender and receiver before any data is sent, keeps it for the whole communication and then releases it, which is how the traditional telephone network works. Packet switching sets up no path: the message is split into packets, each with a header holding the addresses and a sequence number, and every packet is routed independently, so packets can take different routes, arrive out of order and be reassembled at the destination. You need the benefits and drawbacks of each method and where each is suitable, the function of a router in packet switching (reading the destination address, consulting its routing table, choosing the next hop, decreasing the hop limit), and a step-by-step account of how a message crosses a network such as the internet, including what happens when a packet is lost.

fragments.label: Circuit switching
fragments.text: A method in which a dedicated communication path (circuit) is established between sender and receiver before transmission, is used only by them for the whole communication, and is released at the end.

fragments.label: Packet switching
fragments.text: A method in which a message is broken into packets that are sent independently across a shared network, possibly by different routes, and reassembled in order at the destination.

fragments.label: Packet
fragments.text: A small unit of data sent across a packet-switched network, made of a header (control information such as addresses and sequence number), a payload (part of the message) and often a trailer (error-checking value).

fragments.label: Router
fragments.text: A device that connects networks and forwards each packet towards its destination by reading the destination IP address and choosing the next hop from its routing table.

fragments.label: Routing table
fragments.text: A table held by a router that maps destination networks to the next hop (and the interface to use), often with a cost for each route, updated as links fail or become congested.

fragments.label: Hop
fragments.text: One step of a packet's journey, from one router or host to the next.

fragments.label: Time to live (TTL) / hop limit
fragments.text: A value in the packet header that each router decreases by one; when it reaches zero the packet is discarded, so packets that cannot be delivered do not circulate for ever.

fragments.label: Sequence number
fragments.text: A number in the header giving a packet's position in the original message, so the receiver can put packets back in order and notice any that are missing.

fragments.label: Connection-oriented service
fragments.text: A packet-switched service in which the receiver acknowledges packets, so the sender knows what has arrived and resends anything unacknowledged (as TCP does).

fragments.label: Connectionless service
fragments.text: A packet-switched service in which packets are sent without checking that the receiver is ready and without any acknowledgement of delivery (as IP does).
Two ways to carry data across a network

fragments.label: Two ways to carry data across a network
fragments.text: A large network is a mesh of links joined by switching nodes (telephone exchanges or routers). Circuit switching reserves a complete path through the nodes before sending, and all data follows it. Packet switching reserves nothing: the data is split into packets and each node decides, packet by packet, where to send each one next.

fragments.label: Two ways to carry data across a network
fragments.text: Circuit switching: dedicated path set up in advance, used for the whole communication, released at the end.

fragments.label: Two ways to carry data across a network
fragments.text: Packet switching: no set-up; message split into packets, each routed independently over shared links.

fragments.label: Two ways to carry data across a network
fragments.text: Circuit switching is implemented at the physical layer; packet switching at the network (Internet) layer.

fragments.label: Two ways to carry data across a network
fragments.text: The internet is packet switched; the traditional telephone network is circuit switched.
Circuit switching: how it works

fragments.label: Circuit switching: how it works
fragments.text: When a call is made, the exchanges connect a chain of links from caller to receiver. The circuit is established before transmission starts and released once it ends. While it exists, the whole bandwidth of the circuit is reserved for this one communication, whether data is flowing or not, and all data is transferred over the same route at a fixed data rate, so it arrives in order and needs no reassembly.

fragments.label: Circuit switching: how it works
fragments.text: 1 The sender identifies the intended receiver.

fragments.label: Circuit switching: how it works
fragments.text: 2 The network checks that the receiver is available and ready to accept data.

fragments.label: Circuit switching: how it works
fragments.text: 3 A dedicated circuit/channel is established across the network before transmission starts.

fragments.label: Circuit switching: how it works
fragments.text: 4 Data is transferred using the whole bandwidth, all over the same route.

fragments.label: Circuit switching: how it works
fragments.text: 5 The circuit is released once transmission ends.
Circuit switching: benefits, drawbacks and where it is applicable

fragments.label: Circuit switching: benefits, drawbacks and where it is applicable
fragments.text: The benefits come from having the path to yourself: the whole bandwidth, a fixed data rate, data in order and no reassembly. The drawbacks come from the same reservation: set-up takes time and money, nobody else can use the circuit even when it is idle, a single route means no alternative if a link fails, and a single route is easier to intercept. It suits long, continuous, real-time communication.

fragments.label: Circuit switching: benefits, drawbacks and where it is applicable
fragments.text: Benefit: data arrives in order, so no time is needed to reassemble packets.

fragments.label: Circuit switching: benefits, drawbacks and where it is applicable
fragments.text: Benefit: the whole bandwidth is available to the one communication.

fragments.label: Circuit switching: benefits, drawbacks and where it is applicable
fragments.text: Benefit: simple method; fixed data rate along the same path, so no data is lost or disordered.

fragments.label: Circuit switching: benefits, drawbacks and where it is applicable
fragments.text: Drawback: nobody else can use the circuit even when it is idle; bandwidth cannot be shared.

fragments.label: Circuit switching: benefits, drawbacks and where it is applicable
fragments.text: Drawback: less secure, because only one route is used, which is easier to intercept.

fragments.label: Circuit switching: benefits, drawbacks and where it is applicable
fragments.text: Drawback: no alternative route if a link fails.

fragments.label: Circuit switching: benefits, drawbacks and where it is applicable
fragments.text: Drawback: significant cost and time to establish the dedicated connection.
