fragments.label: Line and staff relationships
fragments.text: Line managers have direct authority for core operational results; staff specialists advise or support with expertise. Conflict can occur if line managers see advice as interference or staff specialists lack operational context.

fragments.label: Line and staff relationships
fragments.text: The distinction concerns authority, not seniority. A legal specialist may be highly paid yet advise an operations manager who remains responsible for the decision and its workforce and business-performance consequences.

fragments.label: Line and staff relationships
fragments.text: Staff experts can improve decisions where regulation or technology is complex.

fragments.label: Line and staff relationships
fragments.text: Advice can delay action or be ignored unless roles, escalation rights and final decision authority are clear.

fragments.label: Line and staff relationships
fragments.text: Line managers should supply operational evidence; staff specialists should explain risks and workable alternatives.
What is a span of control?

fragments.label: What is a span of control?
fragments.text: The number of subordinates who report directly to one manager.
How does delayering change structure?

fragments.label: How does delayering change structure?
fragments.text: It removes management levels, usually shortening the chain of command and widening remaining spans of control.
What is delegated and what is retained?

fragments.label: What is delegated and what is retained?
fragments.text: Authority for a task is delegated; the manager normally retains ultimate accountability for the result.
Why can a matrix structure create conflict?

fragments.label: Why can a matrix structure create conflict?
fragments.text: Employees may answer to functional and project managers who set different priorities.
When is geographical grouping useful?

fragments.label: When is geographical grouping useful?
fragments.text: When regions differ in customer needs, culture, law or competition enough to require local decisions.
What is the difference between line and staff functions?

fragments.label: What is the difference between line and staff functions?
fragments.text: Line managers have direct authority for core results; staff specialists advise or support them.

Communication is effective only when the intended meaning is understood and produces the required response. You need to select among spoken, written, electronic and visual methods, identify barriers, explain how communication affects efficiency and recommend improvements.

fragments.label: Communication
fragments.text: Transfer of information and meaning from sender to receiver.

fragments.label: Feedback
fragments.text: A response indicating whether the message was received/understood.

fragments.label: Communication barrier
fragments.text: A factor that delays, distorts or prevents understanding of a message.

fragments.label: Formal communication
fragments.text: Communication through recognised official channels.

fragments.label: Informal communication
fragments.text: Unofficial communication outside formal organisational channels.

fragments.label: Communication channel
fragments.text: The route and medium through which a message travels from sender to receiver.

fragments.label: Two-way communication
fragments.text: Communication in which the receiver responds, allowing clarification and confirmation of understanding.

fragments.label: Vertical communication
fragments.text: Messages moving up or down between different levels of the organisational hierarchy.

fragments.label: Horizontal communication
fragments.text: Messages moving between people or departments at a similar organisational level.
Spoken communication

fragments.label: Spoken communication
fragments.text: Spoken communication is fast and rich and allows immediate questions and feedback. It is useful for sensitive, complex or urgent discussion but may leave no permanent record and can be impractical for a large dispersed audience.

fragments.label: Spoken communication
fragments.text: Face-to-face conversation also carries tone and body language, helping a manager judge concern or resistance. A meeting becomes inefficient when too many people attend without a decision, agenda or recorded action.

fragments.label: Spoken communication
fragments.text: Use conversation for appraisal, conflict or change where emotion and clarification matter.

fragments.label: Spoken communication
fragments.text: Use a briefing for urgent safety instructions, then check understanding and provide a written record where evidence is required.

fragments.label: Spoken communication
fragments.text: Telephone or video adds speed across locations but connection quality, time zones and missing non-verbal cues can reduce understanding.

fragments.label: Spoken communication
fragments.text: A factory supervisor demonstrates a new lockout procedure, asks an operator to repeat it and follows with a one-page checklist. Spoken explanation gives immediate feedback while the written record supports consistent safe practice.
Written communication

fragments.label: Written communication
fragments.text: Written communication provides a permanent record and allows precise, detailed messages. It can be slower to create and read and lacks immediate feedback unless another channel is used.

fragments.label: Written communication
fragments.text: Reports suit evidence and complex recommendations; notices and letters suit stable information; contracts or policies need controlled versions. Poor layout, excessive length or technical language can make a formally correct message ineffective.

fragments.label: Written communication
fragments.text: A record supports accountability, consistency and legal evidence but can make people reluctant to discuss sensitive issues openly.

fragments.label: Written communication
fragments.text: Tailor vocabulary, length and translation to the receiver rather than the sender's expertise.

fragments.label: Written communication
fragments.text: Request acknowledgement or questions where silence would not prove understanding.
Electronic and visual communication

fragments.label: Electronic and visual communication
fragments.text: Email, messaging, intranets and collaboration systems provide speed and scale but can create overload, distraction and security issues. Visual charts and diagrams can make patterns clearer but may oversimplify detail.

fragments.label: Electronic and visual communication
fragments.text: Technology changes transmission, not meaning. An unsuitable channel can spread ambiguity faster, while inaccessible systems exclude employees without reliable devices, bandwidth or digital skills.

fragments.label: Electronic and visual communication
fragments.text: Email suits a searchable record and dispersed audience but long reply chains obscure the current decision.

fragments.label: Electronic and visual communication
fragments.text: Instant messaging suits short operational updates but may interrupt concentrated work and expose confidential data.

fragments.label: Electronic and visual communication
fragments.text: A graph reveals trend or comparison quickly, but axes and aggregation can mislead and should be supported by labels or explanation.
Barriers

fragments.label: Barriers
fragments.text: Jargon, language or cultural differences, status, too many hierarchy levels, noise, overload, poor technology, the wrong channel and lack of feedback can distort meaning. The exam expects the consequence: errors, delay, conflict, weak decisions or lower productivity.

fragments.label: Barriers
fragments.text: Locate the barrier in the communication process. A sender may encode an unclear instruction, the channel may distort it, or the receiver may lack time, trust or knowledge to decode it. The remedy should remove that specific failure.

fragments.label: Barriers
fragments.text: Status can stop upward communication because employees fear criticism; anonymous reporting or psychologically safe meetings can improve the signal.

fragments.label: Barriers
fragments.text: Filtering across a long chain changes detail; direct cross-functional contact or a shared dashboard can reduce delay.

fragments.label: Barriers
fragments.text: Information overload hides priority; summaries, ownership, deadlines and channel rules are better than simply sending more messages.
Improving communication

fragments.label: Improving communication
fragments.text: Choose the channel according to urgency, complexity, confidentiality, audience size and need for a record; simplify language; encourage feedback; train staff; improve systems; shorten unnecessary chains; and clarify responsibility for messages.

fragments.label: Improving communication
fragments.text: One-way communication is fast and consistent for a simple announcement. Two-way communication takes longer but lets the receiver question, clarify and influence the decision. Vertical channels coordinate authority; horizontal channels coordinate work across functions at a similar level.

fragments.label: Improving communication
fragments.text: Feedback is useful only when managers listen and act or explain why they will not; ignored consultation can reduce trust.

fragments.label: Improving communication
fragments.text: Formal networks create accountability, while informal networks can spread knowledge quickly but also rumours and inaccurate information.

fragments.label: Improving communication
fragments.text: Managers should model openness, match access to employee needs and close the loop by confirming decisions and responsibilities.
Communication and efficiency

fragments.label: Communication and efficiency
fragments.text: Good communication reduces duplicated work, errors and coordination delay and helps staff understand objectives and change. However, too many meetings and messages waste time, so more communication is not always better.

fragments.label: Communication and efficiency
fragments.text: Effective internal communication can align purchasing, operations and sales forecasts, reducing excess inventory and missed orders. Externally, timely and accurate communication can preserve customer and supplier trust during a delay or crisis.

fragments.label: Communication and efficiency
fragments.text: Understanding improves task accuracy, reducing rework, waste and customer complaints.

fragments.label: Communication and efficiency
fragments.text: Fast horizontal communication can resolve bottlenecks before they stop production.

fragments.label: Communication and efficiency
fragments.text: Communication has opportunity cost: measure whether a channel improves decisions and action rather than counting messages or meetings.
What makes communication effective?

fragments.label: What makes communication effective?
fragments.text: The receiver understands the intended meaning and can make the required response.
What is the key advantage of two-way communication?

fragments.label: What is the key advantage of two-way communication?
fragments.text: Feedback allows questions, clarification and confirmation of understanding.
How do vertical and horizontal communication differ?

fragments.label: How do vertical and horizontal communication differ?
fragments.text: Vertical communication moves between hierarchy levels; horizontal communication moves across similar levels or departments.
When is written communication valuable?

fragments.label: When is written communication valuable?
fragments.text: When precision, detail, consistency or a permanent record matters.
Why can electronic communication reduce efficiency?

fragments.label: Why can electronic communication reduce efficiency?
fragments.text: Overload, interruptions, access problems and security risks can offset speed.
How should a business remove a communication barrier?

fragments.label: How should a business remove a communication barrier?
fragments.text: Diagnose the specific sender, message, channel or receiver failure and target that cause.

Leadership is influencing and guiding people toward objectives. The current syllabus focuses on leadership roles/qualities, trait, behavioural, contingency, power-and-influence and transformational theories, plus Goleman's emotional-intelligence competencies. Evaluation should always depend on situation rather than assuming one universal best style.

fragments.label: Leadership
fragments.text: Influencing and guiding people towards organisational objectives.

fragments.label: Trait theory
fragments.text: An approach focusing on personal characteristics associated with effective leaders.

fragments.label: Contingency theory
fragments.text: The idea that effective leadership depends on the situation.

fragments.label: Transformational leadership
fragments.text: Leadership that creates a compelling vision and motivates significant organisational change.

fragments.label: Emotional intelligence
fragments.text: Ability to understand/manage one's own emotions and recognise/respond effectively to others' emotions.

fragments.label: Behavioural theory
fragments.text: An approach explaining leadership through observable and learnable task, human and conceptual behaviours.

fragments.label: Power
fragments.text: A leader's capacity to influence decisions or behaviour through position, rewards, expertise, relationships or other sources.

fragments.label: Social awareness
fragments.text: Goleman's competency of sensing other people's emotions, needs and perspectives and taking them into account.
Leadership roles and qualities

fragments.label: Leadership roles and qualities
fragments.text: Directors shape strategic direction and governance; managers translate plans into coordinated action; supervisors lead frontline work; worker representatives communicate employee interests. Important qualities include communication, judgement, integrity, adaptability and ability to motivate, but importance varies by context.

fragments.label: Leadership roles and qualities
fragments.text: Leadership provides direction, aligns effort and sustains commitment when decisions are uncertain or unpopular. Formal position can create compliance; credibility and expertise are often needed for voluntary commitment and useful challenge.

fragments.label: Leadership roles and qualities
fragments.text: Directors need strategic judgement and stakeholder accountability; supervisors need operational knowledge, feedback and consistency.

fragments.label: Leadership roles and qualities
fragments.text: Worker representatives can improve upward communication and trust but may challenge management where interests conflict.

fragments.label: Leadership roles and qualities
fragments.text: A quality is valuable only through behaviour: integrity builds trust when actions match promises and difficult decisions are explained.

fragments.label: Leadership roles and qualities
fragments.text: A director accepts responsibility and sets the recall priority, managers coordinate finance and operations, supervisors brief staff, and worker representatives relay safety concerns. Clear roles reduce delay and protect customers and reputation.
Trait theory

fragments.label: Trait theory
fragments.text: Trait theory looks for personal characteristics linked with leadership, such as confidence, integrity, drive, intelligence and communication. It can inform selection and development but risks assuming qualities alone determine success and may underplay context and learned behaviour.

fragments.label: Trait theory
fragments.text: A trait does not guarantee a business result. Confidence may reassure employees during change, but excessive confidence can suppress evidence and increase strategic error.

fragments.label: Trait theory
fragments.text: Traits are difficult to define and measure consistently across cultures and situations.

fragments.label: Trait theory
fragments.text: The approach helps identify potential but does not explain which behaviour should be used for a particular workforce or task.

fragments.label: Trait theory
fragments.text: Many qualities can be developed, so trait theory should not be reduced to the claim that leaders are simply born.
Behavioural approaches

fragments.label: Behavioural approaches
fragments.text: Behavioural approaches focus on what leaders actually do, including task, human and conceptual behaviours and the balance between task focus and people focus. Behaviour can be observed, learned and adapted, but the same behaviour may not work with every workforce or task.

fragments.label: Behavioural approaches
fragments.text: Task behaviour sets standards, roles and deadlines; people behaviour listens, coaches and resolves conflict. Both can support performance when matched to the cause of the problem.

fragments.label: Behavioural approaches
fragments.text: Clear task direction can reduce error where work is new or safety-critical.

fragments.label: Behavioural approaches
fragments.text: Coaching and participation can develop skill and commitment where employees can contribute useful knowledge.

fragments.label: Behavioural approaches
fragments.text: Behavioural theory is more actionable than a trait list but can still ignore situational constraints.
Contingency theory

fragments.label: Contingency theory
fragments.text: Contingency theory argues that no single leadership approach is always best. Urgency, employee competence, task structure, risk, culture and degree of change influence what works. A crisis may require faster central direction; expert creative teams may perform better with autonomy.

fragments.label: Contingency theory
fragments.text: Situational choice should name the decision, not label the whole leader. A manager may direct evacuation, consult on process redesign and delegate specialist research in the same week.

fragments.label: Contingency theory
fragments.text: Urgency and high safety risk favour clarity and speed; complex innovation favours expertise, challenge and participation.

fragments.label: Contingency theory
fragments.text: A dispersed or inexperienced workforce may need different communication and monitoring from a trusted expert team.

fragments.label: Contingency theory
fragments.text: Continually switching approach without explanation can appear inconsistent and reduce trust.
Power and influence

fragments.label: Power and influence
fragments.text: Leaders influence through formal position, expertise, control of rewards and resources, relationships and credibility. Coercive power may gain short-term compliance but damage trust and commitment.

fragments.label: Power and influence
fragments.text: Legitimate power comes from role; reward and coercive power change consequences; expert power comes from valued knowledge; referent power comes from respect and identification. The useful source depends on what followers need and whether influence must last.

fragments.label: Power and influence
fragments.text: Expert power is strong in technical change but weakens when the leader ignores specialists with better evidence.

fragments.label: Power and influence
fragments.text: Reward power can direct effort to measurable targets but may encourage gaming or crowd out intrinsic motivation.

fragments.label: Power and influence
fragments.text: Credibility and fair process make influence more durable than fear alone.
Transformational leadership

fragments.label: Transformational leadership
fragments.text: Transformational leadership creates vision, challenges old assumptions and inspires followers to support major change. It can increase commitment during transformation but fails if the vision is unrealistic or implementation and resources are weak.

fragments.label: Transformational leadership
fragments.text: The leader must translate purpose into priorities, training, structure, budgets and measures. Inspiration without operational alignment can increase expectations while leaving employees unable to deliver.

fragments.label: Transformational leadership
fragments.text: A credible purpose can reduce resistance and encourage employees to contribute ideas during strategic change.

fragments.label: Transformational leadership
fragments.text: Questioning established routines can support innovation but also create uncertainty and change fatigue.

fragments.label: Transformational leadership
fragments.text: Transformational leadership needs transactional control of deadlines, resources and standards as well as vision.
Goleman's emotional intelligence

fragments.label: Goleman's emotional intelligence
fragments.text: Self-awareness means understanding one's emotions and impact; self-management means regulating reactions and acting reliably; social awareness means recognising others' needs and perspectives; social skills cover communication, relationship-building, conflict management and influence.

fragments.label: Goleman's emotional intelligence
fragments.text: Emotional intelligence improves how a decision is communicated and implemented. It does not prove the decision is technically correct and should complement evidence, ethics and business competence.

fragments.label: Goleman's emotional intelligence
fragments.text: Self-awareness can stop defensiveness from distorting a response to bad news.

fragments.label: Goleman's emotional intelligence
fragments.text: Self-management supports calm, consistent behaviour during conflict or crisis.

fragments.label: Goleman's emotional intelligence
fragments.text: Social awareness and skills help tailor communication, negotiate resistance and rebuild cooperation.
What does trait theory study?

fragments.label: What does trait theory study?
fragments.text: Personal characteristics associated with effective leadership.
Why is behavioural theory useful for development?

fragments.label: Why is behavioural theory useful for development?
fragments.text: It treats leadership as observable task, human and conceptual behaviours that can be learned.
What is the central claim of contingency theory?

fragments.label: What is the central claim of contingency theory?
fragments.text: The most effective leadership approach depends on the situation.
How do expert and legitimate power differ?

fragments.label: How do expert and legitimate power differ?
fragments.text: Expert power comes from valued knowledge; legitimate power comes from formal position.
What makes leadership transformational?

fragments.label: What makes leadership transformational?
fragments.text: It uses vision and challenge to create commitment to significant organisational change.
What are Goleman's four emotional-intelligence competencies?

fragments.label: What are Goleman's four emotional-intelligence competencies?
fragments.text: Self-awareness, self-management, social awareness and social skills.

HRM strategy connects workforce decisions to long-term performance. You must compare hard and soft HRM, evaluate flexible contracts, diagnose and improve employee performance, understand Management by Objectives (MBO), and analyse how IT/AI changes HRM.

fragments.label: Hard HRM
fragments.text: An approach treating labour mainly as a resource/cost to be planned and controlled to meet business needs.

fragments.label: Soft HRM
fragments.text: An approach treating employees as assets whose commitment, development and participation create performance.

fragments.label: MBO
fragments.text: Management by Objectives: managers and employees agree measurable objectives, monitor progress and review results.

fragments.label: Flexible working
fragments.text: Employment arrangements allowing labour time/location/contract to adapt to employee or business needs.

fragments.label: Annualised hours
fragments.text: A contract specifying total hours for the year, with working time varied between periods to match demand.

fragments.label: Compressed hours
fragments.text: Working normal weekly hours over fewer, longer days.

fragments.label: Gig economy
fragments.text: A labour market in which individuals complete short tasks or contracts, often arranged through digital platforms.

fragments.label: Performance appraisal
fragments.text: A structured review of employee performance, development needs and future objectives.
Hard versus soft HRM

fragments.label: Hard versus soft HRM
fragments.text: Hard HRM emphasises workforce numbers, productivity and cost; soft HRM emphasises motivation, development, trust and involvement. Real firms may combine both. The suitable balance depends on skill scarcity, service quality, cost pressure, business objectives and culture.

fragments.label: Hard versus soft HRM
fragments.text: An HR strategy is a connected policy bundle, not a label. Recruitment, contracts, training, rewards, job design and employee relations should reinforce the same objective; conflicting policies can cancel one another.

fragments.label: Hard versus soft HRM
fragments.text: A hard approach can match labour cost and numbers quickly to demand, but insecurity may reduce discretionary effort, retention and service quality.

fragments.label: Hard versus soft HRM
fragments.text: A soft approach can build firm-specific skill and commitment, but training, consultation and secure contracts create cost and take time to pay back.

fragments.label: Hard versus soft HRM
fragments.text: A hospital may use hard workforce budgets and strict safety measures while using soft development and participation to retain scarce nurses.

fragments.label: Hard versus soft HRM
fragments.text: A hotel promises empowerment and service training but gives staff insecure shifts and rewards only the number of rooms cleaned. The hard controls may undermine the trust and quality behaviour the soft policies were meant to create.
Flexible contracts and working

fragments.label: Flexible contracts and working
fragments.text: Temporary, zero-hours, part-time, full-time, annualised hours, flexitime, home working, shifts, job sharing, compressed hours and gig work allow labour to match demand or widen recruitment. Risks include insecurity, coordination difficulty, legal and reputation issues and weaker loyalty or training continuity.

fragments.label: Flexible contracts and working
fragments.text: Contract flexibility changes the quantity of labour available; working-time and location flexibility change when or where employees work. The same arrangement can benefit both sides, or transfer all demand risk to workers, depending on notice, choice, pay and access to development.

fragments.label: Flexible contracts and working
fragments.text: Flexitime lets employees vary start and finish times around agreed core hours. It can widen recruitment and reduce lateness where workers have caring or travel constraints, but customer coverage, team coordination and supervision become harder unless rotas guarantee required staffing.

fragments.label: Flexible contracts and working
fragments.text: Shift working divides extended or 24-hour operations into scheduled periods. It raises asset use and provides continuous customer coverage in hospitals, factories or transport, but night premiums, fatigue and poor handovers can increase cost, errors and safety risk.

fragments.label: Flexible contracts and working
fragments.text: Job sharing lets two employees split one full-time role. It can retain experienced workers and provide continuity when one partner is absent, but handover failures, duplicated communication and unclear accountability can damage service; it best suits work that can be divided with reliable records.

fragments.label: Flexible contracts and working
fragments.text: Annualised hours move labour toward seasonal peaks but can create fatigue or overtime cost if hours are allocated badly.

fragments.label: Flexible contracts and working
fragments.text: Compressed hours reduce commuting days and may improve retention, but longer shifts can harm concentration, safety or customer coverage.

fragments.label: Flexible contracts and working
fragments.text: Gig work gives rapid access to capacity and specialist skill, but control, employment status, quality and availability may be uncertain.

fragments.label: Flexible contracts and working
fragments.text: Home working widens recruitment and may reduce office cost, yet requires outcome measures, secure systems and deliberate team communication.
Measuring poor performance

fragments.label: Measuring poor performance
fragments.text: Indicators include productivity, absence, labour turnover, error and defect rates, complaints and missed targets. Causes may be skill gaps, poor equipment, unclear goals, workload, weak motivation, leadership or reward systems. Diagnose the cause before choosing a solution.

fragments.label: Measuring poor performance
fragments.text: Measures show symptoms, not proof of cause. Compare time trends, departments and benchmarks, then use appraisal, exit interviews, observation and employee feedback to separate ability, motivation, resources and external-demand effects.

fragments.label: Measuring poor performance
fragments.text: If absence rises from 4% to 6%, it increases by 2 percentage points, or 50% relative to the original rate; state which comparison is used.

fragments.label: Measuring poor performance
fragments.text: Higher labour productivity can reflect automation or fewer workers, not necessarily better employee performance.

fragments.label: Measuring poor performance
fragments.text: Low turnover is not always good if weak performers remain and the business needs new skills; high turnover is most damaging where replacement and learning costs are high.
Improving performance

fragments.label: Improving performance
fragments.text: Training, coaching, better job design, participation, clearer targets, technology, reward changes, wellbeing support or better recruitment may help. Evaluate cost, implementation time and whether the problem is individual or systemic.

fragments.label: Improving performance
fragments.text: Match the policy to diagnosis: training addresses an ability gap, clearer objectives address ambiguity, maintenance addresses equipment failure and job redesign or fair rewards may address motivation. Review several measures so one target is not improved by damaging quality or wellbeing.

fragments.label: Improving performance
fragments.text: Appraisal can identify development needs and provide feedback, but biased ratings or a punishment-only meeting reduce trust.

fragments.label: Improving performance
fragments.text: Participation can reveal process constraints and improve acceptance, but needs real authority and management response.

fragments.label: Improving performance
fragments.text: Performance-related pay can focus effort on measurable output but may encourage gaming, short-termism or weak teamwork.
Management by Objectives

fragments.label: Management by Objectives
fragments.text: Managers and employees agree objectives aligned with higher business goals, measures and timescales, then review progress. Benefits include clarity, participation, alignment and performance evidence. Risks include target gaming, narrow focus, measurement difficulty and time spent negotiating and reviewing.

fragments.label: Management by Objectives
fragments.text: Implementation cascades the corporate objective into departmental and individual SMART objectives, agrees resources and authority, monitors milestones, gives feedback and reviews results. Employees should understand how their target contributes to the wider objective.

fragments.label: Management by Objectives
fragments.text: Participation can improve realism and commitment, especially where employees know the process better than senior managers.

fragments.label: Management by Objectives
fragments.text: Objectives must cover quality, customer and team effects as well as easy quantity measures.

fragments.label: Management by Objectives
fragments.text: MBO becomes bureaucratic when targets stay fixed after conditions change or review focuses on blame rather than learning.
IT and AI in HRM

fragments.label: IT and AI in HRM
fragments.text: Systems automate applicant screening, scheduling, payroll, training and performance analytics. Benefits include speed and consistency; risks include algorithmic bias, privacy, cybersecurity, inaccurate data and loss of human judgement and trust.

fragments.label: IT and AI in HRM
fragments.text: AI can predict turnover, match candidates, personalise training and answer routine employee queries. It changes HR work toward data interpretation, exception handling, employee experience and governance rather than removing the need for human judgement.

fragments.label: IT and AI in HRM
fragments.text: Historical recruitment data may encode past discrimination, so apparently neutral screening can reproduce bias at scale.

fragments.label: IT and AI in HRM
fragments.text: Employees need transparency, access controls, correction routes and human review for consequential decisions.

fragments.label: IT and AI in HRM
fragments.text: Automation can release HR time and improve consistency, but system cost, poor data, cyber failure and employee surveillance concerns may offset the gain.
How do hard and soft HRM differ?

fragments.label: How do hard and soft HRM differ?
fragments.text: Hard HRM treats labour mainly as a controllable resource and cost; soft HRM develops employees as assets and partners.
What are annualised hours?

fragments.label: What are annualised hours?
fragments.text: A yearly total of contracted hours allocated unevenly across periods to match demand.
What is a percentage-point change?

fragments.label: What is a percentage-point change?
fragments.text: The arithmetic difference between two percentages, such as 6% minus 4% = 2 percentage points.
What is the first step when performance is poor?

fragments.label: What is the first step when performance is poor?
fragments.text: Diagnose the cause using trends, benchmarks and qualitative evidence before choosing a policy.
How is MBO implemented?

fragments.label: How is MBO implemented?
fragments.text: Align agreed measurable objectives from corporate to individual level, provide resources, monitor progress and review results.
What is a central risk of AI in HRM?

fragments.label: What is a central risk of AI in HRM?
fragments.text: Biased or inaccurate data can make unfair decisions at scale, alongside privacy and trust risks.

Marketing analysis converts market information into decisions. The A2 syllabus focuses on price, income and promotional elasticity; product development and R&D; and sales forecasting using four-period centred moving averages plus qualitative forecasting.

fragments.label: PED
fragments.text: Price elasticity of demand: responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price.

fragments.label: YED
fragments.text: Income elasticity of demand: responsiveness of demand to a change in consumer income.

fragments.label: Promotional elasticity
fragments.text: Responsiveness of demand/sales to a change in promotional spending/activity.

fragments.label: Sales forecast
fragments.text: An estimate of future sales over a stated period.

fragments.label: R&D
fragments.text: Research and development activity aimed at creating/improving products, processes or knowledge.

fragments.label: Product development
fragments.text: The staged process of turning an idea into a tested product that can be launched commercially.

fragments.label: Four-period centred moving average
fragments.text: A smoothed trend value formed from four-period averages and then centred on an actual period by averaging adjacent results.

fragments.label: Qualitative sales forecast
fragments.text: A sales estimate based mainly on judgement, experience and informed opinion rather than a statistical time-series calculation.

fragments.label: Seasonal variation
fragments.text: A regular, repeating difference between actual sales and the underlying trend at the same point in each cycle.
Price elasticity of demand

fragments.label: Price elasticity of demand
fragments.text: Price elasticity of demand (PED) = percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in price. Because price and demand normally move in opposite directions, PED is usually negative. Use the absolute value to classify demand: greater than 1 is elastic, less than 1 is inelastic and equal to 1 is unit elastic. A business can use the estimate to anticipate volume, revenue, capacity and inventory effects of a price change.

fragments.label: Price elasticity of demand
fragments.text: Elastic demand: a price reduction causes a proportionately larger demand increase, so revenue is likely to rise; a price increase is likely to reduce revenue.

fragments.label: Price elasticity of demand
fragments.text: Inelastic demand: a price increase causes a proportionately smaller demand fall, so revenue is likely to rise. Profit still depends on contribution, total cost and capacity.

fragments.label: Price elasticity of demand
fragments.text: PED varies by segment, price range and time. Substitutes, necessity, brand loyalty, share of income and time to switch influence responsiveness.

fragments.label: Price elasticity of demand
fragments.text: The calculation assumes other influences are unchanged. Competitor reactions, promotion, income and product changes can make a historical estimate misleading.

fragments.label: Price elasticity of demand
fragments.text: Price falls from $50 to $45, a change of (−5 ÷ 50) × 100 = −10%. Demand rises from 2,000 to 2,500, a change of (500 ÷ 2,000) × 100 = 25%. PED = 25% ÷ −10% = −2.5, so demand is elastic. Revenue rises from $100,000 to $112,500, but profit rises only if the extra contribution exceeds added production and selling costs.
Income and promotional elasticity

fragments.label: Income and promotional elasticity
fragments.text: Income elasticity of demand (YED) = percentage change in demand ÷ percentage change in consumer income. A positive result indicates a normal good: 0 < YED < 1 is income inelastic and often associated with necessities, while YED > 1 is income elastic and often associated with luxuries. A negative result indicates an inferior good in that market. Promotional elasticity of demand = percentage change in demand ÷ percentage change in promotional spending. A promotional elasticity between 0 and 1 shows a positive but less-than-proportionate response; above 1 shows a more-than-proportionate response. A negative value means measured demand fell while promotional spending rose, but other changing factors may be responsible.

fragments.label: Income and promotional elasticity
fragments.text: YED can inform product mix, capacity and geographic decisions when incomes are forecast to change, but classifications differ between customer groups and over time.

fragments.label: Income and promotional elasticity
fragments.text: Promotional elasticity can compare campaign response and guide budgets, but attribution is difficult when price, season, competitors or distribution also change.

fragments.label: Income and promotional elasticity
fragments.text: An elasticity coefficient describes responsiveness, not profitability. Extra promotion or output can cost more than the revenue gained.

fragments.label: Income and promotional elasticity
fragments.text: Estimates rely on accurate percentage changes and relevant historical data; correlation does not prove that the measured variable caused the demand change.

fragments.label: Income and promotional elasticity
fragments.text: If income rises 4% and demand for premium meals rises 10%, YED = 10% ÷ 4% = 2.5: demand is positive and income elastic. If promotion spending then rises 20% and demand rises 6%, promotional elasticity = 6% ÷ 20% = 0.3: demand responded positively but less than proportionately. The business must compare added contribution with the added promotional cost.
Product development and R&D

fragments.label: Product development and R&D
fragments.text: Product development normally moves through idea generation, screening, concept development and testing, business analysis, prototype development, test marketing and commercial launch. Sources include customers, employees, suppliers, competitors, universities, patents, market research and new technology. Each gate should remove weak ideas before more resources are committed, while retaining evidence about customer value, technical feasibility, cost and strategic fit.

fragments.label: Product development and R&D
fragments.text: R&D can create a defensible USP, improve quality or process cost, replace ageing products and open new markets, supporting future revenue and market share.

fragments.label: Product development and R&D
fragments.text: An offensive R&D strategy aims to lead with innovation; a defensive strategy improves or responds to rivals' products; follow-the-leader reduces pioneering risk but may leave little differentiation.

fragments.label: Product development and R&D
fragments.text: R&D has uncertain outcomes, long lead times, opportunity cost and possible imitation. Legal approval, patents, skills and finance influence whether an idea reaches launch.

fragments.label: Product development and R&D
fragments.text: Testing reduces risk but delays revenue and can reveal plans to competitors; a technically successful product can still fail if the target market will not pay enough.

fragments.label: Product development and R&D
fragments.text: A food producer's prototype scores highly for taste but exceeds the target unit cost by 30%. Business analysis should compare redesign, a premium segment or rejection before national test marketing commits a large promotional budget.
Why forecast sales

fragments.label: Why forecast sales
fragments.text: A sales forecast estimates future demand so marketing objectives and budgets can be coordinated with operations, human resources and finance. It informs capacity, purchasing, inventory, staffing, distribution, cash-flow forecasts and external finance. Underforecasting can cause stockouts, overtime and lost customers; overforecasting can create idle capacity, waste, excess inventory and cash shortages.

fragments.label: Why forecast sales
fragments.text: Forecasts should be disaggregated by product, segment or market when their patterns differ; one total can conceal opposite trends.

fragments.label: Why forecast sales
fragments.text: A forecast is a planning input, not a target that proves itself. Managers should record assumptions, ranges and trigger points for revision.

fragments.label: Why forecast sales
fragments.text: Accuracy matters more when decisions are expensive or hard to reverse, such as factory capacity, recruitment or international entry.
Four-period centred moving averages

fragments.label: Four-period centred moving averages
fragments.text: For quarterly data, add four consecutive periods and divide by 4. Move forward one period and repeat. Because four is even, each four-period moving average lies between actual periods; average two adjacent four-period moving averages to produce a centred moving average aligned with a real quarter. The centred series smooths seasonal and random variation so the underlying trend can be extended cautiously.

fragments.label: Four-period centred moving averages
fragments.text: Keep the first moving averages in chronological order; centring loses observations at both ends of the series.

fragments.label: Four-period centred moving averages
fragments.text: Show each total, division and centring step so follow-through marks remain available after one arithmetic error.

fragments.label: Four-period centred moving averages
fragments.text: For an additive model, seasonal variation = actual value − centred trend for every period with a centred moving average.

fragments.label: Four-period centred moving averages
fragments.text: Average the seasonal variations for the same quarter or season across years to estimate the typical seasonal effect.

fragments.label: Four-period centred moving averages
fragments.text: Extrapolate the trend to the forecast period, then calculate forecast = projected trend + average seasonal variation for that season. Do not mix this with multiplicative percentage factors.

fragments.label: Four-period centred moving averages
fragments.text: A longer smoothing period removes more fluctuation but reacts more slowly to a genuine change in trend.

fragments.label: Four-period centred moving averages
fragments.text: Quarterly sales are 80, 100, 120, 140, 100 and 120 units. First four-period moving average = (80 + 100 + 120 + 140) ÷ 4 = 110. Next = (100 + 120 + 140 + 100) ÷ 4 = 115. Centre these adjacent values: (110 + 115) ÷ 2 = 112.5, aligned with quarter 3. The next four-period average is 120, so the centred value for quarter 4 is (115 + 120) ÷ 2 = 117.5. Repeat across the full dataset. If Q3 actual sales of 120 and 132 have centred trends of 112.5 and 124.5, their seasonal variations are +7.5 and +7.5, so the average Q3 seasonal variation is +7.5. If the trend is extrapolated to 130 for the next Q3, forecast sales = 130 + 7.5 = 137.5 units.
Qualitative forecasting

fragments.label: Qualitative forecasting
fragments.text: Qualitative forecasting uses informed judgement when historical data are limited, the product is new or conditions are changing. Methods include a jury of executive opinion, sales-force composite, customer or distributor intentions and Delphi forecasting, where experts submit anonymous rounds of estimates and revise them after seeing a summary.

fragments.label: Qualitative forecasting
fragments.text: It can incorporate competitor moves, regulation, technology and customer intentions before these appear in a time series.

fragments.label: Qualitative forecasting
fragments.text: Sales staff may know local customers but can deliberately understate forecasts to make targets easier; executives may be overconfident or dominated by status.

fragments.label: Qualitative forecasting
fragments.text: Delphi anonymity can reduce group pressure, but expert selection, time and the framing of questions still affect the result.

fragments.label: Qualitative forecasting
fragments.text: Combine qualitative evidence with quantitative trend data, compare assumptions and update forecasts as actual sales arrive.
Using and evaluating forecasts

fragments.label: Using and evaluating forecasts
fragments.text: Forecast quality depends on relevant data, stable relationships and a method suited to the decision. Time-series analysis is objective and repeatable but extrapolates the past. Qualitative methods can anticipate structural change but are subjective. The strongest decision uses both, separates products and markets, and tests a range rather than presenting one precise figure as certain.

fragments.label: Using and evaluating forecasts
fragments.text: Compare forecast with actual sales and measure error; investigate whether the cause was random variation, biased assumptions or a lasting market change.

fragments.label: Using and evaluating forecasts
fragments.text: Scenario forecasts can show capacity and cash-flow effects under low, central and high demand, making contingency actions explicit.

fragments.label: Using and evaluating forecasts
fragments.text: Forecasts coordinate budgets and resources only if departments share consistent assumptions and revise them together.

fragments.label: Using and evaluating forecasts
fragments.text: A footwear business should not apply one historical trend to fashion, work and leisure shoes if their market growth, competition and sustainability preferences differ. Product-level forecasts and current qualitative research are more useful for inventory and promotion decisions.
How is PED calculated and classified?

fragments.label: How is PED calculated and classified?
fragments.text: Percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price; use the absolute value, with greater than 1 elastic and less than 1 inelastic.
What does a negative YED indicate?

fragments.label: What does a negative YED indicate?
fragments.text: Demand falls as income rises, so the product is an inferior good for that market and period.
Why does promotional elasticity not prove a campaign was profitable?

fragments.label: Why does promotional elasticity not prove a campaign was profitable?
fragments.text: It measures demand responsiveness, not whether added contribution exceeded promotional and fulfilment costs.
What are the main product-development stages?

fragments.label: What are the main product-development stages?
fragments.text: Idea generation, screening, concept development/testing, business analysis, prototype development, test marketing and launch.
How is an additive forecast produced from four-period centred moving averages?

fragments.label: How is an additive forecast produced from four-period centred moving averages?
fragments.text: Centre adjacent four-period averages, calculate actual minus centred trend, average variations for the same season, extrapolate the trend, then add that season's average variation.
When is qualitative forecasting particularly useful?

fragments.label: When is qualitative forecasting particularly useful?
fragments.text: For new products or changing markets where historical data are limited or no longer representative.
How should a business reduce false precision in forecasting?

fragments.label: How should a business reduce false precision in forecasting?
fragments.text: Use relevant disaggregated data, combine quantitative and qualitative evidence, state assumptions and test low, central and high scenarios.

Marketing strategy coordinates objectives, research, resources and the marketing mix into a coherent plan. You must understand marketing plans, make consistent strategic choices, analyse IT/AI, and evaluate international market selection, entry methods and standardisation versus local adaptation.

fragments.label: Marketing plan
fragments.text: A documented set of marketing objectives, research, budgets/resources, actions and controls.

fragments.label: Positioning
fragments.text: The intended perception of a product/brand relative to alternatives in the target customer's mind.

fragments.label: Market entry strategy
fragments.text: Method used to enter a foreign market, e.g. exporting, licensing/franchising, joint venture or direct investment.

fragments.label: Pan-global strategy
fragments.text: A largely standardised marketing approach across countries.

fragments.label: Local adaptation
fragments.text: Changing the offer/marketing mix for local culture, law or market conditions.

fragments.label: Segmentation targeting and positioning
fragments.text: Dividing a market into groups, selecting the group or groups to serve, and designing a clear relative place for the offer in their minds.

fragments.label: Joint venture
fragments.text: A jointly owned business formed with a partner, often combining foreign resources with local market knowledge and access.

fragments.label: Licensing
fragments.text: Allowing another business to use intellectual property or produce an offer in return for fees or royalties.

fragments.label: Marketing control
fragments.text: Comparing actual marketing results with objectives and budgets, then taking corrective action.
Marketing planning

fragments.label: Marketing planning
fragments.text: A marketing plan states measurable objectives, the market and customer research supporting them, target segments and positioning, available finance and people, the coordinated marketing mix, actions, responsibilities, timescales, budgets and controls. It translates corporate objectives into marketing decisions and gives operations, finance and human resources a shared demand assumption.

fragments.label: Marketing planning
fragments.text: Benefits include direction, coordination, resource allocation, risk identification, accountability and a basis for comparing actual performance with targets.

fragments.label: Marketing planning
fragments.text: Limitations include research and preparation cost, uncertain assumptions, rigidity, internal conflict and rapid market or technology change making the plan obsolete.

fragments.label: Marketing planning
fragments.text: A useful plan is reviewed, not ignored or followed blindly. Controls can track sales, share, contribution, acquisition cost, retention and progress against budget.

fragments.label: Marketing planning
fragments.text: If an objective is 8% sales growth without entering a new market, the plan should identify which existing segments and products can deliver it, then test whether capacity, distribution and the promotional budget can support the volume.
Coordinated strategy

fragments.label: Coordinated strategy
fragments.text: Marketing strategy begins with segmentation, targeting and positioning (STP). The business identifies meaningfully different groups, selects those it can serve profitably, and chooses how the brand should be perceived relative to competitors. Product, price, promotion and place then need to reinforce that position and remain feasible within finance, operations and workforce resources.

fragments.label: Coordinated strategy
fragments.text: Consistency with the business means the strategy fits brand, mission, competence and resources; consistency with the product means the message and channel fit its benefits and life-cycle stage; consistency with the market means it reflects target needs, rivals and external change.

fragments.label: Coordinated strategy
fragments.text: Coordination traces interactions: a premium product needs quality evidence, an appropriate price, credible communication and a channel that protects service; constant deep discounting can destroy that position.

fragments.label: Coordinated strategy
fragments.text: A campaign that raises demand without inventory or service capacity can increase complaints and weaken the objective it was meant to support.

fragments.label: Coordinated strategy
fragments.text: The decisive mix depends on the specific objective: rapid share growth, profit, retention, repositioning or international entry may require different trade-offs.
IT and AI

fragments.label: IT and AI
fragments.text: Information technology links websites, e-commerce, CRM, loyalty systems, social listening and marketing analytics so the business can collect data, segment customers, test messages and measure responses quickly. Artificial intelligence can predict demand, recommend products, personalise content, optimise advertising bids, support chatbots, analyse sentiment and update dynamic prices.

fragments.label: IT and AI
fragments.text: Potential gains include faster analysis, lower cost per contact, relevant offers, continuous experimentation and better allocation of promotion and inventory.

fragments.label: IT and AI
fragments.text: Bad, incomplete or historically biased data can produce confidently wrong targeting. Correlation-based predictions may fail when behaviour or the market changes.

fragments.label: IT and AI
fragments.text: Privacy, consent, cybersecurity, opaque decisions, discriminatory outcomes and intrusive personalisation can create legal and reputational damage.

fragments.label: IT and AI
fragments.text: Human review, clear objectives, representative data, access controls and comparison with a simple baseline are conditions for useful AI rather than automatic benefits.

fragments.label: IT and AI
fragments.text: A retailer may use AI recommendations to raise conversion and average order value, but should test whether uplift exceeds software cost and whether new customers or low-data groups receive systematically poor offers.
Selecting international markets

fragments.label: Selecting international markets
fragments.text: Globalisation and economic collaboration can reduce trade barriers, widen markets and enable scale, but also increase competition and expose the business to unfamiliar laws, currencies and cultures. International marketing can extend a product's life, diversify demand and use spare capacity, while adding research, coordination, logistics and adaptation cost.

fragments.label: Selecting international markets
fragments.text: Screen countries for market size and growth, income, segment fit, competition, culture, language, regulation, tariffs, political and economic risk, exchange rates, infrastructure and channel access.

fragments.label: Selecting international markets
fragments.text: Estimate accessible rather than headline demand: a large population may not have the income, distribution or legal access the offer requires.

fragments.label: Selecting international markets
fragments.text: Compare the market with business capabilities, finance and risk appetite. Reliable local research matters because secondary averages can hide regional and segment differences.

fragments.label: Selecting international markets
fragments.text: A weighted score can structure comparison, but the weights express management priorities and uncertain forecasts should not be disguised as facts.

fragments.label: Selecting international markets
fragments.text: Country A scores 8/10 for demand but 3/10 for distribution access; Country B scores 6/10 and 8/10. Choosing A solely for market size ignores whether the business can reach customers. The final judgement should weight the factors linked to the product and proposed entry mode.
Entry modes

fragments.label: Entry modes
fragments.text: Exporting uses domestic production and has lower commitment, but transport, tariffs, agents and limited local control can weaken competitiveness. Licensing gives a local business rights to technology or a brand for royalties; franchising also transfers a business format and support. Both can expand quickly with low capital, but quality, know-how and brand control may be lost.

fragments.label: Entry modes
fragments.text: A joint venture shares ownership with a local partner, gaining contacts, knowledge and sometimes regulatory access, while also sharing profit, control and the risk of conflict or knowledge leakage.

fragments.label: Entry modes
fragments.text: Direct investment through acquisition or a new wholly owned operation gives strong control, integration and retained profit, but requires the most capital and exposes the business to political, economic and exit risk.

fragments.label: Entry modes
fragments.text: E-commerce can test foreign demand cheaply, but fulfilment, returns, payments, taxes, data rules and customer trust still require a local solution.

fragments.label: Entry modes
fragments.text: Choose by required control, speed, capital, risk, local knowledge, intellectual property, product characteristics and regulation—not by a universal ranking.
Standardisation versus adaptation

fragments.label: Standardisation versus adaptation
fragments.text: A pan-global marketing strategy standardises much of the product, brand message, promotion and sometimes price or channel across countries. It can create one identity, reuse R&D and campaigns, speed launches and gain economies of scale. Local adaptation maintains local differences by changing the mix for culture, income, language, law, climate, infrastructure and competitors, increasing relevance and reducing offence or legal failure.

fragments.label: Standardisation versus adaptation
fragments.text: Standardisation can ignore different tastes, usage conditions and regulation; currency and income differences also make one price impractical.

fragments.label: Standardisation versus adaptation
fragments.text: Adaptation increases research, design, inventory, training and coordination cost and can dilute a consistent global identity.

fragments.label: Standardisation versus adaptation
fragments.text: Many businesses use global localisation: retain core brand values and product technology while adapting recipes, sizes, messages, channels or service where evidence justifies it.

fragments.label: Standardisation versus adaptation
fragments.text: Judge each element separately. A standard logo and platform can coexist with locally adapted promotion, product features and distribution.
Data, control and strategy evaluation

fragments.label: Data, control and strategy evaluation
fragments.text: Marketing data become useful only when connected to an objective and a decision. A dashboard should compare actual results with targets and budget, diagnose causes and trigger action. Measures can include sales by segment, market share, contribution, conversion, customer acquisition cost, retention, complaints, distribution availability and campaign response.

fragments.label: Data, control and strategy evaluation
fragments.text: Triangulate internal analytics with current market research; platform clicks omit non-users and do not automatically explain motives.

fragments.label: Data, control and strategy evaluation
fragments.text: Use percentage and absolute changes, suitable benchmarks and the same market definition. One short-term uplift may reflect seasonality or discounting rather than durable strategy success.

fragments.label: Data, control and strategy evaluation
fragments.text: Evaluation should rank the binding condition—customer fit, finance, capacity, regulation, partner quality or data reliability—and state what evidence would change the recommendation.

fragments.label: Data, control and strategy evaluation
fragments.text: An international premium launch may gain reach through a local e-commerce partner, but the product promise, price, service capacity, delivery time and culturally adapted promotion must support the same positioning. High impressions do not compensate for poor fulfilment or negative contribution.
What must a marketing plan contain?

fragments.label: What must a marketing plan contain?
fragments.text: Objectives, research, target and positioning, resources and budget, a coordinated mix, actions, responsibilities, timescales and controls.
What does STP stand for?

fragments.label: What does STP stand for?
fragments.text: Segmentation, targeting and positioning.
Why must a marketing mix be coordinated?

fragments.label: Why must a marketing mix be coordinated?
fragments.text: Each element changes the meaning and feasibility of the others, so contradictions confuse positioning and waste resources.
What is the main AI marketing trade-off?

fragments.label: What is the main AI marketing trade-off?
fragments.text: Faster prediction and personalisation versus data quality, bias, privacy, cybersecurity, opacity and trust risks.
How does a joint venture differ from exporting?

fragments.label: How does a joint venture differ from exporting?
fragments.text: A joint venture shares ownership, control, profit and risk with a local partner; exporting keeps production ownership at home with lower commitment and usually less local control.
What is a pan-global marketing strategy?

fragments.label: What is a pan-global marketing strategy?
fragments.text: A largely standardised product, brand and campaign across countries to gain consistency and scale.
When is local adaptation most justified?

fragments.label: When is local adaptation most justified?
fragments.text: When customer needs, culture, language, law, income, infrastructure or competition differ enough to affect demand or delivery.

Location and scale are long-term operations choices that shape total cost, revenue, speed, quality, resilience and strategic control. A strong answer compares whole-location economics with qualitative risks, then judges whether the business has enough demand and management capacity to gain economies without triggering diseconomies.

fragments.label: Optimal location
fragments.text: The site expected to make the best contribution to long-term objectives after relevant costs, revenues and qualitative factors are considered.

fragments.label: Relocation
fragments.text: Moving all or part of an existing operation to a different site.

fragments.label: Offshoring
fragments.text: Moving an activity from the home country to another country, whether it remains owned by the business or is outsourced.

fragments.label: Reshoring
fragments.text: Returning an activity that was previously moved abroad to the home country.

fragments.label: Scale of operations
fragments.text: The size of a business's productive resources and long-run potential output.

fragments.label: Internal economy of scale
fragments.text: A reduction in average cost arising from growth of the individual business.

fragments.label: External economy of scale
fragments.text: A cost advantage available to businesses because the industry or regional cluster has grown.

fragments.label: Internal diseconomy of scale
fragments.text: An increase in average cost caused by management, communication, coordination or motivation problems as the business becomes too large or complex.

fragments.label: External diseconomy of scale
fragments.text: A cost increase imposed on businesses when growth of an industry or region raises congestion, land, labour or infrastructure costs.

fragments.label: Weighted location analysis
fragments.text: A decision aid that weights factors by importance, scores each site and totals weighted scores while retaining qualitative judgement.
Location factors change with the operation

fragments.label: Location factors change with the operation
fragments.text: Location is strategic, expensive to reverse and usually a compromise. Manufacturing may prioritise input supply, transport, energy, labour productivity and space; a retailer needs customer access, visibility and complementary businesses; an online service may prioritise skills, connectivity, data regulation and reliability. The lowest rent or wage is not necessarily the lowest total cost or highest-profit site.

fragments.label: Location factors change with the operation
fragments.text: Quantitative factors include site purchase or rent, wages adjusted for productivity, transport, utilities, taxes, grants, exchange rates, expected revenue and the capital cost of developing the site.

fragments.label: Location factors change with the operation
fragments.text: Qualitative factors include labour skill and attitudes, supplier reliability, customer convenience, infrastructure, political/legal stability, ethics, environmental impact, management control and brand image.

fragments.label: Location factors change with the operation
fragments.text: Local choices compare neighbourhood access and cost; national choices add regional labour, grants and infrastructure; international choices add tariffs, currency, culture, regulation, political risk and long supply chains.

fragments.label: Location factors change with the operation
fragments.text: A luxury retailer may accept high city-centre rent because footfall and brand status raise revenue. A data centre may instead prioritise reliable low-cost power, cooling, fibre links and legal security. Applying the same checklist without changing the weights would produce a weak decision.
Weighted location analysis: method and limits

fragments.label: Weighted location analysis: method and limits
fragments.text: Use a weighted factor table when several sites must be compared consistently. First choose factors linked to objectives. Give weights that sum to 1 or 100%, score every site on the same scale, multiply each score by its weight and add the weighted scores. Then test whether reasonable changes to weights or assumptions reverse the ranking.

fragments.label: Weighted location analysis: method and limits
fragments.text: Worked scores: market access weight 0.40, labour capability 0.30, logistics 0.20 and political risk 0.10. Site A scores 8, 6, 5 and 7, so its total is (8 × 0.40) + (6 × 0.30) + (5 × 0.20) + (7 × 0.10) = 6.70.

fragments.label: Weighted location analysis: method and limits
fragments.text: Site B scores 5, 9, 8 and 4, so its total is (5 × 0.40) + (9 × 0.30) + (8 × 0.20) + (4 × 0.10) = 6.70. The tie reveals a real strategic trade-off rather than a single obvious answer.

fragments.label: Weighted location analysis: method and limits
fragments.text: Weights and scores are managerial estimates. Add profit/cash-flow forecasts, one-off relocation cost and non-quantifiable risks; do not present a weighted total as certainty.

fragments.label: Weighted location analysis: method and limits
fragments.text: If serving customers quickly is the binding objective, Site A's market score may decide the tie. If specialised labour is scarce and quality failures are costly, Site B may be superior. A small change in the market or labour weight should be recalculated before committing capital.
Offshoring, reshoring and the ownership distinction

fragments.label: Offshoring, reshoring and the ownership distinction
fragments.text: Offshoring describes geography; outsourcing describes ownership and control. A firm can offshore to its own overseas factory, outsource locally, or both offshore and outsource to a foreign supplier. Reshoring may restore speed and control but does not automatically mean every input becomes domestic.

fragments.label: Offshoring, reshoring and the ownership distinction
fragments.text: Reasons to offshore: lower total operating cost, available skills or suppliers, proximity to growing markets, tax or trade access, resource availability and time-zone coverage.

fragments.label: Offshoring, reshoring and the ownership distinction
fragments.text: Risks: longer lead times, tariffs, exchange-rate and political exposure, quality/control gaps, intellectual-property leakage, labour or environmental criticism and single-region disruption.

fragments.label: Offshoring, reshoring and the ownership distinction
fragments.text: Reasons to reshore: automation narrows wage differences, freight/tariff costs rise, demand needs faster response, defects or disruption become expensive, or a home-country origin strengthens the brand.

fragments.label: Offshoring, reshoring and the ownership distinction
fragments.text: Reshoring can raise wages and site costs and requires domestic skills/capacity. Compare total landed cost and risk, not national sentiment alone.
Reshoring as a distinct strategic decision

fragments.label: Reshoring as a distinct strategic decision
fragments.text: Reshoring returns activities to the home country after they were carried out abroad. It may shorten lead times, strengthen oversight and intellectual-property protection, reduce exchange-rate or trade disruption, and support a home-market reputation. It can also raise wage, property and regulatory costs and sacrifice overseas supplier clusters or specialist skills.

fragments.label: Reshoring as a distinct strategic decision
fragments.text: Compare total delivered cost and strategic risk rather than wages alone. Include transport, inventory in transit, quality failure, management travel, tariff exposure, responsiveness, disruption probability and the one-off cost of transition.

fragments.label: Reshoring as a distinct strategic decision
fragments.text: Reshoring may protect dependability and flexibility even when direct production cost rises.

fragments.label: Reshoring as a distinct strategic decision
fragments.text: Moving again creates investment, disruption and redundancy costs.

fragments.label: Reshoring as a distinct strategic decision
fragments.text: Partial reshoring or dual locations may balance efficiency with resilience.

fragments.label: Reshoring as a distinct strategic decision
fragments.text: A fashion brand may reshore final assembly to react to trends while retaining standard component production overseas. The hybrid is worthwhile only if avoided markdowns and faster sales exceed higher home-production and transition costs.
Globalisation changes the location network

fragments.label: Globalisation changes the location network
fragments.text: Trade agreements, digital coordination, global logistics and multinational supply networks widen the feasible choice of sites. A business may separate design, components, assembly, service and distribution across countries to place each activity near the most valuable resource or market.

fragments.label: Globalisation changes the location network
fragments.text: Potential gain: access to specialised clusters and markets can reduce cost or improve revenue and innovation.

fragments.label: Globalisation changes the location network
fragments.text: Potential cost: a longer network increases exposure to tariffs, border delay, geopolitics, pandemics, currency movement and inconsistent standards.

fragments.label: Globalisation changes the location network
fragments.text: A resilient network may use regional production, dual sourcing, postponement or selective buffers even if the cheapest single site has a lower forecast cost.
What determines the scale of operations

fragments.label: What determines the scale of operations
fragments.text: Scale changes when the business increases or decreases its long-run resource base; producing more from the same resources is higher capacity utilisation, not greater scale. Suitable scale depends on owners' objectives, market size and growth, capital, competitor structure, minimum efficient technology, management capability, risk and the scope for economies.

fragments.label: What determines the scale of operations
fragments.text: Expansion can meet demand, lower average cost and finance specialisation, but ties up capital and may create excess capacity if forecasts fail.

fragments.label: What determines the scale of operations
fragments.text: A niche producer may remain deliberately small to protect craftsmanship, control and scarcity value even when technical expansion is possible.

fragments.label: What determines the scale of operations
fragments.text: The relevant question is whether expected demand can use the new capacity at a profitable price for long enough to recover the investment.
Internal economies of scale and the cost mechanism

fragments.label: Internal economies of scale and the cost mechanism
fragments.text: An internal economy must be named and linked to average cost. Purchasing economies arise when bulk orders reduce input price or order cost per unit. Technical economies spread indivisible high-capacity equipment over more output. Managerial economies use specialists more effectively. Financial economies may reduce borrowing or issue cost. Marketing economies spread campaign cost over more sales. Risk-bearing economies can stabilise revenue across products or markets, although diversification itself also costs money.

fragments.label: Internal economies of scale and the cost mechanism
fragments.text: The chain is scale increases → a specific saving or productivity gain occurs → total cost rises more slowly than output → average cost falls.

fragments.label: Internal economies of scale and the cost mechanism
fragments.text: An economy is potential, not guaranteed. Low capacity utilisation, weak purchasing negotiation or management duplication may prevent the saving.

fragments.label: Internal economies of scale and the cost mechanism
fragments.text: Lower average cost can support lower price, higher margin or investment, but competitor response and demand elasticity determine the final performance effect.
External economies and external diseconomies

fragments.label: External economies and external diseconomies
fragments.text: A growing industry cluster may attract trained labour, specialist suppliers, universities, finance and infrastructure. Every suitable firm can benefit even if it has not grown. Continued clustering may also bid up wages and property, overload transport or create shortages: these are external diseconomies.

fragments.label: External economies and external diseconomies
fragments.text: Keep the source clear: internal effects come from the firm's own scale; external effects come from industry or regional growth.

fragments.label: External economies and external diseconomies
fragments.text: Location and scale interact. A cluster can initially lower unit cost, then congestion and scarce labour may make another region more competitive.

fragments.label: External economies and external diseconomies
fragments.text: The business should monitor whether a cluster's knowledge and supplier benefits still exceed its land, wage and disruption costs.
Internal diseconomies and ways to control them

fragments.label: Internal diseconomies and ways to control them
fragments.text: Large operations can suffer slow or distorted communication, coordination failure, bureaucracy, duplicated functions and employee alienation. Decisions take longer, errors increase and motivation or quality falls, raising average cost. Diseconomies may exist at the same time as purchasing or technical economies; the net effect determines average cost.

fragments.label: Internal diseconomies and ways to control them
fragments.text: Decentralisation can shorten decisions and improve local responsiveness but risks inconsistent standards and duplicated resources.

fragments.label: Internal diseconomies and ways to control them
fragments.text: Management by Objectives can align divisions, while ERP and clearer structures improve information; both fail if data or incentives are poor.

fragments.label: Internal diseconomies and ways to control them
fragments.text: Demerger or concentration on core activities can reduce complexity, but may lose cross-selling, shared resources or bargaining strength.
Why is an optimal location usually a compromise?

fragments.label: Why is an optimal location usually a compromise?
fragments.text: Sites combine conflicting cost, revenue and qualitative effects, and the most important factors depend on the operation and objective.
How is a weighted location score calculated?

fragments.label: How is a weighted location score calculated?
fragments.text: Multiply each common-scale site score by the factor's weight and add the products, then test sensitivity and qualitative risk.
What is the difference between offshoring and outsourcing?

fragments.label: What is the difference between offshoring and outsourcing?
fragments.text: Offshoring changes country; outsourcing changes who performs the activity. Either can occur without the other.
Why might a business reshore?

fragments.label: Why might a business reshore?
fragments.text: To improve speed, control, resilience or reputation when automation, freight, tariffs or disruption reduce the overseas cost advantage.
Give the mechanism for a technical economy of scale.

fragments.label: Give the mechanism for a technical economy of scale.
fragments.text: A large indivisible machine is used at higher output, spreading its fixed cost and potentially increasing productivity, so average cost falls.
What causes an internal diseconomy of scale?

fragments.label: What causes an internal diseconomy of scale?
fragments.text: The firm's own growth creates communication, coordination, bureaucracy or motivation problems that increase average cost.
What is an external diseconomy?

fragments.label: What is an external diseconomy?
fragments.text: Industry or regional growth raises costs such as wages, property or congestion for businesses in the area.

Quality means reliably meeting the expectations of the target customer and being fit for purpose, not automatically using the most expensive materials. Quality management moves from detecting defects to preventing their causes and building responsibility across processes, suppliers and employees.

fragments.label: Quality
fragments.text: The extent to which a good or service is fit for purpose and consistently meets target-customer expectations.

fragments.label: Quality standard
fragments.text: A measurable requirement for an input, process, output or service outcome.

fragments.label: Quality control
