fragments.text: Use the table's discount factors; do not add undiscounted and discounted figures together.

fragments.label: Net Present Value (NPV)
fragments.text: Keep the initial investment as a time-zero outflow and show its negative sign.

fragments.label: Net Present Value (NPV)
fragments.text: The discounted year 1-5 net cash flows total $132,000 and initial investment is $120,000. NPV = $132,000 - $120,000 = +$12,000. The positive $12,000 means the project is financially acceptable at the stated discount rate and is forecast to add present value. Accept only if the cash-flow assumptions, risk and strategic fit are credible.

fragments.label: Net Present Value (NPV)
fragments.text: Formula: present value = net cash flow × discount factor. Year 1: $50,000 × 0.909 = $45,450 present value. Year 2: $70,000 × 0.826 = $57,820 present value. Total present value = $45,450 + $57,820 = $103,270. With an initial investment of $90,000, NPV = $103,270 − $90,000 = +$13,270. The positive $13,270 is financially acceptable at the stated discount rate, subject to cash-flow and risk assumptions.
When the methods disagree

fragments.label: When the methods disagree
fragments.text: A project may pay back quickly but generate little later value, or have high NPV but slow payback. Do not average unlike measures. Explain what each method prioritises, link that priority to the business's objective and constraint, and test whether a plausible forecast change reverses the ranking.

fragments.label: When the methods disagree
fragments.text: Sensitivity can recalculate lower sales, higher operating cost, delayed launch, shorter life or a different discount rate. Focus on the assumption with the largest decision impact rather than changing every number mechanically.

fragments.label: When the methods disagree
fragments.text: Cash shortage and high uncertainty increase the relevance of payback.

fragments.label: When the methods disagree
fragments.text: Long-lived projects and shareholder-value objectives increase the relevance of NPV.

fragments.label: When the methods disagree
fragments.text: Management targets may use ARR, but accounting policy can affect comparison.

fragments.label: When the methods disagree
fragments.text: Project A pays back in 2.2 years with NPV $30,000; Project B pays back in 3.6 years with NPV $85,000. A may suit severe liquidity or obsolescence risk; B may add more value for a well-financed firm. Recalculate B under delayed cash inflows before recommending it.
Qualitative and strategic judgement

fragments.label: Qualitative and strategic judgement
fragments.text: Consider alignment with objectives, product/market strategy, capacity bottlenecks, quality, flexibility, skills, employee response, customer service, environmental effects, regulation, reputation, supplier dependence and competitor reaction. Availability and source of finance can constrain even a positive project.

fragments.label: Qualitative and strategic judgement
fragments.text: Forecast reliability must be tested alongside strategic fit, stakeholder effects and risk. Implementation matters: disruption, training, installation, cybersecurity, maintenance and fallback arrangements can change actual cash flows and stakeholder outcomes.

fragments.label: Qualitative and strategic judgement
fragments.text: A mandatory safety or legal investment may proceed despite a weak standalone return.

fragments.label: Qualitative and strategic judgement
fragments.text: A project with good figures may be rejected if it damages a core capability or exceeds management capacity.

fragments.label: Qualitative and strategic judgement
fragments.text: State what evidence would change the recommendation: pilot results, orders, finance rate or sensitivity threshold.

fragments.label: Qualitative and strategic judgement
fragments.text: An automated line has the highest NPV but requires scarce technicians and may interrupt delivery during installation. Phase implementation or training may protect customer contracts even if it slightly lowers the numerical return.
Building the recommendation

fragments.label: Building the recommendation
fragments.text: Start with the verified calculation and decision rule. Compare the competing method, then develop one project-specific benefit and one risk to cash, profit, objective or stakeholder. Finish with a conditional judgement stating the decisive criterion and assumption.

fragments.label: Building the recommendation
fragments.text: Official schemes separate calculation from evaluation: accurate figures do not by themselves justify the final choice. Conversely, qualitative discussion should not ignore a clear positive or negative NPV.

fragments.label: Building the recommendation
fragments.text: Quantitative: result, unit, criterion and comparison.

fragments.label: Building the recommendation
fragments.text: Qualitative: factor, contextual mechanism and business consequence.

fragments.label: Building the recommendation
fragments.text: Judgement: objective, constraint, time horizon and reversal trigger.

fragments.label: Building the recommendation
fragments.text: Choose Project B because its +$85,000 NPV best supports long-term value and finance is available, despite slower payback; switch to A if sensitivity testing shows B's cash inflows fall enough to make NPV negative or if the firm cannot fund the 3.6-year exposure.
What does payback measure?

fragments.label: What does payback measure?
fragments.text: How long cumulative net cash inflows take to recover initial investment.
What data does ARR use?

fragments.label: What data does ARR use?
fragments.text: Average annual accounting profit divided by average investment, multiplied by 100.
What is the NPV acceptance rule?

fragments.label: What is the NPV acceptance rule?
fragments.text: NPV above zero is financially acceptable at the stated discount rate.
Why may payback and NPV rank projects differently?

fragments.label: Why may payback and NPV rank projects differently?
fragments.text: Payback prioritises recovery speed and ignores later flows, while NPV includes timing and all forecast flows.
Name three qualitative factors.

fragments.label: Name three qualitative factors.
fragments.text: Strategic fit, employee/skill impact and environmental or customer consequences; finance and implementation risk also matter.
What should sensitivity analysis identify?

fragments.label: What should sensitivity analysis identify?
fragments.text: Whether a plausible change in an important assumption reverses the decision.
Why is appraisal not a guarantee?

fragments.label: Why is appraisal not a guarantee?
fragments.text: Cash flows, project life, residual value and discount rate are forecasts or assumptions.

Finance strategy connects accounting evidence to long-term choices about investment, working capital, debt, equity, dividends and growth. The goal is not to improve a ratio cosmetically: it is to choose a coherent policy that supports corporate objectives while keeping liquidity, return, control, risk and stakeholder consequences within acceptable limits.

fragments.label: Finance strategy
fragments.text: Long-term approach to acquiring, allocating and controlling finance so corporate objectives can be achieved at acceptable risk.

fragments.label: Annual report
fragments.text: Package containing financial statements and narrative, governance, risk, sustainability and other information for stakeholders.

fragments.label: Audit opinion
fragments.text: Independent auditor's conclusion on whether statements meet the relevant reporting requirements; it is not a guarantee of future success.

fragments.label: Debt finance
fragments.text: Borrowed finance with contractual interest and repayment, usually preserving ownership control.

fragments.label: Equity finance
fragments.text: Owner/shareholder finance with no contractual repayment but possible dilution of ownership and earnings.

fragments.label: Dividend policy
fragments.text: Approach to distributing profit to shareholders versus retaining it for liquidity and investment.

fragments.label: Financial risk
fragments.text: Risk created by fixed finance commitments and inability to meet interest or repayment when cash flow weakens.

fragments.label: Window dressing
fragments.text: Temporary action or presentation designed to make reported position look stronger at the reporting date.
From accounting evidence to strategy

fragments.label: From accounting evidence to strategy
fragments.text: Financial statements and ratios reveal resources, profitability, liquidity, efficiency, financing and investor return. Strategy uses that evidence to diagnose constraints and opportunities: weak liquidity may delay expansion; falling margins may require product, price, cost or process action; underused assets may support growth without major investment.

fragments.label: From accounting evidence to strategy
fragments.text: Use a sequence: objective -> evidence -> diagnosis -> option -> financial and non-financial consequence -> implementation -> control. A ratio target is not an objective by itself unless it supports survival, growth, return or another corporate aim.

fragments.label: From accounting evidence to strategy
fragments.text: Use a balanced set of ratios; improving one can worsen another.

fragments.label: From accounting evidence to strategy
fragments.text: Separate a temporary investment effect from persistent weak performance.

fragments.label: From accounting evidence to strategy
fragments.text: Attach targets, owners, time periods and review triggers to the chosen policy.

fragments.label: From accounting evidence to strategy
fragments.text: Operating margin falls while sales grow and defect returns rise. The strategy should diagnose quality and failure cost before cutting promotion or staff. Better process quality may reduce rework, improve margin and protect reputation even if training initially increases expense.
Annual reports and stakeholder decisions

fragments.label: Annual reports and stakeholder decisions
fragments.text: An annual report may include the financial statements, notes, strategic or directors' report, governance, principal risks, sustainability information and an independent audit report. Notes explain accounting policies and unusual items that headline ratios can hide. Narrative sections add context but management selects how to present its story.

fragments.label: Annual reports and stakeholder decisions
fragments.text: Managers plan and control; investors assess return and risk; lenders assess repayment; suppliers assess payment confidence; employees consider continuity; government and communities consider compliance and impact. The same report supports different decisions.

fragments.label: Annual reports and stakeholder decisions
fragments.text: An unmodified audit opinion increases confidence in reporting, not certainty that strategy will succeed.

fragments.label: Annual reports and stakeholder decisions
fragments.text: Forward-looking statements remain assumptions and should be tested against external evidence.

fragments.label: Annual reports and stakeholder decisions
fragments.text: Stakeholders need information relevant to their own time horizon and exposure.

fragments.label: Annual reports and stakeholder decisions
fragments.text: A high dividend may please an income investor, while a lender may prefer retained cash and lower debt. Employees may focus on continuity and planned restructuring. A strategy answer should identify whose decision is being supported.
Debt, equity and the capital structure

fragments.label: Debt, equity and the capital structure
fragments.text: Debt preserves ownership and interest may be predictable, but raises gearing, fixed cash commitments and covenant/security risk. Equity has no contractual repayment and can absorb uncertainty, but dilutes control and earnings per share and creates expectations of future return. Retained earnings preserve control but have opportunity cost and may be insufficient.

fragments.label: Debt, equity and the capital structure
fragments.text: Match the source to purpose and cash timing. Stable cash flows and low existing gearing can support debt; uncertain, long-payback innovation may suit equity. Compare total cost, availability, flexibility, control and downside survival, not interest alone.

fragments.label: Debt, equity and the capital structure
fragments.text: A debt-funded project raises overall ROCE only if the project's operating return exceeds the existing business ROCE. Finance cost does not determine ROCE direction because ROCE uses profit from operations before interest; finance cost instead affects cash, leverage risk and shareholder return.

fragments.label: Debt, equity and the capital structure
fragments.text: New equity can reduce gearing yet market dilution or weak demand may make it expensive.

fragments.label: Debt, equity and the capital structure
fragments.text: A mixed or staged package can avoid an all-or-nothing choice.

fragments.label: Debt, equity and the capital structure
fragments.text: Current gearing is 40%. A large loan is forecast to raise gearing to 60%. Debt preserves owner control and funds expansion, but interest and repayment risk rise before new cash inflows arrive. Use the 40% to 60% change with cash-flow sensitivity, project NPV and rate risk before recommending the strategy.
Dividend strategy and investor return

fragments.label: Dividend strategy and investor return
fragments.text: Higher dividends increase immediate owner cash return and may signal confidence, but reduce retained earnings, liquidity and self-financed investment. Lower dividends increase dividend cover and funds retained, but may disappoint income investors or signal weakness if communication is poor.

fragments.label: Dividend strategy and investor return
fragments.text: A sustainable policy aligns payout with recurring profit, cash generation, investment opportunities, debt commitments and shareholder preferences. Directors decide dividends; they cannot directly guarantee market price.

fragments.label: Dividend strategy and investor return
fragments.text: Dividend yield can rise because dividend rises or share price falls; interpret the cause.

fragments.label: Dividend strategy and investor return
fragments.text: High cover provides a buffer and retention, but may be excessive where good investment opportunities are absent.

fragments.label: Dividend strategy and investor return
fragments.text: A stable policy can reduce uncertainty but should not force borrowing merely to maintain payout.

fragments.label: Dividend strategy and investor return
fragments.text: Profit is $5m and annual dividend $4m, so dividend cover = $5m / $4m = 1.25 times. Raising payout further offers little profit buffer and may constrain investment. Retain more if a credible positive-NPV project exists; otherwise explain why shareholders should wait.
Growth and other strategies change ratios

fragments.label: Growth and other strategies change ratios
fragments.text: Organic growth can raise inventory, receivables and capacity cost before customer cash and utilisation catch up. Acquisition can add assets, debt and integration cost. Initially, liquidity, margins or ROCE may weaken even if the long-term strategy is sound. Later economies, revenue and productivity must materialise to justify the dip.

fragments.label: Growth and other strategies change ratios
fragments.text: Price changes, quality programmes, automation, outsourcing, international entry and HR policies all affect accounting results. Show the mechanism rather than claiming growth always improves performance.

fragments.label: Growth and other strategies change ratios
fragments.text: Growth financed by debt may raise gearing; equity may dilute ownership and earnings per share.

fragments.label: Growth and other strategies change ratios
fragments.text: Working-capital growth can create overtrading even when profit increases.

fragments.label: Growth and other strategies change ratios
fragments.text: Set leading indicators such as orders, defects, utilisation and collection days before annual ratios confirm the outcome.

fragments.label: Growth and other strategies change ratios
fragments.text: A new factory raises capital employed immediately while profit grows only after commissioning. ROCE may fall in year 1. Judge utilisation ramp-up, order book, cash buffer and expected NPV before labelling the strategy a failure.
Build an integrated finance policy

fragments.label: Build an integrated finance policy
fragments.text: Working-capital, investment, finance and dividend decisions interact. Aggressive growth funded by debt and high dividends can create a cash squeeze even when projected profit is attractive. A coherent package might combine staged investment, selective credit control, retained earnings and a long-term loan with contingency headroom.

fragments.label: Build an integrated finance policy
fragments.text: Stress-test lower sales, delayed receipts, higher cost and interest rates. Decide minimum liquidity, maximum acceptable gearing and review triggers without turning them into rigid universal numbers.

fragments.label: Build an integrated finance policy
fragments.text: Align finance maturity with asset life and cash generation.

fragments.label: Build an integrated finance policy
fragments.text: Protect strategic capabilities rather than cutting every cost to improve a short-term margin.

fragments.label: Build an integrated finance policy
fragments.text: Explain stakeholder conflict and how communication, phasing or safeguards reduce it.

fragments.label: Build an integrated finance policy
fragments.text: Fund the first expansion stage with retained earnings plus a fixed-rate long-term loan, reduce dividend growth temporarily and tighten only overdue credit. Review when utilisation reaches 75% and operating cash meets debt service under the downside forecast.
Limits of the evidence

fragments.label: Limits of the evidence
fragments.text: Accounts are historical, affected by estimates, accounting policy, asset age, inflation, one-off events, reporting-date seasonality and possible window dressing. Acquisitions or discontinued products can break trends. Competitors may use different policies or operate different models.

fragments.label: Limits of the evidence
fragments.text: Financial data omits or incompletely measures employee skill, culture, brand, innovation, quality, environmental impact and customer loyalty. Ratio analysis diagnoses symptoms, not causation. Combine the annual report with budgets, cash forecasts, market research, operational metrics and current external evidence.

fragments.label: Limits of the evidence
fragments.text: Read notes and narrative rather than relying on a ratio table alone.

fragments.label: Limits of the evidence
fragments.text: Audit provides reasonable assurance about statements, not a forecast or endorsement of strategy.

fragments.label: Limits of the evidence
fragments.text: Ask whether later events have made year-end evidence obsolete.

fragments.label: Limits of the evidence
fragments.text: A competitor reports higher ROCE but leases many assets while the business owns them. Different asset financing and age can distort the comparison. Restate where possible or use additional operating evidence before copying the competitor's strategy.
Paper 4 strategic judgement

fragments.label: Paper 4 strategic judgement
fragments.text: A strong answer selects the most relevant financial evidence, connects it to the corporate objective, develops effects across functions and stakeholders, challenges assumptions and states how implementation will be controlled. A list of ratios or generic debt/equity advantages is not strategy.

fragments.label: Paper 4 strategic judgement
fragments.text: Make the recommendation conditional. State which constraint is decisive now, the time horizon and the measurable event that would change the choice.

fragments.label: Paper 4 strategic judgement
fragments.text: Use case figures throughout; do not repeat every appendix number.

fragments.label: Paper 4 strategic judgement
fragments.text: Link finance to marketing demand, operations capacity, HR capability and external change.

fragments.label: Paper 4 strategic judgement
fragments.text: Distinguish management action from outcomes influenced by markets and interest rates.

fragments.label: Paper 4 strategic judgement
fragments.text: Recommend option -> cite decisive ratio/cash evidence -> explain strategic mechanism -> weigh stakeholder and implementation risk -> identify time horizon and reversal trigger.
What belongs in an integrated finance strategy?

fragments.label: What belongs in an integrated finance strategy?
fragments.text: Investment, working capital, source of finance, dividend policy, risk controls and review targets aligned with objectives.
What does an audit opinion not guarantee?

fragments.label: What does an audit opinion not guarantee?
fragments.text: Future performance, successful strategy or the accuracy of management forecasts.
How does more debt usually affect gearing?

fragments.label: How does more debt usually affect gearing?
fragments.text: It raises non-current liabilities and usually raises gearing and fixed financial risk.
What is the central dividend trade-off?

fragments.label: What is the central dividend trade-off?
fragments.text: Immediate shareholder cash return versus retained liquidity and investment finance.
Why may growth weaken ROCE first?

fragments.label: Why may growth weaken ROCE first?
fragments.text: Capital employed can rise before new capacity produces operating profit.
Why can ratios not prove cause?

fragments.label: Why can ratios not prove cause?
fragments.text: They are historical relationships affected by policy, estimates and many possible operational or external drivers.
What makes a strategic judgement strong?

fragments.label: What makes a strategic judgement strong?
fragments.text: A contextual objective, integrated consequences, evidence limits, implementation plan, time horizon and reversal trigger.

Subatomic particles

fragments.label: Subatomic particles
fragments.text: Protons (+1), neutrons (0), electrons (−1, negligible mass). Atomic number = protons; mass number = protons + neutrons. Isotopes share atomic number but differ in neutron count.
Ionisation energy trends

fragments.label: Ionisation energy trends

Bond types

fragments.label: Bond types

Intermolecular forces

fragments.label: Intermolecular forces

Enthalpy change ΔH

fragments.label: Enthalpy change ΔH
fragments.text: Exothermic releases energy (ΔH negative); endothermic absorbs energy (ΔH positive).
Hess's law

fragments.label: Hess's law
fragments.text: Enthalpy change is independent of route. Draw a cycle via a common intermediate and add/subtract arrows to find the unknown ΔH.
Bond energies

fragments.label: Bond energies
fragments.text: ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed)

A focused revision guide to equilibria.
Dynamic equilibrium & Le Chatelier

fragments.label: Dynamic equilibrium & Le Chatelier
fragments.text: Forward/reverse rates become equal at equilibrium. A disturbance shifts equilibrium to partially oppose the change — more reactant → shifts to products; more pressure → shifts to fewer gas moles; more heat → shifts endothermic direction.
Kc

fragments.label: Kc
fragments.text: A catalyst speeds up reaching equilibrium but does not change its position or Kc.

fragments.label: Kc
fragments.text: Kc = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ / [A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ

Reaction kinetics explains why some reactions happen faster than others, using collision theory as the underlying model. At AS level the focus is qualitative — explaining rate changes in terms of collision frequency and the proportion of particles with enough energy to react — while the quantitative treatment (rate equations, orders of reaction) comes in the A2 topic.

fragments.label: Activation energy (Ea)
fragments.text: The minimum energy that colliding particles must possess for a reaction to occur.

fragments.label: Collision theory
fragments.text: The model stating that a reaction only occurs when particles collide with energy ≥ Ea and in the correct orientation.

fragments.label: Catalyst
fragments.text: A substance that increases the rate of a reaction by providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, without itself being used up.
Collision theory & activation energy

fragments.label: Collision theory & activation energy
fragments.text: Not every collision between particles leads to a reaction — only those with enough energy (≥ Ea) and the correct orientation actually react. This is why increasing the frequency or energy of collisions increases the rate.

fragments.label: Collision theory & activation energy
fragments.text: Weak collision (low energy) → particles bounce apart, no reaction

fragments.label: Collision theory & activation energy
fragments.text: Collision with E ≥ Ea and correct orientation → bonds break/form, reaction occurs
Factors affecting rate

fragments.label: Factors affecting rate
fragments.text: Concentration/pressure increase the number of particles per unit volume, so collisions happen more often. Surface area (for solids) exposes more particles to collide with. Temperature increases both the speed of particles and, more importantly, the proportion with energy ≥ Ea. A catalyst offers a lower-energy pathway, so a larger fraction of collisions now exceed the (lower) activation energy.

fragments.label: Factors affecting rate
fragments.text: Doubling the concentration of a reactant roughly doubles collision frequency (for a first-order reactant)

fragments.label: Factors affecting rate
fragments.text: A platinum catalyst in the Contact process lowers Ea for SO₂ oxidation
The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution

fragments.label: The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution
fragments.text: This is a graph of the number of particles (y-axis) against their kinetic energy (x-axis) at a given temperature — an asymmetric curve starting at the origin, rising to a peak, then tailing off. Raising the temperature shifts the peak right and flattens/broadens the curve, while the total area under the curve stays the same (same number of particles). Crucially, the area under the curve beyond Ea — the fraction of particles that can react — increases sharply even for a modest temperature rise.

fragments.label: The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution
fragments.text: At T1, only a small area of the curve lies beyond Ea

fragments.label: The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution
fragments.text: At T2 > T1, the curve flattens/shifts right, and a much larger area lies beyond Ea, even though Ea itself hasn't changed
Rate increases only if collisions occur more often AND/OR more collisions exceed Ea
Catalyst = lower Ea via alternative pathway, not used up
Temperature ↑ → M-B curve flattens/shifts right → more particles exceed Ea
